summary: The Food Inspector, P.W. 4 took a sample of lal mirchi powder from the grocery shop of the respondent. On analysis by the Public Analyst it was found in exhibit PW 1/C that the sample contained nine living meal worms. There was no other evidence in support of the case of the prosecution that the lal mirgi powder was adulterated. It was contended before the Magistrate that the evidence by way of the Public analyst 's report does not satisfy the requirement of the definition of "adulterated article" contained in section 2(1)(f) of the Act. The learned Magistrate accepted this contention and found that the prosecution has failed to prove that the Lal mirchi seed was adulterated and he accordingly acquitted the respondent, but convicted him under section 7 read with section 16 of the . On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation that in the case where food articles for which no minimum standard or purity is prescribed, the moment it is proved that a proportion of percentage of the article not being a proportion or percentage as would be covered by the rule, de minimis non curat lex is putrid, filthy, disgusting, decomposed or insect infested, it would be deemed to be unfit for human consumption and therefore adulterated within the contemplation of section 2 (1) (f). Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The word "otherwise" in sub clause (f)of section 2 does suggest that all the adjectives used earlier refer to the quality of the articles being unfit for their human consumption.

The appellant was convicted by the Munsif, First Class and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months. The foodgrains found in his possession were also ordered to be forfeited to the State. He appealed unsuccessfully to the Sessions Judge, Santhal Parganas, Dumka and his revision in the High Court was summarily dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that he was an agriculturist and was not liable to the penalty under the law because the presumption in his case could not be drawn. HELD: The appellant had successfully proved that he is an agriculturist, and the presumption under paragraph 3(2) could not, therefore, be drawn against him. [901 C] Manipur Administration vs M. Nila Chandra Singh ; , followed. In the present case the appellant produced a number of lease deeds in which leases of various parcels of land were shown to have been granted to him. He also produced receipts of payment of lease money and he cited witnesses who deposed on oath that he and his brother cultivated 80 bighas of land. No doubt, the lease deeds are not registered but for the purpose of a criminal prosecution, it is easy to see that the evidence which was 'brought for ward of witnesses deposing orally was not concocted to set up a false defence. Indeed no adequate reasons were given for rejecting the testimony of one witness on the ground that he being the next door neighbour and has a "soft corner for him".

The defendant took an appeal to the High Court of Calcutta and during the pendency of this appeal, the High COurt appointed a Receiver who was put in possession of the entire estate. On 8th December, 1924, the defendant executed a registered Kabuliyat in favour of the Receiver by which he purported to take settlement of the land in suit for a period of 10 years at a rental of Rs. There was a covenant in the lease that was challenged as invalid and inoperative in law and could not create any rights in the defendant, inas much as the Prodhan had no authority to settle lands of this character. The plaintiff avers that by reason of the payment and acceptance of rent, there were two tenancies for one year each, but on the expiry of the second annual lease which happened on 7th December 1926, the respondent ceased to be a tenant and no fresh tenancy was created by holding over as is contemplated by section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act. The whole controversy in this appeal centres round the point as to whether the defendant was in fact a monthly tenant under the plaintiff or his predecessor. There might have been, according to the learned Counsel, two tenancies, for one years each for two successive periods, but the relationship of landlord and tenant between the parties came to an end on the expiration of the first annual lease. As there was no holding over by the defendant since then as contemplated by sec tion 116, Transfer of property Act, even though no rent was demanded by the landlord after 1926, and the plain tiff 's suit instituted in the year 1943 was obviously time barred. Held, that on the facts of this case it would be quite proper to hold that the tenancy of the defendant is one from month to month since its inception in 1924. The lease was intended to be for a term exceeding one year, but as the intention was not expressed in the proper legal form, it could not be given effect to. It is one thing to say that in the absence of a valid agreement, the rights of the parties would be regulat ed by law in the same manner as if no agreement existed at all; it is quite another thing to substitute a new agreement for the parties which is palpably contradicted by the admit ted facts of the case. It would be pertinent to point out in tiffs connection that in a Second Appeal preferred by the plaintiff against the dismissal of his earlier suit by the lower appellate court, theHigh Court definitely held that the defendant 's tenancy was one from year to month under section 106 Transfer of .

The assessee, Trilok Chand Jain instituted a suit for recovery of Rs. 1,39,722.86 against the defendants, M/s. Dagi Ram Pindi Lal and Smt. Budh Wanti Gulati, w/o Shri Pindi Lai Gulati. During the course of proceedings in the suit, when evidence was being recorded, the plaintiff obtained summons from the court requiring the Income Tax Department to produce in the Court records relating to the Income tax Assessment of the defendants M/S Borizeon Industrial Products (P) Ltd., and Bishamber Nath Kaul. That record was also sent by the IncomeTax Officer in a sealed cover alongwith a letter in which it was submitted that no disclosure of information regarding income tax pertaining to an income tax assessee could be made. It considered the first question in the following four situations: "(a) Where the documents, records etc., in respect of which privilege is claimed were filed by an assessee or a third party before April 1, 1962, but before April I,1964 in respect for assessment years 1964 65 onwards; (b) where the document, records, etc. in respect thereof were filed on or after April 1.

One Mammotty was ill for a long time and was in hospital and he was discharged uncured a month before the execution of the gift deed and remained in his mother 's house afterwards. There were conflicting versions about the nature of the disease and a plea was taken in the case that the gift was made in contemplation of death and was voidable. This plea need not detain this Court because the trial Judge and the first Appellate Court did not accept it. After the death of Seinaba, the present suit was brought by Kunhamu an eider brother of Mammottty for partition and possession of a 6/16 share of the property which he claimed as an heir under the Muhammadan Law, that is to say, by the father or his executor or by the grand father or by his executor. The trial judge and first Appellate Judge did not agree with it. On appeal the High Court held that there was no rule of Muhammadan law which permits such acceptance and that the decision of the High court was right. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) There is a declaration and a tender by the donor Mammetty and as the gift is by a registered deed no question in this behalf can arise. In so far as Mammatty was concerned there was delivery of possession and the deed also records this fact. Possession was not delivered to Seinabai but to her mother, the first appellant, and she accepted the gift on behalf of his wife who had attained puberty and had lived with him, for after the celebration of marriage a husband can receive a gift in respect of minor wife even though her father be living; but Mammastty did not complete his gift in this way. His gift included immovable properties and it was accepted by the mother who took over possession on behalf Of her minor daughter. A gift to a minor is completed ordinarily by the acceptance of the guardian of the Property of the minor Wilayat ul Mal. A mother can exercise guardianship of the person of a minor daughter (Hizanat) till the girl attains puberties after which the guardianship of a person is that of the father if the girl is un 36 2 S.C. India/64 554 married and that of his husband if she is married and has gone to her husband.

The Madras Religious and Charitable Endowments Act 19 of 1951 was enacted to provide for the better administra tion and governance of Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments in the State of Madras. This Court in the Commissioner of Hindu religious and Charitable Endowment, Madras vs Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Mutt, ; held that sections 21, 30(2), 31, 63 to 69 and 89 as amended by Act 27 of 1954 were invalid: Devraja Shenoy vs The State of Mysore, [1963] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 302, followed. In the present case, conditions (1) & (2) are satisfied. But the High Court was of the view that the Commissioner had not determined the cost of auditing the accounts of the temple and proceeded to observe "It is sufficient to say that the demand made of the petitioners ' temple for the payment of a sum of Rs. 1, 62 8 3 nP towards the audit of its accounts in respect of the year 1963 fasli does not rest upon any determination made under section 76(2) and is therefore one made without competence or the authority of law". In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court erred. It was not the case of the respondents in their petition that the amount of contribution payable by the petitioners temple should be prescribed by a rule which remained to be made which means that what was decided by this Court was that no such contribution could be recovered from that temple until such a rule was made, and on that account the demand was premature. If services are provided, assuming that the Venkataramana Temple either does not need the services, or does not obtain the same degree of service as others may. The rules under the Act have to be general. And such rules were in fact framed and were in operation. [920 H; 921 A B] (ii) Under the Act a fee though levied for rendering services of a particular type is not to be, co related to the services performed for each individual who is intended to obtain the benefit of the services.

Section 19(1) of the , provides that an appeal shall lie as of right from any order or decision of a bench of the High Court in the exercise of its jurisdiction to punish for contempt (a) where the order or judgment is that of a single judge, to a Bench of not less than two Judges of the Court; (b) where such order or decisions are that of the court of Judicial Commissioner in any Union territory, such appeal shall be lie to the Supreme Court. Section 19(2) provides that no Court shall initiate any proceedings for contempt either on its own motion or otherwise after the expiry of a period of one year from the date on which the contempt is alleged to have been committed. The appellant filed an appeal under section 19 (1) against the order rejecting the prayer of the alleged contemner for bearing the case piecemeal, contending that no appeal lies to this Court as a matter of right under section19. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: An order merely initiating the proceeding without anything further does not decide anything against the alleged contemnor and cannot be appealed against as a matters of right tinder section 19. In a given case special leave may be granted under article 136 of the Constitution from an order initiating the proceedings. But that is entirely a different matter. What we are deciding in this case is that the present appeal filed under section, 19 (i) does not lie and is incompetent. [510 H] Baradakanta Mishra vs Justice Gatikrushna Mishra, ; , referred to.

The appellant was prosecuted along with another, in the Court of the Magistrate First Class, Delhi under section 6(1 A) of the , for possessing a wireless transmitter in contravention of the provisions of section 3 of the Act and was sentenced to six months rigorous imprisonment. On appeal, the High Court confirmed both the conviction but reduced the sentence to the period already undergone plus a fine of Rs. 500. On an application filed for special leave, this Court gave the same, but limited it to the question of sentence only. Held, that section 6 (1 A), inserted in the Act of 1933 by the amending Act of 1949 did not affect the continuance of the amendment made by the enactment so repealed and that it was in force when the offence was committed by the appellant. The word " text " is comprehensive enough to take in the subject as well as the terminology used in a statute. Another escape from the operation of section 6 A of the is sought to be effected on the basis of the words " unless a different intention appears, the repeal shall not affect its continuance of any such amendment made either by the Act so repealed or in operation at the time of such repeal". The word ' text " was comprehensive enough. To take in a wireless transmittedter, the section does not prohibit the possession of a wireless apparatus. As the Act only gave power to control the establishment, maintenance and working of wireless apparatus, in practice it was found that the detection of unlicenced apparatus and the successful prosecution of the offenders were difficult with the result that the State was losing revenue. To remove this defect, Act XVII of 1933 was passed to prohibit the Possession without licence of a Wireless apparatus. Under section 6, the penalty for such illegal possession of wireless telegraphy apparatus was made an offence but the sentence prescribed was rather lenient.

Under section 36(2) of the Bengal Money Lenders Act, a new decree is passed only for the purpose of substituting the method of accounting sanctioned by the Act for the calculations upon which the original decree was passed and to give an opportunity to the judgment debtor to pay the decretal dues thus ascertained by instalments. But save and except for these, the old decree as well as the adjudications made thereunder are not wiped out and the parties are not relegated to their rights and liabilities under the original cause of action (2). Oramba Sundari was the purchaser at the execution sale and whether or not the money for such purchase was paid by her husband becomes immaterial. Held, that in a proceeding under section 36 of the Act it is not open to the court to go behind the decree and launch an enquiry as to whether the decree holder was in fact a benamidar for another person in respect of the decree. Such enquiry, it seems to us, is altogether outside the purview of the different clauses of section 36 (2) Of the Bengal money Lenders ' Act and these provisions do not recognise any other decreeholder than the one in whose favour the original order was passed. Orambba Sundri vs Manmatha, 72 I.A. 156; Bank of Commerce Ltd. vs Amulya Krishna Babu Roy Chowdhury, 994 decree was based would be changed by substituting the statutory method of accounts in place of what rested upon the contract between the parties. Clauses (b) and (c) contemplate cases where properties have been sold in execution of the original decrees. If the purchaser is the decreeholder himself and he is in possession of the property when the decree is reopened, it is incumbent upon the courtto order restoration of these properties to the Judgment debtor under clause (c). If, on the other hand, the properties had been acquired by strangers either by purchase at the original execution sale or from the decree debtor purchaser, their interests would be protected if they have acquired these rights bona fide as contemplated by cl. (b). Under clause (d), the court has to order the payment of the decretal amount in such instalments as it thinks proper and cl.

The respondent company instituted a suit against the appellant for recovery of Rs. 7,113 7 0 with interest at 6 per cent. per annum in respect of certain transactions in gold and silver effected by the firm as pucca adatias in bullion and cotton at Bombay under the name and style of Habib & Sons. In 1948 the respondent company filed a suit in the Bombay City Civil Court, being Summary Suit No. 233 of 1948 against the appellants for recovery Of Rs. 8,428 7 0 on the ground that the decree was not in existence at the date of the document it operated as an agreement to transfer the decree when it would be passed and that as soon as the decree had been passed the respondent Company became the transferees of the decree by assignment in writing within the meaning of Order XXI, rule 16. The suit was contested on behalf of the appellant company inter alia on the footing that the application for execution filed before the City Civil court not mentioned any of these particulars but merely stated that the Court should declare them the assignees of the said decree as the decretal debt along with other debts were transferred by Habib & sons to them by the deed of assignment dated the 7th February 1949 which was confirmed by the Custodian of Evacuee Property, Bombay and should order them to be substituted for Habib & Co. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court held that the appellant Company could not apply under Order XXI rule 16 for that rule could not properly cover a case where there was no decree at the time of assignment of the property and the term "decree holder" could not cover a party who, in equity might afterwards become entitled to the rights of the actual decree holder. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the High Courts were right in holding that the document under consideration did not transfer the future decree and, therefore, the equitable principle came into play and that when on a true construction of the deed it actually operated to transfer a decree then in existence no equitable principle need be invoked for in that case the transfer was by the instrument itself and as such was by an assignment in pursuance of the assignment in the writing executed before the decree came into existence and the only way in which the transferee could claim that the suit was transferred to him by assignment. Kangati Mahanandi Reddi vs Panikalapati Venkatappa & Anr., A.I.R. , Bhagwant Balajirao & Ors. vs Rajaram Sajnaji & Others, A. I. R. , and Bhagwant Balrajirao and Ors. V. Rajaram Sajmaji & Ors., A I. L. R , referred to.

The respondent was carrying on the business of fabricating steel doors, windows, sashes and other goods. On April 20, 1957, the respondent submitted in pursuance of an invitation by the Executive Engineer, Ajmer Central Division, its tender for providing and fixing "S.H. Windows" and "Composite Window" of certain sizes "in accordance with the specifications, designs, drawing and instructions". The tender was accepted and the respondent carried out the contract. The Sales Tax Officer included in the taxable turnover of the respondent Rs. 23,480/ received under the contract, the amount received under it. He remanded the case with a direction to assess tax on the price for sale of materials only. The Board of Revenue exercising revisional power confirmed the order passed by the Deputy Commissioner observing that the contract undertaken by the respondent was not a contract of service and thus partly liable to sales tax. On appeal, the High Court held that the contracts were divisible between two parts representing the sale of the window, and the labour charges in fixing the same and thus fully liable to Sales Tax. The relevant terms of the tender which was accepted by the executive Engineer were : "Item Rate tender for Works I/We hereby tender for the execution for the President of India of the work specified in the under written memorandum within the time specified in such memorandum at the rates specified therein, and in accordance with all the conditions so far as applicable". This recital was followed by a memorandum setting out the general description,, of the building in respect of which the window leaves, were to be supplied the estimated cost of thecontact and the description and the number of items of work offered to be done ' The items of works offered to the respondent were "providing and fixing" four different types of windows. The respondent offered to execute and complete the "work" mentioned in the written memorandum according to the specifications and conditions. In the view of the High court, the contract was for work, in the execution of which some movable property passed : it was not one of sale but a combination of two distinct and separate contracts, one for the supply or the sale, of goods for consideration, was liable to tax under the Sales Tax Act. On a consideration of all the circumstances, the Court held on a consideration Of all the circum stances that the respondent had agreed to and did supply "motor bus being one for sale" of chattels, they were liable to pay sales tax; but, whether a particular contract is one for work and labour or one for tho sale of a chattel.

The prosecution case was that on November 8, 1967 Shankerlal representing himself to be a broker of foreign machinery parts went to Ram Avtar Prasad complainant and told him that he (Shanker Lal) could arrange for a transaction of sale of foreign goods which would result in good profit to the complainant. The complainant agreed to purchase 200 pieces of the washer plates at the rate of Rs. 38/ per piece. Formal order, it was then agreed, would be sent through Shanker Lal. On November 16, 1967 Shankar Lal handed over the formal order to Ram and stated that the goods would be supplied on the following day. Ram Avtar lodged a report with the police against Shankar Lal after his suspicion had been aroused. Later on that day Shankar Lal and Raj Kumar Agarwalla came to the shop of Ram Avtar. The police did not submit any charge sheet on the basis of the report which had been lodged by the complainant and the accused were discharged. Subsequently, the proceedings were set in motion against Raj Kumar Aggarwalla, Shanker Lal and Saheb Jaman Khan. Charge under sections 420, 468 and 471 Indian Penal Code read with section 120B I.P.C. was framed against all the three accused. Another charge under section 420 read with Section 511 I. P.C., was also framed against Rajkumar Agarwalla and Shankar Lal. Raj Kumar Agarwalala thereafter filed a revision petition in the High Court for quashing the charge against him. The revision petition was allowed by the High court on the ground that so far as Raj Kumar Agawalla was concerned, no case had been made out against him and charges framed against him were consequently quashed.

The petitioner was a resident of Sultanbattery area in the State of Kerala and describing himself as a commuter of the Indian Railways he has alleged violation of fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 19 and 21 and claims reliefs of mandamus to the Union of India for implementing the reports of the Kunzru, Wanchoo and Sikri Committees, appointing a fact finding Commission to inquire and report about the numerous train accidents from 1970 onwards and for several other directions to the Central Government and the instrumentalities connected with the administration of the Railways. The petitioner alleged that the Railways in this country are owned by the Central Govern ment and on account of failure to fulfil the constitutional, statutory and commercial obligations by the Railways adequate safety protection to the passengers and their properties is not available. The Indian Railways Act, 1890 (Act ' for short) has prescribed several safety measures; based upon experience, the Railway Board through which apex body the administration is run and controlled has also prescribed rules and issued instructions which are not being properly implemented. The Union Government had appointed three high powered Committees in the post independence period, namely, the Kunu, Wanchoo & Sikri Committees to investigate into the affairs of the Railway with particular reference to accidents and though detailed and useful recommendations have been made by these committees, there has been no adequate implementation thereof. Particular reference has been made to the unmanned level crossings, increasing human error as a contributing factor to accidents, non allocation of adequate funds for improvements, improper utilisation of the assets and facilities, inefficiency in the administration at different levels, prevalence and increase of indiscipline, frequency of thefts, robberies and murders of passengers, ineffective checking and supervisory system, want of replacement equipment and repairs to bridges as also non provision of adequate facilities to passengers. The Joint Director (Safety) has filed a counter affidavit in answer to the Rule on behalf of the respondents. It has been averred that the recommendations of the Accidents Enquiry Committee were examined and implemented within the limits of financial and material resources. So far as manned level Crossings are concerned there were as many as 14471 of them as on March 1, 1982; unmanning level crosses with a volume of traffic of more than 6000 train vehicle units or poor approach visibility are being manned in a phased manner at the cost of the railways and control at the gate is also being improved. As on June 1,1982 there were about as manyas 27233 unmaned level cross remarks on the Railways and if all of them are to be manned, a capital expenditure of 330 crore rupees would be necessary and similarly an annual recurring expenditure of Rs.44 crores will have to be met. Most of the States have framed rules under the making it obligatory for drivers of motor vehicles to stop short of unmannerned level crossing crossings and observe and then proceed. With a view to educating the users of the roads wide publicity is given through newspapers, cinema slides, commercial broadcasting and the television about the hazards involved while negotiating unmanred level crossing of new level cross promotions in consultation with appropriate State Governments. It had been pointed out that there are nearly 120000 bridges on the Railway out of which 195 are important bridges and almost 9400 are major bridges. It is said that every bridge is annually inspected and continuous record is maintained in regard to every bridge in the bridge register. It was further alleged that unmanunned level crossexamination is undertaken about manning of unmenned level counterings on the railways out of Which 195 are vital bridges and nearly 9400 were major bridges, which are major bridge. It also said that there has not been any instance where the work of bridge rebuilding has been postponed for lack of funds and no accident has occurred owing to structural failure of any bridge or girders. The petition under Article 32 of the Constitution is essentially in the nature of public interest litigation and the petitioner has attempted to voice the grievances of the community availing the services of the said Indian Railways.

The appellants applied for compensation to the Jagir Abolition Officer under section 13 of the Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1953 in respect of their proprietary jagirs. The appellants contended that since the orders passed dismissing the appeals were received by them on April 9 and April 20, 1961, the restitution applications filed on May 6, 1961 were within 30 days of the receipt of the order of dismissal and hence the applications for restoration should be allowed as they were prevented for sufficient cause from appearing at the hearing of the appeals. The Tribunal rejected the applications holding that it was obligatory on the part of the Tribunal to decide an appeal on merits even though there was default in appearance of the appellants and to record its decision regarding the merits of the appeal. On a consideration of the language of section 17(1) of the Jagirs Abolition Act, it is apparent that under Regulation 19(1), it is open to the Tribunal either dismiss an appeal for non prosecution in a case where the appellant does not appear either in person or through his agent or lawyer when the appeal or application is called for hearing. If on the date fixed for hearing or on any other subsequent day to which the hearing may be adjourned, the respondent or applicant satisfies the Tribunal that he had no notice of the date of the bearing or that be was prevented by sufficient cause for appearing when the appeals or applications were heard and declared ex parte, the party concerned may apply for restoration of the Appeal or application as the case may be, and if the party satisfies the Tribu nal that he has no notice thereof of the day of hearing or that he was prevented from appearing when appeal or the application was called for hear ing, the Tribunal may restore the appeal Or application to its file provided that where the other party had appeared in the appeal, or such party shall be given notice and an opportunity of being heard before the order for resto ration of the appellant or application was made. The High Court dismissed the applications on the ground that they were time barred under article 168 of the Limitation Act read with Regulation 55 and 0.41, rr. 17 and 19 of the Civil Procedure Code. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lants: (1) that the Tribunal had no power to dismiss an application for non Prosecution but it is obligatory on its part to decide the appeal on merit even though a default in the appearance of appellants and not to cases of dismissal for want of prosecution under the first part of Regulation 19 (1). HELD: (i) The language of Regulation 20, on its true interpretation, applies not only to a case wherein the appeal has been decided on merits but also to a ease where the appeal had been dismissed for want Of prosecution under Regulation19(1). If an appeal is dismissed for nonprosecution it cannot be said that the tribunal has decided the appeal and 'recorded its decision ' within the meaning of section17 of the Act. [144 H] (ii) The words "decide" in section 17, on their true interpretation apply not only only to cases contemplated by the latter part of regulation 19(2). If the view that is taken as to the interpretation of Regulation 21 is correct, it follows that Regulation 21 applies to the present case and the period of limitation prescribed by that Regulation being 30 days from the date when receipt of order of the dismissal of the ' appeal, the applications of restoration made by the appellants in all the four cases were well within the period Of limitation prescribed under Regulation 21.

One village by the name of Hirmi was dedicated to the temple of Shri Ramchandraji as early as 1857 by Dinanath Sao himself and later on in the year 1896 when a partition took place between his descendants who were up till that time living jointly, all the coshares not only re affirmed the dedication made by Dinnath Sao of this village of Telibandha but themselves dedicated the village to the deities in this temple by accepting the award made by the Panchas. On a consideration of the evidence the Trial Court held that there had been a valid dedication in respect of the village and it was a public religious trust, as Shri Ramchandra temple for which the trust was created, was a Public institution. The High Court agreed with the trial court that the dedication had not been proved but disagreeing with the Trial court, it held that a valid trust had been created in favour of the temple and it did purport to revoke the dedication and to allot the village amongst the members of one branch of the family with only a moral obligation to look after the temple but this later Award had all along remained a dead letter and did not affect the Panch Faisla Award of 1896. The main controversy before the High Court was whether by the Punch Faisli Award of 1796 an absolute dedication of the Village was made in favour Of Shri Ramchandra Swamy temple or whether the village was given in full proprietorship to Ramsaran Lal with only the charge on it to meet the expenses of the Temple. Held, that the use of the words "at that time" in the original necessarily meant " from the profits and income of mouza Telivancorebandha. The use of these words "in that year" by this Award Teli Oriya village was dedicated absolutely to the deity temple of Sri Ramchandra Swamy and Ramsar Raman Lal was not merely a presumption which can well be displaced by what follows in the same document as regards this very property. When all these different provisions are considered it appears to be clear beyond any shadow of doubt that the intention was not to make Ramsar an absolute owner of the land but give him possession and management of the villages for the benefit of Shri Ramachandra Swamy and his brothers. The fact, therefore, that there is not a single word in Bagchi 's award to indicate, even remotely, that in his opinion, the award suffered from any infirmity.

The two appellants were the President of the Avadh Bar Association and the Chairman, Action Committee of the Lucknow Bar Association. There were three charges against them. It was not necessary to refer in detail to the same. The gist of the charge against the appellants was that they had met and resolved that the Chief Justice was acting in a most parti san manner under the influence of the Allahabad Bar. The text of the resolution was this "The Action Committee is of the opinion that the chief Justice is acting in the dis charge of administrative power under clause 14 of the U.P. High Court 's Amalgamation Order, 1948 in a very most partisan manner under its influence of Allahabad Bar quite unbecoming of the office which he held". The High Court discharged the notices. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Chairman of the Action Committee described as contemner No. 2 was actively associ ated with the passing of the Resolution which contained disparaging remarks about the Chief Judge and since he also issued that resolution for publication in newspapers, he is guilty of 'Criminal Contempt '. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The language used by them was unfortunate. Counsel for the appellants rightly said that was not proper and it should not have been passed in that manner. It is the duty of lawyers to protect the dignity and decorum of the judiciary. If lawyers fail in their duty the faith of the people in the judiciary will be undermined to a large extent. [603B C] 2.

The appellant was a tenant for about 20 years in the premises known as " Fida Ali Villa" in Kalyan. The building was purchased by the respondent who gave notice to the appellant to vacate, as he wanted to construct a new building on the site of the old building. The appellant agreed to vacate and the respondent let to him a portion of his new building which 219 was riot far from "Fida Ali" Villa. The respondent brought a suit for ejectment on the ground of non payment of rent and sub letting of the premises. The defence of the appellant was that under the terms of the lease he had the right to sub let the premises, and as to the claim on the grounds of nonpayment of rent be deposited the arrears of rent in court. The trial Court held that subletting was lawful in spite of section 15 of the Bombay Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act 1947 (Bom. 57 of 1947). He also passed a decree for Rs. 445 on account of rent remaining due and dismissed the respondent 's suit for eviction. On appeal, the Assistant Judge reversed the order of ejectment holding that section 15 did not prohibit sub letting and under section 13(1)(e) of the Act the landlord bad the right of evict the tenant on account Of sub letting which it was alleged had resulted in the termination of the tenancy. The High Court affirmed the order passed by the trial court. Held, further, that even if any other law allowed subletting, e. g., section 108 of the Transfer of Property Act, the sub letting would, because of section 25 of the Contract Act and section 23 of the Indian Contract Act, enforcement of the agreement would produce the (1) A.I.R. 1949 Bom. 222 and (2) that even assuming that to be so and proceeding on the facts found in this case the plea of waiver could not be raised because as a result of giving effect to that plea the Court would be enforcing an illegal agreement and thus contravene the statutory provisions of section 16 based on public policy and produce the very result which the statute prohibits and makes illegal. The maxim " must not be understood as meaning that where a transaction is vitiated by illegality, the person left in possession of goods after its completion is always and of necessity entitled to keep them. Its true meaning is that, where the circumstances are such that the Court will refuse to assist either party, the consequence must, in fact follow that the party in possession will not be disturbed ". The maxim ' Ex dolo malo non oritur actio, is limited by no such qualification. The proposition to the contrary strikes as hardly worthy of serious refutation. Wherever the illegality appears, whether the evidence comes from one side or the other, the disclosure is fatal to the case. No consent of the defendant can neutralise its effect. A stipulation in the most solemn form, to waive the objection would be tainted with the vice of the original contract and void for the same reasons. wherever the contamination reaches, it destroys ".

The appellant Board conducted secondary examinations in the month of March 1990, whereat the marks awarded, after the formalities of valuation by the examiners of the answer sheets in each subject were found tampered with, the marks initially obtained and the marks increased due to tampering, and also indicated the proposed punishment, if in the enquiry it would be found that marks were tampered with the knowledge or connivance or at the instance of the candidates or parents or guardians. They would not be entitled to appear through an Advocate, but the parents or guardian would be permitted to accompany the students at the time of enquiry, but they are not entitled to take part in the inquiry. It did not obtain the approval of the Divisional Board and therefore, the impugned notification was without authority of law. The High Court directed the Board (a) to allow all the candidates referred to in the Notification of August 31, 1990 to appear at the S.S.C. examination to be conducted in March 1991 by the Board; and (b) to declare the untampered results of nine named candidates therein. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Board that the impugned Notification was vitiated for the reasons that the Standing Committee itself did not record any reason in support of its conclusion that the examinees/parents/guardians were parties to the fabrication and the fabrication was done at their behest. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The finding of the High Court that the Examination Committee had no power to take the impugned decision, etc., without approval of its Divisional Board is clearly illegal and cannot be sustained. [798C] 1.2 It depends on the nature and gravity of the misconduct to be dealt with by the disciplinary authority. In proof of the charge it was held that it is the duty of the Examination committee, etc. to maintain purity of examination and if examinee is found to have used unfair means at the examination, it is not open to the High court to interfere with that decision merely on the ground that different view could possibly be taken on the evidence available on the record. The Examination Committee has jurisdiction to take decision in the matter of use of unfair means not only on direct evidence but also on probabilities and circumstantial evidence. If the evidence is such that the tribunal can say: "we think it more probable than not the burden is discharge but, if the probabilities are equal, it may be not discharged". [799E F] 1:3 In the light of the finding, normally the appeals are to be allowed, the judgment of the high Court is set aside and the impugned order of the Board is upheld.

The appellants were charged under section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code for criminal conspiracy to cause the offence of criminal misconduct punishable under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution case was that during the progress of investigation and after the houses and shops of the accused persons had been searched, Ram Kishan took Labhu Ram aside and proposed that the three firms would be prepared to pay Rs. 2,000 if the case was hushed up and that Madan Lal was to be sounded. Madan Lal refused to have anything to do with such a proposal but as the accused persisted in their offer it was ultimately decided that a trap should be laid for them at Delhi in Madan Lal 's house. It was further alleged by the prosecution that during progress of the investigation, and after houses and shop of the appellants had been raided, Ram Krishan took Labu Ram aside, and proposed to pay a sum of Rs. 5,000 by way of illegal gratification which offence was, however, not committed by him. The Special judge who tried the case found the appellants guilty under both heads of charges and sentenced them to three months ' rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs 500. On appeal the High Court reduced the sentence on Gian Chand to the term of imprisonment already undergone and a further fine of RS. 500. There was no dispute that the amount was actually paid to Madan Lal even though he said he could do nothing to help the appellants who begged him somehow to help them out of the impending prosecution. Held, that section 5 (2) Of the Prevention Of Corruption Act provides by section 2 that "notwithstanding anything in section 21 of the I.P.C., a railway servant shall not be deemed to be a public servant for any of the purposes of that Code except those mentioned in Chapter IX". The object of the Act as set out in the preamble is to make more effective provision for the prevention of bribery and corruption. A new offence of Criminal misconduct by a public servants is created by section 5 and under sub section (2), it is made punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years or with fine or with both. The offence is of four kinds or categories. Bribery as defined in section 161 I. P.C. if it is habitual, falls within clause (a). Bribery of the kind specified in section 165, if it was habitual, fell within clause(b) contemplates criminal breach of trust by a Public servant and the wording takes us to section 405 of the Code. It is with cl. (d) that it can come into play only when there is no offer to give an acceptance of a bribe by apublic servant. The word "obtains" on which much stress was laid does not eliminate the idea of acceptance of what is given or offered to be given, though it connotes also an element of effort on the part of the receiver. One may accept money that is offered or solicit payment of a gratification, or extort the bribe by threat or coercion; in each case he obtains a pecuniary advantage by abusing his position as a public Servant. The words "corrupt or illegal means" find place in section162. If a man obtains a monetary advantage by the abuse of his position, he will be guilty under sub clause (d). Sections 161, 162 and 163 refer to a motive or reward for doing or forbearing to do something, showing favour or disfavour to any person, or for inducing such con duct by the exercise of personal influence. It cannot be laid down as an absolute rule that the laying of traps must be prohibited on the ground that by so doing it is out of an unwilling person is different from the acceptance of bribe from a voluntary giver and that before a charge under section S 5(1), sub clause(d) could be sustained, there must be threat or inducement proceeding from the public servant or duress or extortion practised by him to obtain the pecuniary advantage.

The appellant Bank filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 76,368.04 P. against the legal representative of the deceased principal debtor Harilal Parmanaddas Adatia and his surety ' original defendant 2 Chitranjan Rangnath Raja. The principal debtor executed a demand promissory note in favour of the Bank on September 16, 1957 and on the same day the principal debtor also passed letter of continuity of the bond and the promissory note Ext. 31 in favour Of the Bank. Along with the two demand promissory notes simultaneously the surety executed a letter of guarantee Ext. 32 in favour by the Bank and the Principal debtor executed another letter of guarantees Ext. 33 in favour favour of 'Along with two demands promissory notes, simultaneously the sureties executed a bond Ext. 83 in favourof the Bank, and the principal creditor also passed letters of continuity and the bank filed a Suit for recovery against the surety. The trial court found that there was negligence on the part of the bank with regard to the safe custody of the pledged oil tins but as the contract of guarantee entered into by the surety with the Bank was independent of the pledge of goods given by the principal, the surety was not discharged from his liability under the guarantee. On appeal by the sureties, the High Court held that the surety had agreed to become surety on the principal amount decreed by the trial court and that as in this case the entire security was lost on account of the negligence of the creditor Bank, yet the surety would not be discharged from the obligation undertaken under the letter of Guarantee. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Bank that in view of clauses 5,7 and 13 of the letter Of guarantee, Ext.31 even if it is held proved that security of pledged goods was lost or without the consent of the surety parts with the security, the bail would not lie to this court and it would stand disposed of accordingly. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant Bank was the plaintiff and its suit was decreed by both the trial Court and the High court. [924C] 2.1 In order to attract section 141 it must be shown that the creditor had taken more than one security from the principal borrower at the time when the contract is entered into and irrespective of the fact whether the surety knew of such other security offered by the Principal, if the creditor loses or without his consent of both parts with security the surety will be discharged to the extent of the value of the security. In the instant case, as found by the High Courts and not controverted, the principal defendant had offered two securities, one the pledge Of goods and the other personal guarantee of the sureties. The surety agreed to give personal guarantee on the specific understanding and with the full knowledge of the respondent Bank that the principal ' debtor was offering another security, namely, pledge of good goods. The bond executed by the said surety in good faith contracted to offer personal guarantee against the proper performance of the contract evidencing advance of loan and methods of its repayment, or a guarantee covering Bank 's utter disregard of its responsibility or to use the words of the High COurt, the Bank ' s utter negligence in failing to exercise the care of a prudent man which one would expect in management of one 's own affairs ? The surety in the good faith agreed to offer his personal guarantee and with full knowledge thereof that the Principal ' debtor had offered security by way of pledge ofgoods and the goods were to be in the custody of creditor Bank.

The lands in suit were comprised in six survey numbers. The appellant was the son of Amritrao, respondent No. 1, before us. Formerly, the lands in dispute lay within the province of Central Provinces and Berar; later they fell within the State of Madhya Pradesh, and now they were in Bombay. The lands in question were originally comprised in two survey numbers stated in paragraph one of the plaint. They lay in village Nawabag, a jagir village of Ellichpur (now Archalpur) taluq of Berar and we shall give some more details of that Jagir. In 1923 there was a dispute between the jagirdars and the patels about the latter 's right to get if bighas of " patelki inam" lands were given as emoluments of his office to the working patel from the Rokade family. The dispute was referred to the Nazim who was the local representative of the then sovereign authority, and the decision of the Nazim was expressed by saying that he granted the inam of a bigha and a half from year to year for each netan; it was also stated that this was supported by old judicial usage. The order made by the Government further stated that the aforesaid lands would be recorded in the name of Amritaji Patel as his patel "patelki Inam" lands, so long as the service is performed by any member of the family, the land are joint family lands subject to partition etc. among the members of the families. On this part of the case the appellant claimed that he had a share in the emoluments of the patel 's office and that Government had no right to resume "p Patelki inam lands and regrant them to respondent No 1. Held, that under r. VI(2) read with r. V(2), the appellant was entitled to his share in 'the "Patelki inams" lands as an undivided brother of Amritarao, Patel. The settlement will be made with the head member of a family holding the office or enjoying the inam and who will be held alone responsible to Government, and in no case will the Government interfere to compel the actual incumbent of an office to make over any portion of his regulated service grant to other branches of the ' family, as service grants cannot be divided according to the orders passed by the revenue authorities in respect of matters mentioned therein.

The question for determination in the appeal was whether on the facts and circumstances of the case, the entire property held by the deceased valued at Rs. 12,23,794/ was chargeable to estate duty. The assessment in question related to the estate of Hajee Mahomed Hussain Sailt, the father of two respondents, who died at Bangalore on March 22, 1955 leaving the said properties. The said property comprised shares and securities of the value of Rs. 25,778/ , and immovable properties at Bangalore and Madras respectively valued at RS. 5,42,500/ . The assessment related to estate of Hazee Mohamed Hussain Sailts, the grandfather of the two respondents who died on March 23, 1955, leaving the aforesaid properties. On behalf of the Controller of Estate Duty, the following points were raised : (i) that the concept of joint family did not apply to Cutchi Memons and that a cutchi Memon 's son did not acquire any interest by birth in the property inherited by his father from his ancestors; (ii) that in any case there was no scope for raising any such contention after the enactment of 'he Shariat Act of 1937, and thereafter of the . " The question as to which personal law, sects among the Muslims, such as the Khojas and Memons, would be subject to in matters of property succession, succession and inheritance arose in Bombay as early as 1847. On that finding he held that neither the said evidence nor the fact of their having paid succession duty on one third of the said estate only concluded the issue before him viz., that the rules of Hindu law including the rules as to joint family property and its devolution by survivorship constituted the customary law of Cutchi memons in Madras and Bangalore. He rejected his contention that as there was only one solitary decision of the High Court of Bombay which limited the application of Hindu Law to matters of succession and succession only, the Bombay view was the correct one. The different petitions and the orders thereon set out earlier and ranging from 1909 to 1930 showed, (i ) that the respondents ' family was in Madras till about 1930 when its members partly shifted their activities to Bangalore, and (ii). that in all these petitions the stand taken by the members of the respondents family was that the family properties were treated as joint family properties. Held: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the Khoja Memons in Bombay had regulated their affairs since they had settled down amidst Hindus, according to Hindu law not only in matters relating to succession and property but also in matters other than those specified in section 2 of the Act. (2) In the absence of proof of a special custom as to succession the Hindu Law of inheritance would apply to cutchi memors, and therefore when a Cutchi was Memon widow dies issueless, her property would be governed by the Hindu law as to stridhan. A year later in Elia Sait vs Dharanavva, A.I.R. (1954) Bom. 2 48, X of 1938 was not extended at first to the Civil Station area in Bangalore where the deceased and the members Of his family had settled up and carried on business. The question which arose in the suit was whether the respondent, the widow of one of them, was entitled, as against the appellant, the eldest son of the deceased by his first wife, lo one eighth share according to Mahomedan law or only to maintenance under Hindu law which applied to the Cutchi, Memons were governed by Hindu Law.

Rule 49 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 provides that excisable goods produced, cured or manufactured in any place and consumed or utilised (i) as such or after subjection to any process or processes; or (ii) for the manufacture of any other commodity whether in a continuous process or otherwise in such factory or place or premises specified under rule 9 or store room or other place of storage approved by the Collector under rule 47, shall be deemed to have been removed from such place or Premises immediately before such consumption or utilisation. Rule 49(1) provides that no excisable goods shall be removed from any place where they are produced, manufactured or manufactured or any premises appurtenant thereto, which may be specified by the collector in this behalf whether for consumption, export or manufacture of Any other commodity in or outside such place until the excise duty leviable thereon has been paid at such place and in such manner as is prescribed in these Rules or as the Collector may require, and except on presentation of an application in the proper form and on obtaining the permission of the proper officer on the form: "Rule 49. (1) Payment of duty shall not be required in respect of excisable goods made in a factory until they are about to be issued out of the place or property specified under Rule 9 or are about or to be removed therefrom from such factory, place premises, store room, or other places of storageapproved by the proper officers. " The appellants do not dispute that the different kinds of fabrics which are manufactured in the mill are liable to payment of excise duty on their removal from the factory. They also do not disputed their liability in respect thereof. It is the contention of the appellants that no duty of excise can be levied and collected in respect Of yarn which is obtained at an intermediate stage and, thereafter subjected to an integrated process for the manufactured of different fabrics. Indeed, on a writ petition filed by the appellants, the Delhi High Court held that yarn obtained and further processed within the factory for the purpose of weaving the same into fabrics, will be liable to pay excise duty in view of the amended provisions of Rules 9 and 49 of Central Excise Act, 1944. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that even assuming that there can be fictional removal as provided in the Explanation to Rule 9 and rule 49, there cannot be such fictional or deemed removal without the specification of the places where the excisable goods are produced; cured or if such excisable goods were used in the manufacture for any other purposes in the same place, this cannot be done without payment of duty at the place and, in the manner prescribed.

The petitioner filed his objections to the said scheme along with several others. After a number of adjournments, the Hearing Authority empowered under section 68 C of the Act was able to conclude the proceedings by April 26, 1979 and it was alleged that the Authority in the course of hearing ob served that it would finalise and approve the scheme by 21.5.1979. The petitioner filed original suit No. 145 of 1979 on the file of Civil Judge, Bulandshahr for a declaration that the scheme published under section68 C of tho Act was illegal, void and ultra vires and for an injunction restraining the defendants in the suit from finalising and approving the scheme and acting upon it after it was published. The State Transport Undertaking filed its objections to that scheme along With several others, the hearing authority empowered under Section 68 of the , was able. Thereafter, the petitioner filed a writ petition before the High Court for staying the hearing of the suit till the disposal of a special leave petition before this Court since the question relating to maintainability of suits of similar nature was involved in the said special leave Petition. The learned Single Judge declined to grant the request of the petitioner and fixed the suit for arguments on November 8, 1985. Aggrieved by the order of the learned Single judge, the Petitioner filed a Writ Petition in the High court which was also dismissed. Against the order passed by the learned single Judge, the petitioners filed a Special Leave Petition before this court against the order dated August 8, 1986 of the Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court. The question for consideration in this case is whether a suit is maintainable in a civil court for an ad interim injunction restraining a Hearing Authority appointed under Section68 D of the (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act ') from proceeding with the hearing and approving of a scheme published by section 68C either with or without modification. Dismissing the Special Leave petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of the civil courts is impliedly barred from entertaining suits of the present nature. The juris of the Civil Courts is impliedly excluded from entertaining suit of the instant nature. [544G] 2.1 In cases of the other nature where invariably reliance is placed by the private operators on Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, a writ Petition lies before the high Court. In such cases a suit was hardly the remedy which can be availed by them.

The appellant was charged under section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and section 161 Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that Miss Eylene (P.W. 2) used to live in 1962 with her father at Fazilka. She developed illicit connection with someone and became pregnant. In April 1963 she went to Ambala to her maternal aunt who is employed as a sister in the Ambala Air Force Hospital, and gave birth to a son there in July 1963. The appellant asked Russel Niel and his wife to make arrangement for the bringing up of the child. Russel n Nathaniel told them that if they wanted to save themselves they should make some settlement with him and demanded a bribe of Rs. 1,000/ . But Mr. M. P. Singh, D.I.G., who recorded his statement and called two witnesses to witness the proceedings produced seven currency notes of the denomination of Rs 100/ each. The numbers of those currency notes were noted and Russels Neniel was then instructed to pass on the money to the appellant. Rusrosel Nani gave a signai and immediately D.S.P. Mukatdhari Singh turned up and recovered the currency notes from the pocket of the appellant 's brother in law. The Special Judge accepted the prosecution case as correct and convicted the appellant of the charged framed against him and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years and to pay a fine of Rs 5001 or in default to undergo simple imprisonment for a further period of six months under section 161, Indian Penal code and ordered the substantive sentences to run concurrently. The High Court maintained the conviction of the appel lant under s 5(2) of Prevention of corruption Act and section I5(1) (d). In appeal by special leave it was contended that the concealment of the birth of an illegitimate child was not an offence under the Indian Penal Penal Code or any other criminal statute and if the appellant had obtained money from RusselNathaniel, it cannot be said that the appellant has obtained a gratification for doing or forbearing to do any official act, or for showing or forbearing to show in the exercise of his official functions, favour or disfavour to any per son.

The appellant was convicted under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 by a Special judge who sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for three months and to pay a fine of Rs. 500 in default to suffer further rigorous imprisonment. No separate sentence was passed under section 6(c). The charge framed against the appellant was that on or about May 12, 1952 he had accepted Rs. 100 as illegal gratification from V. section Doraiswamy as a motive or reward for doing an official act and showing in the exercise of his official functions favour to whomsoever in seeing that a speedy and favourable settlement of the claim cases preferred by him against the Bengal Nagpur Railway was subsequently the Eastern Railway. The charge under section 161 I.P.C. read with section 5 (1) (d) of Prevention of Criminal misconduct for the corrupt and illegal use of his Official position as a public servant to obtain pecuniary advantage for himself punishable under section S.5(2), clause (d), of the Act was alleged to have been committed by him. The Special judge rejected this contention and was satisfied that in the interests of justice, the appellant should be put on his trial in a Court of competent jurisdiction for offences under section 165 I. P.C., and section 5, (2) read with s.5 (1), clause(d). On appeal by special leave: Held, that the sanction accorded was a valid sanction. The only point which had been argued before this Court was whether there was a proper sanction in the case was a question serious enough to justify the granting of a certificate. Gokulchand Dwarkadas Morarka vs The King, (1948) L.R. 75 I.A. 30, referred to.
