Section 18(1)(a) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950 provides that an "intermediary 's grove" is bhumidhari property. Rights in it are part of bhumidhari rights. After the coming into force of the Act, what could still be sold in execution of the decree was the right in trees of groves as these contin ued to vest in the intermediary. This means that "grove land" and an "Intermediary" 's groves are equated and groves were on ly collections of trees in plots of land so as to preclude cultivation in them. The uncut trees are deemed to be parts of the "land". Section 18(i)(a), therefore, provides that where an intermediary could enforce his right against the mortgage or after the Act came into force, he would proceed against trees in groves and the view taken by the execution court, that there is a distinction between trees and a grove and grove land should have been upheld by a Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court (Lucknow Bench). Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: Under the general law, trees, before they are cut, form parts of 'land '. And an inseparable part is always included in the whole. In view of this very clear legal position, it is not necessary even to consider previous definitions or to make out specious or unrealistic distinctions between standing uncut tree, which are parts of grove and grove land. The proposition is well settled, under the general Law, that trees, after they came into existence under section 18 of the , in the State of Uttar Pradesh, new bhumidhari right came into exist under section 6(h) of Act read with section 73 of the .

The prosecution case was sought to be proved by the ocular testimony of PW4 Biju and PW5 Anil, both aged about 13 years at the time of occurrence and the other evidence. Both the eye witnesses supported their statements recorded under Section 161 Cr. P.C. during their testimony in court. The trial Court on the basis of prosecution evidence found accused No. 1 guilty of an offence punishable under Section 302 IPC and sentenced him to suffer rigorous imprisonment for life. Accused Nos. 2 to 6, namely, Rajan, Preman, Viswan, Sura and Shajan were found guilty of offences under Sections 143, 147, 148, 341, 323, 324, 326 and 302 read with Section 149 I.P.C., but no separate sentences were awarded on any of those counts. On an appeal before the High Court, the conviction and sentence was set aside. In view of the limited notice issued by this Court, it is directed that issue notice limited to the question as to the nature of offence and the quantum of sentence. No orders on bail. It is in this background that we have to consider the nature and nature of the offence committed by the four appellants. According to the prosecution case there was enmity between the two groups on account of illicit distillation and suspicion of information being passed on to the Excise officials. However, no evidence was led in support of this allegation by the prosecution and no motive for commission of the crime was established at the trial. The postmortem on the deceased was conducted by Dr. Sivasankara Pillai PW12. He had found as many as 38 injuries on the injured. Most of the injuries found by him, however, were abrasions on different parts of the body though the deceased had also suffered stab wounds on the right upper arm and left elbow and sharp weapon injuries on his hands and legs. The bones of the legs and arm had been fractured.

The assessee, Standard Triumph Motor Co. Ltd., is a non resident company having its place of business at Coventry in the United Kingdom. It entered into a collaboration agreement with the Standard Motor Products of India Ltd. (Indian Company) in November, 1939 whereunder the assessee was entitled to royalty of five per cent on all sales effected by the Indian Company. This amount of 5 per cent less the Indian tax had to be remitted to the assessee in the Sterling currency. The assessee 's accounting year was the year ending 30th September. With respect to 101 its Indian income, it was filing its returns through the Indian company. The collaboration agreement between the assessee and the Indian Co. expired in November 1970. For the assessment years 1967 68 and 1968 69, the assessee filed returns in which it stated that it was maintaining its accounts on mercantile basis. It did not dispute its liability to assessment. In these returns, it disclosed a royalty income of Rs. 1,600 and Rs. 4,57,311 respectively. When it came to filing of the return for the assessment year 1969 70 (year ending 30.9.1966), the assessee admitted a royalty of Rs, 925,257 but filed a nil return saving that it had been maintaining its account on cash basis. The I.T.O. completed the assessment for the first two assessment years on the basis of the returns. For these assessment years 1969 70 and 1970 71, however, he refused to accept the assessee ' 's plea that it is maintaining its books on mercantile foundation alone and since it did rot actually receive any income in all these four years no tax was payable by it. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeals holding that the assessment orders for the past years relating to the asses see reveal that the method of accounting was mercantile, that for the A.Y. 1967 68, the assesses did not actually receive the amount nor did it take credit for the said amounts in its books at Coptry. The Tribunal also held that the assessee had not been following any particular method of accounts regularly over the past year years. For this reason, the High Court answered the question in the negative i.e., in favour of the revenue and against the assessee. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in answering the question against the assessee. [102B] 1.2 In the instant case, it is clear that eventuality will never arise in regard to the income with which were are concerned because that income will have to be remit to the nonresident by obtaining an irre vocable letter of credit and will thus be received only outside India.

The appellant was convicted for an offence under section 302 Indian Penal Code read with section 34 for the murder of one Lahu Vithu Patil on the night between May 23, and 24, 1960 at village Pasarde. Four persons Rama Krishna Patil accused No. 1, Bhiva Doulu Patil accused Nos. 2 (now appellant before us) and Deoba were alleged to have taken part in murder of Lahu Santu Patil. The trial court convicted the appellant on the testimony of the approver and found corroboration for the approver 's testimony in the statement of Nanu Sintu Sutar, P.W. 7 who had prepared the knife alleged to be used for the offence on March 17, 1960, and hi, motive to commit the murder because of the suspicion he had about his wife having a liaison with the deceased. The High Court on appeal found corroboration in material particulars; from the evidence of Santu 1W. 6 brother of Deoba to whom Deoba had made a confession of his participation in the offence the discovery of the 'knife at the instance of accused No 1 and the knife being found blood stained and the unusual character of the knife which fitted in with the dimensions of the injurious caused to the deceased, were very extensive and according to the medical evidence they could have been caused with the knife. On appeal by special leave the appellant contended that there should be corroboration of the accomplice 's story because the knife was got prepared by accused No1 and the appellant nine weeks before the murder and that fact by itself will not corroborate the charge under section302 read with s 34 of the Indian Penal code against the appellant. Held, further, that though the conviction of an accused on the evidence testimony of an accomplice cannot be said to be illegal yet the courts will, as a matter of practice, not accept the evidence Of such a witness without corroboration in materials particulars. The law may be stated in the words of Lord Reading C. J., in Bhuboni Sahu vs The King, (1949) L.R. 76 I.A. Mad. 308, 836 position in which he can hardly fail to have a strong bias in favour of the prosecution ; the real danger is that he is telling a story which in its general outline is true, and it is easy for him to work into the story which is untrue.

The appellant was a public servant within the meaning of section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. On or about December 11, 1962, he was charged in the Court of Special Judge for an offence under section 5 (2), read with section 5, (1) (d) of ' the Prevention Of Corruption Act and section 161 of the Indian Penal Code. The case of the prosecution was that on July 8, 1961, the appellant committed these offences by obtaining a sum of Rs. 180/ for Sri A.D. Singh, Executive Engineer (Electrical) from Ramprit Singh, P.W. 2 by resorting to corrupt and illegal means or by otherwise abusing his position as public servant. The Special Judge accepted the prosecution case as true and convicted the appellant under section 161 I.P.C. and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for five years. The High Court dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment of the Special judge. In appeal to this Court it was contended that upon the findings recorded by the High Court, the appel lant could not be convicted of the charges because he was not a "public servant" within the language of section 81 I. P.C., in view of the language Of section 81 of the . HELD: (i) The appellant was an officer in the service or pay of the Corporation as defined in section 21, cl. (12), Indian Penal code and therefore a 'public servant ' within the expression "corporation engaged in any trade or industry" includes a banking, insurance or financial corporation, a river valley Corporation and a corporation for supplying power, light or water to the public. [687 E] (ii) The word "officer" used in section 2(1) of Prevention of corruption Act means that there must be some person employed to exercise, to some extent, and in certain circumstances, a delegated function of Government. He is either himselfarmed with some authority or representative character, or his duties are immediately auxiliary to those of some one who is so armed. The decision in Reg vs Ramajirao Jivbaji was considered by the Calcutta High Court in Nazamuddin vs Queen Empress, A.I.R. , referred to.

The appellant was tried and convicted under r. 125(9) Defence of India Rules, 1962 for contravening cl. 4(b) of the Maharashtra Jowar (Restriction on Purchase 'and Sale and Control of Movement) Order, 1964, and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months and fine of Rs. 500/ , in default further rigorous imprisonment. The sentences were directed to run concurrently. In appeal before this Court it was contended that r. 141(2) was ultra vires because it laid down a rule of evidence contrary to the law contained in section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act. HELD: Rule 141 (2) falls within section 3 because it is essential to the scheme of the Defence of india Rules. The Rules must necessarily provide for the publication of orders made under the Rules and they must also provide for proof in judicial proceedings of the fact of publication. [273 E] In the instant case the order of the High Court maintaining the forfeiture of the seized stock of juar set aside and the rest of the order maintained. [272 F G] Rule 141(1) is within the powers conferred by section 3 (1). Section 3 gives very wide powers. It seems to us that r, 141( 2 falls within s.3 because it does not enable the Court to order forfeiture of juari seized stock. In the result the appeal is partly allowed and the order maintaining the sentence is set aside. [274 A B] The order of High Court maintained. The forfeiture of seized stock was ordered in respect of contravention of cl. 3 of the Jowrar ( Restriction on purchase 'and sale Control of movement) Order 1964, but it did not contain any provision authorising the court to forfeit the juar seized from the house of the appellant because, he says that the Maharashtra State Jowarsar (restrictionon Purchase and Sale) Order 1965, was contrary to an existing act does not matter because section 43 of the defence of India Act provides that "the provisions of this Act or any rule made thereunder or any order made under any such rule shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any enactment other than this Act. " The section contemplates that the rules may be inconsistent with existing legislation but by virtue of section 43, if otherwise valid, they would have effect, notwithstanding that they are inconsistent with the existing legislation.

One Kunwar Singh was a practising lawyer and after finishing his work for the day he left the Fatehgarh court along with the brother lawyers, Brijendra Singh Yadav and Om Prakash Dubey. They were proceeding on their bicycles and as they reached a spot near Barhpur Block, Violet is alleged to have shouted "The Vakil has come". Sia Ram fired a shot from his gun as a result of which Kunwar Singh fell down. All the accused thereafter ran away. The other lawyer, Om Prakash Pandey, contacted the District Magistrate and the Superintendent of Police vainly attempting to have the dying declaration of Kunwar Singh recorded. A person called Soney Lal also alleged to be an eye witness lodged the First Information Report at the police station at about 5 45 p.m. The Superintendent of police K. N. Daruwala reached the spot of occurrence shortly before 6 p.M. and sent it for postmortem examination. Dr. Rizvi who performed the postmortem examination found a firearm wound on the left upper chest of the deceased. There were lantern marks around the injury. The evidence of PW 4 is clear on the part played by the appellant Sia, Ram Chandra, had moved an application before the Additional District Magistrate (Judicial) who was conducting the committal proceedings that he was not known to the witnesses and therefore he should be put up for being identified in an identification parade. The Public Prosecutor objected to that request. The Magistrate upheld the objection and refused to direct that a parade be held. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the State Government except in regard to Shri Ram whom it convicted under section 302 read with section 109. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) A person may for example invite another casually or for a friendly purpose and that may facilitate the murder of the invite. But unless the invitation was extended with intent to facilitate the commission of the murder, the person inviting cannot be said to have abetted the murder. It is not enough that an act on the parts of the alleged abettor happens to facilitate its commission of crime. Intentional aiding and therefore active complicity is the gist of the offence of abetment under the third paragraph of section 107. Apart from the words attributed to Violets, there is nothing at all to show that she was aware of the nefarious design of SiaRam and his associates. [626 F G] (2) The High court erred in holding on the complicity of VioLetter 's conduct a meaning which it does not naturally bear. The words of Vialet are at best in the nature, of a circumstance and they do not, without more, necessarily justify the inference that she Was a party to the murderous design.

In the year 1959, two persons by name Ramachandra Budhya and Govind Dhaya were murdered by some people. In all 11 accused including one Deoram Maruti Patil were brought to trial for the murder of Vishwanath before the Court of the Additional Sessions judge, Kolaba. The charge against them was that they, in view of their common grudge against the deceased combined together and did away with the deceased. The Sessions Judge found that the prosecution witnesses were not speaking the truth and that the version given by accused 2 was the probable one. In appeal to the High Court it was contended on behalf of the State that when three of the four named accused, who were charged under section 302 read with section 34, of the Indian Penal Code, were acquitted, the court could not convict only one of the accused on the basis of constructive liability and that in the present case on a fair reading of the entire judgment it would be clear that the learned judges meant to hold that persons other than the acquitted accused conjointly acted with the convicted accused. Held: (i) In the first illustration, the Court certainly can convict two or more of the named accused if it accepts the evidence that they acted conjointly in committing the offence. But what is the position if the Court acquits 3 of the 4 accused either because it rejects the prosecution evidence or because it gives the benefit of doubt to the said accused ? Can it hold, in the absence of a charge as well as evidence, that though the three accused are acquitted, some other unidentified persons acted conjointaneously with one of them ? (ii) In such cases, either the trial court or even the High court in appeal may be able to come to the conclusion that the acquittal of some of the persons named in the charge and tried will not necessarily displace the charge under section 149 because along with the two or three persons convicted were others who composed the unlawful assembly but who have not been identified and so have not yet been named.

Section 15 of the , provides that the rate of duty and tariff valuation, if any, applicable to any imported goods shall be the rate and valuation in force on the date on which the goods are actually removed from the warehouse. Section 15(1)(b) clearly requires that the rates of duty, rate of exchange and tariff applicable to all imported goods shah be the rates and valuationin force on that date on the dates on which a bill of entry in respect of such goods is presented under that section; (c) in the case of goods cleared from a warehouse under section 68, on the day on which goods are actual ly removed from a ware house under section 69, on tho date onwhich the goods were actually removed, the bill of Entry shall be deemed to have been presented on thedate of such entry inwards. Section 16 provides that an importer of any warehoused goods may clear them if the import duty leviable on them has been paid; and (d) in a particular situation whether customs duty is payable at the rate prevalent on a particular date or not has to be determined under the four corners of the . The petitioner placed orders on M/s. Metalic metal Indus tries Pvt. Ltd., Singapore for the supply of MSCR defective sheets or coils on 30th May, 1984. On 4th April, 1988, the petitioner 's clearing agent filed six bills of entry for ex bond clearance. However, the bills of Entry were returned with the remark that "please obtain no objection from the income tax". This was endorsed on 24th August, 1984 and the petitioner states that thereafter he came to know that the income Tax Authorities had imposed ban under section 132(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The petitioner asserted that he was ever ready and willing, rather was anxious, to get the material on payment of the then prevailing customs duty. However due to circumstances beyond the control of the petitioner, that it to say, by the order of the Incometax Authorities, the goods could not be released. This factor was not of the Petitioner 's making, according to the petitioner. On 30th March, 1988 the Income tax Department issued the necessary no objection certificate, thus lifting the ban. On April 4, 1988 a notice was issued to the revenue authority to appear before this Court. It was contended on behalf of the respondents that for the payment of duty the liability of the peti tioner to pay the duty is the duty at the time of clearance of the goods. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1. Article 32 of the Constitution guarantees the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of fundamental rights. If there is breach of the fundamental rights, the Petitioner can certainly have recourse to Article 32 Of the Constitution provided other conditions are satisfied. But this Court has passed an order on 22nd April as indicated hereinbefore. It is stated that the goods have been cleared pursuant to that order. The revenue would be at liberty to take appropriate action in accordance with law for the recovery of the dues.

The appellant was the Managing Director of Dharwar Urban Co operative Bank Ltd. which went into liquidation and in that capacity he was receiving a yearly remuneration from the Bank and the properties were sold in payment of a debt binding on the family and therefore the sale in execution of the payment order could not be challenged as the sons were under a pious obligation under the Hindu Law to discharge their father 's debts not tainted with immorality or illegality, which lays open the whole estate to be seized for the payment of such debts. Held, that even after partition the sons could be made liable for the pre partition debts of the father if there was no proper arrangement for the payments of such debt at the time when the partition was effected although the father could have no longer any right of alienation in regard to the separated share of the sons. The liability of a father, who is a managing director and who draws a salary or a remuneration, incurred as a result of negligence in the discharge of his duties is not an avyavaharika debt as it cannot be termed as " repugnant to good morals". In Hindu law there are two mutually destructive principles, one the principle of independent coparceiiary rights in the sons which is an incident of birth, giving to the sons vested right in the coparcenary property, and the other the pious duty of the son to discharge his father ' debts not vitiated by the partition. The obligation of a son to pay the debt of his father unless it is for an immoral or illegal purpose, continues till the debt is paid off and the pious obligation incumbent on the sons to see that their father "s debts are paid, prevents the sons from asserting that the family estate so far as their interest is concerned is not liable to purge that debt.

Section 3 of the Rajasthan Passengers and Goods Taxation Rules, 1959 provides that in cases covered by the second proviso to sub rule (1) of rule 8 and by subrule (ii) of that rule the lump sum fixed by the State Government as payable in lieu of the tax on fare or freight, as the case may be shall be deposited in cash into a Government Treasury or a Sub Treasury in equal quarterly instalments payable within 15 days from the 31st day of March, the 30th day of September and 31st of December every year. The petitioners who are seven in number challenged the Act by way of writ petitions under article 32 of the Constitution on the ground that they were repugnant to articles 301 and 304 as being a restriction upon inter State trade, commerce and intercourse, to article 19 as involving an unreasonable restriction upon their business of the petitioners and also to article 14 as discriminating between this mode of transport and the Railways. The Act was passed in 1959 for levying a tax on passengers and goods carried by road or inland waterways. The power to enact the Act purports to be derived from Entry No. 56 of the State List in Sch. VII to the Constitution, which reads: "156. Taxes on goods and passengers carried by motor vehicles" and though the measure of the Tax is furnished by the amount of fare and freight charged, it does not cease to be a tax On fares and freights being a different tax, cannot be levied under the Entry and thus the tax is without authority of law. Held, that the levy of tax cannot be said to offend articles 301 or 304 of the Indian Constitution. The word 'shall ' was held to be directory only in that case, by Coutts Trotter, C. Now, Rules 8 and 8 A and the notification only lay down what lump sum payment has to be in each case, if a lump sum is being paid. The mandatory language of the Rules and the Notification still retains the permissive character of the section, but only lays down what the amount must be, if lump sum pay is made in lieu thereof, of payment of the 'tax calculated on actual fares and fares. If the two Rules and notification are read in this way, the mandatory language is limited to the prescribing of the lump sums rates.

% The appellant, a private limited company having set up an industrial unit in engineering industry, served notice of retrenchment on 56 workmen alleging non availability or raw material to utilise the full installed capacity power shedding limiting the working of the Unit to 5 days a week and the mounting loss. Subsequently negotiations took place between the Union and the appellant leading to an agreement dated 1st April 1974 whereby the workmen who were sought to be retrenched were taken back in service with continuity of service by the appellant and the workmen on their part agreed to co operate with the management in implementing certain economy measures and in increasing the productivity so as to make the undertaking economically viable. Simultaneously, the workmen demanded a revision of the wage scales and the Labour Court by its award directed that all the workmen shall be reinstated in service from 1st August 1974 with full back wages, permitting the appellant to deduct any amount paid as retrenchment compensation from the amount payable to the workmen as back wages. The appellant challenged the Award before this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) It would be appropriate to award 75% of the back wages to the workman to be paid in two equal instalments. [567B] (2) The direction given by the Labour court that all workmen shall he reinstated shall be paid 75% Of the back Wages after deducting the amount paid to them as wages when recalled for work since the date of retrenchment and adjustment of the retrenchment compensation towards the amount found due and pay able. The award shall stand modified to the effect that the retrenched workmen who are now reinstated shall he paid 75 % of the backwages after deducting 50% of their back wages from the date they offered to resume work till their reinstatement. [568C] (3) It is not for this Court to be a regular court of appeal but it confers a discretionary power on the Supreme Court to grant special leave to appeal, inter alia, against the Award of any Tribunal in the territory of India. The scope and ambit of this wide constitutional power cannot be exhaustively defined. It cannot obviously be so construed as to confer a right to a party which he has none under the law. The Court will entertain a petition for special leave in which a question of general public importance is involved or when the decision would shock the conscience of this Court. the lndustrial Disputes Act is intended to be an self contained one and it seeks to achieve social justice on the basis of collective bargaining, collaboration and arbitration. Awards are given on circumstances peculiar to each dispute and the Tribunals are to a large extent free from resrtrictions of technical considerations imposed on courts. A free and liberal exercise of the power under Article 136 may materially affect the fundamental basis of such decisions, viz., quick solution of such disputes to achieve industrial peace. Though Article 136 is couched in widest terms, it is necessary for this court to exercise its discretionary jurisdiction only in cases where Awards are made in violation of the principles of natural justice causing substantial and grave injustice to parties or raises an important principle of industrial law requiring elucidation and final decision by this Court or disclose such other exceptional or special circumstances which merit consideration of this court (See Bengal Chemical & Pharmaceutical Works Ltd., Calcutta vs Their Workman) ; Bengal Chemical and Pharmaceutical Works Limited, Calcutta vs their Workman, [1962] Supp. 2 SCR 136 at 140; Management of Paniltole Tea Estate vs The Workmen, [1959] Suppl. 2 S.C.R. 136 at 141; Management 's Union for India & Anr. Employers in relation to Calcutta Dock Labour Board and ors.

The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 302 I.P.C. for committing the murder of his wife Churl (26) and was sentenced to death. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that the confessional statement exhibit PH was not admissible in evidence as it was not recorded in the manner prescribed by section 164 Cr. P.C., the same is inadmissible in evidence. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The decision in Nazir Ahmed 's case also covers the case in hand and that on the principles there applied, here to oral evidence given by Mr. Khanna on behalf o the State conceded that in view of the a decision, a confession recorded by a second class magistrate cannot be put in evidence under sections 74 and 80 of the Indian Evidence Act. [434C D] (2) The fact that the accused alone was with Churi deceased in the house when she was murdered there with the Khokhri and the fact that his relations of the accused with the deceased, ts would be shown hereafter. were strained would, in the absence of any cogent explanation by him, point to his guilt. The evidence of Nagju (PW 2) mother of the deceased shows that the ac cording to Bhagat Ram was illtreating Churi. It is well established that the discovery and arrest of the suspected offender is one of the essential steps in the course of an investigation (see in this connection H. Rishbud & Inder Singh vs The State of Delhi, [1964] 4 S.C R. 435 referred to. (3) In view of section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, any Presidency Magistrate and Magistrate of the First Class and any Magistrate specially empowered in this behalf by the State Government may, if he is not a police officer record any statement or confession made to him in the Course of an investiga tion under this chapter (Chapter XIV of the code) be under any other law for the time being in force or at any time afterwards before the commencement of the enquiry of trial.

Section 82 of the Transfer of Property Act provides that where property subject to a mortgage belongs to two or more persons having distinct and separate rights of owner ship therein, the different shares in or parts of such property owned by such persons are, in the absence of a contract to the contrary, liable to contribute rateably to the debt secured by the mortgage. Section 83 of the Act provides inter alia that where the property subject lo a mortgage belonged to two and more persons have distinct and independent rights of owners ship therein the different share in or part of such properties owned by them are, In the absence Of a contract between them either in the mortgage deed or otherwise, regarding their respective shares of responsibility in the Rs. 10,000 the total aggregate sum due at the date of the mort gage from the three of them is applied in satisfaction of the mortgage debt and the balance of Rs. 20,000 is retained by A. 5,000 and C 's would be 5/10 of Rs 15,000 which comes to Rs. 2,500. The plaintiff claimed that each of the three mortgagors was liable for a half of that sum namely Rs. 80,000 from each of them and that each one of them was liable under Order XXXIV of the Civil Procedure Code in proper form. Schedule A contains a list of the rest of the mortgaged properties which belong exclusively to the defendants, 24 182 Round Tank Lane (which belonged exclusively to him) to the decree holder for a sum of Rs, 89,485 12 plus costs. The amount which went towards satisfaction of his claim and costs then outstanding was only Rs. 1,19,116 11 0 in satisfaction Of the first mortgage and the later decretal charge; Rs. 11,519 11 0 was paid by Tarak, Kedar and Naku to the Hooghly Flour Mills on the same day. In addition to this Rs. 16,000 was paid to the Mills in full satisfaction of their claim and cost then outstanding. The Mills executed a reconveyance of the remaining properties to the mortgagors in release of the mortgages on the 10th of March, 1943, for a consideration of Rs., 80,507 7 8 from the two defendants. In execution the mortgagee proceeded against the proper ty of the plaintiff alone (as Tarak 's son) and during the pendency of the execution, assigned her rights in the decree to the said Hoohghly Jute Mills. The mills continued the execu tion and on the 11th March, 1944, the claim was satisfied in this way. An order of the Court was obtained sanctioning sale of a part of the property, 20 Round tank Lane ( which belonged exclusively exclusively to M/s. Gyarsi Dassi (died 1945) I I.L.R. at 586 and 16 Round Road Lane for Rs. 29,667 10 with interest against each defendant. The sanction of the court was necessary because the judgment debtor Hari Lall (present plaintiff) was a minor. The trial Court decreed the suit but on appeal the Chief Justice of the High Court disagreed and held that it was not proper to introduce into the matter any extrinsic principle to modify the statutory provisions. Held, that section 82 must exclude section 43 because when there is a general law and a special law dealing with a particular matter, the special excludes the general. In the present case the whole law of mortgage in India including the law of contribution arising out of a transaction of mort gaged, was now statutory and was embodied in the Transfer Of Property Act read with the Civil Proce dure Code. The words "the con tract" can only refer to the main contract between the promisors on the one side and the promisee on the other.

Appellant No. 1 is a Bachelor of Engineering (Civil) having secured first class with distinction getting 69.96% marks from Karnataka Univer sity. Shri Rajendra appellant No. 2 is a graduate of Engi neering (Mech.) from Karnataka University and secured 66.40 marks in the qualifying examination. The Govt. of Karnataka by notification dated 4th April, 1985 invited applications for recruitment of Asstt. Engineers (Civil). The selections were to be made on the basis of marks obtained in the competitive examina tion and marks secured in the interview, in accordance with the K.S.C.S., (Direct Recruitment) Rules, 1973. According to these Rules total marks for qualifying examination were kept at 100 and 50 for interview. Thus the marks allotted for inter view amounted to 33.3% of the total marks. Applications were invited for 300 posts of Civil Engineers and 100 Mechanical Engineers initially and subsequently added additional posts of 150 Civil Engineers. Both the appellants applied for the posts of their choice in Public Works Department, Government of Karnataka. Appellant No 1 secured 29.50 marks out of 50 marks in interview and 69.95 marks out Of 150. The 2nd appellant obtained 24.83 marks in his interview and 66.41 marks in qualifying examination thus in all 91.23 marks out to 150. Both appellants were not selected in merit as the last candidate selected for the above posts secured higher marks than the appellants. The appellants filed a petition before the Karnataka Administrative Tribunal challenging the Rules on the ground that the percentage of marks for viva voce as 33. 3 were excessive and in violation of the decisions of this Court. The Tribunal by its order dated 24th May, 1990 dismissed the petitions and the appellants aggrieved against the aforesaid decision have approached this Court by grant of special leave.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. Their appeal was dismissed by the High Court on the question of sentence and see no justification to take a view different from what has been said about him by the high Court. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The confession of co accused person cannot be treated as substantive evidence and can be pressed into service only when the court is inclined to accept other evidence and feels the necessity of seeking for an assurance in support of its conclusion deducible from the said evidence . [403C D] 2. In a case involving the killing of the District Magistrate in his office, better investigation was expected and the State should have taken great care to ensure that every loophole in the investigation was plugged at the fight time in ac cordance with law. It is unfortunate that lapses have oc curred. P.S.S., Appeals dis posed of. [404D E] 3. In the instant case, Sadanand must have been the common reaction of all the ashramites including Yadav and Sadiq. Thus, this could not be a feature to supply the link for establishing conspiracy. Prosecution also relied upon a feature, which if accept ed, could provide some link between the two for the commis sion of the offence. According to the prosecution, Yadav was regularly visiting Sadanand at the jail. The jail records do not support such visits. According ly, the prosecution case that Yadav made this statement, he appears to have made the statement following assault on him. Even if it is accepted that Yadav has made the statements as alleged, can the same be utilised against Sadanand is the next aspect for consid eration. Obviously, when Yadav was beaten up, he must have had been anxious to ensure tricking that the assault stopped. His plea in such a situation would neither be voluntary nor natural. It would not be proper to rely upon the same for any purpose. [414E F] 4. The prosecution has also led evidence to show that after the arrival of Sadanand, at the Jail enforcement of rules became slack and there was a regular flow of food from outside. jail officials were also entertained by Sadanand. This type of evidence, even if accepted, does not establish conspiracy because Yadav, being a follower, was likely in the usual course to meet Sadanand and the fact that they were meeting at regular intervals by itself would not estab lish conspiracy. The Prosecution relied on an event of 11th April, 1983 by examining P.W.4. This witness who was a convict staying in the same jail stated that his wife had an interview with him in the jail by paying bribe of Rs.2 or Rs.3 on 11 4.1983. While he was talking to his wife, he saw accused Yadav talking to Sadanand; He over heard Yadav telling Tripathi that his work would be done within an hour or so. Sadanand appeared to be happy on being told so.

The dispute between the four appellants companies and the respondents workmen was referred for adjudication to the Industrial Tribunal by nine references orders on various dates between April to December 1959. The main dispute which gave rise to the references was with respect to wages, dearness allowance and gratuity. The references included other items but it was common that wages and dearness allowance prevalent in the four companies had been continuing since 1950 when the last award was made between the parties. It may also be stated that there was noserious dispute before the Tribunal as to the financial capacity of the companies and further, as the first company controls the other three companies, the wages and Dearness Allowance are the same so far as the clerical and subordinate staff are concerned. Held, that in applying the industry cum region formula for fixing wage scales the Tribunal should lay stress on the industry part of the formula if there were a large number of industrial concerns in the same region carrying on the same industry; but in doing so the Tribunal must when making comparisons take into account the total wage packet packet (i.e. basic wages fixed by it as well as dearness allowance) and then compare it with the total wages packet of comparable concerns and thus arrive at a just figure for basic wage, for each category of factory workmen. The Tribunal was right in following the trend that has begun in this region and in fixing the same scale of dearness allowance for subordinate staff and factory workmen as in the case of clerical staff. So far as subordinate and clerical staff areconcerned, there is no reason to disagree with the rate of dearness allowances fixed by the Tribunal.

A part of the consideration for this simple mortgage consisted of moneys borrowed by both the brothers on bonds executed by both of them. This simple mortgage deed provided that the mortgagees would bear the expenses of the Nand Deep and debit the same to the mortgagors in the mortgage account. On March 10, 1900, Shiddappa executed a usufructuary mortgage (exhibit D 52) in favour of Lalchand Bhavanchand Gujar and Tuljaram Bhavanchand respectively for Rs. 1,300 made up of Rs.1,100 due under a previous mortgage and Rs. 200 presently advanced in cash. That deed provided: that the mortgage money would be repaid within a period of three years and that the mortgagors would pay the judi and incur expenses of Nand Deep, i.e., keeping a lamp always burning before Shri Tholaba Deity in the village of Nipani. The mortgagees by a Kabuliyat were sanctioned by the Mamlatdar on May 5,1900. Shiddha having died, his four sons were added as party defendants to this suit and then on their own application they were transposed to the category of plaintiffs. The trial court passed a decree for possession declaring that both the mortgages had been satisfied. On appeal the District Court held that by the Rajinama, Shriddappa intended to convey the title in the mortgaged property to the mortgagees and hence Shiddanappa 's heirs, the plaintiffs 1 and 2 could not claim redemption of Shiddana one half share in the suit land. The High Court dismissed both the appeals. In appeal to this Court by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that under section 74 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code as it stood at all material times, the Raj inama passed by Shiddhasappa did not extinguish the title of the mortgagors and that inasmuch as the mortgages were subsisting, the defendants could not acquire title by adverse possession. HELD : (i) On a correct interpretation of section 74, where there are more occupants than one in respect of the same occupancy each occupant has his own rights and the fact of registration of one of them as the registered occupant attracts the operation of the Code and confers certain rights or imposes certain obligations on the registered occupants as laid down in the Code but does not take away the rights of other occupants. It is true that if any of the occupants other than the registered owner desires to relinquish his occupancy, he cannot himself give a notice of relinquishment but must give it by and through the registered dealer Nevertheless the registered user, in the absence of any authority, express or implied, to be clearly pleaded and strictly proved, has no inherent or independent (1) , 89 702 right to give any such notice so as to affect the interests of the other occupants.[706 B C] (ii) In view of the observation of the Judicial Committee in Khiarajmal vs Daim, [1904] L.R. 32 Ind App. App. No. 22 of 1945 which was filed by defendants 1 to 4 and L.P.A. No 16 of 1945, which was dismissed by this Court on March 15, 1909, the position of law applicable to those facts and that law was nothing but the provisions of section 73 of the code. [706 G] (iii) The contention that annappa 's interest in the property was extinguished by reason of the adverse possession exercised by the mortgagees since at least 1905 when the claim of the Annappa to get the mortgaged properties registered in his name failed, cannot affect the subsisting right of redemption of the mortgages or operate to shorten the period of limitation prescribed for a suit for redemption.

The respondent, a company incor pated under the Indian Companies Act dealing in carbon paper, typewriter, ribbon, stepler machines and steplers, despatches the said goods from its head office at Bombay to its branch office at Kanpur wherefrom sales there of are effected in the State of Uttar Pradesh. During the course of the assessment proceedings for the assessment year 1956 57, the respondent claimed that carbon paper not being paper falling within the ambit of Entry No. 2 of the Schedule to the Notification but a specialised article used for copying purposes, its turnover had to be assessed at the rate of 2 per cent prescribed for unclassi fied goods and not at the rates of 6 paise per rupee i.e. 6% prescribed in the aforesaid Notification. The Sales Tax Officer taxed the turnover of carbon paper for the period commencing from July 1, 1966 to June 30, 1966 at 6%. The validity and correctness of this order in so far as it related to the levy of tax on carbon paper at 6% and ribbon at 10% was challenged by the respondent by means of a writ petition before the High Court which allowed the same and quashed the levy. Hence this appeal. Dismissing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: The mere fact that the word 'paper ' forms part of the denomination of a specialised Article is not decisive of the question whether the article is paper as generally understood. [838E] Attorney General vs Winstanley ; , referred to. In popular parlance, the word "paper" in the common parlance or in the com criminatory sense means paper which is used for printing, writing or packing pur poses.

The respondents I to 4 were employed by the appellant as seasonal masons in the year 1946. In 1951, the partners of the appellant Mills purchased the building machinery and other equipment of another sugar mill at a time when they were not proprietors of the Sugar Mills at Bulandshahr. On January 19, 1955, the General Manager served a notice on the respondents 1 to 4 stating that they had disobeyed his orders and thereby committed misconduct under Standing Order No. L(a). They were asked to submit their explanation as to why action should not be taken against them under the Standing Order. The Labour Union by its letter dated January 31, 1955 denied the charges. On February 2, 1955 the General manager served a second notice on respondents 1 and 4 stating inter alia that they bad disobeyed their order of transfer and thereby committing misconduct under standing Order No L(A). They also stated that the bonus for last year at Amroha would be probably equal to II months wages and at Bulandshahr equal to about 4 or 5 days ' wages. The Industrial Tribunal by its award held that the management was within its rights and that as the respondents I 1 to 3 had disobey ed the order of the management, they were properly dismissed by the management. On appeal, the Labour Appellate Tribunal held that both the concerns i.e., the Mills at Amroha and the mills at Bulandshahr formed one unit, the Appellate Tribunal had no jurisdiction to set aside that finding under section 7(1) of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants: (i) The right to transfer is implicit in every contract of service and is too wide the mark; apart from any statutory provision, the rights of an employer and an employee are governed by the terms of contracts between them or by the rules necessarily implied therefrom. It is conceded that there is no express agreement between the appellant and the respondents where under the appellant has the right to trans fer his employees from one concern to another of his in the circumstances of this case, the transfer from one branch to another was valid or amounted to victimization; (ii) The question whether a person employed in a factory can be trans ferred to some other independent concern started by the same employer at a stage subsequent to the date of his employment. HELD: (1) It is not a condition of service of employment of the respondents either express or implied that the employer has the inherent right to the transfer them to a new concern stared by him subsequent to tho date of their employment. The respondents also relied upon a Government Order No 6122 (ST)/XXXVI A(S) T 1953 in support of their contention that the order was bad. By this order the Government of U.P. had directed that the employment of seasonal workmen in all vacuum pan sugar factories in the Uttar Pradesh should be governed by rules contained in the annexure thereto. Rule I in the said annexure is to the following effect: " A worker who has worked or but for illness or any other unavoidable cause would have worked in a Factory during the whole of the second half of the last preceding season will be employed in this season in such factory. " This rule does not prevent the employer to transfer an employee if he has the rights to do so under the contract of Service or under any statutory provisions. [922 H] (2) The employer in the present case had no such right. [936 B] (3) It was well within the powers of the Labour appellate Tribunal to entertain the appeal.

The appellant company which was formed in 1965 and went into production the same year, was exempted from the provisions of Chapter V A of the , until the provisions Of Chapter V of the Act were enforced in the area where the appellant 's factory was situated. However this exemption was withdrawn with effect from May 31, 1969 by a notification of the Government. The appellant company questioned its liability to pay special contribution under Chapter VA by filing a writ petition in the High Court of Gujarat under article 226 of the Constitution. The writ petition was dismissed on September 7, 1971 and the present appeal has been filed pursuant to a certificate granted by the High court under article 132(1) and 133(1)(c) of the constitution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. When extending the Act to different establishments, the relevant (1) ; 6 SCR 913 1092 Government is given the power to constitute a Corporation for the administration of the scheme of Employees ' State Insurance. The course adopted by modern legislatures in dealing with welfare scheme has uniformly conformed to the same pattern. The legislature evolves a scheme of socioeconomic welfare, makes elaborate provisions in respect of it and leaves it to the Government concerned to decide when, how and in what manner the scheme should be introduced. [1091C D] 2. When the whole Act is brought into force in the whole of India, it would not be necessary to retain this Chapter. Then all contributions will be made under Chapter IV. It may be noted that Chapter VA was inserted, as pointed out above, by an amending Act only in 1951. The object of the amendment was to make an equitable distribution of contribution by all employers. It was not considered fair that only employers of these regions to which the benefit provisions were extended should alone make contributions and thereby help to set up a corporation. [ 1091E F] 3. In the instant case, the appellant company 's contention proceeds on the fundamental misconception that the payment of contribution directed to be made by the employer under the or other similar payment or benefit under various social welfare legislations must either be labelled as a tax or a fee in order to attain legitimacy or not at all. The idea that such payment, contribution or whatever name is given to it should be so pigeon hold and fitted in stems from a misunderstanding of the Scheme of our Constitution in regard to social welfare legislation. Apart from the preamble which promises to secure to all its citizens, "justice, social economic and political", the State is enjoined by the Directive Principles of State Policy to secure a social order for the promotion of the welfare of the people". [1092F G] 4. The scheme is analogous to a deferred insurance policy which parents often take out on the lives of their children, but which are to be effective only from a future date after the children attain a certain age, though premium is liable to be paid right from the start. Merely because the benefits to be received are postponed, it cannot be said that there is no quid pro quo. It is true that ordinarily a return in proe senti is generally present when fee is levied, but antiquaneity or contemporaneity of payment and benefit is not the most vital or crucial test to determine whether a levy is a fee or not. In fact, it may often happen that the rendering of a service or the conferment of a benefit may only follow after the consolidation of a fund from the fee levied.

The petitioners demand regularisation of their services claiming to be daily rated workmen for a long time in the mines of the Diamond Mining Project, Panna of the National Mineral Development Corporation Ltd. Their demands are of regularisation and "equal pay for equal work" on the ground that they were discharging the same duties as the regular workers. The management has throughout denied the petition ers ' claim and alleged that, in fact, the petitioners have been continued on rolls on humanitarian grounds for several years, even though there was no work for them; and as such, there is no question of regularising the petitioners and giving them the pay of regular workers when in fact they are not doing any work for a short time. Allowing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The principle of regularisation of a daily rated workman and payment 'to him of the pay equal to that of a regular workman arises only when the daily rated worker is doing the same work as the ordinary workman and there being a vacancy available for him, he is not absorbed against it or not even paid the equal pay for the period during which the same Work is taken from him. On the clear findings in this case, this is not the position. This petition must, therefore, fail. [620C D] 2. The principles of regularisation are not the situation. This principle has been reiterated at the hearing before this Court. In spite of our above conclusion, keeping in view the offer made on behalf of respondent No. 2 in the counter affidavit together with Annexure R V thereto which was reiterated at tile heating before us, we direct that all the 63 daily rated workers including the 54 petitioners herein mentioned in the aforesaid Annexure RV to the counter affidavits be given the benefit of the Voluntary Retirement Scheme framed by respondent No 2 and they be paid the specified amounts in addition to their all other dues.

The suit out of which the appeal arises was brought by the appellants claiming title to and recovery of possession of a property known as the Azambad Tea Estate which comprised about 378 acres of land in Touzi No. 911 of Darjeeling Collectors. This property was set out in Schedule A to the plaint and besides a claim was also made to certain other items of the movable and certain other tenures, but this appeal is not concerned with these others which were set out. The appellants contended that when by the sale in execution of the mortgage decree obtained by the National Agency Co. they purchased the property mortgaged it was only the interest of Ismail that passed to them and not those of his co sharers who were no parties to the mortgage, there was one further transaction to which we must advert before passing on to the next stage of the proceedings. After the mortgage by deposit of title deeds in favour of the National agency Co., Ismail transferred his entire interest in the mortgaged property, that is, in the equity of redemption, to his wife Mst. To complete the narrative of the relevant facts, very soon after the purchase in Court auction in execution, the heirs of Azam Ali brought a suit (58 of 1931) to set aside the decree and the sale therein passed to it no title except to the extent of 2 1/2 as share belonging to Mohd. Ismail, the plaintiffs had by their purchases acquired from the several co sharer directly or mediately, the entire 16 as. share in the property assuming that their vendors had any such right. The suit was decreed as prayed for and the property was sold in execution by the decree holder on September 24, 1931. Ltd. to the Azamabad Tea Estate, but nothing turns on this, for even if that transfer was not effective that would not help the plaintiffs so long as they could not displace the title of theNational Agency Co., and that the co heirs were estopped from questioning the validity of the mortgages of the entire interest effected by him under section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act and that in any event the claim could not be accepted without careful scrutiny of the facts. Held, that the proper order to pass would be to remit the matter to the trial Court for recording a finding as regards the reality of the sale on the evidence already on the record and to pass an appropriate decree in the suit, that was, if the sale under exhibit 12(i) were held to be real, the appellants would be entitled in addition to the 8 pies share decreed to them by the High Court, to a further 2 as.

The appellant was tried by the Sessions judge of Karimnagar in what used to be the State of Hyderabad (now part of the State) under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code for the murder of his brother Baga Rao, and sentenced to death. The conviction and sentence were affirmed by the High Court of Andhra Pradesh. Held, that the omission complained of in the instant case should not have a more farreaching effect than the omission to carry out the provisions of section 162 or section 360 of the Code. Abdul Rahman vs The King Emperor (A.I.R. , followed. In cases exclusively triable by a court of Session it is the duty of the magistrate, while holding a preliminary inquiry, to satisfy himself that the documents referred in section 173 had been furnished to the accused and if he found that the police officer concerned had not carried out his duty in that behalf, the magistrate should see to it that is done. If the Magistrate was of opinion that it was necessary in the interests of justice to take the evidence of any one or more of the other witnesses for the prosecution, he may take such evidence also. The fact that the accused got the copies in the Sessions Court before the statements of the prosecution witnesses were recorded by that court without any avoidable delay within a few hours after the occurrence. Abdul Rahim vs The State of Assam ([1955] 1 S.C.R., 1069), referred to. In the present case the omission alleged in the first information report should not be allowed to have such a far reaching effect as to render the proceedings including the trial before the court wholly ineffective.

The respondent Municipality, after having obtained the approval of the Government issued a notice under section 153A(1) of the Bombay District Municipal Act, 1901 as adapted and applied to the State of Saurashtra and as amended by Act XI of 1955 (hereinafter referred to as the Act), to show cause in writing within a period of one month from the date of receipt of the notice why it should not be directed to arrange for the discharge of the effluent through a covered pucca drainage and for pumping it over a distance of about 8 miles in the Ran ' area of Cutch near Kuda, as shown in the plan annexed to the notice. The appellant replied that the effluent was being discharged until 1943 through a Katcha Channel running parallel to the railway line in the direction of Halvad. In 1944 it was felt that as the water of some of the wells in the areas known as Harijanvas and Kolivas close to the vicinity of the channel might be affected another channel was constructed for discharging the effluent, which was at a considerable distance away from Kolivas and Harijanvas, still further away from the city which lies on the western side of the railway lines. It was pointed out that during the last 3 or 4 years periodical surveys of water of various wells in city had been taken by the appellant and these tests had shown that the water was not in any way polluted by reason of the effluents being discharged through the existing channels, that all the papers and reports relating to the tests carried out periodically by the appellants were available for inspection by the respondent Municipality and that they could be inspected by appointment. The Special Officer decided Issue No. 4 in the affirmative and held that the question whether the discharge Of the effluent from the factory of the respondent company was polluting water and adversely affected the fertility of the soil was one for the subjective satisfaction of the Municipality, and was beyond the scope of the enquiry before him. On appeal by special leave to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (i) that the Special Officer had not erred in holding that the existence of a nuisance of the kind mentioned in section 153 A(1 ) of the Act was a matter for the objective satisfaction of Municipality and beyond the powers vested in him under the Act; (ii) that if the requisition in the notice is objected to, the objection includes not only to the allegation of the existence existence of the nuisance in terms of sub section (1) but also to the direction as to the manner in which the discharge should be discharged. HELD: (1)(a) The scheme under section153A is to leave it to the subjective satis faction of the municipality as to whether a particular state of fact exists and on finding that it does exist to proceed further and do something more, then the fact in question is not collateral but is a part of the very issue which the Municipality has to enquire into and that ceases to be justiciable. [395 C] (b) The words "to hold an enquiry into the matter " clearly suggest that the special officer must enquire into the entire matter where a party objects absolutely to the, notice and the requisition contained therein.

The Railway Stores (Unlawful Possession) Act, 1955 is a measure providing for punishment of persons in unlawful possession of railway stores who cannot satisfactorily account how they came by the same. By section 2 "railway stores" are defined to mean any article (a) which is the property of any railway administration and (b) which was used or intended to be used in the construction, operation or maintenance of a railway. Section 3 defines the offence as also the measure of punishment therefore. It reads: "If any person is found, or is proved to have been in possession of any article of railway Stores reasonably suspected of being stolen or unlawfully obtained, and cannot account satisfactorily how he came by, the same, he shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to five years, or with fine, or both. " Before anyone can be charged with the offence under section 3 it must be shown that he was in possession thereof of railway property which by definition of section does not include all articles which are 'the property of a Railway administration but only those which were used or meant to be use for the construction or operation of a rail. Mere unlawful possession would not fulfil the requirements of section 2(b). Some evidence will have to be led to the effect that the goods conformed to the specifications of the Indian Railway Standards, they held that they belonged to any particular railway administration. The prosecution must also prove that the articles were being actually used or were intended to 'be used for by the railway.

The respondent landlord terminated the lease by a notice under section 106 of Transfer of Property Act, but she remained in possession and enjoyment of the shop carrying on small kirana business. She died in September 1966. The demised premises were governed by the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950 for short the 'Act '). Section 13(1) thereof postulates that "notwithstanding anything contained in any law or contract no court shall pass any decree or make any order in favour of the landlord, whether in execution of a decree or otherwise evicting the tenant so long as he is ready and willing to pay rent thereof to the full extent allowable by the Act" unless the landlord proves to the satisfaction of the Court any one of the grounds enumerated in Clauses 'a ' to 'k ' thereof. The action for ejectment was initiated by the respondent on the premise that on the death of the tenant, the appellants have no right to continue in occupation of the demised premises. The Trial Court dismissed the suit on the ground that Smt. Anandi paid and the respondent accepted the rent after determination of the lease. So she was a tenant holding over. During the pendency of the appeal, the Act was amended through Rajasthan Premes (Control) of Rent & Eviction Ordinance 26 of 1975 which was replaced by Act 14 of 1976. The definition of 'Tenant ' in section 3(vii)(b) makes the legislative intent manifest that from the date of the Amendment Act came into force, on the heirs of the deceased tenant, his surviving spouse, son, daughter and other heir in accordance with personal law as applica ble to him, who had been, in the case of premises leased out for commercial or business purposes, ordinarily had been carrying on business with him/her in such premises as member of his family upto his death. The appellants contended that the lease hold right is an heritable estate and on death of a tenant in September, 1966, the tenancy came to a terminus with its determination by issuance of notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of property Act and the legal representatives do not succeed to the estate of the respondent tenant so as to prosecute the proceedings. The trial court dismissed the Suit on the view that Smt Anandi was the tenant holdingover. During her life time, she had not carried on the business with her till date of her death.

The appellant Board maintains a Contributory Provident Fund where the contribution is on the basis of basic wage, the Board and the employees contributing equally. The workmen claimed that all workmen of the Board should have the same and similar benefits and that therefore there should be no distinction between the Board 's Contributory Provident fund scheme and the scheme under the Employees Provident Fund Act. The Industrial Tribunal held that if the interests realised by the State were excluded from consideration, there would be surplus in favour of the appellant Board. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the workmen that the State Government is the financier of the Electricity Board which charges interest now at the rate of 6.25 per cent as against the previous 4 per cent per annum; and that the contribution under the Act is 8 per cent whereas under the Board scheme it is 6.26 per cent. The employees also contended that the services of the workers of the company are liable to be transferred from one establishment to another both which may not he covered by the same scheme under Act and therefore it will bring about serious injustice if they were deprived of their benefits under the Provident Fund Scheme, and such anomalies will be removed by making the benefits under both the schemes similar. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Tribunal had dealt with the matter in a perfunctory way. It should be directed to dispose of the matter afresh in the light of the observations made in this judgment. [44E] Gramophone Co. vs Its Workmen, [1964] II L.L.J 131 and Gramophonone Co., vs its Workmen, ; , referred to. 2.1 The Tribunal did not look into the Act at all. Whether in view of the statutory obligations laid on ii the various sections just now referred to in analysing the capacity of the board to bear any additional burden in the matter of provident fund or other amenities the same considerations that applied in the case of private commercial concerns could be applied is a rather difficult question. In fact the decision might very often depend on a close analysis of the financial condition of the Boards. [45F G] 2.2 The various sums payable under the provisions of section 67 have to be deducted before the profits could be ascertained. Even with regard to the depreciation reserve, the provisions Of section 68 may have to he taken into account.

The respondent who is the wife of the appellant filed an application before the Magistrate under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 for grant of maintenance by the appellant on the ground that her husband was guilty of wilful neglect and was unable to fulfil his primary responsibility of discharging his marital obligations. The Magistrate dismissed the application holding that the husband having been found to be impotent, this should be a just ground for the wife to refuse to live with the husband and hence she was entitled to the grant of the maintenance. In revision before the High Court, the appellant contended that it is now well settled by a long course of decisions of various High Courts that impotency is no good ground or reason for the husband to refuse live with her husband and therefore the wife is not entitled to maintenance if she refused to live alongwith the husband merely because her husband had been impotantent. The respondent further submitted that the various authorities of the High Courts seem to have overlooked the legal effect of the second proviso to sub section (3) of Section 125 of Cr. P.C. under which a wife could refuse to reside with her deceased husband if there was a just reason for doing so. The said proviso may be extracted thus: " Provided further that if such person offers to maintain his wife on condition of her living with him, and she refused, such Magistrate may consider any grounds of refusal stated by her, and may make an order under this section notwithstanding such offer, if he is satisfied that there was just groundfor so doing. " On behalf of the respondent it was contended: (1) that it was now well established by a series of decisions that impetency is not good ground for refusing to live apart from her husband; and (2) that in any case, the various Authorities of the Bombay High Courts seems to have ignored the legal consequences of the first proviso to subsection (3). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 In view of the decision of this Court in Velayudhan vs Sukmari a Single Judge observed as follows: "Where it is proved to the satisfaction of the court that a husband is impotable and is unable to discharge his marital obligation, this would amount to both legal and mental cruelty which would undoubtedly be a valid ground for refusal of the wife 's refusal to livewith her husband. [706C] 1.2 In the instant case, there was no dispute and the case will have to be decided on the point of law that arises on the contentions raised by the parties before the courts below as also in this Court. Both the High court and the Metropolitan Magistrate clearly found that the appellant was physically incapable of having sexual relations with the respondent. In other words, the concurrent finding of fact by the Courts below is that the appel lant was impotsuent and was, therefore, unable to perform his marital duties, found himself bound by the decisions of the Madras High Court in Jaggavarapu Basawamma 's case (supra).

The suit property is described in two parts in the schedule to the plaint. The first part consists of a large extent of vacant land which is referred to in these proceedings as Parade Ground. The second part is covered by Survey Nos. 162, 163, 164 and 165 on which structures of old Lancer 's lines are standing and certain evacuees were Occupying at the time of the suit. This second part consists sometimes referred to as Lancers quarters and also sometimes as Rasala Lines. The plaintiffs ' case was that by Resolution No. 37 dated 19th January, 1984 published in the Bhavnagar Darbar Gazette dated 24th January 1948: "The Bhavnagar State bestowed the rights of the State of Bhavnagar to effect sales of land in the Municipal area of Bhav Nagar City in Bhavnagar and by a further order No. 77 of dated 29th February, 1948 the State vested the said lands except four plots of land mentioned therein in the survey numbers referred to In part 2 of the Schedule to the Plaint. The plaintiff claimed damages for this wrongful occupation of the Parade Ground from 1st January, 1964 till they vacate the wrongful encroachment and hand over possession to the plaintiff. So far as the Lan cercer quarters or Rasala Line is con cerned it was stated in the plaint that the structures in the land covered by the Survey numbers referred ted in part 2 o the schedule did not belong to the plain tiff, that the same were occupied by the State Government and subsequently by refugees, and that the plaintiff allowed the land and the structures thereon to be used free by the Government. However, they were entitled to recover rent or compensation in respect of this land for the period from 1 st January, 1954 till delivery of possession. The Union of India filed a written statement which was adopted by the state of Gujarat. It was contended by the defendants that the Parade ground was used by the Ex Bhavna gar State forces and that barracks and other military build ings used for accommodation of Ex Bhavnagar state forces known as Lencer ' 's Lines were in existence for a long time prior to 1948 in the suit property known as Rasla Lines and that consequent upon the Bhav Nagar State acceding to the Indian Union and consequent on the Federal Financial Inte gration of States, accommodation, lands and buildings in the use or occupation of Ex State forces were transferred to the Government o[ india and became its property. The Trial Court held that the plaintiffs had proved their title to the suit land and that they were in possession in the Suit property till 7th July, 1952 when physical posses sion was handed over by the military engineers of the Gov ernment of India to the State Public Works Department of the Government of Saurashtra. However on the ground that in respect thereof Rasala lines the plaintiff had admitted that they did not own the buildings thereon, they are not entitled to recovery possession of the lands covered by survey numbers de scribed in the second part of the schedule.

The appellant was a class III servant employed as a metal examiner in the Railway Carriage Workshops at Ajmer. He was charged under section 161 Indian Penal Code for having induced the said Nanak Singh to deliver to him currency notes of the value of Rs. 150 by dishonest representation that he could secure a job for the said Kallu. The Special judge convicted him of the offence under section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and sentenced him to suffer rigorous imprisonment for six months and one year respectively in regard to the same, both the sentences to run concurrently. In appeal by special leave: Held, that the appellant was an officer within the meaning of section 21(9) and therefore a public servant fell within the definition of a 'public servant contained in section 2 of the prevention of Corruption act II of 1947. Ram Krishan vs Delhi State, A.I.R. 1918 Lah. (2) I.L. R. 7 Madras 18, 690 and Queen vs Nachimuttu, I. L. R., , referred to. The appellant was not an officer but a mere contractor bound by his engagement but not by the terms of his office or employment to pay a certain proportion to the Government. There was no delegation to him of any authority for coercion or interference nor was he an assistant appointed to help any one who was vested with such authority. The duties which he performed were immediately auxiliary to those of the Works Manager who, beside being an officer of the Government was also armed with some authority or representative character qua the Government and was therefore a 'officer ' within the expression of that term as used in section 21 (9) Indian Penal code.

The lands in question were acquired for the Synthetic Drugs Project Factory of the Indian Drugs and Pharmaceutical Ltd. by the Andhra Pradesh Government by Notifications issued on June 19, 1961 and January 18, 1962 under the Land Acquisition Act. The Special Deputy Collector awarded a total compensation of Rs. 4,29,360. This compensation was received by Rashid himself during his lifetime. Later two more parcels of agricultural land (admeasuring 22 Acres 24 Guntas and 8 Acres 23 Guntas) situated at Qutbillapur in Medchal Taluk belonging to Rashid where acquired for Hindustan Machine Tools, Units I and II by the Government Notification issued on November 1, 1963 and February l, 1964 under the Act. Though the former notification was issued during his life time and the latter after death possession of both the lands was taken after his death by the government on December 4, 1963, and March 15, 1964 and by two separate awards both made on January 31, 1963 the Special Deputy collector awarded a compensation of RS. 20,45,000 for the lands acquired by the State Government at figures awarded by the Special Dy Collector for those lands.
