The Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 was enacted to bring about an agrarian re ordering so pivotal to the progress of our rural economy. Haryana, happily a granary of our country is one of the States where land reform laws are likely to generate great changes by banishing big concentration of Natur 's bounty in a few feudal hands creating an enthusiastic sense of distributive justice and exploiting the productive potential of land by the possessive passion of the landless many. So strategic is land reform that special constitutional concern has been shown for this programme. Naturally the State enacted the Act whereby ceiling on land ownership was set; surplus lands were taken over for settling ejected tenants and others, peasant proprietorship created. The scheme of the Act with which we are concerned is fairly simple and somewhat scientific, although its language, what with frequent amendments dovetailed from time to time, has made for ambiguity, obscurity, marginal inconsistency and a rich crop of litigation. Indeed, the conflict of opinion at the High Court level and the bone of contention before us arise from this drafting deficiency Legal Preface: A thumb nail sketch of the Punjab Act is a prefatory necessity. The defines 'small land owner ' [section 2(2)] having in mind the optimum ownership in the given conditions. 'Permissible area ' [Section 2(3)] is a cognate concept limiting the maximum permissible extent a person may hold, and so long as he does not have any excess, he is a small landholder. He can evict the tenants from his holding and be in actual enjoyment as provided by the Act. If, however, he has lands beyond the permissible area, he becomes a large land owner and has to cough up the excess. However, he was given the option to choose there best area he desires to keep, called 'reserved area ' ' [ section 2(4)] and then he must make available to the State such excess as called surplus area [section 10A]. This creation of a surplus pool or reservoir is vital to the success of the statutory project since, by distribution of such lands, rehabilitation of ejected tenants, and landless persons is to be "accomplished". Even if a person is small holder, it is quite on the cards that, by inheritance or other operation of law, or by voluntary transfer he may acquire lands in excess of the permissible limit. In short, the legislative mandate is that every agricultural holder in the State shall hold no more than the permissible Area and the surplus in the hands of large holders, whether acquired by voluntary transactions or involuntary operation of laws will go to feed the surplus pool. With this end in view, the Act has been amended to block all escape routes unearthed by the law makers as often as the High court has upheld certain patterns of alienations and oblique dealings by interpretative process. A study of the history of the legislation suggests an unspoken criticism about judicial approach which we will refer to later. Suffice it to say that the law is interpreted a radical agrarian measure; its basic goals are to cut down large holdings and distribute lands to various landless people according to a design design and to foster, according to legislative policy, an agrarian community of peasants proprietors.

The plaintiffs instituted an action in the Court of the Additional District Judge Chanda for a decree for possession of property (including the Zamindari of Dhanora) and movable specified in Schedules annexed to the plaint, and for an order declaring their right to receive the balance of compensation remaining to be paid. The plaintiffs relied upon the following genealogy Gangashah Niru Bhakta Sakru Kajur Thakur Thakur Thakur Thakur Sitaram Tanba Chatturshah Thakur Thakur (dead) Nilkanthah Pratapshah Dawaltshah Ranwirshah Prakoshta Sakhar Karbah (Platff. Shah dead) No. 1) No, 2 (dead), Hanmantrao Amarshah Basu Chandarsha Karbah Niranshah Died Dec. 9, (dead). Hanmant Rao Amarshih devised his estate in their favour. The branches of Sakru and Kajur became extinct a long time ago. The branch of Hiru (who was 327 the eldest among the five sons of Gangashashah) because extinct with the death of Amarsheh on December 6, 1950, was granted to Sitaram ancestor of Amshah as an impartible estate devolving by the rule of primogeniture; that the Zamindari on that account devolved upon Pratapshah and Zamindari devolved upon them under a will executed on December 3, 1950 whereby Amarshasha devised his Estate in their own favour. On December 8, 1950 Amarsahah devised their estate in favour of Sitaram. The first plaintiff claimed that he was entitled to the Zamindari as on the death Of Amarsh on January 27, 1951 and the plaintiffs claimed the other estate of Am Sheohah, as devisees under his will. The defendants contended that Dayaram the first defendant took wrongful possession of the Zamindari and other property movable and immovable of Amreshah. The Trial Court held that the plaintiffs were entitled to receive compensation in respect of the Malguzari lands and the decision of the Compensation Officer did not operate to deprive the plaintiff of the right to those lands or compensation payable in respect thereof; and that the will set up by the plaintiffs represented the true relationship between the descendants of Gangashhah and the defendants. The High Court also held that on the facts no suspicion as to the genuineness of the will dated December 3 was arose, and that it was not shown that in making the order the Governor had acted in exercise of the power conferred by the Chanda Patent; that in any event the decision was contrary to the customs and the law governing the Zamindari, that the decision did not oust the jurisdiction of the Civil Court. On appeal by special leave: HELD : (i) The right to determine it is true vests in the Governor but the power is exercisable in accordance with and not in violation of the custom of the family. When a holder of the zamindari is removed, the Governor is bound to hand over the Zamindari to the next heir in the order of succession if the Zamindar removed had died and the heir will get the right. The provision not approved as that on a death of a Zamindar, the estate should in default of a son devolve upon his widow. Government, however, after weighing the arguments urged, decided that it Was conducive to the interests of the Zamindarees that the succession should devolve only upon a male member of thefamily and the clause was altered accordingly.

Section 12(3) (a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 provides for the passing of a decree for eviction first where the rent is payable by the month and there is no dispute regarding the amount of standard rent or permitted increases recoverable under this Act the tenant shall be deemed to be ready and willing to pay such amount if before the expiry of the period of one month after notice referred to in sub section (2) he makes an application to the Court under sub section(3), of section 11 and thereafter pays or tenders the amount specified by the court. The respondent landlord terminated the tenancy of the appellants inter alia on the ground that the appellants were in arrears of rent for more than six months. The appellants filed a suit for recovery of possession of a portion of the ground floor of a building on the grounds: (1) that they were in arrear of rent from 1st September, 1964 and (2)(a) that there was no dispute as to standard rent within one month of the service of the notice terminating the tenancy. The trial court gave a decree in favour of the respondent for possession of the premises. The Appellate Court confirmed the judgment of the trial court. In an application under article 227 of the Constitution the Bombay High Court held that when the respondent paid all arrears and costs of the suit on 23 December, 1964 it could not be said that the respondent did not comply with the provisions of section 12( 3) (b) of tho Act. Allowing the appeal by special leave the Court ^ HELD: The view of the Gujarat High Court nullifies the provisions contained in section 12 and Explanation thereto and confers a right on the tenant where the legislation does not contemplate such a right. The provisions in section 11(3)(a), deal with orders which may be passed by the Court during the pendency of the application disputing the rent. Provisions in section II (4) of Act deal with order which may have been passed consequent upon dispute as regards standard rent. It is only when an application disputing rent is made within the time contemplated by Explanation I to section 12 of the Act that the provisions in sub s.(3) and (4), of Section 11 are attracted. [637 B C] Ambalal vs Badaldas, ; , referred to.

The respondent company was a company incorporated in what was then British India having a capital of Rs. 3,600 divided into 360,000 shares of Rs 10 each. The Aluminium Limited, a company registered under the provisions of the Indian Companies Act, 1913, held 359,790 shares in the chargeable accounting periods ending on December 31, 1939 and December 31., 1940, and December31, 1943, and January 31, 1941, respectively. In exercise of the power given to it by article 105 of the articles of association of the respondent company, the Aluminium Ltd. appointed three permanent directors on the board of directors of the Company. Two of these directors eventually retired and only one, namely, Mr. L. G. Bash who continued to be a director of the company nominated by the Aluminium Limited. The respondent company thereupon appealed to the Incometax Appellate Tribunal which reversed the decision of the Excess Profits Tax Officer and held that in computing the standard profits the statutory percentage should be taken at 10 per cent. per annum and not at 8 per cent per annum. The Commissioner of Excess Profits tax, West Bengal, has now come up on appeal to this Court with a certificate under section 66A(2) of the Income tax Act. Held: (i) Under article 90 when Mr.L.G. Bash as agent of the Aluminium Company attends a general meeting of the Respondent company he has to produce the resolution of his principals authorising him to cast the votes of his principal. The votes he casts are not his votes but are the votes and of the aluminium Ltd. In such a situation, in the eye of the law, the controlling interest remains vested in the Aluminium Co Ltd. and is at no time vested in Mr. Bash. (ii) Under Article 90 when a shareholder holding the majority of shares authorises an agent to vote for him in respect of the shares so held by him, the agent acquires no interest, legal or beneficial, in, the shares. The title in the shares remains vested with the shareholders. The shareholder may revoke the authority of the agent at any time. In spite of the appointment of the agents the shareholder may himself appear at the meeting and cast his votes personally. Therefore, the share being always subject to his will and ordering, the control interest which the holder of the majority shares has never passed to the agent.

The respondent was serving as an Accountant Grade II in the Electricity Department of the former State of Hyd erabad. On 1st October, 1957, he opted to the Service under the Board and ceased to be an employee of the Government with effect from that date. In 1960, the Board framed Recruitment and Promo tions Regulations in the exercise of its powers conferred on it under section 79(c) of the Electricity (Supply) Act, 1948. The Regulations were subsequently amended on 16th December 1966. The amended Rules prescribed that the posts of Accounts Superintendents were to be filled by promotion of I Division Clerks on the basis of seniority cum merit on their having passed Part I and II of the S.A.S. examination. On 30th December, 1966, some persons junior to the respondent were promoted on their Having passed the S .A. Examination while promotion was denied to the respond ent as he had not passed the examination. The respondent made several representations one such representation being on 24th December 1970. On 21st November 1972, the respondent opted to continue in the Government service or to opt to the Board. On 31st November, 1972, a Writ Petition before the High Court was dismissed and the respondent preferred an appeal to a Bench of the Karnataka High Court which held that the writ petition ought to be dis missed on the ground of inordinate delay and laches on the part of the respondent and also on the grounds that in view of the later Resolution of the Board dated 5th January, 1970, it was no longer open to the res pondent to rely on the resolution dated 19th May, 1969. On behalf of the appellant, Karnataka Electricity Board it was contended before this Court that the High court was in error in construing the relevant provisions of the Regulations and the Resolutions and holding that the respondent is exempted from passing the S A.S., examination before qualifying for the promotion. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The Resolution dated 19st May,1969 as exempting the allottees from passing a Departmental Examination I and Kannada language test is only as regards services where the rules do not specifically require the passing of the examinations and the language test.

A letter dated 14.9.1988 sent to this Court by Smt. Nilabati Behera alias Lalita Behera was treated as a Writ Petition under Article 32 of the Constitution for determining the claim of compensation made therein consequent upon, the death of her son Suman Behera, aged about 22 years, in police custody. The said Suman Behara was taken into police custody on 1.12.1987 by respondent No.6 Sarat Chandra Barik, Assistant Sub Inspector of Police, Jaraikela Police Outpost under Police Station Bisra, Distt. Sundergarh in Orissa, in connection with the investigation of an offence of theft and detained at the Police Out Post. At about 2 p.m., the next day on 2.12 .1987, the petitioner came to know that the dead body of her late son Suman was found on the railway track near a bridge at some distance from the Jaraiampur Railway Station. There were multiple injuries on the body of Suman Behrahera when it was found and obviously his death was unnatural, caused by those injuries. The allegation made is that it is a case of custodial death since Suman Beuria died as a result of the multiple injuries inflicted to him while he was in police detention; and thereafter his dead body was thrown on the Railway track. The prayer made in the petition for award of compensation to the petitioner, mother of Suman Sehera, for contravention of the fundamental right guaranteed under Article 21 of the constitution, is for award Of compensation to her, the mother of the deceased, for violation of the constitutional right to life guaranteed under article 21 of Constitution. The State of Orissa and its police officers including Sarat Chander Barik Assistant Sub Inspectors of Police and Constable No.127, Chhabil Kujur of Police Out post Jeraikela, Police Station, Bisra are impleaded as respondents in this petition. The defence of the respondents is that Suman Beeta managed to escape from police custody at about 3 a.m. on the night between the 1st and 2nd December, 1987 and it was likely that he was run over by a passing train after he had escaped from Police custody. In short, on this basis the allegation of custodial deaths was denied and consequently the respondents ' responsibility for unnatural death of Suman behera. It would, however, be appropriate to spell out clearly the principle on which the liability of the State arises in such cases for payment of compensation and the distinction between this liability and the liability in private law for payment Of compensation in an action on tort. It may be mentioned straightaway that award of Compensation in a proceeding under Article 226 by this Court or by the High Court under Article226 of the Constitu tion is a remedy available in public law, based on strict liability for contravention Of fundamental rights to which the principle of sovereign immunity does not apply, even though it may be available as a defence in private Law in an actions based on tort, through a suit instituted in a court of competent jurisdiction or/and persecute the offender under the penal law. This is what was indicated in Rudul Sah and Ors. vs Ravikant section Patil, ; , referred to.

The two prisoners have been sentenced to death for an offence under section 302 Indian Penal Code and the petitions filed by them to the President of India for commutation of the sentence are reported to have been rejected by the President recently. Before considering the merits of the application, this Court would like to observe that the constitutional right to freedom of speech and expression conferred by article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution, which includes freedom of Press is not an absolute right, nor indeed does it confer any right on the press to have an unrestricted access to means of information. The Press is entitled to exercise its freedom of circulation and expression by publishing a matter which does not invade the rights of other citizens and which do not violate the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security of the State, public order decency and morality. But in the instant case, the right claimed by the petitioner is not the right to express any particular view or opinion but the right asserted by him is not that they can always and without good reasons be denied the opportunity to interview a condemned prisoner. The existence of a free Press does not imply or spell out any legal obligation on the citizens to supply information to the press, such for example, as there is under section 161(2) of Criminal Procedure Code. No data has been made available to us on the basis of which it would be possible for this Court to say that the two prisoners are ready and willing to be interviewed. Rule 549(4) of Delhi Administration Manual for the Superintendence and Management of Jails, which is applicable to Delhi, provides that every prisoner under a sentence of death shall be allowed such interviews and other communications with his relatives, friends and legal advisers as the Superintendent thinks reasonable.

The respondent mortgaged a tea garden called the "Ishanchandrapar Tea Estate" to M/s. Das Bank Ltd. On January 19, 1950 the Bank instituted mortgage suit against the respondent on the original side of the Tripura High Court for recovering the amount due under the mortgage. On February 28, 1950, the respondent moved an application asking for damages from the Receiver on the ground that the fire had occurred due to his negligence. The Subordinate Judge decreed the suit on May 31, 1956 but he allowed the respondent 's cross objections and enhanced the damages to Rs. 4,525. He directed that the Receiver should pay the amount within two months failing which the amount should be recovered from the security of Rs. 50,000. Civil Miscellaneous First Appeal No. 22 of 1956 filed by the Receiver against that order was dismissed for default by the Judicial Commissioner on December 18, 1959. On October 4, 1961 respondent filed in the court of the Subordinate Judge, Execution Petition No. 39 of 1961 against the Receiver and the appellant praying that execution do issue against the appellant as directed by the Court. The appellant filed an appeal against that Order but it was dismissed on June 29, 1970. In appeal to this Court, HELD: Under section 150 of the Code of Civil Procedure, save as otherwise provided, where the business of any court is transferred to any other Court, the transferee Court has the same powers and is entitled to perform the same duties as those respectively conferred and imposed by the Code upon the transferor Court.

The appellants are dealers in food grains supplied to the Regional Food Controller diverse quantities of wheat. The Sales Tax Officer levied tax under the U.P. Sales Tax Act on the aggregate of the price of wheat by the appellants, rejecting the contention raised by the appellant that the wheat supplied was not sold by them to the Controller. In appeal, the Assistant Commissioner (Judicial) Sales Tax held that the turnover resulting from supplies of wheat was not taxable since there was no "sale" within the meaning of the U .P. Sugarcane (Regulation of Supply and Purchase) Order, 1959. The order was confirmed by the Additional Judge (Revisions) Sales tax. The High Court following its earlier judgment in Commissioner of Sales Tax, U. P., Lucknow vs) an Bilas Ram Gopal, held that there was a "sale", within the term 'sale" under section 2(h) of the Act and therefore the sales made to the appellant were sales within the definition of the word 'sale ' in section 2 (h) thereof. The appellants appealed to this Court with special leave. It was contended on behalf of the appellants that the transactions of supply did not result in sales and were on that account not exposed to sales tax, because steel products were supplied pursuant to the directions of the Iron and Steel Controller made under cl. 10B of the Order there being no mutual assent between the parties to the transaction. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The expression "sale of goods" in section 4 of the provides by its first sub section that a contract of sale of goods is a contract where the seller agrees to transfer the property in goods to the buyer for a price paid or promised : a transaction in which an obligation to supply goods is imposed, and which does not involve an obligationto enter into a contract cannot be called a "Sale" even if the person supplying goods is declared entitled to the value of goods, which is determined or determinable in the manner prescribed. Assuming that between the licensed dealer and the Controller there may be some arrangements about the place and manner of delivery of wheat, and the payment of " controlled price", the operation of cl. 3 of the order and thereafter fifty per cent of the wheat daily procured or purchased by him every day beginning with the date of commencement of the levy until such time as the State Government otherwise directs. The price at which the wheat is sold is the maxi mum price fixed in the Wheat (Uttar Pradesh) Price Control Order, 1960 as notified by the Government of India. Delivery of the goods has to be given by the dealer to the regional Food Controller or a person authorised by him in that behalf. The dealer has no option but to sell the specified percentage of wheat to the State Govern ment.

The appellant Abdul Latif Wahab Sheikh, was in jail from November 12, 1985 onwards awaiting trial on a charge of murder. He was due for release from prison on June 23, 1986. On that day, however, an order for his detention was made under the provisions of the Gujarat Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1985. The mandate of Article 22(4) of the Constitution is that no law providing for preventive detention shall authorise the detention of a person for a longer period than three months unless the Advisory Board has reported within the period of three months that there is in its opinion sufficient cause for such detention. Section 10 stipulates that in every case where a detention order has been made under section 11 of the Act, the State Government shall, within three weeks from the date of detention of the person under the order, place before the Advisory board the grounds on which the order has be made, the representation, if any, made by the detenu and the report, ifany, of the authorised offi cer. What is important for the purposes of this case is that section 11 stipulates that a detention shall not bar the making of a subsequent detention order under the Act against the same person, subject to the proviso that if there were no fresh facts, the maximum period for which a person may be detained shall not extend beyond the expiry of a period of 12 months from the day of detention under the earlier detention order. The period of 3 weeks stipulated by section 11 expired on July 14, 1986 and the appellant was entitled to be released on July 19, 1986 as no reference had been made to the Advisory Boards within the time stipulated by Section 11 of Act. But he was not so released. This state of affairs continued till August 7, 1986 when the order of detention dated June 23,, 1986 was revoked and a fresh order of deten tion was made on the same facts on the very same day. In the meanwhile, the order for detention had been challenged by filing a writ petition in the High Court. Consequent to the revocation of that order that writ petition was withdrawn as having become infructuous and another writ petition, out of which the present appeal arises, was filed questioning the second order of Detention dated August 7 , 1986.

The respondent, a father of the respondent, filed an application for setting aside the decree passed in Special Civil Suit No. 84 of 1977 on the ground that he had torn off the award and, therefore, the respondent was compelled to rely upon a photo copy of the original award which was produced with the application. The petitioner filed his objections to the application but did not file any application within the prescribed limitation of 30 days. The trial Judge rejected the objections filed beyond the period of limitation and for the reasons that (1) the notice was already given to the party concerned about the filing of the award, (2) the time for making an application to set aside the award had expired and no such application was made (3) the award was not set aside under section 30 and (4) that the award is not remitted under section 16(5) of the Act. The High Court dismissed the civil revision application which challenged the award in this case. Dismissing the special leave petition, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The conduct of the parties that there was an arbitration agreement and by signing the award it could be said that the parties had agreed to refer the dispute to the arbitrator. This agreement was done twice, firstly by signing an endorsement below the award; secondly by entering into an agreement in the form of a letter dated 14th August, 1978 (Exhibit 40). In that view of the matter, there is no such express or implied prohibition nor any inability of the Judge concerned. In this case, it may be useful to refer to the observations of this Court in Prasun Roy vs The Calcutta Metropolitan Development Authority and another, A.I.R. 1988 S.C. 205 where all the relevant authorities on this point have been discussed. [539E F] 2. It is clear from the narration of facts that the party had agreed that both of them should abide by the award dated 20th January, 1977 and that its interpretation should be left to the Arbitrator himself. It was not relevant according to the Judicial Committee, whether they decided it rightly or wrongly, they had jurisdiction to decide the question which was before them (namely, whether the suit was barred as res judicata) and they did decide it. [540F G] 3. In the light of the facts and circumstances of the case, there can be no doubt that on this aspect the petitioner is not entitled to challenge the award. The Civil Court had jurisdiction in taking cognizance of the Award under sections 14 and 17 of the . This question had come up for consideration before the Judicial Commis sioner in Amir Hassan Khan vs Sheo Baksh Singh, ; , where this Court observed that interminable time consuming, complex and expensive court procedures impelled jurists to search for an alternative forum, less formal, more effective and speedy for resolution of disputes avoiding procedural claptrap and this led them to the . However, the way in which the proceedings under the Act are conducted and without an exception challenged in Courts, has made lawyers laugh and legal philosophers weep. This Court further observed that experience shows and law reports hear ample testimony that the proceedings u/s 9 of the Civil Procedure Code have become highly technical accompanied by unending prolixity, at every stage providing a legal trap to the unwary.

A suit had been instituted by one Kumar Dakhineswar Malia against Rameswar Malia, Rani Bhaba Sundari and others for partition of the Searsole Raj Estate. One Bhagabati Charan Mitra was appointed receiver of that estate in August, 10, 1908, and a final decree for sale was made on February 26, 1929. In execution of this final decree the mortgaged properties were sold at a Court i sale and were purchased by Deva Prasanna Mukerjee for Rs. 59,000. This sale was confirmed by the Court on June 30, 1931. A large sum remaining still due to Deva Prasanta Mukerjee he applied for and on October 30, 1935, a petition (exhibit 2) was filed in the Court of the Subordi nate Judge praying that under the circumstances aforesaid, the Court may be pleased to strike off this execution case keeping the attachment in force. Neither the original nor a certified copy of the order made on that date by the executing court on the application for executions of decrees relating to execution Case No. 118 of 1936 was forthcoming but the parties have definite agreed that the order is substantially and correctly entered in column 20 of exhibit F which is a certified copies of extract from the Register of applications for execution of decrees pertaining to execution case No. 117 of 1936 and that the said attachment is cancelled and the decree in question is recorded as adjusted as stated by learned pleader for the judgment debtor according to the adjustment mentioned but not detailed in this petition of June 2, 1939. Held, (i) The order of January 30, 1937, was a final order which brought the Execution Case No 118 of 1935 to an and the attachment continued, not because there was a pend ing execution proceeding but because a special order was made under Order XXI, rule 57, as amended by the High Court. Ram Kumar De vs Abhoya Pada Bhattacharjee (I.L.R. , followed. (ii) Under Order XXXVIII, r. 11, where after an order of attachment before judgment a decree is passed in favour of the plaintiff it is not necessary upon an application for pro ceeding execution of such a decree to apply for re attachment of the property. In cases where attachments in execution had already been entered, the question arose whether the effect of an order 'striking off ' was that the attachment made upon application for execu tion was itself struck off or whether it remained notwithstanding such an order. It was not necessary for the Court to consider whether the assignment is such as to establish a debtor and creditor relation between the assignee and the debtor so as to bring the case within the purview of the Act.

One Venkatacharyulu was the Karta of a joint family consisting of himself and his four sons. The appellant was his concubine since 1945 until his death on February 22, 1949. By two registered deeds purporting to be sale deeds dated April 15, 1946, (Exbts. A 1 and A 2), he transferred certain properties belonging to the joint family. In 1947 after the execution of exhibit A 1 & A 2 there was a disruption of the joint Hindu family and a severance of the Joint status between Venkatachallulu and his sons. In 1954 his widow and sons instituted O.S. No. 12 of 1954 against the appellant for recovery of possession of the properties alleging that the documents dated April 14, 1946 were executed without consideration or for immoral purposes, and were void. The trial court dis missed O. S. No., 62/54 and decreed O.s. 63/54, the decree for possession in respect of the said properties being conditional on payment by the respondents of the value of improvements made by the appellant to the properties. From the decrees passed by the High Court, the present appeals have been filed by special leave. It was common case that future illicit cohabitation was not the object or consideration for the transfers under exhibit A1 and exhibit A 2. The transfers were without consideration and were by way of gifts. The gifts were not hit by sec. 6(h) of the , by reason of the fact that they were motivated by a desire to compensate the concubinine for her past services. In the alternative, the respondents contended that assuming that the transfers were made in consideration of past cohabitation, they were hit by section 6(g) of . But the properties gifted under exhibitA 1 and exhibit 2 were not covered by section 2(d) as a subsisting consideration for his subsequent promise to transfer the properties to her. The past cohabitations were the motive and not the consideration for them for the transfer under exhibit R1 and A2. Held, further, that in view of the decision of this Court in Balo vs Parbati (I.L.R. [1940] All. 370, it is common case law that future illegal cohabitation is not the purpose or consideration of the transfers. The assignment was without consideration by way Of gift and as such was not bit by section 5(h).
