Section 29(2)(a) of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908 provides that where any special or local law prescribes for any suit appeal, appeal or application a period of limitation different from the period prescribed therefor by the first schedule the provisions of section 3 shall apply as if such period were prescribed therefor in that Schedule. The appellant who was one of the respondents in an election petition challenged the validity of section 29(1)(a), on the ground inter alia (i) that the right to prefer the appeal should be conferred by the Code of Civil Procedure but that it was sufficient if the procedure for filing of the appeal and the powers of the Court for dealing with the appeal were governed by that Code; and (ii) that sub section (2) will apply even to a case where the first Schedule to the Limitation Act had not prescribed any period of time of limitation for an appeal, but a special law prescribed a period different from that prescribed therefor under the First Schedule. Held, (per Subba Rao, J., dissenting), that the expression "appeal under the Code" in article 156(2) of Sch. 11 of the Limitation ' Act means an appeal governed by the code of Civil procedure so far as procedure is concerned. It will be noticed that no argument was raised in that case that the appeal was governed by section 116A of the Representation of the People Act and it was not necessary in order to be an "appeal" under the Civil Procedure Code, 1908, for the purpose of computing the period of 30 days prescribed by section 117A(3) of that Act. The expression "appellate jurisdiction" in the first limb of sub section 2 of section 28 would include a suit or an appeal ' even though it is not of a type for which a period Of limitation is prescribed in the First schedule because it is enough if the special law prescribes a period which is different from any period prescribed in that schedule. The word "appeal " occurring in the second limb of clause (a) to section 29 would include an appeal or an application under a special or general law which is of a kind for which no period of Limitation is prescribed In order to deal with the second ground given by my learned brother it was necessary to reproduce the provisions Of section 29, sub section(2), of the Act. They run thus: "Where any special and local law prescribe for any suits appeal or applications a period o limitation differentfrom the period fixed therefor by that first schedule by the application of the first part of sub sec tion (2), the court is enabled to dismiss suits, appeals and applications filed beyond time.

The appellant was a person providing transport service in the District of Mathura. He questioned the validity of the Order dated May 22, 1986 passed by the District Magis trate declaring Plot Nos. 701 and 703 in the Town Area, Baldev (Mathura) as a bus stand/halting place of Baldev, where the stage carriages were directed to stand for the purpose of allowing the passengers of Baldev to get into and to get down from the stage carriage vehicles in a writ petition, Civil Miscellaneous Writ Petition No. 501 of 1986 filed before the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution of India challenging the said bye laws. The High Court was of the opinion that section 76 of the Act conferred wide powers on the District Magistrate 'to fix the places for the bus stand andhalting places '. It was further held that since the impugned order did not specifically state that the bus operators could allow the passengers to get up and pick up the passengers, it could not be construed as an order fixing the area as a Bus stand. It should be stated at this stage that after the impugned Order was passed, the Town Areas Committee gave a contract to a private contractor to collect that fees payable by the bus operator for making use of the area in question which was within its jurisdiction for stopping their buses in accord ance with the order passed by District Magistrate and the letter dated 10.10.1986 written by the Executive Officer of Baldev Town Area Committee, Baldev to the President of the said Municipality requiring all the bus opera ties to stop their buses at the bus stands fixed by the district Magistrate. After the Writ Petition was dismissed, the Executive Offi cer issued a notice to the appellant calling upon him to stop his buses at that bus stand fixed by him. The appellant challenged the order before this Court by special leave. It is contended on behalf of the appel lant that the District Judge had no power to appoint any area as bus stand under section 76 and that could be done only under section 68(2)(r) of the . Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.

Section 3 (1) of the , provides that if any person contravenes any order made under section 3 (a), he shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year and shall also be liable to fine. Section 7 states that "any person who attempts to contravene, or abets a contravention of any order passed under section 4 shall be deemed to have contravened that order". On January 3, 1959 the Central Government promulgated the Punjab Paddy (Export Control) Order, 1959 in exercise of the powers conferred by section 3 of the . Para 2 of this Order states: "3. (1 ) If the Central Govern ment is of opinion that it is necessary or expedient so to do for maintaining or increasing supplies of any essential commodity or for securing their equitable distribution and availability at fair prices, it may by order provide for regulating or prohibiting the production, supply and distribution thereof and trade and commerce therein." On January 4, 1959, the Central Govt. promulgated the Pepsu Paddy(Export) Control Order, 1960 in exercise Of the powers under section 7 of the Act. The appellants took the matter in revision to the High Court but the revision petition was dismissed on November 4, 1965. It was contended on behalf of the respondent that there was no attempt on the part of the appellants to commit the offence of export and it was merely a preparation on the parts of the appel lant and as a matter of law a preparation for committing an offence is different from attempt to commit it. The preparation consists in devising or arranging the means or measures necessary for the commission of the offence. On the other hand, an attempt to export paddy to Delhi was a direct movement towards the commission after preparations were made. In order that a person may be convicted of an attemptto commit 'a crime, he must be shown first to have had an intention to commit 'the offence, and secondly to have done an act which constitutes the actus reus of a criminal attempt. The sufficiency of the actuus reukus is a question of law which has led to difficulty because of the necessity of distinguishing between acts which are merely preparatory to the commissionof a crime and those which are sufficiently proximate to it to amount to an attempt 'to commit it, and that if a man buys a box of matches, he cannot be convicted under section 2 (a) if he approaches the stack with the matches in his pocket but, if he bends down near the stacks and lights a match which he extinguishes on perceiving that he is being watched, he may be guilty of an attempts to burn it. Sir James Stephen, in his Digest of Criminal Law, article 50, defines an attempt as follows: "an act done with intent to commit that crime, and forming part of a series of acts which would constitute its actual commission if it were not interrupted". The question to be considered in this appeal was whether upon the facts found by the lower courts any offence has been committed by the appellants. Held, further, that there is no provision in the Act which makes a preparation to commit an offence punishable.

The Sassoons agreed to transfer their Managing Agency of the said companies to Messrs. Agarwal and Company, Chidambaram and Rajputana Textile (Agencies) Ltd., by letters dated the 3rd September, 1943, 16th April, 1943 and 27th April 1943 respectively. The Sassoon executed in favour of M/s. Agarwal & Co., Chidambaram Mulraj and Company Ltd., and Rajputani Textiles (Agences) Ltd. were the Managing Agents of E. D. Sassoon United Mills Ltd., under agreements dated the 24th February, 1920, and the 2nd October, 1934 respectively, and they agreed to transferred their managing Agency to Messrs Agarwal and Co. Chidambaram Mulaj and Company Limited, and Rajputna Textile (agencies) Limited by letters of the 3nd September,1943, 16st April, 1944, and 27rd April 1943. The agreement was to be effective from the 1st December, 1943. All that the transferees obtained under the deeds of assignment and transfer executed by the Sassoors in their favour was an income bearing asset consisting of the office of Managing Agents, the Managing Agency Agreement and all the rights and benefits as such Managing Agents under the agreements and no part of the consideration paid by the transferees to the Sassoon and Company had accrued to them during the chargeable accounting period. The profits and gains of the whole year seem to me clearly relate to the business carried on both by the assignor and the assignee taken together and are hence taxable as income accruing to both and apportionable as such between them. But it is not correct to approach the consideration of this case as though, the decision in Lakshminarayan Ram Gopal and Son, Ltd., vs The Government of Hyderabad, [1955] 2 S.C.R. 869 was turned upon the question whether any income could accrue to the managing Sassoff on the dates of the respective transfers of the Managing Agencies to the transferees. Held, that the mere ownership of Managing Agency cannot as a matter of law be treated as the source of 'income ' as explained above, any term in the Managing agency Agreement between the principal and the agent entitling only the assignee to receive the year 's remuneration and negativing to the assignee any direct recourse to his quondam principal for his share of the income, cannot have the effect of denying to the assigningor a substantial right to a share in the remuneration, if otherwise he has a vested right thereto. Lakshminarayan R. vs The State of Hyderabad ([1955] 1 S.T.C., 869), relied on.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. On appeal, a Division Bench of the High Court confirmed both the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the soliloquy of the accused admitting his guilt was not an extra judicial confession as the courts below held it to be. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) A statement whether communicated or not, admitting guilt is a confession of guilt. But there is a clear distinction between the admissibility of an evidence and the weight to be attached to it. A confessional solil hundy is a direct piece of evidence. It may be an expression of conflict of emotion; a conscious effort to stifle the pricked conscience; an argument to find excuse or justification for his act; or a penitent or remorseful act of exaggeration of his part in the crime. The tone may be soft and low; the words may be confused; they may be capable of conflicting interpretations depending on witnesses, whether they are biased or honest, intelligent or ignorant, imaginative or prosaic, as the case may be. [90 F G] (2) A confession is a statement made by an accused admitting him guilt. What does the expression "statement" mean? The dictionary meaning of the word does not warrant any such extension; nor the reason of the rule underlying the doctrine of admission or confession demands it. Admissions and confessions are exceptions to the hearsay rule. [91 G H] (3) A confessional Soliloquay is a part of the concept of "confession". In this context a decision of this Court in Bhogilal Chunilal Pandya vs The State of Bombay, [1959] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 310 referred to.

The appellant was working as Divisional Manager at Delhi, the general insurance business was nationalised and its management was taken over by the Central Government under General Insurance (Emergency Provisions) Ordinance, 1971 replaced by Act 57 of 1972. The services of the appellant and others stood transferred and vested with the custodian. Under the Act, the Board of Directors was empowered to terminate the service of the officer/employee of the insurer. The appellant challenged it in a writ petition in Delhi High Court which was dismissed on November 11, 1983 and was confirmed by the Division Bench in Letter Patent Appeal No.351/1984 dated April 23, 1984. Section 7 of the Act provides that every whole time officer or other employee of an existing insurer employed in connection with his General Insurance business, immediately before the appointed day, shall become an officer/ employee of the Indian Insurance Co. in which the undertaking of the Corporation to which the service relates has vested and would hold his office on the same terms and conditions as would have been admissible to him if there had been no such transfer, as referred to in paragraph 3. He shall continue to remain an officer unless and until his employment, in the transferee company is terminated or the terms and condition are duly altered by any other scheme framed under the Act. By notification dated April 29, 1976 the Central Govt. also framed the scheme called the General Insurance(Rationalisation of pay scales and other Conditions of Service of Development Step) Scheme, 1976 which came into force on May 1, 1976, the details of which are not material for the reason that service of appellant was terminated in terms of the existing rule 5 of the Rules. Pursuant thereto, the Central Govern ment framed the New India Assurance Co. Ltd. Merger Scheme, 1973 with effect from December 31, 1973. Thereunder by Rule 3, the undertaking was transferred to the respondent; under Rule 5 the existing whole time Officer etc.

The Collector of Mayurbhanj issued a notice on February 3, 1970 by which he invited tenders for the grant of li cences for establishing 70 outstill shops for 1970 71. Ajodhya Prasad Shah gave the highest bid for a group of seven shops, in one lot, for Rs. 34,000/ per month. His bid was accepted and his name was entered in the prescribed register, and the entry was signed by the successful bidder and the Collector. Ajendra Prasad Shah deposited Rs. 329 of 1970) in the High Court with the allega tion that the Collector was not acting according to law as the State Government had issued instructions to him not to. issue the licenses. The State Government and the other respondents traversed the claim in Ajodhya Prashad Shah 's writ petition and pleaded, inter alia, (i) that the bids at the auction were not satisfac tory and, in the interest of the State revenue, the State Govern ment had passed the orders for not accepting Aj Ayodhya Prasad 's bids; (ii) that it was a tax which was not contemplated by section 38 of the Bihar and Orissa Excise Act, 1915; (iii) that as the petitioner was the highest bidder on February 20, 1970 and his bid was entered into in the bid register and the Entry was signed, the petition er was entitled to the grant Of the exclusive privilege under section 22 by virtue of section 6(a) of the Amending Ordinance irrespective of the validity of rule 103 (1) of Board 's Excise Rules; and (iv) that he had already enjoyed the benefit under the license and had volun tarily participated in the auction, and was not entitled to an order for its refund. The High Court quashed the direction of the Collector dated April 15, 1970 for reauctioning the licence and declared that rule 103(1) was ultra vires the Act.

The appellant was charged with having entered into crimi nal conspiracy with approver Dinkar Sakharam between 19 December 1967 and 4 January, 1968 at Deolali Camp for the purpose of committing the murder of Narendrakumar and com mitted house breaking and thefts in the house of his grand father Dr. Nanavati and to murder his grandson Narendra Kumar. The prosecution case was as follows: Accused No. 3 thought that he had committed two murders prior to that date but nothing happened to him. Dinkar at first expressed his inability to undertake the job. Accused No 2 and Dinkar took Narendra out with the intention of murdering him but because ofcertain interruptions they could not muster courage to achieve that object. On 27 December, 1967 accused No. 1 called Dinkar and told him and accused No 2 that he was going to Nasik in connection with some court work and they should murder Narendra and that he would look to everything after his return from Nasik. The police came to the tailor 's shop made enquiries about the piece of cloth which was found in the tailors ' shop, made enquiries and ultimately accused No, 2 and one Dinkar entered the house by breaking open the lock and found that Narendra was not in the 'house, that the whole house had been ransacked and the back door was ajar. The dead body which had on it khaki shorts and white shirt of Narendra was seen alive by Kewal Ram, owner of the betel shop on 26th December,1967. On 25th January 1968 accused No., 3 was arrested. Dinkaran and accused Nos. 2 and 3 made various statements and led the police to various places. Several articles stolen from the house were recovered from the possession of Dr. Lilavati. Nanawati were recovered.

On July 4, 1967 a draft scheme was published which included among other lands an area admeasuring 1,37,961 sq. meters of which appellant as Karta of a Hindu undivided family was the lessee. On May 10, 1968 Government granted sanction to the draft scheme. Before the Town Planning Officer the appellant claimed compensation for deprivation of his right in the land at Rs. 50 per sq. by his order made on November 4, 1971 the Town planning Officer awarded compensation to the appellant at the rate of Rs. 2.40 p. per sq.; the total compensation awarded was Rs. 3,31,455. Not satisfied with the decision of the Town improvement Officer the Appellant preferred an appeal before the Board of Appeal which reduced his claim to Rs. 9.50 p. by reducing his claim for compensation to Rs, 9. 50 p. The appellant 's grievance was that the compensation awarded is inadequate and further that the apportionment of compensation between the lessor and the lessee was not proper. He also questioned the propriety of reserving such a large area of land for the scheme. The Board of appeal held that the appeal was not maintainable as the Act did not provide an appeal from a decision of a Town Planning officer on matters dealt with by him in his order dated November 4 1971, and that the matter should then go back to the Board for a decision on the adequacy of the compensation; if however it found that the Board 's appeal was incompetent, he would urge the grounds challenging the constitutional validity of the Act at this stage and the matter be remanded back to Board of Appeals for a determination on the sufficiency of the Compensation.

The testator appointed his brother as the guardian of his minor daughters as well as of his foster son. He left the management of his properties to his brother and provided that as soon as his minor daughter attained majority he should give to them per head one veli nanja land and one vela of punja land in vattam No. 149 in village Nagampadi 976 and further provided that the said Seetharama should deliver possession of the remaining properties to their son immediately after he attained majority. It was also provided in the will that Seetharamma should pay to the minor daughters the income from the properties devised to them after the death of the testator. After the two daughters were married and became major, Balakrishnan paid them certain monies as due to them out of the income of the properties in May 1942. Thereafter he used to pay 224 kalam of paddy and Rs. 175/in cash towards their properties after deducting the kist each year. In 1949 the two sisters claimed possession of their lands and their claim was that they were entitled in law having regard to the provisions of the will to select their respective one vehi of anja land and another veli land from out of their land in Vattam 149. The appellant did not accept this right of selection and contended that the daughters were entitled to their lands taking into account lands of good and bad quality. Held, that on a fair and reasonable construction of the Will it was clear that the testator intended that each daughter should select the land to be handed over to each son and therefore there could be no question of the legatees making the selection in the order in which they were named in the Will. It is only when the uncertainty is so great that there is no way of resolving it and finding out the intention of the executant that section 89 comes into play. But where the uncertainty was of a less degree and the intention Of the testator to gift certain property is clear, though there may be some difficulty because there is more property of that kind than actually bequeathed, that (1) (1860) 5 N. 125 980 980 the benevolent rule should be applied to carry out the intentions of a testator which clearly show that he intended to bequeath something which could be made definite by choice; and (2) where it is not possible to say on the construction of a will that the legatee himself indicated the selection or appointed a third person to make the selection but still intended to make a gift which could he made certain by selection made by the legatee, the English rule of construction that in such cases the testator meant the legatee to select should be applying in India also and the decision in Narayanasami Gramani 's case was correct.

The plaintiff and the defendants were in joint possession of the plots in dispute, being co bhumidars, because after the abolition of Zamindari by the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act 1950, the plaintiff appellant, Mohd. Bashir and Mohd. Rasheed used to manage the properties which were joint and used to give her share and assured her that her share would be properly looked after and protected by them. Thus, having gained the confidence of the plaintiff, the first and second defendants went on managing the properties and off and on gave her share so that she may not suspect their evil intentions. The plaintiff further alleged in her statement before the trial court that during consolidation proceedings separate plots were carved out and she was never informed about any proceedings by the defendants and was under the Impression that her name shall be entered in the record during the consolidation proceedings. The allegation of the plaintiffs that the defendants had committed fraud was stoutly denied. The trial court decreed the suit for joint possession in respect of Chakbandi plot Nos. 201 and 274 only. As regards plot nos. 93, 94 and 106, the dismissal of the suit by the trial Court was upheld. In second appeal, it was contended on behalf of the defendants mainly on the ground that the respondents were in separate occupation of the land or plots in question and the plaintiff had absolutely no concern with them. It was further alleged that although at some time before, the lands in dispute were joint but during consolidation operations the plots were occupied by Adhivasi who having acquired the rights of a Sirdar under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1950, and therefore, the suit was barred by section 49 of the said Act. It is also contended that although there was no evidence to prove that the plaintiff was prevented from filing a petition under section 9 of the U .P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953 or that the defendant assured the plaintiff that her names shall be recorded in the Record during consolidation proceeding and was assured by the defendant that they would take proper care of her share in any proceedings that may be instituted. This was accepted by the District Judge and should not have been interfered with by the High Court in second appeal. The High Court proceeded on the basis that there was nothing to show that any fraud was practised upon the consolidation authorities so as to make the order a nullity. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 A clear finding of fact after consideration of the evidence that a clear fraud was committed during the Consolidation operation either by the parties or by somebody else as a result of which the rights were sought to be extinguished. [867C] 1.2 In view of the clear decision of this Court, referred to above, the High court erred in law in holding that the present suit was not barred by Section 49 of U. P. Consolidation Act.

The petitioner, a Minister of the Union of India, took the oath as the other ministers are required to take. He maintains that yet in view of the fact that the Constitution describes him as the Prime Minister, while being sworn into office, he describes himself as Prime Minister and this practice is in vogue eversince 1950. The oath register is by the incumbent signed as Prime Ministers and all other ministers sign as Ministers. He further indi cates that describing Shri Devi Lal as Deputy Prime Minister is descriptive only and for all purposes he is a Minister and there is no 3 constitutional sanction for the post of Deputy Prime Minis ter as such. Relying on a bench decision of this Court in the case of Virji Ram Sutaria vs Nathalal Premji Bhavadia & Ors., , it was contended that the prescribed oath should be divided into two parts, one which is descriptive and the other which contains the sub stantial part. And according to him, as long as the substantial part is properly followed, a mere mistake or error in the descriptive part would not vitiate the oath. Dismissing the writ petition for the reasons indicated above, this Court, HELD: 1. The essential requirement of Article 173 read with Form VII A was that the person taking the oath or making the affirmation would bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution and uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India. The words which precede this portion are merely descriptive of the person and of his nomination as a candidate. " In view of this clear statement made by the learned Attorney General that Respondent No. 1 is just a Minister like other members of the Council of Ministers though he has been described as Deputy Chief Prime Minister but the description of him as Deputy Cabinet Minister does not confer on him any powers of the Prime Ministers, along with his other submis sions, we think the first contention raised by the petitioner has no force. So far as the second contention is con cerned, the petitioner himself does not press it.

On 1st November, 1948, 859 night shift operatives of the carding and spinning department of the Carnatic Mills stopped work some at 4 p.m. and some at 5 p. m. The strike ended completely. The apparent cause for the strike was that the management of the Mill had expressed its inability to comply with the request of the workers to declare the forenoon of the 1st Nov., 1948 as a holiday for solar eclipse. On the 3rd November, the strike ended totally and the apparent cause of the strike which was that it was an illegal strike since the textile industry was notified as a public utility industry and there could be no legal strike without a proper issue of notice in the terms prescribed by the . No such notice had been given. In view of this finding he upheld the view of the management that the continuity of service of the workmen was broken by the interruption caused by the illegal strike and that as a consequence the workers who participated in such strike were not entitled to annual holidays with pay under section 49 B (1) of the Factories Act, they lost the benefit of holidays that they would have otherwise got under the rules. Held, further, that on a proper construction of section 49B(1) 29 222 of the , the management was right in its decision that the stoppage of work for a period of two to four hours and such non permitted absence absence from work cannot be regarded as interruption of service by a body of persons employed in any industry acting in combination, or a concerted refusal or a refusal under a common understanding of any number of persons who are or have been so employed to continue to work or accept employment.

Section 292 I.P.C. provides that no prosecution could be legally sustained in the circumstances of the case, the film having been duly certified for public show by the Central Board of Film Censors, acting within their jurisdiction under the Act, thereby sanctioning the public exhibition of the film, does it furnish a justification in law in doing the act which, in the absence of such certification, may constitute an offence under section 292 I P.C., notwithstanding. The prosecution alleged that the fascinating title was misleadingly foul and beguiled the guileless into degeneracy. If the producer can irrefutably establish that he is actually justified by law in committing the act or alternatively, that he entertained a mistake of fact and in good faith believed that he was justified by Law in committing it, then also, the exception operates and the bona fide belief, although mistaken, eliminates the culpability. The resolution of the problem raised in this case thus becomes simplified. If, as here, the Board of Censorors acting within its jurisdiction under section 5B has to consider, before certification, all the points section 292 Cr. P. C., prescribe. Indeed neither the Penal Code nor the can go beyonds the restrictions sanctioned by the Constitution and once the special law polices the area it is pro tanto out of bounds for the general law. At least as a matter of interpretation, section 79 I. P .C. resolves the apparent conflict between section 292 IPC and Part II of the Act relating to certification of films.

The petitioner was the Government Pleader for the Patna District, authorised to represent 'Government in all civil cases. During the currency of his term a plurality of nine Assistant Government Pleaders was appointed and one of them was put in charge of a bunch of land acquisition cases. The petitioner challenged the power of Government, like any other litigant, to appoint any other lawyer except under him and never by excluding him. He went to the extent of writing to Government: "I am, therefore unable to comply with your instruction in allowing any Assistant Government Pleader to work in this case. I shall myself conduct this case and have enough time for it." The petitioner contended that his client 's claim as the sole representative of Government in courts is not a legal cover for seeking lucre but for vindicating the inviolability of the high public office of Government Pleader by politicking men in the Secretariat or by practitioners of favouritism dressed in 'little brief authority ', a deeper issue in which the Bar has a stake and the Bench must also be concerned. The time has come for State Governments to have a second economic look not only at litigation policy but lawyer 's fees rules (like rule 115 in the Bihar instance) especially in mass litigation involving ad valorem enormity and mechanical professionalism. Even a ceiling on income from public sector sources may be a healthy contribution to toning up the moral level of the professional system. After all, the cost of justice is the ultimate measure of the rule of law for a groaning people. Government and other public sector undertakings should not pamper and thereby inflate the system of costs. Maybe, this petition would not have been filed had the prospect of income without effort not been offered by Government Rules. A closer look at the legal stand may be helpful.

The appellants held out of a total issue of 800 shares of the Navjivan Mills Ltd., Kalol, a public limited company. Between the years 1943 47, the Mills purchased 5,000 shares of Bank of India Ltd. At an extraordinary general meeting of the shareholders of the Bank of lndia held on May 6, 1948, a resolution was passed increasing the share capital of the bank and for that purpose offering new shares to the existing shareholders in the proportion of one new share for every three shares held by the shareholders. The appellants agreed to the allotment of these shares and ultimately transferred them to a private company Jesinghbai Investment Co. Ltd. The assessment of the seven appellants was reopened under section 34(1)(a) of the Indian Income Tax Act by the Income tax Officer on the footing that, the release by the Mills amounted to a distribution of "dividend" within the meaning of section 2(6A), it was still dividend within the ordinary meaning of that expression and was taxable as income in the hands of the appellants. The order of the Income Tax Officer reassessing the income of the 7 appellants was confirmed in appeal by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and by the Tribunal. At the instance of the appellant, the High Court reframed the question as follows: "Whether on the facts and circumstances of the case, the distribution of the right to apply for the shares of The Bank of India amounted to distribution of dividend within section 2 (6A) of Indian Income tax Act. " Held, that the High court was right in holding that the distribution by the appellants amounted to 'dividends ' within the extended definition of that term in section 2.(6A).

The appellant was elected to the Haryana Legislative Assembly from Jind Legislative Assembly constituency. The first respondent was declared elected. He filed an election petition under section 81 of the Representation of People Act, 1951 for short). To this petition, the returned candidate as well as all other candidates who lost the election were impleaded as parties. After going through the pleadings of the parties, the Court ascertained the points on which parties were at variance and framed appropriate issues. The Election Petition reached the stage of recording evidence. It appears an application was filed by the appellant seeking permission to produce and examine witnesses whose names were set out in the application. It was averred in the petition that the names of the witnesses whom he desired to produce were already mentioned in the appropriate paragraphs of the election petition and that the petitioner would keep the witnesses present. The learned Judge to whom the Election Petition was assigned made an order on November 29, 1982 that as and when witnesses are produced, appropriate orders will be passed determining whether the witnesses could or could not be produced. In the meantime, the evidence of election petitioner was being recorded. It appeared that again on January 11, 1983, the appellant submitted a list of witnesses intimating to the Court that he desires to examine them. This was objected to by the returned candidates. The Judge after hearing the parties made an Order upholding the objection raised by the first respondent that the purpose for which the witnesses were offered is not mentioned in his list and therefore, the election petitioner could not he permitted to examine more witnesses whose name had not been mentioned in that list of witness submitted in accordance with the relevant provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure and the rules framed by the High Court. Accordingly, the learned Judge held that except Bahre son of Sher Singh, no other witness could be examined and that as soon as the evidence was recorded, the court would proceed to record the evidence on behalf of the returned petitioner; and thereafter the matter will be set down for hearing oral arguments of the learned counsel of either side. It is this order which was questioned in this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The obligation to supply the list of candidates within the time prescribed under sub rule (1) of Rule 1 of Order XVI is in respect of witnesses to procure whose presence the assistance of the Court is t necessary. And this ought to be so because the court wants to be satisfied about the necessity and relevance of the evidenceof such witness whose presence will be procured with the assistance by the Court. [532C] 1.2 The obligation cast on every party to a proceeding to present a list Of witnesses who it t proposes to call either to give evidence or to produce documents without applying for summons under Rule 1.

% The appellant, a double M.A. and holding a Doctorate applied in response to an advertisement that appeared in Hindi Daily Bhirgu A Chetna and Dainik Jagran on May 18, 1980 for the post of Principal. Pursuant to this decision of the Selection Committee, the Manager of the College issued an appointment order dated April 27, 1981 to the appellant informing him that the Committee of Management had appointed the appellant as Principal on one year probation in the scale of 550 1200 at initial pay alongwith DA admissible under the rules. The appellant was required to present himself before the Manager and take over the charge within 10 days of the receipt of the order failing which the appointment would be void. On receipt of this letter, the appellant wrote to the Manager that as permitted by him he has assumed charge of the post and he has convened an urgent meeting of the staff to be held on the same day after college hours in the teachers ' room. It appears that the State Government was contemplating to bring about a radical change in the mode, method and power of appointment of teaching staff in non government aided schools and accordingly Secretary to the Government of U.P. Education Department issued an order dated May 1, 1981, communicated by a radiogram to the various authorities. It reads as under: "From Secretary to Govt. of U P. No. 1701/l5 7 FI 1 (27)/81 dated 1.4.1981 Stop all fresh selections and appointments of Principals Headmasters and teachers including recruitment by promotion in all non Government aided secondary schools except minority institutions pending further orders(.) District Inspectors to ensure non drawal of pay of teachers appointed after his date(.) Detailed instructions follow(.)" Pursuant to the receipt, the District Inspector of Schools, Ballia had sent a copy of it to the College. There was some dispute between the parties as to whether this copy of the radiograms was received by the Management of the college but there is a letter dated May I, 1981 addressed by the District Superintendent of Schools to the Director of Education, U. P., the Deputy Director of School, VI Region, Varanasi, District Inspector Of Schools, wherein it was stated that as soon as G.O. No 1701 /15 7F (27)81 dated 7 4.1981 in regard to the prohibition on appointments is received in this office, it has been sent by letter No. 60/81 82 dated 8.4 1981 and it had been received by him by the clerk of his office on 8.5.1981 and the message of the G. O. have been sent to the experts by telegram. Hence in such a situation there is no question of appointment on the post or of Principal, and therefore the appointment of the appellant alleged to have been made on May 1. 1981 was not valid. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the radiagram dated April 7, 1981 contained an order of the State Govt.

The petitioners, manufacturers of tyres to whom the fabric is supplied "impregnate the fabric with rubber and weave it into a fabric in the same way as is being done by the first petitioner. Thus, the petitioners allege that they manufacture "a textile" and also that it serves as part of raw material for what ultimately goes into the manufacture of a fabric. After indicating the manner in which and substance out of which "rayon tyre cord fabric" is made and its composition, the petition sets out item 22 of the first schedule of the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1941 as the applicable entry covering the goods manufactured by the petitioners. This item reads as follows: "18. All cotton fabrics, rayon or artificial silk fabrics shall have the meanings respectively assigned to them in Items Nos. 1, 4, 19, 20, 21 and 22 of First Schedule to the Central Excise and Salt (Central) Act, 1944." Section 2(C) of the Additional Duties of Excise (Goods of Special Importance) Act 1957 lays down that "2(C), the words and expressions 'sugar ', 'tobacco ', shall have their meanings respectively assign to them In Items Nos., 1, 2, 4 19, 21, 22 and 22. The petitioners state that the manufacturers of the tyres to which the fabric was supplied " Impregnating the fabric" with rubber fall under entry 18 of the Schedule of the Rajasthan Sales Tax Act, 1954 (the Act ') contended that the goods now sought to be taxed are not the "end product". Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. There is no sufficient reason for overriding and discarding the High Court 's view that there was no error apparent on the face of the record and 502 that the taxing authorities should be left to determine whether the "tyre cord fabric ' is more correctly capable of being described as a fabric or as merely cordending to pass off as ar textile fabric This is really a technical question. In any case, it is a question on which two views seem possible on apparent facts. And, neither of the two views can be rejected outright as untenable. [501D E] 2. The High Court was right in not interfering with the decisions of the taxing Authorities at this stage. There was no appeal by the State of Rajasthan. It does not, therefore, seem propel for us to finally decide on merits the question argued before it in the appeals by the Delhi Cloth Mills which are before us unless we could have decided the matter in favour of the appellant.

The appellant company was engaged in construction of coal washeries on contract basis in different collieries and also doing allied work. The management held domestic enquiry into the incident and found him guilty of committing theft. He was accordingly dismissed from service. The dispute arising therefrom was referred under Section 10(1)(c) of the Act to Labour Court Dhanbad for adjudication. The Labour Court registered the case as refer ence case No. 4 of 1988 and issued notice to the parties. The parties entered appearance and filed their respective pleadings. When the matter was thus pending consideration, the respondent seems to have written to the Government stating that it would be difficult for him to attend the Labour Court, Dhanbad since he has been residing at Hajipur and it would he convenient for him if the case is trans ferred to Labour court Patna. That application was made without intimation to the management. The Government howev er, has acceded to the request of the respondent and without opportunity to the Management transferred the case to Labour Appellate Court, Patna. The Notification issued in that regard reads as follows: " NOTIFICATION Patna dated 8th August 1988 S.O. In exercise of powers conferred by sub section (1) of Section 33 B of the , the Governor of Bihar after careful consideration of the application of the petitioner Shri Shivajee Prasad Sinha wherein he has prayed for the transfer of adjudication proceedings to Patna keeping in view the difficulties expressed by him to attending the labour court, Dhanbad regu larly due to his residence at Hajapur is pleased to withdraw the proceeding shown in Annexure 'A ' pending before Labour Court. " The management moved the High Court by way of writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution to have the Notification quashed. The High Court did not agree and summarily dismissed the writ petition with an observation: "Since no prejudice is being caused to the petitioner and no allegation of mala fide has been made against the presiding officer, Patna, we are not inclined to interfere with the order under challenge. This application is dismissed" The management in the appeal challenged the Government notification withdrawing and transferring the pending case from the Labour court Dhanbad to Labour Tribunal Patna. Since the impugned Notification has been issued under Section 33B of the .

The appellant was the manager of a Hotel Imperial, New Delhi. The main contention on behalf of the hotel was that the reference was incompetent inasmuch as it did not specify how many of the 480 workers of thirty different categories working in the hotel were involved in the dispute. Held, further, that even if the workman is entitled to be represented by an officer of a trade union of which he is a member, the reference in this case does not mention any officer of the trade union but mentions the union itself. The nature of the dispute is also specified in the terms of reference. It was entirely unnecessary for the purpose of section 10 where the dispute was of a general nature relating to the terms Of employment or conditions of labour of a body of workmen, to mention the names of particular workmen who might have been responsible for the dispute, and it could not be denied on the facts of this case that there was a dispute between the hotel and its workmen and it went to this length that the hotel decided to dismiss a large number of workmen on October 7, 1955. State of Madras vs C. P. Sarathy, [1953] S.C.R. 334, followed. The fact that more than three years have passed since the reference is made does not make the reference incompetent merely because it was mentioned therein that the workmen will be represented only by some officer, such as its president or secretary and it is that officer who will really represent the workmen before the tribunal, and there is no force in this appeal.

The appellant, a bushings and bearings imported by the appellant, was entitled to the benefit of exemption under the Notification No. 281 Cus/76, granting part exemption from payment of Customs duty in respect of the rod bushes and camshaft bushes imported by it. Before the Customs, Excise and Gold (Control) Appellate Tribunal, the bushments and bear ings were the same and as the bearings came under the Heading No. 84.63 and not under Heading 84.06, they are not entitled to claim any exemption for the bushes, even if they are parts of such engines. Secondly, it was contended by the Additional Solicitor General that even assuming that Heading No 84.07 also contemplates parts of the engine, such parts must be all the parts constituting the engine or engines, and, therefore, even though they perform the same functions, they were distinct and separate, yet there is no material for holding that the bushes which have been imported by appellant, are parts, of the engines referred to in Heading No, 84.6. The Notification provides that the articles specified in column (2) of the Table annexed hereto annexed and falling under Heading No .84.06 are exempt from payment Of a certain portion of the customs duty. Paragraph 2 of column (1) of Table annexed to the Notification, which is relevant for our purpose, not only refers to internal combustion piston engines but also to 'parts thereof '. The notification further provides that "the articles specified therein and failing under Heading Nos. 8406 are exempted from payment .of a certain part of the Customs duty. Para 2 of paragraph 225 column (3) of Notification No,. 281 C.us dated 2.8.1976, as amended A from time to time, reads as follows: "Notfn. No. 282.Cus. The articles specified In column(2) are exemptfrom payment of a certain percentage of the duty of Customs leviable thereon which is specified in the First Schedule to the . as is in excess of the rate specified in corresponding entry in column(3) thereof. Heading 8406 does not, however, contain or refer to the parts of internal combustion Piston engine engines, but also specifically mentions the 'part 's thereof, that is to say, parts of those engines. Heading No: 84.05 does not refer to "parts" of such engine. Non mention of "part ' in Heading 84,06 has given rise to a controversy between the parties. It may be that the Notification has been inartistically drafted. It is, however clear that the notification not only intends to grant exemption to internalviation pistonson engines, yet also to "Part 's" thereof. When, therefore the intention is clear and manifest, it will be unreasonable to take a narrow view of the Notification and not to extend its benefit to the part parts of engines referred in Heading Nos, 8406 and 83. To accept the contention made on behalf of the respondents that as heading No.8406 does does not mention 'the parts ', the Notification is inapplicable to the Parts, will be to amend the Notification which the court will not do.

The appellants filed a suit for declara tion that they were entitled to be in enjoyment and pos session of Saint Syed Moosa Shah Khadiri Dargah in Madras for a period of 27 days in all in the months of February, March, June, July, October & November each year and to restrain the defendants from interfering with the plaintiffs ' right and management in the Dargah. The Trial Court decreed the suit and in the operative part held that the plaintiffs were entitled ted to manage the Dargah for 27 days i.e. from February 1, to February 27. The High Court took the view that the Courts below proceeded upon an erro neous assumption as if it was the duty of the defendants to prove by what hostile assertions of title and possession ouster had been established. It further held that after the decree in Civil Suit No. 116 of 1909 also nega tived the right of any management by Wazir Bee and Mohideen Bi and from this it was clear that the females were totally excluded from the right or claim of any share in the management or offerings, the plaintiffs who were claiming through Fathima Bee were also not entitled to any relief. The widows of Sayed Gulam Dastagir Sahib also could not claim any right of ownership or posses sion in a Dargah and on that account they were pleading an ouster of Fathiman Bee from the fight or management of the Dargah or any claim in the offerings, and even if she had got any right, the same was lost as she did not claim no right till her death. It was further held by this Court that after decree in C.S. 116 Of 1909, the right to manage was divided between the two sons each taking six months for himself. According to this arrangement the branch of Sayed Ismail Sahib used to remain in management for the months for Janu ary, April, May, August, September and December and the branch branch of Gulam Dhatagir Saheb for the other six months, namely February, June 1, July October and November each. The present suit relates to the controversy between the decendants of the branch. According ly after the death of Fathi ma Bee in 1957, the appellants being her son and daughter associated themselves in management of Dargah with their mater nal uncles and the sons of the maternal uncles were getting share of the income of the Wakf. The plaintiffs alleged that thus Fathna Bee had 1/5th share in 6 months i. e. 36 days Fathilima Bee left surviving one son and two daughters. The appellants filed written statement taking the plea that their father was a Mujawar along with two daughters, namely, Abdul Gaffer Sahib and Fathma Bee in proportion of 2:2:1 respectively.

The 1st respondent was a gangman in the employ of the Central Railway. At that time his wages were Rs. 18 per month plus dearness allowance. With effect from the 1st November 1947, the Railway Board under the Ministry of Railways introduced a scheme of grant of compensatory (city) allowance and house rent allowance at rates specified in their memorandum No. E47 CPC/14 dated 1st December 1947. As a result of this scheme certain railway employees stationed at specified headquarters were eligible for the allowance aforesaid at certain specified rates. The 1st Respondent thus became entitled to the allowance of Rs. 10 per month. The appellant appeared before the Authority and by his written statement contested the claim on the ground that the house rent allowances which was 1348 the subject matter of the claim was not "wages" within the meaning of section 2(vi) of the Act. The Authority condoned the delay and set aside the order condoning the delay. Held, that the rules which must be included in the terms of contract between the employer and the employee contemplate that an employee posted at one 173 1352 of the specified places would be entitled to house rent Allowance; but that as soon as he is offered Government quarters for his accommodation he ceases to be so entitled to whether he actually occupies or does not occupy the quarters offered to him. The rules clearly provide that the allowance will not be ad raissible to those who occupy government quarters or to those to whom such quarters have been offered but who have refused to take advantage of the offer.

In Writ Petition 434 of 1980, the detenu is one Indru 's Ramchand Bharvani; while in Writ Petition 435/80, the detenus are carrying on business in diamonds and precious stones in partnership under the style of "M/s. Gems Impex Corporation". 35, New Marine Lines Bombay, since 1971. On November 16, 1979, the Customs Officers at Bombay raided the premises of the firm and seized two cameras and three wrist watches worth about Rs. 55 lakhs and also some jewellery and Rs. 1,40,000 in Indian currency and two gold sovereign coins. The detenus were arrested on November 23, 1979 and interrogated. During interrogation, the petitioners claimed that the gems and other articles seized were not smuggled goods but were local materials locally acquired. They also gave the names of four persons from whom these gems had been acquired. Both the father and the son were arrested and were produced before a Magistrate. They were released on heavy bail subject to the condition that they would attend daily before the Customs officers and cooperate in the investigation. This condition was later on related. On February 16, 1980, an order of detention dated February 15, 1980 purporting to have been made under section 3(1) of the (for short called COFEPOSA) by the State Government was served on the detenus. The grounds of detention were also served on them alongwith the order of Detention on February 18, 1980. On March 25, 1980 the wife of the detenu addressed a letter to the first respondent (Under Secretary to the Government of Maharashtra), requesting him to furnish the detenus with the material relied upon by the detaining authority in the grounds of Detention. On April 3, 1980 copies were received by the detenus from the State Govt. under their covering letter dated March 31, 1980 and were actually received by them on April 3. 1980. The detenu also made a representation to the State government which, according to the information furnished at the Bar by Mr. Salvi, Secretary in the Home Department, was declined. The Central Government advised the State Gov ernment to supply the copies. Thereupon, it seems, that within three days the copies were put in a course of communication to the detenus by the Union Government under their cover covering letter, dated March 14, 1980 which, in fact, was received by him on March 25.

The Gujarat High Court recorded a very lengthily order though the reasoning in support of the non maintainability of the joint appeal was confined to a couple of pages only. The High Court in its order referred to ss 258, 410, 417 and 423 of the Code and came to the conclusion that the scheme of Chapter XXXI of the code as disclosed by these sections and particularly by section 419 was against the maintainability of a joint appeal by the State against an order acquitting several accused persons tried jointly. On the view that the Full Bench decision holding a joint appeals to be maintainable in law was not binding on it. On behalf of the respondents, it was contended that r. 6 in Chapter XXVI of the Bombay High Court Appellate Side Rules (which are applicable to the proceedings in Gujarat High court) was inconsistent with Chapter XXXI Of the Code of Criminal Procedure, with the result that a joint Appeal by several accused person convicted at one trial must be held not to be contrary to any provision of the said Code. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The power to frame this rule is specifically conferred on the High Court by section 554(2)(c) Cr. P.C. and r.6 does not seem to us to be inconsistent with any provisions of the aforesaid Code. Holding this rule to be valid in agreement with the decision of the Full bench, the competency of a Joint appeal by several persons convicted at a joint trial has also to be upheld. [879 E F] Mahadeolal Ranodia vs The Administrator General of West Bengal, ; , referred to.

The appellant was a firm registered under section 26(A) of the Income tax Act, 1922. Prior to the constitution of the firm, the partners were members of a Hindu undivided family. The family which consisted of Meyyappa Chettiar and his two brothers carried on money lending business in India and in the former Federated Malaya States and it was assessed under the Indian Income Tax Act, 1918. There was a disruption of the joint family status on June 2, 1938 and thereafter the members of the family continued the business as partners. In the course of assessment for the year 1939 40 it was claimed by M that having regard to the severance of joint family nature, the income from April 13, 1938 to June 2nd, 1938 was not liable to be taxed by reason of the provisions of section 25(3) and (4). The Income tax Officer accepted the fact of partition amongst the members. but rejected the contention that the family was not entitled to relief under section 25 (3) of 1922 Act except for the income received from the house properties in Malaya. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that there was no discontinuance of the business within the meaning of section25(3). The High Court also held that when a Hindu Undivided Family carrying on a business which was taxed under the 1918 Act became disrupted and the members continued the firm business there after as partners there could be no discontinuance but only succession by the firm of the said business. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The assessee received the entire profits of the foreign business in British India and the entire income were assessed to income tax in the hands of the assessee under the 1922 Act. [908 G] Commissioner of Income tax, Madras vs section V.R.M. Palaniappa Chettiar and Others ; , followed.

The respondent entered into a contract with the Public Works Department of the Government of Gujarat on September 6, 1965 for manufacture and supply of kiln burnt bricks to the said department for the construction of the Capital Project, Ghandhinagar. Large quantities of bricks were manufactured and supplied under the contract and the applicant received payment for the same in accordance with the agreed rates. The assessee made an application under section 52 of the Bombay Sales lax Act, 1959 on November 19, 1967 to the Deputy Commissioner of Sales Tax to determine the question whether the said supplies of bricks by the respondent to the Public works Department were sales or works contract. The Deputy Commissioner held that the supply of bricks was sales. At the instance of the assessee, the Tribunal referred the following question of law to the High Court: "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the transaction envisaged by the contract entered into by the applicant with the public Works Department for the manufacture and sale of kiln burning brick work is a works contract ?" The High Court answered the question in favour of the respondent holding that the transaction was a works Contract. In coming to that conclusion, the High court held as follows: "In view of certain distinguishing features of the contract with which we are concerned, it would be difficult to hold in the light of the special features and characteristics of the contracts with which this Court are concerned that the decision of the Supreme Court in Chandra Bhan Gosain 's case is clearly distinguishable on facts. The contract in that case though prima facie word "cd as regards the relevant clauses in similar fashion as the contract in the instant case is in fact cast in a different mould and it would he difficult to held in the absence of any standard formula by which one can distinguish a contract of Sale from contract for work and labour. The question is not always easy and has for all time vexed jurists all over. The distinction between a contract Of sale of goods and a contract for works and labour is often a fine one. A contract of sale is contract whose main object is the transfer of the property in and the delivery of the possession of a chattel as a chattetel to the buyer. (Halsbury 's Laws of England Third Edition Volume 34 page 6.) The contract withwhich we are dealing here is found in a tender for the supply Of materials containing a memorandum of the conditions. The nature of work is described as manufacturing and supplying kiln burn bricks for construction of Gandhinagar . The question will depend upon the true construction of all the terms and conditions of the document when there is one. The questions will depend on the intention of the parties executing the contract. As we have observed in this case, the property was entirely of the assesee. He had not only to manufacture that but also to stack them for facilitating delivery.

The petitioner was an assessee under the Income tax Act and Wealth Tax Act during the assessment year 1976 77 and was liable to pay income tax and Wealth tax in accordance with the rates prescribed by the Finance Act, 1976 which was passed by the Lok Sabha during its extended period which was extended under the provisions of the House of People (Extension of Duration) Act,1976 after the expiry of five years from the date appointed for its first meeting. The petitioner contended that the duration of the house of the People could have been validly extended only when a Proclamation of Emergency was in force under the proviso to clause (2) of Article 83 of the Constitution and since the two Proclamations of Emergency dated 3rd December, 1971 and 25th June, 1975 were either ultra vires the Constitution or had ceased to be in operation by the time the House had not been published in the official Gazette of the Government of India. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1(a) The resolution passed by both Houses of Parliament approving the two resolutions of Emergency as required by clause (1) of article 352 of the Consti tution should have been published for the very same reason which compelled the Government to publish the Proclimations in the Official Gazette. [446C] (b) The production of the Lok Assembly Debates and of the Rajya Sabha containing the proceedings of the two Houses of parliament relating to the period between the time when the resolutions were moved in each of the three Houses of the Parliament and the time, when the resolution was duly adopted amounts to proof of the said resolutions. [441E] (c) The reports of the proceedings are widely circulated. The newspapers, radio and television are also the other modern means which give publicity to all Acts and resolutions of Parliament and Legislatures of the States. The publication in the Parliamentary Debates though after 455 some short delay is adequate publication of the resolutions approving the Pro clamations by both the Houses of Legislature as set out earlier in the course of this judgment is not sufficient compliance with clause (c). [441G H] 2(a)(i) It is seen that any public notification issued under Article 364(1) has to be published in a official Gazette as provided by Article 366(19) of the Constitu tion. The procedure of the both Houses is made under Article 118(1), of the constitution which reads thus: "118.(1) Every House of Parliament may make rules for regulating, subject to the provisions Of this Constitution, its procedure and the conduct of its business. (2). Until rules are made under clause (i), the rules of procedure and standing orders in force immediately before the commencement of this Constitution with respect to the Legislature of the Dominion of India shall have effect in relation to Parliament subject to such modifications and adaptations as may be made therein by the Chairman of the Council of States or the Speaker of the Houses, as the case may be. .". [442G H; 443A] (ii) The proceedings of both Houses are not open to challenge.

The appellant filed an application in the District Court for a declaration that the said premises were private property and for an order setting aside the said decision. The District Judge decreed the suit in favour of the appellant holding that the premises did not constitute a temple and set aside the decision of the said authorities. On appeal, the High Court reversed the judgment and decree passed by the Trial Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that cl. (b) of article 133(1)(a) could not apply as the judgment & decree passed against it did not involve directly or indirectly a claim or question res pecting property of the value of Rs. 20,000/ or more and that the appeal did not involving any substantial question of law. HELD: The High Court was wrong in proceeding on the assumption that whether the property was a private or a public temple was incapable of valuation as it could have in either case no market value. It may be observed that the appellant 's case was that the subject matter of dispute in the suit was the private property of his family and that it was alienable property and therefore capable of a valid transfer. That being so, capitalising that value at twenty times the annual rental value, the value, of the property would come to more than Rs.20,000. The refusal of the High court to grant leave was based on the observation that whether property is a private temple or a Public temple, it was incapable Of valuation. But as observed earlier, the appellant did not have to pay court fees as it would in the case of an ordinary suit on a valuation made by him therefor.

The respondents claimed that they should be given cash allowance in lieu of the tiffin arrangements at present made by the appellant, and they urged that the practice started by the appel lant of employing retired persons was mainly inspired by humanitarian considerations. When it appeared to the appellant that some employees who had retired found it difficult to maintain themselves and their families, the appellant sympathetically and generously considered their request for re employment and that is, the basis on which some of the re employments have been made. Held, that the question posed by the respondents ' demand must be considered. The fact that the re employed persons have made an affidavit supporting the practice adopted by the appellants can have no material bearing in dealing with the point; in the very nature of things, the said re employed person are bound to support the appellant. The result is that the appeal fails and is dismissed with costs. Chandi Charan Banerjee vs Their Workmen, [1960] 1 S.C.R. 571, referred to. In the instant case, as many as 6 persons have been re employed and the correspondence between the parties on this subject shows that the respondents felt that the policy adopted by them in re employing the retired personnel was not based solely on humanitarian grounds. When the respondents had raised a dispute on this point in 1960, the State Government refused to make a reference on the ground that only 4 cases of reemployment had been brought to its notice, and so, the problem did not call for any consideration at that stage.

The respondent was an employee of the East India Railway and was a subscriber to the State Railway Provident Fund. He elected to be governed by the Provident Fund Sterling Accounts Rules, whereunder payment of the provident fund credited in his account in rupees was on retirement to be made in sterling. On August 26, 1947, Browne retired from service, the Deputy General Manager, Eastern Railway, wrote a letter on July 27, 1955, to the Chief Accounts Officer communicating the sanction of the General Manager for payment of special contribution to Provident Fund to Browne in sterling in terms of r. 1410(1) of the Railway Establishment Code. Another communication was received from Browne (who had apparently by then migrated to the United Kingdom) on February 22, 1956 by which he requested that the amount standing to his credit in the Provident fund Account be remitted to him by Bank Draft on the District Bank Water Street, Liverpool. After Browne retirement of Browne, in order to carry out that obligation, the Accounts Officer of the railway made out two cheques in the name of Brown and sent them to the Reserve Bank for conversion of the amount in sterling and to transmit the fund in sterling to the bankers of Browna in England. The Reserve Bank was the only authority which could permit such conversion in view of the 31 currency restrictions imposed by the Government of India. For purpose of conversion and transmission of the amounts to Brown, the Reserve bank was the agent of the Railways. Until the money was converted into sterling and was transmitted by the Reserve Banks to Brownee, the money remained at the disposal of Railway Administration. The Railway Administration then drew two cheques one for Rs. 14,428 8 9 and another for Rs 23,018 11 10 in favour of the ReserveBank of India with instructions to convert amounts covered by the cheques into sterling, and to remit it to Browna Bank, Birmingham. The Union of India again applied for removal of attachment on the ground that the money represented provident fund money and was immune from attachment under the law and that the attachment was "illegal and without jurisdiction". The executing court overruled the objection observing "that the attachment issued by the Court on December 8, 1956, was perfectly in order. the moneys attached by the court lost their character as Provident Fund moneys long before they were attached and hence they were not immune from the attachment as claimed by the objector. The High Court confirmed the order passed by the executing court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that by sending the two cheques to the Union Bank of India in performance of the manner of Payment prescribed by Browne the debt was discharged, and the money must be deemed to have been paid out to the subscriber Browne. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The order of attachment of the money into which the two letters drawn by the Railway Administration were converted on encashment was contrary to the terms of section 3 of the . The High court was in error in holding that the moneys in the hands of the Bank had ceased to be provident fund and was liable to be attached.

An employee who wilfully or anti socially holds up the wheels of production or undermines the success of the business is a high risk and deserves, in industrial interest, to be removed without tears. The management took the Court into confidence to explain why the employee was discharged. He was consequentially shifted to the post of clerk handling posting of bins and collection of payments but the workman, although denied direct access to correspondence in the Receipt and Dispatch section, made attempt to elicit information from the section with a view to pass it on to outsiders '. The upshot of these activities of which the management was alerted was a loss of confidence in the employee. Therefore, the action was claimed to be legal and immune to judicial interference. Security of employment is the first requisite of a worker 's life. The second equally axiomatic consideration is that a worker who wilfully and anti socially held up the wheel of production Or undermines his success of business isa high risk, and deserves in industrial interests, to he removed without carved and proving the objec tionable conduct which has undermined his confidence so that the tribunal may be satisfied about the bona fides of the 'firing ' as contrasted with the colourable exercise of power hiding a not so innocuous purpose. The worker, Michael, through his Union, protested against the 'sack ' order as victimisation of a Trade Union activist but the management denied and the reference to trade union activities by the worker was more 'to create a ground for the workman 's claim and has been leveled as a matter of habit and routine. The basic plea of the management is that the action being a simple termination without a sting, the process and consequence of a disciplinary action were not attracted. The Management, however took the view that the motivation for the termination was the suspicion which lurked in the mind of the Regional Manager that information regarding tenders was being passed on by the workman. It is significant that this Court used language and laid down law very much like in the earlier cases and did refer to the precedents on the point. For instance, Vaidialingam J., (as he then was) speaking for the Court made the following observations: "The right of the employer to terminate the services of his workman under a standing order like cl.17(a) in the present case, which amounts to a claim 'to hire and fire ' an employee as the employer pleases and thus completely negatives security of service which has been secured to industrial employees through industrial adjudication, came up for consideration before the Labour Appellate Tribunal in Buckingham & Carnatic Co. 2 SCR 822) wherein the view taken by the Labour Court was approved and it was held that even in a case like the present the requirement of bona fides was essential and if the termination of service was a colourable exercise Of the power or as a result of victimisation or unfair labour practice, the industrial tribunal would have the jurisdiction to intervene and set aside such termination. " The management, however, took the court into confidence that it was 'not possible to hold this order to be based on any conceivable misconduct '. In the light of what we have indicated, it is clear that loss of faith is often a subjective feeling or individual reaction to an objective set facts and motivations. The Court is concerned with the latter and not with the former, although circumstances may exist which justify a genuine exercise of the power of simple termination. In a reasonable case of a confidential or responsible post being misused or a sensitive or strategic position being abused, it may be a high hazard to keep the employee, once suspicion has started and a disciplinary en quiry cannot be forced on the master.

The petitioners, who were the State of U.P., Dr. R.M. Sahay and his team of doctors and para medical staff, who arrived in Khurja on 21st April, 1986, examined about 122 patients. One hundred and eight patients were operated upon, 88 of them for Cataract which, with the modern advances in Ophthalmic Surgery, is considered a relatively minor and low risk risk surgery surgery. Dr. Sahay returned on the 24th April and undertook himself some ameliorative treatment. But the operated eyes had been damaged completely. Similar mishap, but on lesser scale affecting some patients, repeated itself at Moradabad. Some of the victims were later sent to and treated at Dr. V.P. Hospital at Jaipur where he was scheduled to conduct similar operations at another "Eye Camp". However, this Court by its order dated 26th September, 1986 directed the Indian Medical Council and the Union of India to be impleaded as parties to the proceedings. In the Writ Petition, the petitioners have made serious allegations about the very bona fides of, and the intention behind, the sponsoring of the iII fated "eye camp" and have alleged that motives of monetary gains by way of State and International subsidies. The prayers in the writ petition are that: (1) the victims of this medical misha p be given expert rehabilitatory treatment and appro priate compensation; (2) the Government do conduct a thorough investigation as to the conditions which rendered a medical misadventure of such a scale possible and evolve proper guide lines which will prevent recurrence of such tragedies; and (3) appropriate legal action be instituted against Dr.R.M., Sahay and their team and also against officers of the Government who, according to allegations committed serious breaches of duty in sanctioning permission for the conduct of the "eya camp" without ensuring a strict compliance with the conditions prescribed in the guidelines prescribed by the Government in that behalf and in not effectively dis charging the duties enjoined upon them to over see the satisfactory and safe functioning of the camp. At the directions of this Court, each of the injured victims had been paid a sum of Rs.5,000.00 by the State Government by way Of interim relief. The amount shall be deposit ed as was done in the matter of distribution of interim relief with the District Judge who shall arrange to dis tribute the same in accordance with the procedure adopted at the time of administration of the interim relief, and this Court directed that the victims otherwise satisfy the conditions of those schemes. Disposing of the Writ Petitions, this court, HELD: 1. The Revised guidelines dated 9.2.1988 arrived at after a careful study of all aspects of the problem are quite comprehensive. However, in a case where the plaintiff developed meningitis as a result of some infection in the apparatus used in the operation it was held that there must have been some negli gence by the hospital staff for which the hospital authority was responsible. (page 232) 2. The prescriptions re ferred to by the said sub committee of the Indian medical Council may be considered for incorporation in the Revised Guidelines of 9th February, 1988. Government States and Union, incur enormous expenditure of public money on health care, but the standards of cleanliness and hygiene in public hospitals unfortunately leave greatly to be desired. Purity of the drugs and medicines intended for man use would have to be ensued by prior tests and inspection.
