One Ram Kishori Lal Sao, a resident of Asansol in Bengal died in September 1927. The plaintiffs respondents filed a suit for a declaration that a deed of gift dated March 10, 1940, executed by Sumitra Devi in favour of her daughter Kamala Devi was void and inoperative beyond the lifetime of Sumitra Devi and was not binding on the reversion as she had only a life interest in the corpus of the property and there was no justifying legal necessity for the alienation made by her. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court affirmed that decision. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants, inter alia, (i) that there were no compelling reasons for the High court which was the appellate Court to differ from the appreciation of oral evidence by the learned Subordinate Judge who had the advantage of seeing the witnesses with regard to the question of the ante nuptial agreement said to have been made at Deoghar and the acceptance of such a gift by Nand Lal father in law of Kamala Devi; (ii) that even accepting the findings of the final Court of fact as correct, the gift being of a reasonable portion of the estate of Ram Kishori Lai Sao and in pursuance and fulfilment of an ante naptial agreement made by Sumitra ' at the time of the preliminary settlement of the marriage negotiations at Deughar was for spiritual benefit of Ram Kishore Lal and valid in Hindu law; (iii) that it was not proved by reliable evidence that Sumitra Devi had made a "sankalpa" of the gift of four houses when the bride was given in marriage and the question whether Sumitra Devi was competent to make a gift under the Hindu Law, even as it stood prior to the enactment of the . HELD: (i)(a) The finding of the courts below that there was antenuptial arrangement by Sumitra wife that she would give four houses at Asansool of the value of Rs. 20,000 to her daughter as marriage dowry is not correct. It has been held in Churaman Sahu 's case that there is a moral or religious obligation of giving a portion of it of the joint family property for the benefit of the daughter and the son in law, and a gift made long after the marriage may be supported upon the ground that the gift when made fulfils that moral or legal obligation. The finding by the final court of fact is that there has been anten uptial agreement by Sumitra Debi Devi that she will give four house at Asirsol, of the values of Rs 20,00 to her daughters as marriage and dowry. It was open to Sumitra Devi to fulfil that promise as a religious act which conferred spiritual benefit upon her deceased husband, irrespective of the consideration whether she made a ' sankalna ' at that time of marriage or not. [463 D E] (b) If a promise is made of such gift for or at the request of the donor, and attested by at least two witnesses, it may be made afterwards in fulfilment of the promise. The Explanation to section shows that "property" includes immoveable property acquired by a female Hindu at a partition or by gift from any person whether a relative or not, before, at or after her marriage, or by her own skill or exertion, or By purchase or by prescription, or in any other manner whatsoever, and also any such property held by her as stridhana immediately before the commencement of this Act.

The election to the Baghapurana Constituency (District Faridkot) to the Punjab Legislative Assembly took place on May 31, 1980 and the counting was done on June 1, 1980. Tej Singh secured 25694 votes whereas Avtar Singh (appellant) secured 25571 votes. The margin between the votes secured by Tej Singh (respondent) and Avtar Singh was only 123 votes. Avtar Singh filed an election petition in the Punjab & Haryana High Court against Tej Singh alleging that he was guilty of committing corrupt practices, detailed in the petition an(l in the Statement of facts. Ruplal supported the appellant but Bhagat Puran Singh and Jagdish Chander secured 140 and 2856 votes respectively. The trial court dismissed the petition holding that the allegations of corrupt practice indulged in by Tej singh have been clearly proved. The High Court also held that the allegation of corrupt practices indulged in had been clearly established. Allowing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: 1.1 In view of the very narrow margin of votes (123) between Tej Singh and Avtar singh, a strong presumption and possibility that the votes polled in favour of Rup Lal would have gone to Avtar Singh cannot be ruled out and that would have doubtless materially altered the result of the election. [419D E] 1.2 The appellant has proved beyond reasonable doubt that Tej Singh had indulged in corrupt practices particularly when the printing of the posters by Tej. Singh has been clearly admitted by him as indicated above. It is also clear to us that in view of section 123(2) of the Act having been adopted by the first respondent (Tej. Singh), which have been fully proved, the irresistible inference and inescapable conclusion that can be arrived at is that Tej singh had actually paid for the posters which were printed at his instance and Rup Lal was not collected with the printing by the posters.

The appellant, a Forest Minister in the Council of Ministers headed by Shri Bhajan Lal, was personally very keen on giving him an office of profit. In order to achieve this objective, he got an Ordinance being Ordinance No. 44 of 1982 promulgated by the Governor. The ordinance inter alia provided that the constitution of a Forest Development Board would be constituted with a view to appointing the said Devinder Sharma as its Chairman. It was further alleged by the appellant that after having failed to threaten and demoralise the appellant through indirect means, the respondent, Bhajan Lal called him to his official residence on July 26, 1983 through the Acting Chief Conservator of Forests and criminally intimidated him to withdraw the writ petition and pursuant to that, eleven officers withdrew from the petition. The appellant filed an application for contempt against the respondent in the High Court complaining of interference by the respondent with due course of judicial proceedings. The application was admitted and a rule nisi was issued upon the respondent. The respondent appeared in the rule and opposed the same by filing an affidavit denying all the allegations made against him by the appel lant. The learned Single Judge of the High COurt took the view that there were circumstances to indicate that it was not a fit case in which the Court should exercise its jurisdiction under the Act. In that view of the matter, the learned Judge dismissed the application and discharged the rule niisi. It is apparent from the facts stated above that the allegations against the appellant, if proved would consid erute a criminal contempt. The High Court did not exercise its jurisdic tion or power as conferred on it by Article 215 of the Constitution when it imposes a punishment for contempt.

The respondents were the daughter and grand sons of the original plaintiff Vinayakbhat. The lease provided that in default of payment of rent the tenant 's rights would come to an end. On 18th August, 1870, Ladha Ibrahim sold his tenancy rights to one Girdhari Balaram Lodhi for Rs. 7,999. The sale deed provided for the payment of the agreed rent in the month of Pousb every year and stated that in case of default the tenant or his heirs would have no right over the land. On the same day the purchaser passed a rent note in favour of Ramabai. The rent note provided for payment of Rs. 999 for the lease, and also agreed to pay 1011/2 yearly rent at Rs. 80 per maund during her lifetime and after her death a yearly amount equal to the assessment of the two lands to the heirs of expires. The respondent claimed that he was entitled to the whole compensation money as the tenants rights had ceased by forfeiture for non payment of rents. The trial court refused to interfere with the discretion of the trial judge in granting relief against forfeiture but observed that the defendants having obtained relief against the forfeiture thrice before should not expect to get it for a fourth time if they again made default in the payment, and that without prejudice to the above contentions he should be granted relief against forfeited. On appeal by special leave: Held, that section III (g) of the , as amended in 1929 embodied a principle of justice, equity and good conscience which must be held to govern even agricultural leases and where there was a forfeiture by denial of the landlord 's title a notice in writing determining the lease was necessary. It is not safe to say that the court must and will always insist upon certain things when the Act does not require them, and the facts of some unforeseen case may make the court wish it had kept a free hand. If the purpose of the rule as to notice is to indicate the intention of the lessor to determine the lease and to avail himself of the tenant`s breach of covenant it could as effectively be achieved by an oral intimation as by a written one without in any way disturbing the mind of a chancery judge. That it was not so was apparent from the circumstance that the requirement of a notice under writing to complete a forfeiture has been dispensed with by the legislature in respect to leases executed prior to 1929 or even prior to the coming into force of the Act or to leases made between 1882 and 1930 the principle of equity applicable is the one contained in sub section (g), as it then stood. The law in India and England on this subject was not the same and it could not be said that this sub section enacts or enunciates any general principle of Equity, equity & good conscience and according to it the institution of a suit for ejectment would be sufficient indication on the part of the ' landlord for determination of the lease. The rights and obligations under those leases have to be determined according to the rules of law prevailing at the time and the only rule applicable seems to be that a tenant cannot by his unilateral act and by his own wrong determine the leasehold unless the lessor gives an indication by some unequivocal expression of intention on his part of taking advantage of the breach. On no principle of equitable justice is a tenant entitled to a notice for determining a lease for nonpayment of rent under section 114 of the and that if at the date relief is asked for the position has been altered so that relief cannot be given without causing injury to third parties relief will be refused, but if that position is not altered so, no injustice will be done there is no real discretion and the court should make the order and give the relief.

Section 7D of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 as amended by Act 35 of 1969 provides that certain persons occupying land for not less than ten years to be deemed tenants notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in section 52 or any other provision of the , shall be deemed to be a tenant if he or his predecessor in interest was in occupation of such land on the 11th day of April, 1957, on the basis of that deed, notwithstanding the fact that the lease was granted by a person who had no right over the land or who was not competent to lease the land. The High Court took the view that the benefit of section would apply only to persons whose occupa tion of the private forests or unsurveyed lands had a lawful origin in the sense that they had either bona fide believed the lands to be Government 's lands of which they could later seek assignment or had taken the lands on lease from persons whom they bona fide believing to be competent to grant such leases or had come into posses sion with the intention of attorning to the lawful owners or on the par ties of arrangements like varam etc. which were only in the nature of licences and fell short of a leasehold right. It was not within the contemplation of the legisla ture to confer the benefit Of protection on persons who had wilfully trespassed upon lands belonging to others and whose occupation was unlawful in its origin. The expression "in occupation" occurring in section 7D must be construed as meaning "in lawful occupation". In the present case, the finding of fact entered by the High Court is that the appellant had come in possession of the lands by trespass. His plea before the Courts below was that he was himself the owner of the area having acquired title to it by adverse possession. In such circumstances the High court was in error in holding that the appel lant was not entitled to the protection of section 7 D. The appeal, therefore, must be dismissed.

The appellant was found in possession of the goods on 21 4 1967. On opening them six of them were found to contain cigarette lighters of "Imco Triplex Junior" and "Made in Austria". Each of the six boxes were tightly packed with jute cloth and secured by iron strips. The remaining five boxes contained 50 sealed tins of flints for cigarettelighters which bore the following writing: "Tego Lighter Flints of Superior Quality Made in Germany". On opening they, six of these boxes were found written "Dubai" and 'Made ' in West Germany" inscribed on them. A panchnama was prepared before Panchas. Section 9(1) of the Wild Life Protection Act, 1972 provides that no person shall "hunt" any wild animal Specified in Schedule T. 2 (16) in a comprehensive manner: "2(16) 'hunting with its grammatical variations and cognate expressions, includes. (a) capturing killing. poisoning. snaring and trapping of any wild animals and every attempt to do so (b) driving any wild Animal for any of the purposes specified in sub clause (a). 51 of the Act provides for penalties. 9(2) is an offence under sec. No court shall take cognizance of any offence against this Act except on the complaint of the Chief wild Life Warden or such other officer as the State Government may authorise in this behalf. " What emerges from a perusal of these provisions is that cognizance of an offence against the "Act" can be taken by a Court only on the complaints of the officer metioned in Sec. In these circumstances even if the jurisdictional police purported to register a case for an alleged offence against, Sec. 210(1), would not be attracted having regard to the position that cognizance could only be taken on the report of the Officer mentioned in that section. Even where a Magistrate takes cognisance of an offences instituted otherwise than on a police report and an investigation by the police is in progress in relation to the same offence, the two cases do not lose their separate indentity. The section seeks to obviate the anomalies that might arise from taking cognisance more than once. But, where as here cognisance can be take only in one way and that on the complainant of a particular statutory functionary there is no scope or occasion for taking cogn cognizance more than Once and, accordingly, Section 210 has no role to play. The view taken by the High Court on the footing1g of section 210 is unsupportable. It cannot be said that the complaint does not spell out the ingrediants of the offence alleged. A complaint only means any allegation made orally or in writing to a Magistrate with a view to his taking action, that some person, whether known or unknown. has 'committed an offence. P.C. which saves the inherent power of the High court, to make such orders as may be necessary to prevent abuse of the process of any Court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice, has to be exercised sparingly and with circumspection. In exercising that jurisdiction the High Courts would not embark upon and enquiry whether the allegations in the complaint are likely to be established by evidence or not.

The law in its majestic equality, forbids the rich as well the poor to sleep under bridges, to beg in the streets and to steal bread, lampooned Anatole France. The reality of this caricature of equal justice under the law, whereby the poor are priced out of their liberty in the market, is the grievance of the petitioner. His criminal appeal pends in this Court and he has obtained an order for bail in his favour "to the satisfaction of the Chief Judicial Magistrate". The direction of this Court did not spell out the details of the bail, and so the magistrate ordered that a surety hl a sum of Rs. 10,000/ be produced which, in actual impact, was a double denial of the Bail benefit. For one thing the miserable mason. the petitioner before us could not afford to procure that huge sum or manage manage a surety of sufficient prosperity. Affluents do not hefriend indigents. For another, the magistrate made an odd order refusing to accept the suretyship of the Petitioner 's brother because he and his assets were in another district. If mason and millionaire were treated alike, egregious inegality is an increditability. Likewise geographic allergy at the judicial level makes mockery of equal protection of the laws within the territory of India. India is one and not a conglomeration of districts, untouchably apart. When this Court 's order for release was thus frustrated by magisterial intransigence the prisoner moved this Court again to modify the original order "to that extent that petitioner be released on furnishing surety to the tune of Rs 2,000 or on executing a personal bond or pass any other order or direction as this Hon 'ble Court may deem fit and proper". From this factual matrix three legal issues arise ( 1 ) Can the court under the Code of Criminal Procedure enlarge, on his own bond without sureties, a person undergoing incarceration for a non bailable offence either as undertrial or as convict who has appealed or sought special leave ? (2) If the Court decides to grant bail with sureties, what criteria should guide it in quantifying the amount of bail and (3) Is it within the power of the court to reject a surety because he or his estate is situate in a different district or State ? This formulation turns the focus on an aspect of liberty bearing on bail jurisprudence. The victims, when suretyship is insisted on or heavy sums are demanded by way of bail or local bailors alone are presona grata, may well be the weaker segments of society like the proletariatariat, the linguistic and other minorities and distant denizens from the far corners or our country with its vast diversity. In fact, the grant of bail can be stultified or made retrospec tively and expensive if the court is powerless to dispense with surety or to receive an Indian bailor across the district borders as good or the sum is so excessive that to procure a wealthy surety may be both exasperating and expensive. The problem is plainly one of the human rights, especially freedom vis a vis the lowly. This poignant import of the problem persuaded the Chamber Judge to invite the Supreme Court Bar Association and the Citizens for Democracy to assist the Court in decoding the Code and its provisions regarding bail. There is already a direction for grant of an bail by this Court in favour of the petitioners and so, the merits of that matter do not have to be examined now. That is why we have decided to examine the question from a wider perspective bearing in mind prisoner 's rights in an * Justice V. Social Justice is the signature tune of our Constitution and the little man in peril of losing his liberty is the consumer of social justice. There are several considerations which deter an accused from running away from justice and risk of financial loss is only one of them and that too not a major one.

The assessee had advanced Rs. 3,21,460 to another concern, the Bombay Fine Worsted Manufacturers ' Castle Mills. In the assessment year 1951 52, the assessee claimed under section 15C of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, exemption from tax in respect of 6% of the capital employed in 'Eldee ' as a newly established undertaking and sought to include in the computation of the Capital so employed Rs.3,21460 advanced to 'Castle '. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim but the Appellate Assistant Commissioner modified the assessment and directed in clusion of the amount advanced to the assessee in the calculation of capital invested for the purpose of 429 section 15 C. An application submitted under section 66(1) of the Act to the Tribunal to refer a question which it was contended by the Commissioner arose out of the order of the Tribunal was rejected and the petition of the Commissioner under section66(2) for an order directing the Tribunal 'to state the case and refer it to the High Court was also dismissed. With special leave, the Commissioner appealed to this Court. The question in dispute before the revenue authorities was whether the business called 'Cartle ' at Bombay was a branch of the assessee. Held: (i) Under section 66 (2) invests the High court with jurisdiction to require the Appellate Tribunal to state a case and to refer it, if the Appellate Tribu nal has misdirected itself in law in arriving at its finding. The refusal of the tribunal on the view that a question of law does not arise out of tho order is not conclusive. The High Court has the power merely to advise the Tribunal on questions of law arising out of an order of Tribunal. Such a question may arise out Of the findings of the Tribu als, and also if the Tribunal has misdirected himself in law, arriving at a finding, it cannot be regarded as a finding not giving rise to a question liable to be referred to the Court. Non inclusion of the income of 'Ctastle" in the assessment of the asses see may have been a relevant circumstance, but its effect had to be considered in the light of other circumstances on which the Appellate Assist ant Commissioner had relied.

The Minister in charge of Irrigation Department was directed to file his personal affidavit. In the writ petition filed by him, Duggal respondent challenged the notification dated January 29, 1974 fixing the seniority of the engineers n the Irrigation Department of the Punjab Government. During the course of the hearing of the writ peti tion, an order was made by the High Court on November 18, 1974 that the Minister concerned might give a personal hearing to the parties and thereafter pass the necessary order in the matter. The Minister concerned thereafter heard the parties, and made a speaking order on February 18, 1975 affirming the earlier seniority list. The writ petition was then amended and 97 in the amended petition. Dugdgal respondent also challenged the validity of the later order of February 18 , 1975. At the resumed hearing of this appeal before this Court, the Advocate General for the State of Punjab has contended that looking to the facts of the case if the High court came to the conclusion that the minister was a necessary or proper party, this Court should not interfere in the matters. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The direction for impleading of the Minister as a party was given by the Supreme Court with a view to apprise the Minister of the allegations made in the petition and thus to afford him an opportunity of controverting those allegations, if he so deemed proper. Taking the totality of the facts and circumstances of the ease, this court does not feel persuaded to interfere with the order of the High Courts adding the Minister ' as a respondent to the writ Petition. [97E F] 2. The High Court was in error in directing that the Secretary concerned should file his affidavit. It is essentially for the Minister to decide in the light of the allegation made in petition as to whether he should or should not file an affidavit.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant. An application was made by the Cantonment Executive Officer, Ambala, on January 7, 1960 for realisation of a sum of Rs. 64950 from the respondent under section 259 of the Act on the ground that the amount was due as arrears of rent on the basis of a lease in favour of the respondent. The Magistrate held that he had jurisdiction and issued warrants for attachment of the movable property of the Respondent on June 13, 1961. Thereupon the respondent went in revision to the Sessions Judge, Ambala contending that the magistrate had no jurisdiction to realise the arrears of rents due under a lease under section259 of the Cantonment Act and in any case that could not be done without taking into account the objections of the respondents. The Sessions Judge accepted the view of the Sessions judge and set aside the order of the Magistrate dated June 13. 1961. The High Court having refused the certificate, the appellant obtained special leave from this Court. It was urged on behalf of the appel lant that the Magistrate acting under section 260 of the , acts as a persona designata and therefore his order under that section is not revisable under sections 435/439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and the Sessions Court and the High Court had no jurisdic tion under those provisions to interfere with such an order. ^ HELD: (i) Section 259 does not bar the right of the Board as an owner or holder of land and buildings to take action for recovery of rent thereof by suit under the general law of the land is not taken away by the section. It may be that the section provides for recovery by suit also and as such it wilI not be possible for the Board to recover rent of its land and building by suit for such rents are entirely outside the section and the right to recover it is ultimately traceable to the Act inasmuch as this liability has arisen by reason of the exercise of a power exercised or performance of duty by the Board under express provisions of the statute and the Rules. [345 D E] (ii) Section 258 provides that in the event of non compliance with the terms of any notice, order or requisition issued to any person under this Act, or any rule or bye law made thereunder requiring such person to execute any work or to do any act, it shall be lawful for the Cantonment Authority after giving notice in writing to such person, to take such action or such steps as may be necessary for the completion of the act or work required to be done or executed by him, and all the expenses incurred on such account shall be recoverable by the board.

The appellant was appointed as a section salesman and his services were controlled by the head office through its territory office situated in Delhi. The various correspondence and other evidence produced before the Labour Court showed that the appel lant is required to send reports about the publicity and advertisement of placing posters, holders, cinema slides and suggest means to canvass the sale in this area. Some of the documents relate to matters of publicity in melas, some relate to the existing position of the stock of the goods of the company in the area and the action taken to ameliorate stocks. It was not the duty of the appellant to procure orders for the company. None of the salesmen were employed to sell the product of the Company in any particular area or collecting the sale proceeds and depositing the same with the Company. However, the Tribunal noted that the appellant was required to supervise the work of the local salesmen and local travelling salesmen appointed in the areas of his operation as well but it was only incidental to his main function of canvassing and promoting the sale of the product in the four districts allotted to him. On these facts found, the Tribu nal came to the conclusion that the termination of the services of the appe lant by the respondent company was legal and justified and if not to what relief he was entitled to. It is against this order the appeal was filed. In order to come within the definition of workman under the Industrial Disputes Act as it stood in the year 1973 when the appellant 's service was terminated, the employee has to be under the employment to do the work for one of the types of work referred to in the section i.e. manual, skilled and/or clerical in nature. The finding of the Tribun al on the nature of the work is a finding on a question of fact and it is also borne out by the document produced before t he Labour Court. It would not have interfered with that finding had this Court differed from the Labour court on the question whether the appellant is a workman. In the light of the holding that the is not applicable to him, and in view of the fact that a long period of over 16 years has passed it would be unjust to leave the appellant without any remedy at this stage. [474A B] Burmah Shell Oil Storage & Distribution Company vs Burmah Colliery Management and Staff; , ; D.S. Nagraj vs Labour Officer, Kamal and others, 1973 F.J. (42) P. 440, J. Dechane Distributor vs State 476 of Kerala and others; , referred to.

The appellant Company entered into a contract of lease with the Gwalior State Government (Sanitary Engineering Department) for a period of one year in Samvat 1999. The lease was extended for a further period of ten years subject to payment of enhanced rent as agreed upon between the parties. Since proceedings were initiated on 16.7.1952 to eject the Company, the Company filed Suit No. 14 of 1960 for declaration of title and perpetual injunction. Issue No. 1(1) in that suit was in the following words: "Whether the plaintiff in accordance with paras 5 & 6 of the plaint was a `gair Maurusi tenant ' and now by virtue of the Revenue Administration and Ryotwari Land Revenue and Tenancy Act Samvat 2007 has become a `Pakka Tenant '. If so, what is its effect on the suit?" That issue was answered in the negative. The High Court held that the Company was not a 'pakka ' tenant ' within the meaning of section 181 read with section 2(h) and was, therefore, not liable to be proceeded against in terms of section 182. Allowing the appeal by the State, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Section 182 of the Code is attracted. That section reads: "182. Rights and liabilities of Government lessee (1) A Government lessee may be ejected from his land by order of a Revenue Officer on one or more of the following grounds, namely: (i) that he has failed to pay the rent for a Period of three months from the date on which it became due; or (ii) that the term of his lease has expired or (iv) that, he has contravened any of the terms and conditions of the grant: Provided that no order for ejectment of a Government lessee under this sub section shall be passed without giving him an opportunity of being heard in his defence". It was in terms thereof that the company was not 'a pakka tenant ' as found by the High Court in the earlier judgement, and, therefore it was, according to the said Act, an ordinary tenant. The finding of the Additional Collector is a finding of fact based on evidence and is not liable for be questioned in these proceedings. His finding shows that large amounts are due and payable by the Company as rent and that the rents have remained unpaid for a long period far in excess of three month from the dates on which they became due. In the circumstances, the impugned Order of the High court dated 20.9.1980 in Misc. Petition No 84 of 1978 is set aside. The Order of Additional Collector dated 1.10.1977 in Case No.1 75 76A 39: 182 shall stand restored.

The Orissa Land Reforms Act 16 of 1960 received the assent of the President on October 17, 1960. By section 1(3) of the principal Act it was provided that the Act shall come into force in whole or in part on such date or dates as the Government may from time to time by notification appoint and different dates may be appointed for different provisions of the Act. By a notification issued on September 25, 1968 certain provisions of an Act other than those contained in Chs. III and IV were brought into force. By Act 13 of 1965 amendments were made in the principal Acts : the expressions "ceiling area" and "privileged raiyat" were defined by clauses (5) & 24 of section 24 and the expression "classes, of land" was defined in section 2(5 a). The original Chs., III andIV of the Principal Act were deleted and were substituted by fresh provisions. Nothing need be said about the amendments made in Ch. IV because in these groups of appeals the validity of these provisions is not in issue. It may suffice to say that Ch. III (sections 24 to 36) as amended deals with the right of the landlord to resume land for personal cultivation, the extent of that right, and the proceedings for resumption of land. Chapter IV as amended dealt with the preparation and publication of draft statement showing ceiling and surplus lands by the Revenue Officer and section 44 provided for payment of compensation at a rate which is less than the market value of the land falling within the ceiling limit as originally fixed under 1960, and section 52 imposes a ceiling on future acquisitions. It was provided thereby: 5 96 "The foregoing provisions of this Chapter shall, A mutatis mutandis, apply where lands acquired and held under personal cultivation subsequent to the commencement of this Act by any person through inheritance, request, gift, family settlement, purchase or otherwise together with the lands 'in his personalcultivation at the time of such acquisition exceeds his ceiling limit. By the amendment made in section 1 (3) the expression 'law in force ' must be "construed only in the constitutional sense and not in the sense of its actual operativeness", and on that account it must be held that "there was a ceiling limit already provided by the principal ' Act as it was 'law ' in force" within the meaning of that expression as used in the second proviso to article 31 A. By virtue of section 45 of the said Act "the interests of the person to whom the surplus lands relate and of all land holders mediately or immediately under whom the excess lands were being held stand extinguished and the lands vest absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances". The State of Orissa amended the principal act by Act 13 Of 1965 which provided for compensation not based on the marketvalue of the lands failing within the Ceiling limit as initially fixed under section 47. Section 45 provided for settlement of surplus lands vested in the Govern ment under section 45 with persons as raiyats in the order of priority mentioned therein and section 51 imposes a Ceiling on future acquisition acquisitions. The Act was amended by Act 15 of 1965 which came into force on July 1, 1949. By an amendment made by the Constitution (Seventeenth Amendment) Act, 1964 it was clearly enacted that under any law which provides for the acquisition by the State of any land in an estate in the personal cultivation of a person is guaranteed by the second Proviso only where the land is within the maximum limit applicable to him under any laws for the time being in force. On the plain words of the proviso the law prescribing the ceiling limits must be in force at the date of acquisition. In order that property may be validly acquired compulsory the law must provide for the transfer of ownership or right to possession of any property to the State or to a corporation owned or controlled by the state, and by virtue of s. 45 of Act the rights of the Land holders were sought to be extinguished or modified.

A deed of surrender was executed by a Hindu widow to recover 341 possession of the properties belonging to the last male owner during the lifetime of the widow from persons who acquired title to the same by adverse possession against the widow. The widow 's estate was in this case completely extinguished by adverse Possession exercised by the defendants, and she had, in fact, no interest left in her which she could make a surrender of in favour of the reversions. It is true that a surrender may and in the majority of cases does take the form of transfer, e.g., when the widow conveys the entire estate of her husband without consideration and not as a mere device to share the estate with the reversioner, in favour Of the latter, but reservation of such small benefit absolutely necessary for her maintenance does not invalidate a surrender as has been held by the Privy Council in Sreeramulu vs Kristamma (I.L.R. , referred to. Held, further, that where there is no necessity for alienation, the interest which she herself holds and which she can convey to others, is not an indefeasible life estate but an estate liable to be defeated on the happening of certain events which in Hindu law cause extinction of the widows 's Estate in the same way as if she suffered physical or civil death, there isno conceivable reason why the reversioner should not subject to any question of fraud or collusion that might arise, be in a position to recover possession of properties from (1) Vide Vaidyanatha vs Savithri, I.L .R. Surrender is not alienation and as the reversioner does not derive his title from her, there was no principle of law under which the acts of the wife could bind him.

The petitioners were plaintiffs. They instituted a suit in a representative capacity under Order 1 rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the Court of the Additional Senior Sub Judge, Barnala for a declaration that they were the owners in posses sion of the suit land along with some others, that the Gram Panchayat Mehal Kalan, Tehsil Barnala, District Sangrur in the State of Punjab (the Panchayat) had no sort of right in the suit lands and that the suit property had been wrongly shown as belonging to the Panchayat by the entries made in the revenue records which were not binding on the plaintiffs and for an injunction restraining the Panchayat from interfering with their possession. The Panchayat filed a revision petition before the High Court of Punjab and Haryana in Civil Revision Petition No. 571 of 1986. The learned Judge who heard the Revision petition came to the conclusion that the issues involved in the case were not triable by a civil court by virtue of section 11 read with section 13 of the Act and accordingly he held that the Suit was not maintainable before the civil Court. Aggrieved by the said finding recorded by the trial court, the Panchayat filed an appeal before the Punjab andHaryana High Court which came to be conclusion that since the question involved in this suit was simply one of title to the suit Land and it was not necessary to decide whether the suitland was shamlat deh or not and whether the land had validly vested in the Panchayat or not being shamlat, it had jurisdiction to try the suit. Aggrieved, the petitioners preferred this petition under Article 136 of the Constitution of India requesting the Court to grant leave to prefer an appeal against the decision of the High court. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The above decision is clearly distinguishable from the present case since in this case the Panchayat which had been impleaded as a defendant had raised the plea that the land in question belonged to it as shamlat k deh and that it had been vested in it. It will not be possible in the circumstances for the civil court to make a declaration in favour of the plaintiffs without deciding the question whether the property in question was shamil deh or whether it belonged to the Gram Panchayats or not. Reliance was however placed by the learned counsel for the petitioners on a decision of Punjab & Haryana High Court in Bhagu and Ors., vs Ram Sarup and Ors, [1985] Punjab Law Journal Page 366 in which the suit had been held to be maintainable in a civil Court even though the defendant had contended that the said land belonged to him or that it did not belong to the Village Panchayat.

The respondent Electricity Board issued a notice to the appellant Electricity Board under section 49(1) of the Andhra Pradesh State Electricity Board General Conditions of Supply Regulations, 1981 for supply of electricity to a person. The appellant Board did not pay the consumption deposit or additional consumer deposit within 15 days from the date the demand notice if there be any delay in payment, the consumer was obliged to pay surcharge thereon equal to 1 1/2% per month or such other percentage to be fixed by the Board from time to time, of the demanded amount for each month of delay or part thereof. The deposit was liable to be reviewed by the Electricity Board fromtime to time and having regard to the factors mentioned in the said clause, it was submitted that regulation 7 of the Orissa State Electricity board General Conditions Of Supply Regulations 1981 providing that no interest would be payable on security deposit is just and reasonable and is not arbitrary or violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. On behalf of the appellant Board it was contended: (i) The Electricity Board has power to demand additional security but the average consumption of three months should be taken as the basis for calculating the amount of such security; (ii) The clause relating to non payment of interest on the amounts due to the Board is in the form of cash for one month and bank or insurance guarantee for two months. The rate of interest payable on fixed deposit because the nature and character of a security deposit was basically different from fixed deposit. The consumption deposit cannot be equated to the deposit in a bank and interest could be demanded as of right; (iii) The Board is clearly in the position of a trustee in respect of this money since the money is deposited by the consumer in trust with the Board to secure the Board against default in payment of electricity bills, and therefore, it is not in dispute that the prevention and eradication of smuggling was a proper and legally attainable objective and that this is sought to be achieved by the relevant law; (iv) The respondent Board has fixed the period of security deposit equal to the amount payable for each day 's consumption of electricity estimated for a period of approximately three months, but that would depend upon the billing cycle adopted by the Haryana State Electricity Boards. State Electricity Electricity Board AIR 1 990 Andhra Pradesh 58 at pages 68 69 it was observed: "It is also stated by the board that huge sums are required by it as rotating capital; that it borrows large amounts from organisations like L.I.C. and Banks; that It pays interest to them, and that in such circumstances it is well entitled to require the consumer to co operate by paying their bills regularly, by giving security deposits, and by conforming to the terms and conditions of supply. The liability of Electricity Board to pay interest on security deposited is hardly sufficient to secure payment to the respondent Board for violation of any condition of supply in the context of wide scale theft of energy, tampering with the meters and such other methods adopted by them; (v) The said consumption security deposit serves not only to securing the interest of the Board for any such violation but should serve as a deterrent on the consumer, in discharging his obligations towards the Board.

The recruitment to the different cadres in the Telecommuni cation Research Centre was later discontinued.) (b) by transfer of Group A Field Officers recruited through the Union Public Service Commission by written examination followed by an interview, (These officers belong ing to this category. They were recruited in four batches in 1965, 1967, 1970 and 1973. The Class I posts in the P & T Department consisted of the following posts: 1. Director (Senior Adminstrative Grade Level I) 2. Additional Director (Junior Administrative Grade Level II 3. Assistant Directors (Senior Class I). The Posts of Deputy Directors, Assistant Directors and S.T.Os Grade I are filled by the following methods: 1010 (a) by direct recruitment through the union Public Service Commis sion, (the petitioners belong to this Category; (b)(i) by promotion from Group A field Officers recruited by the Union P &T Directorate, and (ii) by transfers of Group B Field Officers who are Posts and Telegraphs departmental promotees belonging to the Indian Telecommunications Service Group. The direct recruits to which category the peti tioners belong were not given any Special Pay in these grades and they are given only the pay at the pay scales prescribed for them. It is stated that the total number of officers who are getting Special Pay is of the order while only about 25 officers who arc direct recruits working in the telecommuni tation Research centre are not given Special Pay paid to the others holding the same posts. A number of representations had been made earli er by the direct recruits but all in vain. It appears that at the official meeting held in May, 1979 with Shri J.A. Dave Secretary, Communications, Government of India there was consensus on the question of granting of Special Pay to the direct recruit as in the case of transferred officers as can be seen from the letter written by the Association on the petitioners (Annexure XIX) and that the Director Tele communication Research Centre also recommended for granting Special Pay accordingly. Dismissing the petitions, this Court, HELD: 1(a) The first question relating to denial of promotional opportunities to the petitioners according to the Recruitment Rules is left open to be decided by the Central Administrative Tribunal. The appellant was employed as a munshi in the appellant 's Bidi factor at Bhandara. The appellant had framed a charge sheet against him in respect of certain acts of misconduct, gross negligence of duty, insubordination etc. on May 13, 1965. An enquiry in respect thereof was held on May 15th after receipt of written statement from Nathu. Holding that the charges levelled against him were proved, the employer dismissed the third respondent with effect from August 1, 1965 and the said respondent filed an application challenging the order of dismissal before the Labour Court under section 78(1)D of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946 on the 5th August. His complaint was that the charge sheet was not proper, that the Head Office of the appellant had no authority to deal with his case under the Standing Orders, that no evidence was allowed or filed on behalf of the employer and that the finding was based only on his statement and in particular his cross examination. He had been forced to append his signature to a certain paper without the same having been read over to him. The Labour Court after holding an enquiry took the view that the findings of the enquiry officer were perverse, that it was not necessary for an employee first to approach the employer or to follow the procedure laid down in section 42(4) including the proviso before he could apply to the Labour court for relief under section 7 8 (1) D.P.C., and directed reinstatement of the third Respondent with all back wages.

The contesting respondents had been occupying the property under a registered lease for a period of 20 years which expired on 31.7.1971. They served a notice on the appellants claiming the right to contin ue in possession after 31.07.1971 as tenants from month to month. The appellants did not accept the claim and filed before Munsif, Ranchi a case purporting to be an application under section 12 of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Evic tion) Control Act, 1947. The respondents contested the application and raised several points in defence which were rejected by the trial court. The Judicial Commissioner agreed with the findings of the trial Court on merits and concluded in paragraph 48 of thejudg ment thus: "In view of the findings in the case, it is not necessary to deal with this aspect now. Apart from pleading that the application under sec tion 12 was not maintainable and the allegations contained therein were incorrect, the respondents also stated that the heirs of late S.N. Ganguli had formed a partnership as a result of which a new month to year tenancy was created, and the respondents, therefore, were not liable to eviction. The parties differed on several questions of fact which, in view of findings of fact in the ease, it was not necessary for them to be detailed. The trial court accepted the appellants ' case that they are the successors in interest of the lessor company, and that being so, according to the terms of the deed of lease (Ext. 4) 1 have no hesitation in saying that the deed is subsisting and the parties are having the relationship of lessors and lessees and also landlords and tenants respectively. No month to day to month tenan cy had been created. " The respondents filed a regular appeal from the decision before the District Judge, Ranchi designated as Judicial Commis sioner, and he also went into the entire controversy thoroughly. Both the parties led full evidence both oral and documentary and the case was tried by the learned Munsif in the same manner as the trial of an eviction suit. The judgment of the High Court indicates that the scope in which the argu ments by the parties were addressed was the same as in a second appeal, and it was therefore not open to the High court to reverse them under section 100 C.P.C. The question is whether the petition which was filed by the appellants as an application u/s 12 should be treated as a plaint and the impugned proceeding as the one in a suit followed by an appeal and a second appeals. With the assistance of learned counsel for the par ties, we have gone through the relevant papers in the instant case and are satisfied that both the parties dealt with every aspect of the case from their respective angles elaborately, and led their full evidence, both oral & documentary. On the disputed issues of fact between the parties, the proceeding arising out of the appellant 's application before the learned Munsiff should be held as a suit and his decision as a decree. It has to be kept in mind that it is the same court before which both a suit under section 11 and an application U/s 13 are to be filed. The High Court while deciding the disputed questions in favour of the present appellants instead of confirming the decree of 977 the Munsif directed them to file a fresh application u /s 12(3) for a formal decree of eviction. In view of these circumstances, it would be helpful to examine the provisions of the section 12 which is quoted below: "12. Extension of period limited by lease. (1) If a tenant in possession of any building held on a lease for specified period, in tends to extend the period limited thereby, he may give the landlord at least one month before the expiry of the period covered by the original lease subject to a maximum of one year.

The appellant a registered Society filed the suit out of which this appeal arises in the court of the District Judge, Jaipur City. The counsel engaged by the appellant were Sri Satya Narain Sharma and Sri Shyam Bihari Agarwal. The suit was later transferred to the Court of Additional Dis trict Judge No. 1, Jaipur city where it was renumbered as Suit No. 116 of 1974. After the institution of the suit, an election of the office bearers of the Society was held on 1.6.1973 and according to the appellant 's case one Sri Laxman Das Swami was elected as the Secretary. On 4.9.74 a prayer for withdrawing the suit was made by one Hari Narain Swami through another lawyer claiming to have been elected as Secretary of the society. In support of his claim, he had produced certain documents on the basis of which the Trial Court allowed the suit to be withdrawn. According to the case of the appellant, Hari Narain Pandit was not elected as a Secretary and had no locus standi to withdraw the suit. Since no notice was given of his application for withdrawal of the Suit either to the then Secretary Laxman Das Mahant Swami or to the learned advocates Sri Satya Narayan Sharma or Sri Shyam Sunder Agarwal, through whom the suit had been instituted, none of them had any knowledge of the order passed by the Court.

The appellant was charged along with the accused Nos. 2, 3, 5 and 6 with having on or about July 11, 1953 transferred by sale 10 High Denomination Bank Notes of the Denomination of Rs. 1,000 each to one Velji Lakhamshi Joshi for Rs.1,800 at the rate of Rs 180 per note and thus contravened the provisions of section 4 of the Ordinance read with section 109 Of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court acquitted both the accused persons but convicted them under section 7 read with s.4 thereof and sentenced each to pay a fine of Rs 8,000 and in default suffer six months ' rigorous imprisonment and the co accused of the offence with which they had been charged were awarded varying sentences of fine with which however we are not concerned. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that Ordinance promulgated under the emergency powers vested in the Governor General under section 72 Of the 9th Sch. of the Government of India Act, 1935, and that as soon as the declaration that the emergency was at an end was made on April 1, 1946, the original position was restored and the Ordinance in question which had been promulgated in exercise of the emergency power ipso facto lapsed when the emergency is declared to have ended, (b) that in the alternative, section 72. Of the Act having been thus restored with effect from April 1 1946, one must look to its terms as they originally stood to justify the continuance of the ordinance in question after April 1 9, 1946 and therefore on the expiration of that period, viz., on the 1st April 1946, Ordinances made after the passing of the Act automatically came to an end. Held: (i) The Ordinance in dispute having been promulgated during the period between June 27, 1940 and April 1. 1946, was perpetual in duration and continued in force until it was repealed; (ii) that the Ordinance lapsed or ceased to be in operation on July 11. 1953, the date on which the offence in question was committed by the appellant and the appellant was rightly convicted by both the courts below.

Section 302 I.P.C., read with section 354(3) of the Criminal Procedure Code, demands special reasons for awarding the graver sentence, and to borrow the reasoning in Rajendra Prasad 's case that death sentence on death sentence is Parliament 's function. Interpretative non application of death sentence when legislative alternatives exist are within judicial jurisdiction. The onerous option to spare the lives of the appellants to be spent in prison or to hand them over to the hangman to be jettisoned out of terrestrial life into "the, undiscovered country from whose bourn no traveller returns" is the crucial function this Court has to exercise in the present appeal. Sir Winston Churchill, in his oft quoted observation, said: The mood and temper of the public with regard to the treatment of crime and criminals is one of the most unfailing tests of the civilization of any country. " In the case on hand, the High Court analysed the evidence liberally applied the rule of benefit of doubt and climaxed its judgments with sentences of death and imprisonment for life on the various accused who were eventually held guilty. On appeal by special leave it was contended that life imprisonment which strictly means imprisonment for the whole of the man 's life, but in practice amounts to incarceration for a period between 10 and 14 years may, at the option of the convicting court, be subject to the condition that the sentence of imprisonment shall last as long as life lasts where there are exceptional indications of murderous recidivism and the community cannot run the risk of the convict being at large. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. A decision on a question of sentence depending upon the facts and circumstances of a particular case, can never be regarded as a binding precedent, much less 'law declared ' within the meaning of article 141 of the Constitution so as to bind all Courts within the territory of India. An inferential finding of facts is the inference which the Judge draws from the direct or perceptible facts, (ii) statements of the principles of law applicable to the legal problems disclosed by the facts; and (iii)judgment based on the combined effect of (i) and (ii), above. [1069 A B] 2. When a sentence of death is passed it is subject to confirmation by the High court under section 366(1) of Cr. P.C.

The appellant was in service upto 30th April 1958 when he was prematurely retired. The appellant claimed that he had worked to the entire satisfaction of his immediate superior officers and higher authorities and had earned a number of certificates highly appreciative of his work. He also alleged that there had been an enquiry in 1949 by Shri A. K. Bose, Deputy Director of Investigation, who was appointed by the Commissioner of Income tax as the Inquiring Officer. The preliminary enquiry had been conducted by Shri G. section Srivastava, Inspecting Assistant Commissioner of Incometax, Meerut. That first charge was that he made various investments in the name of various members of his family far in excess of and disproportionate to the known sources of his income. His high standard of living and expenditure were also mentioned there. The third and last charge gave particulars of thirteen assessment cases in which the appellant was alleged to be either "grossly negligent, careless, inefficient, and/or corrupt in the performance of his duties as Income tax Officer". The appellant 's defences included confused nature of charges characterised by him as "vague, over lapping, intermingled" and wrongly joined together. He further pleaded that there has been an inquiry in 1949, by Shri R. N. Srivastava, Asstt. Inspecting Commissioner, into some of the matters mentioned in the charges, and about others in 1952 by Shri S. Srivastava and another Inspecting Assistant Commissioners, who were pursuing the appellant for some unknown reason which he did not find anywhere. The questions raised by the appellant depended on findings of fact. All relevant facts had been examined by the officer who held the enquiry and by the punishing authority. No mala fides against either the Inquiring Officers, Shri A R. K., Bose, Dy. Director Investigation, or against the punishing Authority was alleged. There were, however, suggestions that Shri G section Srivastava and Shri R N. Singh, Inspecting Asstt. Commissioner, were pursuing their appellant for certain unknown reasons which we do not find mentioned anywhere. On 4th March, 1971, the High Court refused the certificate of fitness of the case for appeal to this Court observed that questions had been attempted to be raised before it in asking for certification which had not been argued at the time when the first appeal was heard by the High court. The two authorities cited: The State of Assam & Anr. vs J. N Roy Biswas, and R. T. Rangachari vs Secretary of State, do not help the appellant. If an inquiry is held, at a particular stage, possibly to determine whether regular proceedings should be drawn up or started, it does not debar a departmental trial. That was the nature of the previous enquiries. It appears that it is only after the appellant 'S activities had become more than notorious that further enquiry was undertaken and regular charges framed. The defence of the appellant seemed something similar to the much too common a defence of his accused in criminal trials attributing all their misfortunes to the hostility of the police. The question whether the appellant, was given a reasonable opportunity to lead evidence and to be heard or not is largely a question of fact; it is not uncommon for astute Govt. servants, facing such enquiries, to give long lists of witnesses and documents so as to either prolong an enquiry or to prepare grounds for future litigation. Unless the exclusion of evidence is of a kind which amounts to a denial of natural justice or would have affected the final decision it could not be material. In the case before this Court, it has not even been shown how the witnesses whose production was said to have been disallowed could help the appellants ' case on specific charges. Indeed, it was for the appellant to satisfy the departmental authorities which had looked into the case upto its final stages, that he suffered some injustice which to be set right. The plea that the appellant has been subjected to trial on allegations which had been the subject matter of previous enquiries overlooks that no charge was framed as a result of any previous enquiry.

The appellants were the last purchasers of manganese ore within the State of Andhra Pradesh. The appellants contended before the Sales Tax authorities that their sales of manga nese ore to the Mines and Minerals Trading Corporation in short called M.M.T.C. were complete within the state of Andhra pradesh. The Sales Tax Authorities held that these contracts were intrinsically linked and connected and the sales effected were held to be sales in the course of export out of the territory of India. The High Court came to the conclusion that the appellants were not the last purchaser but the M. M.T.,C. was liable to pay the tax. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the State that there were six contracts and it had been the case of the appel lants that the contracts were different, and, therefore, there should be examination of five other contracts. It may be stated here that counsel for the State did not dispute that the decision in Serajuddin 's case was applied to one of the six contracts but he disputed the application of the ruling in Serrajuddin ' case to the other five contracts. The reasons given by counsel for State were these: Only one contract was referred to in the High Court. The case of M/s. Binani Bros. (P) Ltd. vs Union of India & Ors., [1975] Supp. S.C R 169, relied on. F.O.B. contracts with the manganese merchants and the S.T .C. entered into direct contract with their foreign buyers. The S. T.C., alone agreed to sell the goods to their foreign buyer and, consequently, the purchase by the merchant from the mine owner was the last purchase in the State. It had to be appreciated that quite often merchants dealing in goods which are exported out of our country enter into what is called string contracts for purchase of the goods from the factory or the mines for sale to exporters for saleto foreign buyers, and the Trading Corporations are often the only authorities allowed to export out Of their country. These corporations entering into direct contracts with their Foreign buyers for export. The directions given by the Corporations to the merchants to place the goods on board the ship were pursuant to the contracts of sale between the merchants and of the Corporation. These directions were not in the way of export, because the export sale is an independent one between the Corporation and their foreign sellers. The taking of the Goods from the merchants ' place to the ship was completely separate from the transit pursuant to export sale (See Seraj Mohammaduddin ' s case at pp. 184). In string contracts or chain contracts delivery is made by the original seller and eo instanti it is delivered in implement under each separate contract in the chain. In chain or string contracts starting between the mills or mines or factories and their immediate buyer and ending with the ultimate buyer through several intermediaries not only does the mill give and its immediate buyer take actual delivery but eoinstanti each middleman gives and takes actual delivery This process of delivery of possession goes all along the chain at the same moment when delivery is effected to the steamer. See Duni Chand Rataria vs Bhuwalka Brothers Ltd., ; , referred to.

The appellant was employed with the respondent M/s Bharat Electronics Limited as Salesman at its Delhi Sales Depot on a salary of Rs. 520 per month from 8th December, 1973. His service was abruptly terminated by letter dated 12th October 1974 with effect from 19th October, 1974. Consequent upon this termination, an industrial dispute was raised and the Delhi Administration referred the following dispute to the Labour Court for adjudication: "Whether the termination of services of Shri Mohan Lal is illegal and/or unjustified and if so, to what relief is he entitled and what directions are necessary in this respect?" As the respondent management at one stage failed to participate in the proceedings, the reference was heard ex parte and the Labour court made an award on 2nd May, 1977 directing reinstatement of the appellant with continuity of service and full back wages at the rate of Rs 520 per mensem from the date of termination till reinstatement. Subsequently, respondent moved for setting aside the ex parte award and seeking permission to participate In the proceedings which motion was granted. The respondent inter alia contended that the appellant was a salesman appointed on probation for six months and subsequently on the expiry of the initial period, the period of probation was extended upto 8th Sept., 1974 and on the expiration of this extended period of Probation, his service was terminated by letters dated 12st October, 1975, as he was not found suitable for the post to which he was appointed. The Labour Court held that the termination was neither illegal nor improper nor unjustified and the claim of the respondent was negatived. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The termination would constitute retrenchment and by a catena of decisions it is well settled that where pre requisite for valid retrenchment as laid down in section 25F has not been complied with, retrenchment bringing about termination of service is ab initio void. In other words, it does not bring about a cessation of service of the workman and the workman continues to be in service. According to him unless the workman has put in continuous service for not less than one year his case would not be governed by section 25 F.

The appellant was appointed an Inspector of Consolidation by order dated October 5, 1953 of the Settlement Commissioner of Patiala and East Punjab States Union. The appointment was on temporary basis and terminable with one month 's notice. On February 5, 1955, the appellant was served with a charge sheet setting out his mis demeanour, an enquiry was held in respect of the alleged misdemeanour and his employment was terminated because in the view of the settlement Officer with which view the Deputy Commissioner agreed. The appellant challenged the authority of the Deputy Commis sioner or the Settlement Officer to hold the enquiry and submitted a memorial to the Minister for Revenue affairs. Having failed to obtain relief, the appel lant applied to the High Court for a writ under article 226 of the Constitution quashing the order dated March 17, 1965 on the ground inter alia that the order of dismissal from service was in contravention of article 311 of the Constitu tion as no reasonable opportunity to show cause against the order. The High Court held that the appellant had been a temporary servant and had no right to hold his post he was occupying and by the impugned order the appellant 's services were terminated in exercise of authority reserved under the terms of employment, and no penalty was imposed upon him. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the protection of article 31 (2) of the Consti tution applies as much to a temporary public servant. The protection of Article 311 (2), therefore, applied as much as to a permanent public servant, but an order discharging a probationer following upon an enquiry to ascertain whether he should be confirmed is not of that nature x x x. The third proposition in the latter (Gopi Kishore Prasad 's case) refers to an enquiry into allegations of misconduct or inefficiency with a view, if they were found established, to imposing punishment and not to an inquiry whether a probationer should be confirm ed.

The State Government issued a Notification No. SRO 161 dated March 25, 1969 for selections to be made to posts of Professors in the colleges. By another Notification No,. SRO 161 HTETE dated July 25,1969 those rules were replaced by the rules made by the Governor specifically for the appointment of Professors which were called the "Jammu and Kashmir Professors of Colleges (Selection) Rules, 1969". The Commission set out the reasons for its decision and finally made its recommendation on merits. The Commission was consulted on the suitability of the candidates for promotion as Professors and the second requirement of clause (b) of sub section (2) of section 133 was also complied with. It was not provided by section 133 of the Constitution that all the members of the Commission should have interviewed all or any of the candidate, or that it was not permissible for the Commission to entrust the selection to a committee consisting of only one of its members, so long as the Commission reserved to itself the right to approve or disapprove the Committee 's report and actually discharged that constitutional responsibility. No argument to the contrary has in fact been urged for our consideration. Had the Commission de facto abdicated its power in favour of some committee composed of strangers to the Commission the position might have been different. Here, it was also not so. It would thus appear that the High Court erred in holding that the Commission was not consulted in the manner required by section133 of the constitution and that the selection made by it was invalid for that reason. With this finding the appeal by certificate is allowed.

The privilege conferred on the Legislature of a State is subject to the freedom conferred by article 19(1)(a) and (g) of the Constitution. Article 194(3) of that Constitution provides for powers, privileges and immunities enjoyed by the House of Commons at the commencement of this Constitution. The provisions of clauses (1), (2) and 3 shall apply in relation to persons who by virtue of this constitution have the right to speak in, and otherwise to take part in the proceedings of, a House of the Legislature or any committee thereof as they apply in respect of members of that Legislature. Article 195(3)(b) provides for power, privileges etc., in the State Legislatures and the members and committees of a House or Houses of Parliament and of the members com mittees of a house of such Legislature, shall be such as may from time to time be defined by the Legislature by law, and until so defined, shall, be those of the House Of Commons of the Parliament of the United Kingdom and its members and Committees at the beginning of this period. The petitioner who was one of the oldest members of the Bihar Legislative Assembly made a speech on May 30, 1957, and the official authorised report was published and made available on January 2, 1958. On August 18, 1958, there was a debate in the Bihar Legislature when M. P. N. Singh, one of its oldest Members of the Assembly made speech the gist of which was a criticism of the administration of Bihar as run by Dr. section K. Sinha, Chief Minister and cited certain instances of favouritism. At this stage the Speaker held that a portion of the speech was objectionable and ordered it to be struck off and expunged. The action of the Privileges Committee raised constitutional points affecting the petitioner fundamental right of freedom of expression. The Legislature cannot have such privilege as will deprive the citizens of their fundamental rights which are guaranteed by the Constitution, specially the right of free expression under article 19 (1) (a). It is true that a law made by Parliament in pursuance of the earlier part of article 105(3), or by the State Legislature in pursuance Of the earlier portion of article 194(2) will not be a law making in exercise of constituent power like the law which was considered in Sankari Prasad Singh Deo vs Union of India, ; , referred to.
