The appellants made applications to the State Transport Authority for grant of temporary permits to ply their vehicles on the route. The U.P. State Road Transport Corporation (Corporation for short) also made an application for three temporary permits for the same purpose and the application was granted while the application made by each of the appellants was rejected on the ground that once a scheme has been published in view of the provision contained in section 68 F(1 A) the Corporation alone to the exclusion of others is entitled to apply for temporary permit and if such an application is made by the Corporation and granted no one else is entitled, to obtain a temporary permit. This decision of the State Authority was upheld both by the State Road Appellate Tribunal and the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that in respect of the route a scheme had been prepared and published under section 68C of Chapter IV A of the . Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Section 68 F (1 C) clearly envisaged a situation where application for a temporary temporary permit is not made under section68 F(I A) by the corporation. And there was felt need for providing transport service on the routes in question. [986C D] 2. The State Transport Appellate Tribunal as well as the High court fell into an error by interpreting section 68F(1 C). The correct approach would be that keeping in view the strength of the vehicles fixed by the competent authority, the authority should first examine the application for number of temporary permit made by it. If the Corporation has made application for temporary permits covering all the vacancies the matter ends there. But if the Corporation does not apply for all the permits but only for some, the inescapable conclusion is that for the remaining strength the Corporation had made no application for the temporary permits and section 68 E F( 1 C) would be squarely attracted. [987A B] 3. The correct interpretation would be to that keeping the strength in view section 68 of Chapter III A of it is undoubtedly true that the Corporation enjoys a preferential treatment in the matter of obtaining permits. The authority under the Act must not ever lose sight of the fact that the primary consideration must be the service available to the travelling public. While interpreting the provisions of the undoubtedly the competing claims between the Corporation & the other private operators may be examined with reference to the provisions contained in the Act. But the overall consideration namely the service is for the benefit of the travellingpublic should never be overlooked for a moment. Reverting to the facts of this case if the approach of the High Courts is accepted it would lead to a startling result.

A Hindu governed by the customary law of the Punjab succeeds to his maternal grandfather 's estate, is the property in his hands ancestral property qua his own sons. This is the short and interesting question of law which arises in this appeal. The appellant is the son of Sarup, respondent 10. On March 22, 1927, he executed a registered mortgage deed in respect of the said properties in favour of Shibba, the ancestor of respondents I to 9 for Rs. 5,000. Subsequently on April 12, 1929, he sold the equity of redemption to the said mortgagee for Rs, 11,000 and in suit No. 145 of 1946 filed by the appellant in the court of the Sub Judge, Panipat, from which the present appeal arises, the appellant had claimed a declaration that the two transactions of mortgage and sale in question did not bind his own reversionary rights, because the impugned alienations were without consideration and were not supported by any legal necessity. The trial judge held that the property inherited by respondent 10 was 'not ancestral property ' qua the appellant, and so it allowed the appeal preferred by respondents 1 to 9 and dismissed the appellant 's suit. In second appeal the High Court took the view that the appeal had in fact been properly filed, but even so it did not ask respondents 1 9 to go back to the District Court, but condoned the delay made by the said respondents in the presentation of the appeal before itself and proceeded to deal with the appeal on merits. The High Court further held that there was " a great deal to be said in favour 'of the proposition that unless the land came to a person by descent from a lineal male ancestor in the male line, it should not be treated as ancestral property or that such property in the hands of a daughter can be given that description. Mahajan J., as he then was, who delivered the main judgment of the Full Bench of the High court conceded that there had been " a considerable deal to he said in his favour and that the question as to whether the property which the daughter 's son inherits from his maternal grand father is ancestral property is not free from doubt and he referred to the conflict of judicial opinion on the said point. Held, further, that the decision of the first Full Bench was wholly unsustainable as a decision on the point of the relevant custom. The doctrine of stare decisis is not so imperative or inflexible as to preclude a departure therefrom in any case, but its application must be determined in each case by the discretion of the court, and previous decisions should not ordinarily be followed to the extent that error may be perpetuated and grievous wrong may result.

The appellants were tried by the Additional Sessions Judge, Birbhum, on charges under section 449 and 307/34 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on the night of 14th November 1950 when Haji Ebrar Ali was sleeping on the Verandah of his hut, these appellants came there and while one of them armed with a dagger while the other three held him down. Fortunately, the injury inflicted on Haji E brar Ali did not prove fatal. The jury returned an unanimous verdict of guilt against all the appellants on both charges. The Sessions Judge accepted that verdict and convicted the appellants under sections 449 and 302 read with section 34 of the Penal Code and sentenced them to rigorous imprisonment for four years under section 307/149 and to rigorous imprison ment for two years under s. 449 of the I.P.C. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) There can be no doubt that the words "in order to" have been used to mean "with the purpose of". If the purpose in committing the house trespass is the commission of an offence punishable with imprisonment for life, the house property trespass becomes punishable under section 450 of the Code. (ii) Section 449 prescribes the punishment for house trespass if it is done "in Order to" the committing of any offence punishablewith imprisonment. Section 451 makes punishable, lurking house trespass or house breaking, if committed "inorder to" tho committing of an act punishable with death. The words " in order to have been use by the legislature not only in section 449 of I. P.C., but in the two succeeding sections 450, 451 and 457 will apply it the house trespasser or lurked house trespass, or lharking house breaking by night are committed for the purpose Of the offence indicated in those sections. Whether or not the purpose was actually accomplished is quite irrelevant in these cases. (iii) The fact that the murder was not actually committed would not affect the applicability of section 449 I.

The appellant filed a suit for declaration of his title as collateral within four degrees of Gurdial, who was a Sarswat Brahmin, resident of Pathankot in the district of Gurdaspur and the last male holder of the properties in suit. The respondent contested the suit mainly on the grounds (i) that the suit for a mere declaration was not maintainable; (ii) that there was no custom whereunder the collaterals of the father who was the last female holder excluded the daughter from succession to the self acquired property of her father and had, therefore, failed to discharge the onus that was thrown on her as a result of the production by the appellant of the Riwaj i am of 1913 and consequently the appellant must succeed. The Subordinate Judge decreed the suit in respect only of the lands in suit and ordered the parties to bear their own costs. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court modified the decree of the Subordinate Judge to the extent that the declaration in the appellant 's favour was made to relate only to the land in Khata No. 2 of village Kingarian which was held to be ancestral. On an application made by the appel lant on the 26th August 1949 the High court granted him a certificate of fitness to appeal to the Federal Court. After the commencement of the Con stitution of India the appeal has come before this Court for final disposal. The first question raised before the Supreme Court was as to whether there is a custom in the Gurdaspur district governing the parties under which a collateral within the fourth degree excludes the daughter of the last Hindu holder from succession even though they were within the four degrees. Held, that the appellant has failed to discharged the initial onus that he was initially on him and that being the position no burden was cast on the respondent which she need have discharged by adducing evidence of particular instances. In order to enable the appellant to displace the general custom recorded in Rattigan 's book so as to shift the onus to the respondent the appellant should produce a Riwaz i am which is a reliable and trustworthy document, has been carefully prepared and does not contain within its four corners contradictory statements of custom and in the opinion of the Settlement Officer is not a record of the wishes of the persons appearing before him as to what the custom should be, it would be a presumptive piece of evidence in proof of the special custom set up, which if left unrebutted by the daughters would lead to a result favourable to the collateral 's.

Section 5 of the Indian Stamp Act II of 1899 provides that when in the case of any sale, mortgage or settlement several instruments are employed for completing the transaction, only one of them called the principal instrument is chargeable with the duty mentioned in Schedule 1, and that the other instruments are chargeable each with a duty of one rupee. The question was whether a separate duty was payable in respect of Government stocks under the provisions of the Stamp Act, 1891 over and above what was paid under section 74 sub section (1) of the Finance Act, 1910 on account of other investments. Held, that though enjoying different capacities he is the same individual who functions though in different capacities and conducts his affairs in the various capacities which he enjoys but as a single individual. He is not one individual when he is acting as a trustee of a particular estate and he is not a third individual when acting as an executor or administrator of a deceased person. In whatever capacity he is exercising all the powers as the full owner qua whatever right, title and interest be enjoyed in the property, whether it be an absolute interest or a limited one. He may be the absolute owner of the property or may have a life interest therein, he may have had a mortgagee 's interest or lessee therein, but whatever interest be enjoys in that property will be the subject matter of the power which he executes in favour of the donee. The transaction is a single transaction whereby the donor constitutes the donees jointly and severally his attorneys for him and in his name and on his behalf to act for him in his individual capacity and also in his capacity as managing director, director, managing agent, secretary or liquidator of any company in which he is or may at any time thereafter be in terested in any such capacity as aforesaid and also as executor, administrator, trustee or in any capacity whatsoever as occasion shall require. The fact that the donor of the powers of attorney executed it in different capacity is not sufficient to constitute the instrument one comprising distinct matters and thus requiring to be stamped with the aggregate amount of the duties with which separate instruments each comprising or relating to one of such matters would be chargeable under the Act, within the meaning of section 5.

The assessee was carrying on business in Bhavnagar which was formerly an Indian State. In 1948 the Raj Pramukh of this newly formed State instituted the Saurashtra Income tax Ordinance, 1949. This Ordinance was in force for one year only the assessment year 1949 50. In assessing the profits of business by the two appellant companies for the years 1949 50 the Income Tax Officer had to proceed in accordance with the provisions of this Ordinance. For the purpose of calculating the depreciation allowance to which the assessee was entitled in computing the profits or gains of the business, the written down value had to be computed by deduction from the actual cost of depreciation allowance which was allowable under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 if it had been in force and a claim had been made supported by prescribed particulars. No. 1721,041 and in the case of the Master Silk Mills Ltd., the appellant in C.A. Nos. 601 and 602 of 1962) the Master silk Silk Mills Limited was the assessee. Appeals Nos. 599 & 600 of 1962 were filed before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner as well as the Income tax Tribunal which took a different view and held that this expression "or which would have been allowed to him if the Indian income tax Act 1922, was in law in force in the past" in section 13(5)(b) of the Saurashtra Incometax Ordinance,1949. The High Court answered the question in the affirmative but gave a certificate that it was a fit case for appeal to the Supreme Court under section 66(1) of tile Indian Income Tax Act. On behalf of the assessee it was contended: (i) that no deduction should have been made on the strength of the words "actually allowed" used in section 10(5) (b) read with the Taxation Laws (Part B States) (Removal of Difficulties) Order, 1950, paragraph 2 and the Notification No. 19 (S.R.O.477) dated 9th March 1953 under section 60A the written up value was to be determined after deducting depreciation allowance allowed under such laws, even though not claimed". (ii) that it is only when a difficulty is actually experienced in giving effect to the Indian Incometax Act that the provision of the Order can come into operation in a particular case. in the cases now under consideration, he argued, no such difficulty was actually experienced and so paragraph 2 would have no application. 227 of the Finance Act, 1950 is that paragraph 2 of the Removal of Difficulties Order must be applied according to its terms.

The petitioner, an instrumentality of the State of Karnataka, in favour of the Mysore Construction Co. (M.C.C.) and his writ petition and a further writ appeal in the Karnataka High Court having been unsuccessful, he has preferred this Spe cial Leave Petition from the judgment of the High Court in the Writ Appeal. The petitioner is aggrieved by the award of a contract by the Karnataka Power Corpora tion Ltd. (K.P.C.), an instrumentality. of the state of Karnataka in favour othe Mysore Construction Company (M C.C.). His writ petition & a further appeal in this Court having failed, he preferred this special leave petition from the Judgment of the Division Bench in the writ appeal. Allowing the Special Leave Petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The stipulation of time element within which the information asked for in para V should be supplied is also of some significance; it specifically requires the information to be supplied along with the application for tender forms. It may not, therefore, be correct to read para I in isolation and treat it as the only condition precedent for the supply of forms of tender. T. which have to be complied with before the applicant can be eligible for supply of tender forms, these include, if not all, at least such of those documents referred to in para v(d) as have a direct bearing on the three condition outlined in para l.

Section 5 B of the East Punjab Evacuees ' (Administration of Property) Act, 1947, provides that any person aggrieved by an order made under section 38(which corresponds to the previous section 5 A) may prefer an appeal in such manner and within such time as may be prescribed to the Custodian General where the original order has been passed by the Custodian or Additional Custodian or authorised Deputy Custodian but there was no provision for revision of such an order. The appellant who was a displaced person from Lahore had taken possession of the Danepur Road House on October 10, 1947. In pursuance of that exchange, Malik Sir Firoz Khan Noon is said to have taken possession in Punjab Khore presumably by way of attornment 1120 of tenants who were in actual cultivating possession of lands. Under section 5A of the Act the position so far as the positive portion is concerned has to be judged as if the repealing Act had not been passed, while under section 58 of the Central Act XXXI of 1950, the position in respect of matters covered by it would have to be determined as if that Act were in force on the day on which such thing was done or action taken. Held, further, that the revisional power cannot be exercised when there was an appeal provided but no appeal was filed, that it was open to the Assistant Custodian who appeared before the Custodian in support of the notice for revision or to the allottees of the property in whose interest the revisional order appears to have been passed and to file an appeal under the Act as persons aggrieved.

The appellant, a locality in the city of Bombay, is studded with small hardware businesses where pipes and fittings, nuts and bolts, tools and other small products are made and/or sold. These establishments, well over a thousand, employ a considerable number of workmen in the neighbourhood of 5,000 although each unit has (barring four), less than the statutory minimum of 20 workmen. This heavy density of undertakings and workers naturally produced an association of employers and a Union of workmen each recognising the other for the necessary convenience of collective bargaining. Apparently, these hardware merchants huddled together in the small area, were getting on well in their business and in their relations with their workmen, and this goodwill manifested itself in ex gratia payments to them of small amounts for a number of years prior to 1965 when trouble began. Although rooted in goodness and grace, the annual repetition of these payments ripened, in the consciousness of the workers into a sort of right nothing surprising when we see in our towns and temples a trek of charity seekers claiming benevolence as of right from shop keepers and pilgrims especially when this kindly disposition has been kept up long years. The compassion of yesterday crystallises as the claim of today, and legal right begins as that which is humanistically right. Anyway, the hardware factories of Nag Devi, made of sterner stuffs in the year 1965 abruptly declined to pay the goodwill sums of the spread out past and the frustrated workmen frowned on this stoppage by setting up a right to bonus averring considerable profits for the Industry (if one may conveniently use that expression for a collective coverage of the conglomeration of hardware establishments). The defiant denial and the consequent dispute resulted in the appointment of a Board of Arbitrators under section 10A of the Industrial Disputes Act to arbitrate upon twelve demands put forward by the Mumbai Kamgar Sabha, Bombay (the Union which represents the bulk of workers employed in the tiny, but numerous, establishments). This led to the recognition in law of the right of the workmen to get other kinds of bonus which do not depend upon nor are necessarily connected with the earnings of profits by the industrial concern. The Tribunal did not enter the merits of the claim but dismissed it in limine on the score that the demand for bonus was barred by res judicata the arbitral board 's decision negativing the bonus for 1965 being the basis of this holding. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) There is hardly any doubt that custom has been recognised in the past as a source of the rights to bonus as the several decisions cited before us by Shri Desai make out and section 17(a) of the Bonus Act in a way recognises such a root of title. Vaidialingam J., in Churakulam (1), referring to some of the precedents, observed: "In Ispahani 's case this Court had to consider a claim for Puja bonus, in Bengal, and the essential ingredients, for sustaining such a claim when it is based on an implied agreement between the employers and employees creating a term of employment for payment of Puja bonus or that even where no implied agreement can be inferred, it may be payable as a customary bonus, this Court in the said decision specifically dealt with a claim by two sets of workmen, based on profit of the business but the workmen fell outside the ambit of the legislation by express exclusion or exemption.

Respondents 1 and 2 to those Writ Petitions are the State of Haryana and the High Court of Punjab and Haryana respectively. Respondents 3 to 11 were appointed directly from the Bar to the Haryana Superior Judicial Service. Some of the more important grievances of the petitioners are that their seniority qua direct recruits is wrongly and unjustly made to depend upon the fortuitous circumstance of the date of their confirmation in the Superior Judicial service; that even if a substantive vacancy is available, the confirmation of a promotee in that vacancy is postponed arbitrarily and indefinitely, that promotees are treated with an unequal hand qua direct recruit for example, a promotee despite his satisfactory performance and the availability of a substantive post in which he can be confirmed, is continued in an officiating capacity until after a direct recruit completes his probation and is due for confirmation, and that, the High Courts apply the principle of rotation as between promotees and direct recruits at the time of their their confirmation when, in fact, that the relevant rules provide for is the application of a rule of quota at the times of their appointment. The petitioners who were officiating continuously in the Higher Judicial Service of the State as Additional District and Sessions Judges for two or three years prior to the appointment of Respondent 3 directly to that service lost their seniority over him by being allotted a date of confirmation which was one day later than the date on which he completed his probationary period. These rules were originally framed by the Governor of Punjab in consultation with the High court, in exercise of the powers conferred on the Governor by the proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution. Rule 12 as it stood originally was revived with effect from April 1, 1970 with retrospective effect from 4, 1970, and restored the rule of seniority as it existed originally in the 1963 Rules. In Haryana, Rule 12 provided that the seniority of the members of the service, whether direct recruits or promoted officers shall be determined by the length of continuous service (in a post in the service irrespective of the dates of confirmation).

A mortgagor in possession might grant a lease conformable to usage in the ordinary course of management but was not competent to grant a permanent lease unusual terms or authorise the use of land in a manner, or for a purpose different from the mode in which he himself had used it before he granted the mortgage. He is however liable for destructive waste is acts which are destructive or permanently injurious to the mortgaged property if the security was insufficient or would be rendered insufficient by such acts. In other cases a distinction was drawn between English mortgages and other mortgages and it was considered that the mortgagor in India remained the owner and when in possession could prima facie exercise the rights of ownership inclusive of the power to grant leases of the mortgaged properties. The question whether the mortgagor had power to lease the mortgaged land has got to be determined with reference to the authority of the mortgagor as the bailiff or agent for the mortgagee to deal with the property in the usual course of administration would be operative against the mortgagee. Held, further, that a lessee from the mortgagor acquires no interest whatever in the property demised to him. A person taking a lease from a mortgagor after the mortgage does acquire an interest in the equity of redemption and can claim to redeem that footing.

Clause 68 of the Contract provides for appointment of an arbitrator and when the petitioner has legally invoked clause 68, he sent the bills on July 12, 1979 but payment was not made. For the first time he sent notice on Nov. 28, 1989 to the respondent for reference to arbitration. On receipt thereof, the respondent filed an arbitration suits in the Calcutta High Court under sections 5, 12 and 33 of the for short the Act. The learned Single Judge held that the claim was hopelessly barred by limitation, there was no proof that the petitioner had sent any claim in July 1979. Since the Claim was made long after 10 years the arbitration cannot be proceeded with. Accordingly finding that it to be an exceptional case for interference, the learned Single judge cancelled the arbitration clause 68 of contract in matter Nos. 1326, 1364 and 1365/90 dated November 23, 1990. On further appeals, the division bench by its order dated December 18, 1992 in Appeal Nos 104/90 etc. dismissed the appeals. Thus special leave petitions arise out of Arbitration Agreement said to be executed by the petitioner on May 27, 1978 which provided that the respondent had to execute the work within 9 months. It was his claim that while executing the work he sent bills on 7, 1979 and payment was also not made, the petitioner having abandoned the contract even assuming that any claim was as a fact made in July, 1979, he had not taken follow up action thereafter for well over 10 years. The question for consideration is whether the High Court was justified in permitting the respondent to rescind the contract of Arbitration provided in clause 68 in matter No. 13 26. Allowing the Special Leave Petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. Clause 68 provides reference to an arbitration of all or any of the disputes or differences enumerated therein that have arisen between the parties at the instance of either party to the contract. It empowers either partyto issue notice calling upon the Engineer to refer the dispute or difference for arbitration. In this case, as found by the High court that though the petitioner was said to have made the claim for payment for the first period in July 12 1979 and the respondent having not acted thereon till November 28,1989 for long 10 years he did not move his little finger to approach the Engineer and later the Court. For these reasons, it is an exceptional one and the courts below have justifiably exercised their discretionary power and jurisdiction under sections five and 12(2) (b) to grant leave to a contracting party to have the arbitrator or umpire removed and the arbitration agreement entered into with other contracting part revoked. Where the Court grants such authority consequentially arbitration agreement shall cease to have effect in respect of the difference or dispute. It flows therefrom that there exist implied power vested in the court permitting a party to avail the remedy under sections5 and 12 to rescind arbitration agreement. In all cases it is not a condition precedent that there should in the first instance be an order appointing an arbitrator or he should enter upon reference for adjudication. In given circumstances and the factual background the Court may be justified to exercise the power under section 5 and 12 (2) of the Act regulates the limitation for the arbitration proceedings. The appellants obtained a preliminary decree on June 26, 1947 on the basis of a mortgage. The property mortgaged was an Estate within the meaning of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. That property included both Bakasht lands as well as other lands. The Act came into force after the passing of the aforesaid preliminary decree. Thereafter the mortgagees applied under section 14 of the Act and got determined the compensation to which they were entitled under the Act. It was said that they did not proceed any further in that proceeding but on the other hand filed on June 18, 1958 an execution petition to execute the mortgage decree against the appellants was dismissed for default of the judgment debtors on September 12, 1959. A second application raising the same ground of objection ( Misc. Case No. 110 of 1959) was filed by the judgment debtor on September 8, 1960 after examining the contentions of the parties. Therein the execution court came to the conclusion that the objection raised by the Judgment debtors is barred on the principles of res judicata and further that the same has no merits. This decision as mentioned earlier was affirmed by the appellate Court but reversed in second appeal by the High Court. The two questions that arise for decision in this appeal are (1) whether the objection as regards executability of the decree pleaded by the judgments debtors is barried by principles of Res judicata and (2) whether a mortgage decree has become unexecutable in view of the provisions of section 4(d) of the U.P. Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1960. HELD: The decision of the majority of the judges in the Full Bench decision in Sidheshwar Prasad Singh vs Ram Saroop Singh [1962] Supp. 3 S.C.R. 564 is not correct. In construing section 4 (d) it would not be right to assume that the interests of the debtors affected by the provisions Of the Act do not fall within the protection of the said Act and again at page 578 "Having regard to the said scheme, it is difficult to confine the application of section 6 only to execution proceedings in which the decree holder seeks to proceed against the estate of the debtor. In fact an execution proceeding to recover the decretal amount from the estate which has already vested in the State would be incompetent because the said estate no longer belong to the judgment creditor.

The appellant challenged his order of detention under section 3(1)(i) of the (COFEPOSA for short) by filing a writ petition before the High Court and that application, had been dismissed. As many as six contentions had been advanced before the Supreme Court, the point relating to denial of a fair hearing before the Advisory Board has not been noticed by the High court as a contention on behalf of the appellant, but counsel for the respondent did not dispute the allegation on the basis of the record as also the papers available with him that the department was represented at the hearing before its Advisory Board by a Deputy Collector of Customs. The position, therefore, is that on 25th November, 1986 while the detaining authority was assisted by a Dy Collector and a Superintendent of Central Excise, the detenu was denied the assistance of a retired Assistant Collector of Central excise. On the recommendation of the Advisory board, the detention order was confirmed. The appellant challenged this order before this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. It is not for this Court to examine and assess what prejudice has been caused to the appellant on account of such denial. This Court has reiterated the position that matters relating to preventive detention are strict proceedings and warrant full compliance with the requirements of law. In view of the position of law and the facts of the case, it must be held that the refusal by the Advisory Boards to permit the appellant to be assisted by Sundararajan as a friend was bad and continued detention of the appel lant became vitiated. Accordingly, this appeal is allowed and the order of deten tion is quashed. [793G H; 789A B] Nand Lal Bajaj vs State of Punjab, ; , referred to.

In September 1946 there was food shortage in the country. The Government of India issued a notice under sub r. (2) Of r. 75 A(2) of the Defence of India Rules, 1939, to acquire the requisitioned goods and acquired movable property under the rules made under the Defence Of India Act, 1939. He further held that there was no service of the orders on the mills which were in possession of the goods on September 30, 1946, as required by r. 74 A(1) (i). Held, that service of such an order is necessary on the person who can place the goods in question at the disposal of the requisitioning authority and until that is done there cannot be any valid and effective requisition. The notice of acquisition in this case was served on the managing agents of the mills as such there had been proper service of notices of acquisition, for it was not in dispute that no goods were actually appropriated towards the pucca delivery orders concerned, the property in the goods passed to the Government of india on September thirty, 1946. Held, further, that the notice of the decision to acquire was given to the various managing agents on September 10, 1946 and the notices of requisition were properly served on them through the managing agent and therefore these orders effected a valid requisition of the said goods mentioned in the schedules attached thereto. It was not correct to say that the order of requisition was not good service or reasonable way of service in the case of notices under r. 76 A(3) of 0. XXIX, r. 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

The assessee is a Private Limited Company. The assessment year concerned is 1963 64. Sometime in 1955 56, a notice was issued to the assessee under Section 23A of the Income Tax Act, 1922. Apprehending that it may become liable to pay additional tax under the said provision, the assessee set apart a sum of Rs. 6,52,000 in its books for the year ending March 31, 1956. Out of this amount an amount of Rs 2,02,000 was transferred to the profit and loss account during the year 1958 59 with the result that a sum continued to remain and was shown as a provision set apart to meet the taxation liability which the assessee called a contingent liability. At the same time the assessee had been contesting the proceedings taken against it under Section23A. Though it failed at the earlier stages, it succeeded ultimately in the Letters Patent Appeal filed by it in the East Punjab High Court. In so far as the item in question is concerned it held that it was a reserve and should be included in its capital for the purposes of the Act. The High Court answered the same in favour of Revenue and against the assessee following the decision of this Court in Metal Box Company of India Limited vs Their Workmen, it held: "The distinction between provision and reserve is stated in the following words: "In other words the broad distinction between a provision and a reserve is in commercial accountancy fairly well known. Provisions made against anticipated losses and contingencies are charges against profits and therefore to be taken into account against gross receipts in the P.& L. accounts and the balance sheet. On the other hand, reserves are appropriations of profits, the assets by which they are rep resented being retained to form part of the capital employed in the business. Bearing in mind the aforesaid broad distinction we will indicate how the two concepts are defined and dealt with by the " Applying the said test it must be held that the provision made by the assessee in its Books for meeting the anticipated liability of tax (under Section 23 A) was indeed a provision, and not a reserve. The assessee itself called it a provision.

The petitioners, who were direct recruits to the Indian Railway Service of Engineers (Class 1) were subjected to competitive written and personality tests and in the nature of things only the very best could emerge out successfully. On the other hand, temporary Assistant Officers, (temporary Assistant Engineers) and others concerned were informed that six of them would be absorbed into the Indian Railways Service of engineers (Class I) every year, this figure in the subsequent years was increased from time to time when in 1975, the figure as increased stood at 25 per year. The net result was that after absorption, 107 Officers were residually left unabsorbed in the year 1976 by the time of filing of the connected writ petitions in Katyani Dayal 's case and they too were finally absorbed in 1979 by what was described as a "blanket order". Before hand on September 17, 1965, the Railway Board had taken a decision to the effect that the Officers so absorbed into Indian Railway service of Engineers would be given weightage in seniority "on the basis of half the total years of continuous service in working posts in Railways prior to their permanent absorption into Class. 1, subject to a maximum weightage of five years". The then writ petitioners, describing themselves as members of the Federation of Temporary Officers Association, Indian Railways joining with them, their President Vice President and Secretary of the aforesaid Federation as writ petitioners approached this Court by way of a representative capacity to seek relief in their seniority status. The principal claim of the writ petitioners was that officers were appointed to temporary posts on the cadre of Engineers and that their seniority had to be reckoned on the basis that of their length of continuous services, though they conceded that in any given year, the candidates appointed as Engineers on the date of selection by the Union Public Service Commission. The challenge was to the authority of the Railway board to create such an unclassified parallel service, something outside the preview of the Indian railway Establishment Board. Notwithstanding the procedure of selection so adopted, the writ Petitioners contended that they were recruited in Class I service and supported their claim on diverse grounds so as to obtain the result that all Assistant Engineers formed one class under the Indian Indian Railway Establishment Board; that the development of law had gone a long way so as as to shed the views expressed in Kattani Dayal"s case justifying demolition of the demarcation between the two services made as it was in Katakyani Lal 's Case, and those that were recruited by selection, but both by Union Public Services Commission, terming it as arbitrary and not permissible under the equality clause in the Constitution. It was further contended that principles of constructive res judicata would bar the re agitation of the issues decided in Katalani Dayal vs Secretary, Home (Police) Department, Government of Bihar & Ors., [1988] Supp. SCC 519, Dr. O.Z Hussain vs Union of India, ; and Direct Recruit Class II Engineering of officers Association vs State of Maharashtra & Others, ; , referred to. Dismissing the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The distinction and the classification of the temporary Assistant Officer and members of Indian Railway Services of Engineers Class I fell clearly to be identified and marked. The only method of fusion was by means of a phased absorption as noticed in paragraph 9 of the Report detailed above. The scheme having met with approval of this Court cannot by mere passage of time be taken to have become vulnerable by subsequent exponence and dimension of Article 14 of the Constitution, for the reason that it had nexus to the object sought to be achieved, which mainly was efficiency of service, and that both the services had started separately and never became one. This Court in Katnani Dayals case specifically said that relief of equality was being denied to the then petitioners because of the history, origin, and structure of the Services. No opinion was expressed however as to the validity of the given weightage of half of the length of service to Temporary Assistant Officers.

The Saurashtra State Public Safety Measures (Third Amendment) Ordinance, 1949, which was passed "to provide for public safety, mainte nance of public order and preservation of peace and tranquillity in the State of Saurashtra", by the insertion of sections 7 to 18 which deal with the establishment of Spe cial Courts of criminal jurisdiction in certain areas to try certain classes of offences in accordance with a simplified and shortened procedure. Section 11 provided that "all offences under the Indian Penal Code shall be investigated, inquired into, tried and otherwise dealt with according to the provisions hereinafter contained", and section 12 empowered the State Government by notification to constitute Special Courts for such 'areas as may be specified in the notification". The appellant contended that sections 9 and 11 of the Ordinance were discriminatory in that they infringed article 14 Of the Constitution. Held, (per PATANJALI SASTRI C.J., PATANJULAM CHANDRASEKHARA AIYAR J. dissenting) that section II of the Saurashtra Ordinance in so far as it authorised the State Govern ment to direct particular "cases" to be tried by Special Courts was void as offending against the equal protection clause of the Constitution, and the notification which had been issued under that part of the section could not be held to be invalid or ultra vires. Benoarilal 's case ([1952] S.C.R. 889) distinguished. Per PATANJAL CHANNADHADAS J. (PATANJALI sAR C. J., PATANNADHAM HASAN JJ. dissenting), that section 11 of Saurashtra Ordinance, in so much as it empowered the Government to direct "offences" classes of offenses "classes of offences", made it the duty of the State government to make a proper classification, that is to say, a classification which must fulfil both conditions, namely, that it must be based on some intelligible differentia distinguishing the offences grouped together from other offences and that differentia must have a reasonable relation to the object of the Act as recited in the preamble. The Legislature has left it to the State Govt.
