Rule 7 of the Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation Rules, 1950 provides that in every case of termination of service by act of employer even if such termination involved was a consequence of transfer or closure of the undertaking was to be treated as 'retrenchment ' for the purposes of notice compensation etc. The employer terminated the services of some of the employees during the initial period of probation and of some others during the extended period on the ground of unsatisfactory service. Thereupon an industrial dispute was raised questioning the legality of their termination and the State Government referred the dispute to the Labour Court for adjudication under section 10 of the . The Labour Court held, overruling the stand of the employer that section 25F had no application, to the effect that the discharge was invalid. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation that the termination of services amounted to retrenchment as defined in section 2(oo) of the and those orders were bad for non compliance with the provisions of section 25 FF of the Act. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The expression 'termination of service for any reason whatsoever ' is not defined in the Act and it is true that an artificial definition may include a meaning different from or in excess of the ordinary acceptation of the word which is the subject of definition; but there must then be compelling words to show that such a meaning differ from or are in excess Of the ordinary accepted connotation of the term. [787C D] 2. When a portion of the staff or labour force is discharged as surplusage in a continuing business, there are (a) termination of the service of a workman; (b) for any reasons whatsoever; and (c) otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action. If such a position were adopted, the termination would be ab initio void for violation of principle of natural justice or for not following the procedure prescribed for imposing punishment. It is not necessary to dilate on the point nor to refer to the earlier decisions of this Court in view of the later two pronouncements of this court to both of which one of us was a party.

The assessee South Eastern Railway disposes of unclaimed and unconnected goods for money consideration. On 1 April, 1952 the assessee applied to the Commercial Tax Officer for cancellation of the registration of the assessee as a "dealer" under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. The Commercial Tax officer examined the case and did not accept the contention that the assessee was not a " dealer". On 6 June 1959 he made an order rejecting the application on the basis that the disposal of unclaimed goods for valuable consideration was a regular feature of the asses see 's activities, and that therefore the assessee fell within the scope of the Act. The assessee applied in revision before the Assistant Commis sioner of Commercial Taxes. The Board held that a transfer of property was involved in the auction held by the assessee and that consequently a sale of goods took place. The High Court also dismissed the other case on the same ground as found favour with it in the earlier case, and answered the question in favour of the Revenue. In these appeals the question is whether the assessee Railway in each case is a "business" for the purpose of as sessment under the Act, and therefore liable to assessment under that Act. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The activity of so disposing of the goods was adjunctive to the principal activity of the carriage of goods by the Railway. It seems to South Eastern railway was a 'dealer" for purposes of the Bengal Reve nue (Sales tax) Act 1941. In the other cases, the assessee Eastern Railway disposed of scrap and unserviceable material lying with it. The case is covered directly by the decision of this Court in the District Controller of Stores, Northern Railway, Jodhpur vs The Assistant Commercial Taxation Officer and Another, [1976] 37 S.T.C. 423.

The appellants were convicted of the offence under section 120 read with section 409 I.P.C., and all of them except Vishnu Prasad, were also convicted of certain offences arising out of the overt acts committed by them. Dalmia was a Director and Chairman of the company. He resigned from these offices in 1942 and was succeeded by his brother J. Dalmia on March 19, 1949. The period of criminal conspiracy charged against the appellants was from August 1954 to September 1955. Dalmia 's defence was that be had nothing to do with the details of the working of the Company, that he had authorised Chokhani, in 1953, to purchase and sell securities and that thereafter Chokbani on his own purchased and sold securities; that he used to go to Dalmia on the day following the receipt of the advice for confirmation of the contract of purchase or sale of securities, and that after Dalmia 'S approval the vouchers about the purchase of those securities and the crediting of the amount of the sale price of these securities to the account of the Insurance Company with the Chartered Bank, as the case may be, used to be prepared. He denied that Dalmia had said that the investment of funds would be in the discretion of Chokhani, and added that Dalmia was not authorised to purchase or sell securities on behalf of the insurance company unless he was authorised by the Chairman. The trial court convicted the appellants under section 477A read with s.409 I. P.C. and all the sentences were confirmed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that (i) the transactions were genuine commercial transactions, and (ii) they had not been delivered to the Insurance company by Bhagwati Trading Company and yet Chokhani made payment of the purchase price from out of its funds to the Union Agencies when funds were needed and also or providing funds in the Insurance Co 's account with the United Bank of India and Rs. 35,00,000 on behalf Of the Insurance Companies. Held: (i)(a) It is not possible to believe that the amounts which his company viz., Bhagwati Trading Co., received from the Insurance Corporation must have purported to be on account of securities sold to the insurance companies as that was the business which Bhagwati Trading company professed to do and, according to him, he knew that it had suffered losses as a result of sharespeculation business in 1954 55 and that the Delhi Office was short of liquid funds to meet these losses.

The Government of Bombay sanctioned certain rules called "The Allocated Government Servants ' (Absorption, Seniority, Pay & Allowances) Rules, 1957. Those rules governed the servants who were allotted to the State of Gujarat on reorganisa tion. By sub section (1) of section 115 it was provided that every person who immediately before the appointed day was serving in connection with the affairs of any of the existing States specified therein shall, as from that day be deemed to have been allotted to serve in connection With the affairs Of the successor State to that existing State. By section 117 power was conferred upon the Central Government to give directions to any State Government that may appear to be necessary for the purpose of giving effect to the provisions of sections 114, 115 and 116 of the Act. Under the proviso to sub section(7) it was laid down that conditions of service applicable immediately before November 1, 1956 shall not be varied to his disadvantage except with the previous approval of the Central Govern ment. Section 116 provided for the continuance of officers in the same posts. The appellants were allotted permanent posts in the Secretariat Service of the State under section 81 of the Bombay Reorganisation Act. By virtue of section 8 of the States Reorganization Act 37 of 1956, the new State of Bombay which included the territories of the former States of Saurashtra and Kutch was formed. Section 115 provided for continuance of Officers in the said posts. By the proviso it was further provided that conditions Of service applicable to every person allotted to another State shall not he varied to their disadvantage except With the previous sanction of the Government. Section 117 empowered the Central Gov ernment to give such directions to the States. Those provisions were substantially the same as those of sections 115, 116 and 117 of the . The appellants contended that the order violated r. 138 of the Recruitment Rules framed by the Govern ment of Bombay in 1957; (2) that the transfer of the latter Saurashtra and the Kutch States Secretariat personnel to the Gujarat Secretariat per se was not open to objection; (3) that it violated the provisions Of section 81 in that it altered the conditions of serv ice of the applicants; and (4) that r. 13 only dealt with the existing servants and did not prevent any additional members from being amalgamated in the ministerial staff in the secretariat. The High Court held that since the order purported to amalgamate the former Saurashtra and Saurashtra States Secretariats were absorbed in the districts, integration of the services was complete and any transfer thereafter to the Secretariat could not and did did not amount to absorption in equivalent posts. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants : (1 ) that the expression "absorption" has not been used in the order but that will not justify an inference that there was no intention to absorb the former and Kutch States personnel in the Secretari tories. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1)(a) Under section 115(7), a guarantee was given to every allotted public servant that his conditions of ' service shall not not be changed except with prior approval of Central Government. The protection could not be removed by the rules made by the State subsequent to November 1. 1956 unless the previous consent of the central Govern ment was obtained thereto. It is true that the ministerial service personnel in these States were posted and assigned duties in various districts in Saurashtra and Gujarat. But in the absence of evidence to show that the previous approved approval of tho Central Government was obtained, their right to be absorbed in equivalent post in the new state of Bombay and later in the State was not thereby affected. It was conceded and rightly, that the State has the authority to transfer, subject to the Constitution and the rules framed under article 309 any public servant to render service which by his training and aptitude he was competent to do.

Section 5(2)(a) of the Punjab General Sales Tax (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967 provides that in respect of declared goods the tax (sales or purchase) shall not exceed the prescribed limit and shall not be levied on the purchase or sale of such goods at more than one stage. The petitioners of the second category purchase oil seeds for use in manufacture of edible oils. The surplus oil seeds were sold to other dealers, registered or unregistered, inside and outside the State of Punjab. Both these commodities are essential commodities to which the Central Sales Tax Act applies. Certain provisions of these Amending Acts are challenged on the ground that they offend section 15 of the Central Act and are also unconstitutional being in violation of Articles 14 and 19. The Punjab General sales tax (Amendment & Validation) Ordinance, 1967 was passed in 1948. Restrictions and conditions in regard to tax on sale or purchase of declared Goods within a State. Every sales tax law of a State shall, in so far as it imposes or authorises the imposition of a tax on the sale or Purchase of such Goods inside the State shall not exceeding three per cent of the sale Or purchase price thereof, and such tax shall not he leviable at morethan one stage: Provided that in the case of goods liable to purchase tax, the stage of purchase of such declared goods by the last dealer liable to pay tax under this Act; and (b) the taxable turnover of any dealer for any period shall not include his turnover during that period of any sale or purchases of declared 'goods at any other stage than the stage so mentioned. It was contended on behalf of the petitioners that section 2(ff), 5(1) second proviso and 5(ii)(a)(vi) were in conflict with section 15 and were also unconstitutional as being in violative of Articles 19 and 301. HELD: (i) The provisions for taxing purchases of cotton were challenged on a ground that there was a possibility of the tax being levied at more then one stage, the provisions of the first proviso notwithstanding. [547C] (ii) There is no indication either in the Act or the rules, on the basis of which it will be entitled to be supplied with all the material information, relevant for sustaining a request for refund. If the Central Legislature makes it mandatory that the tax can be collected only at one stage in our opinion, it is not enough for the State to say that a person, who is not liable to tax, must nevertheless pay it in the first instance and then claim refund refund, at a later stage. [548D E] (iii) The question as to how far a party can ask for refund without the order of assessment being set aside by appropriate proceedings is highly doubtful; because at the time when the actual order of assessment is passed, in certain eases it may not be possible for a party to say whether he is entitled to exemption or not, under sub cl. (vi) of section 5( 2), of the Act. If a person is not assessable for payment of tax at all, at any time, the collection of a 'tax from him, with a possible contingency of refund at a subsequent stage will not make the original levy valid; because, if particular sales or purchase are exempt from taxation altogether, they can never be taken into account, at some stage, for the purpose of calculating or arriving at the taxable turn and for levying tax.

The appellants were the representatives of three original plaintiffs who instituted a suit (being O.S. No. 30 of 1934) in the Court of the District Judge, East Tanjore for enforcement of a mortgage against the present respondent who was defendant No. 1 in the suit and six other persons. The suit was contested by all the defendants except defendant No 1 against whom it proceeded ex parte, and there was a preliminary decree passed on May 15,1937, by which a sum of RS. 1,08,098 was directed to be paid by defendant No .1 and defendants 3 to 7 in default of which the plaintiffs were declared entitled to apply for a final decree for sale of the mortgaged properties and the suit was dismissed against defendant No 2. Against this decree two appeals were taken to the Madras High Court, one by defendant Nos. 3 to 6 being Appeal No. 48 of 1938 who contended that the mortgage debt was one and indivisible and even though different amounts were mentioned as payable by two groups of defendants in the decree, the decree holders were bound under the terms of the decree to release the entire mortgaged property even on payment of the amount directed to he paid by them under the decree as scaled down by the High Court in favour of defendant Nos 2 to 7. During the pendency of these appeals, the Madras Agricultur ists ' Relief Act (Act IV of 1938) came into force and appli cations were made by defendants 2 to7 to the High court praying that in the event of a decree being passed against them, the decretal debt might be scaled up in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The High Court rejected these applications on the ground that as the decree had already been passed by the Madras Court definitely negativing his claim to any relief under the Agriculturists ' Relief Acts, such application was not entertainable by the lower court. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the view taken by the District judge was right and should not have been disturbed. The fact that in this case it was a puisne mortgagee and not a mortgagor whose application for relief under section 19 of the Madras Agriculturists ' relief Act was allowed does not make any difference in principle. The ratio decidendi in all these cases is not applicable to the case before us. Arunachalam Pillai vs Seetharam, [1940] 2 M. 39 300 decisions referred to.

Section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 provides that nothing contained in sections 28 or 29 shall be deemed to bar a party to a suit, proceeding or appeal mentioned therein in which a question of title arises and is determined, from suing in a competent court to establish his title to such premises. The plaint in the suit filed by the appellants in the City Civil Court clearly asserts that the first plaintiff was entitled in law to sublet the premises to the second and third plaintiffs and that there had been a lawful subletting of the premises by him to them. The City Civil Judge held that it had jurisdiction to entertain the suit but did not record any decision on the merits of the appellants ' case. On appeal, the High Court disagreed with the view of the judge of the City civil court that he had no jurisdiction to try the suit and dismissed the suit on the ground that there bad been no lawful subletting by the first appellant of the said premises to them being contrary to law the latter had deprived himself of the protection of the Act. On further appeal, Held: (i) The High Court correctly decided that the suit was not one between a landlord and a tenant merely because the defendants denied the claim of the plaintiffs. (ii) Section 29A expressly provides that no finality should be attached to the decision of a court trying a suit under section 28 on a question Of title de hors the Act but by virtue of a claim made thereunder must be determined by a Court specified in section 28 and a title de dehors the Act may be determined in any other court of competent jurisdiction.

The respondent, a private company, was incorporated under the name and style of Oriental Metal Pressing Works Ltd., hereafter called the Company. On May 26,1955, the appellant transferred his business to the company. On July 7, 1955, Dadoba had died leaving a will whereby he purported to appoint the appellant Govind the managing director of the Company in his place from the date of his death. Shortly after Dadoba 's death disputes arose between the appellant and the respondent. The appellant was contending that he had ceased to be a director on account of his failure to attend the directors ' meetings. He also alleged that the appointment of the appellant as managing director by the will of Dadoba, was void under section 312 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court accepted all the contentions of the respondent and made the declarations claimed. The company appealed from this decision to the High Court at Bombay. The appeal came up for hearing before a bench of two Judges of that Court. In the eventual result according to the opinion of the majority of the learned judges, the appeal was dismissed and the decree of the City Civil Court was confirmed. It appears that while the appeal pending in this Court, the respondent sold his holding in the Company to the appellant. The High Court took the view that the word "assignment" in section 312 included "appointment", and so, such an appointment would also be void under the section. Held, that the High Courts were right in holding that sections 254 and 317 of the Act impliedly indicate that there should be no perpetual management. Section 312 was intended to prevent a director from appointing his successor when section 255 permits him to do that. In order, however, that a directors may exercise this power of appointment, there must be a vacant office of a director. The vacancy would again be caused by his death or by the expiry of the term of his office. It would follow that the Act contemplates an appointment by a director of another person as director to take his office, when made vacant by his resignation or death or the expiry Of the term Of his office and that since the new Act was a consolidating Act it must be deemed to have continued the policy of the earlier Act and, therefore, for the purpose of section 312 an "assign assignment" must include an "appointment". The word "resignation" in the section included " appointment", and not appointment of his successor by a directors.

The respondent landlady filed an eviction petition against the appellants and one other partnership firm, carrying on business in the name and style of M/s. Adeshwar Glass Mart on the ground that the appellants had unlawfully and without the consent of the respondent sublet the said shop let out to the respondent. The Trial Court held this ground established and passed a decree for eviction as sought by the respond ent. The appel lants preferred an appeal against this decision to the Appellate Authority under Section 23 of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and 419 Rent Control) Act, 1960 being the Court of Small Causes at Madras. The said appeal was numbered as H.R.A. 156 of 1979. The Appellate Authority dismissed the said appeal upholding the finding of unlawful subletting by the appellants. The appellants then preferred a Civil Revision Petition being C.RP. No. 44 of 1981 in the High Court of Madras against the decision of this Court in Chhotelal Pyarelal, the partnership firm and others vs Shikharchand, In that case an eviction peti tion petition was filed by the respondent landlord against the appellant a partnership firm under clause 13(3)(iv) and (vii) of the Central Provinces and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949. The appellant raised a preliminary objection that the application against the partnership Firm was not maintainable without joining its partners as re spondents. It was held by this Court that it is only by virtue of the provisions of order 30 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, that a firm can sue and be sued in its own name without the partners being impleaded. It would be merely a case of misdescription of the respondents to the application and this misde scription can be corrected at any stage of the proceedings. In the instant case, no such objection has been raised at all till the stage of Special Leave and it is certainly not open to the appellants to raise such an objection at a very late stage and thereby delay matters for a number of years.

Section 2(a) (i) defines "vacant land" by providing that if the extent of the holding of a person is in excess of the ceiling area, the person shall be liable to surrender the land held in excess. If an individual or a family unit holds land in excess Of the ceiling limit, the excess would have to be surrendered to the State Government. The Andhra Pradesh Act was enacted with a view to imposing a ceiling on vacant land, other than land which is mainly used for the purpose of agriculture and agriculture in this connection includes horticulture, but does not include raising of grass, dairy farming, poultry farming, breeding stock and cultivation or the growing of such plants as may be prescribed by the Rules, and, moreover, in order to fall within the exclusion, the land must be entered in the revenue or land record before the appointed day as for the purposes of agriculture, and must also not have been specified in the master plan for a purpose other than agriculture. That power stood transferred to Parliament and as a first step towards the eventual imposition of ceiling on immovable property of every description, the Parliament enacted the Central Act with a avowed object to imposing ceiling on urban immovable property and acquisition of such property in excess thereof of the Ceiling limit and all matters connected therewith or ancillary and incidental thereto should be regulated in the State of Andhra Pradesh by Parliament by law and an identical resolution in the same terms was passed on the next day by the Andhra Pradesh Legislature Assembly. The definition of "family unit" in section 2(f) is materially in the sense that it is used or is capable of being used for purposes ancillary thereto, including horticulture, forest land, pasture land, waste land plantation and tope; and includes land deemed to be agricultural land under this Act. Section 10 is the key section which imposes ceiling on the holding Of land by providing a declaration in respect of his holding by every person whose land exceeds the ceiling limits and the Tribunal is required by section 9 to hold an enquiry. The ceiling area in the case of a family units consisting of father, mother and three minor sons or daughters, the lands held by all these persons would have been clubbed together and then the ceiling areas applied to the aggregate holding.

A dispute regarding an individual employee was referred to the Industrial Tribunal, Calcutta. The case of the company was that on January 18, 1953 certain workers of the Hot Mills section resorted to an illegal stoppage of work and on the next day all the three shifts of the hot mills section commenced a 'slow down strike. This resulted in a tripartite conference between the Labour Commissioner of the Government of West Bengal, the General Manager of the Company and the President of the Union. The workers ' committee protested against the closing of two shifts and the trouble continued till April 8, 1953 when the company issued a notice to the workmen that unless they voluntarily recorded their willingness to do normal work, they would be considered as no longer employed by the Company from 2 p.m. on April 10, 1953. On September 23, 1953, another notice was issued by the company lifting the lock out with effect from June 6, 1953 and thereafter in the concluding portion the notice states " The services of all other workers shall be deemed to be discharged with effectfrom the date of the lockout really meant that the Company refused to employ the respondent workmen during the period when the place of employment was closed. " On September 17, 1953 another notice dated September 23. 1953, which extended the date for joining to October 2, 1953 again said that " all employees on the Works rolls of the factory on August 23, and who wish to report for duty, must resume work between 6 a m. on Friday, the 18th September, 1953". The third notice stated inter alia that in consequence of the illegal strikes which took place on several previous dates, the management had no option but to declare a look out of the entire Works except some special shifts, really terminated the services of the respondent by discharging them with effect From August 24, 1953; then in the fourth portion the notices states " All employees on Works rolls on the 23rd August, 1953 & 10 p. m. On Saturday, September 19, 1953 the Company issued a third notice, which stated inter: "All employees on The Works rolls Of the company on August 3, 1953 on their regular shift. If however, any worker in the vicinity of the Works is unable to resume duty on account of illness, he should report himself to the Company 's Medical authorities or if unable personally to attend, send written intimation of his sickness to the company by Saturday the 19th September. " The three notices were read together against the background of events which bad happened prior to August 23. It was contended for the workmen in which the prayer is for payment of full compensation and it was sufficient to state that no question of principle is involved. Held, that the two Tribunals below have misdirect ed themselves as to the true scope and effect of the Standing Orders in question and their decision with regard to the seven workmen mentioned above cannot be supported. It has been somewhat faintly suggested that if the notices bear the construction which they put on them, the respondent workman did not join on or before Saturday but failed to produce evidence satisfactory to the Tribunal of their absence as required by the notice dated 9th September 1953, and therefore, they were not entitled to be taken back as of right and without any condition. It may be that some of the workmen could have presented themselves earlier than they actually did, but that does not prove that the company refused to take only those workmen who had failed to produced satisfactory evidence of their Absence.

The University of Rajas than invited applications for the post of Professor in the department of Botany. The Selection Committee constituted under section 5 of the Rajasthan University Teachers and Offi cers (Selection for Appointment) Act, 1974 held interviews on 20th June, 1989 and selected Dr. Nathawat for the said post. Dr. Urea Kant who was already selected and kept in the reserve list was appointed as Professor in a department of the Bot any. The syndi cate of the University approved the list and appointed Dr. G.S.Nathawat on the said posts. Dr, who were not selected filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the appointment of Dr. Uma Kant on the ground that the Selection Committee was not constituted in accordance with law and objection was also raised that once a selected person joins the post, the reserve List stood exhausted and the person named in the reserved list could not be appointed against a future vacancy. The learned Single Judge held that the constitution of the Selection Commit tee was valid but as regards the appointment to Dr.Urea Kant from the reserve lists it was held that once the selected person join the post then selection made by the Committee was exhausted and that the person mentioned in the Reserve List could not he appointed against any future vacancy, and that once again a selected candidate joins the Post, the reserved List stood revived and the persons named in that reserve list could be appointed. The Division Bench upheld the order of the Single Judge and dismissed the appeals. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In matters relating to educa tional institutions, if two interpretations are possible, the courts would ordinarily be reluctant to accept that interpretation which would upset and reverse the long course of action and decision taken by such educational authorities and would accept the interpretation made by such Educational Authorities. [421C D] 1.2 The High Court was wrong in taking the view that a regular vacancy of Professor having arisen on the retirement of Dr, G. S.Nathwat on 30th September, 1989 again a fresh Selection Committee should have been constituted and no appointment on such post could have been made from the reserved lists prepared by the Selection Commi sioner on 20.6.1989.

The petitioners are owners of plots of land in areas round about Bombay, commonly known as Greater Bombay. They have all similar but separate grievances with respect to the development plan prepared and published under the Act. In Writ Petition No. 228 of 1966, the petitioner 's complaint is that the list of sites reserved for public purposes was for the first time submitted by the second respondent to the Development Committee on February 8, 1964 showing for the second time that a major portion of the petitioners ' lands were earmarked for a recreation centre and green belt in the development Plan of 'P ' Ward of Greater Bombay should be removed, that their lands should be redesignated as reserved for industrial purpose, that the order of the Assistant Engineer, Bombay Municipal Corporation rejecting the petitioners proposal for construction of two factory buildings and lavatory blocks should be quashed and a declaration be made that sections 9, 10, 11 12 and 13 of the Act are ultra vires the Constitution of India. The petitioner contended (i) that the power vested in the competent authority at its sweet will and pleasure to refuse permission to execute a decree for eviction violated the right to hold property under article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution, on the ground that there were no principles in the Act itself to guide the competent authori ty in the exercise of his will and discretion was met by saying that the restrictions imposed would not be held to be unreasonable as "the ban imposed on eviction is temporary though. its duration is not definite; (ii) that by the combined operation of sections 4 and 11(3), the local authority could easily delay the acquisition of any land designated for a public purpose under section 7 of the , for 14 years and if resort was had to power,% under section 17 of revising the development plans at the end of this period of 14 years; (iii) that even assuming that the State Legislature could pass the Act, nevertheless its provisions regarding the levy of contribution towards the cost of the scheme and all other matters relating to the working of the Scheme were unauthorised and unreasonable and that the powers vested in tho Town Planning Officer and other authorities under the Bombay Town Planning Act were unguided, arbitrary and uncontrolled and as such infringed the fundamental rights of the petitioner under articles 14, 19(i)(f), 31 and (g) and 31 of the Constitu tion. HELD: (1) The provisions of sections 14, 15 and 16 would again become operative with the result that the acquisition might be delayed for a further period of ten years. [285 C] (2) Under section 8 various particulars had to be published and sub mitted to the State Government along with the development scheme inclusive of a report of the surveys carried out by the local authorities, a report explaining the provisions of the development planning plan, a Report of the stages by which it was proposed to meet the obligations imposed on the local authori ties. The authority must therefore look into all material available to it including the tentative plans and the final development plan and then make up its mind as to whether a commencement certificate should be granted or not.

The petitioner who appeared in person (in W.P. No. 234 of 1968) and section Khanduja, for the Union of India (in C.A. Nos. 1528, 1900 and 2118 of 1968), contended that there was no territorial dispute as there was a well established boundary running roughly along the northern edge of the Rann of Kutch as shown in the pre partition maps which needs to be demarcated on the ground. The claim was supported by survey maps, correspondence between the officials of Kutch State and the British Adminis tration, assertions made in the Annual Administration Reports for 75 years before 1947 Statistical abstracts relating to British India, Bombay Administration Reports Gazetteers, Memorandum on Indian States and a number of official publications, and by the Resolution of the Government of Bombay, dated 305 February 24, 1914. Macdonal Survey appears to support the claim was the conflicting alignments in the survey and other maps, the claims made were about the location of the boundary line, and the operative part of the award declared the alignment of the boundaries which had under the terms of the agreement relating to the procedure for demarcation to be filed by pillars on the alignment. It was agreed by the two Prime Ministers that a part of Berubari Union which was allotted to India under that Award and was in occupation of India was to be ceded to Pakistan, and enclaves within Pakistan but in occupation Of India de lure were to be exchanged for similar enclave of Pakistan within Indian territory. The agreement between the two States was reached purely as an executive act, and no legislative sanction was obtained by the Government from the Union Government of India to its implementation. The dispute related to the boundary between the State of Gujarat in India and West Pakistan regarding which there were disputes and much friction, and it was agreed that both sides put forward their claims, (d) that there is no clear evidence of demarcation of a boundary acceptable to the parties now or in the past, (e) that the area is in different state at different seasons in the year, for part of. the year it is water and for the remaining part it was land; and (f) that both side put forward its claims, and (g) that in any case will not be later than one month after the cease fire, Ministers of the two Governments would meet in order to agree on the determination of the border in the light of their respective claims. Held: (per Hidayatullah, C.J., Sikri, Bachawat and Mitter, JJ.) : (i) Article 1 read with the First Schedule to the Constitution made Kutch into a part C State and under the second paragraph of Part C itself its territory comprised all territories which by virtue of an order made under section 290A of the Govern ment of India Act, 1935, were immediately before the commencement of the Constitution being administered as if they were a Chief Commissioner 's Province or a Chief commissioner 's province specified in the Order. It could not be said that there will be a cession of Indian territory and the rule earlier laid down by this Court applies if no constitutional amendment is required the.

The mortgagor borrowed Rs. 5,500 from one Rabindra Nath Chakravarty and executed a deed of mortgage whereby he agreed personally to repay the amount and encum bered his share in Mauzas Bansjora and Simitanr for repayment of the amount borrowed with interest at the rate of Rs. 1/8/ per mensem and further agreed that in default of payment, the mortgagee do recover the amount due by sale of his interest in Mauza Bansjuna, Simitan and Bahaldih. By the mortgagedeed the mortgagor also agreed that the mortgagee did receive the amountdue as royalty from the tenants under mining leases in Mauza Bahaldhih in the month of Aswin of the Vikram year and the second in the first month of Chaitra. On June 14, 1922, the mortgagor assigned his interest to one Mahendra Nath Rai and on October 2, 1927 he assigned his share of the coal fields in Mauza Khaldih to one Moyee Devi. Thereafter in execution of a money decree obtained against the mortgagor, his right, title and interest in mauz Bahaldjih was sold on January 16, 1937 and after th sale was confirmed possession of Mauza Baha dih was taken by the auction purchaser on April 7, 1937. By two deeds dated June 18, 1946, Manimala Devi the plaintiff in the suit out of which this appeal arises obtained assignments of the rights of the mortgagees under the two deeds executed by Manimala Lal Chakravartity and Indra Nath Chakrabarty to secure payment of Rs 5,000 advanced to him and interest thereon. The covenants of this mortgage deed were substantially the same and such differences as there are in the covenants have no bearing on the questions to be decided in this appeal. It was agreed that these properties had not been encumbered to any person and that he was in peaceful possession of the mortgaged property described in Sch. (kha) and (kha). By paragraph 13 the mortgagor undertook to pay interest at a rate of RS. 1,000 every year, and the mortgagee was, in default, of payment by the tenants, competent to realise the same. By para 14 the mortgagor agreed that he would compensate the mortgagee in respect of the amounts remaining to be realised.

The appellants employ as many as 7.000 workmen in those factories. In order to provide transport facilities to its employees to come to the factories from their respective villages, the appellants provided transport which would pick up passengers from Pune or Khed or Vadgaon or Alandi or places enroute to TELCO Factory at Pimpri and back. For this journey a nominal charge of Rs. 10 per month was realised by the appellants from the employees. Similarly, for the transport facilities provided to the employees from Pimpri Railway Crossing and onwards to TILCO factory, they were charged at the rate of Rs 5 per month. A charge of RS. 2 per month levied for the Transport of employees from Chinchvad Village to TALCo factory at Pimgra and back was levied for transport of employees. The appellants contended that in future no charges would be realised from the appellants and they would he provided free transport as in the case of supervisory staff, that even if a nominalcharge is realised from employees that would not make the transport a public service vehicle carrying passenger; so as to attract the provisions of section 3 which is the charging section of the Act. Dismissing the appeals by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The tax can be levied only on passengers who are carried by a stage carriage which is of the nature of a public services vehicle. [361E] 2.1 In view of what we have already said, it is not necessary for this Court to go into such meticulous details because the legal position appears to be clear enough. As counsel for the appellants has already undertaken not to charge any amount from the employee for providing transport facilities, the point has now become more or less academic. The Commissioner appears to have dismissed the appeals of the appellants 5 9 SCI/78 as he felt bound by the judgment of the Bombay High Court which had held that the transport vehicle provided to employees by the company would be a publicservice vehicle.

The appellants, who were residents of the locality and had objected to the grant of a licence for a temporary cinema to respondent No. 3 Prem Narayan son of Ganpatlal Chouksey, proprietor Chitra Talkies, Lalbagh, Burhanpur (M.P.) against which a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution by the appellants was dismissed in limine by a speaking order by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur on 6th March 1978. The second respondent made an application on 5th December 1975 for grant of licence for the temporary cinema and the District Magistrate having jurisdiction issued a no objection certificate vide his order dated 10th February 1976 for a period of six months. This licence was renewed upto 30th June 1976 and there was a further renewal up to 30th September 1976. A subsequent application for renewal was turned down by the Distt. Magistrate by his order on 29th June 1977 on the ground that Paras Talkia with permanent cinema licence which was closed, has now been functioning in the locality, and therefore a renewal of the licence for "a temporary cinema in the same locality would not be proper". The appellants filed a writ petition under article 226 questioning the validity of the order of the State Government conceding inter alia that they were the residents of tho locality and that they had objected thereto to the granting/renewal of licence on the grounds that there is a mosque a madrasa and a temple in the vicinity or the place where the cinema house was to be constructed, and even though their objections were upheld by the licensing authority, the District Magis trate, they were not heard in the appeal preferred by the third respondent and, therefore, the order granting the no objection Certificate is violative of the principles of natural justice. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that District Magistrate was not influenced by the fact that there was an mosque and a Temple in the nearby vicinity of the place wherein the proposed cinema house is to be built but he was influenced by an extraneous consideration, namely, re opening of Paras Cinema with a permanent cinema license while rejecting the application of third respondent for renewal of his licence by the order dated 29th 6 1977. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellants did not file any objection at that stage "no objection" certificate was granted to the third respond ent. Thereafter, when an application for no objection certificates is made, objections have to be invited in the prescribed manner. If after taking into consideration the objections, a no certificate is granted, there ends the matter subject, of course, to any properly constituted legal proceedings, conceivably a writ Petition under Article226. But sub section (3) of section 5 of the Act is unambiguous when it provides for an appeal only at the instance of a person aggrieved by the decision of the licensing Authority refusing licence. A fortiori, every objector to renewal is not entitled to file an appeal if licence is granted rejecting his objections.

Under a contract dated August 3, 1957 the defendant agreed to sell to the plaintiffs 40000 tons of float iron lying in the mining area and gave them the right to win and remove the iron ore. The plaintiff 's suit for specific performance was decreed by the Trial Court. On appeal the High Court allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there was no concluded contract between the parties and that in breach of the contract, the defendant failed to apply for and obtain the necessary consent of the central government to the assignment of the mining lease. HELD: The plaint in O.S. No. 46 of 1957 was not an acceptance. There was no other acceptance either oral or in writing. Mere mental assent of the plaintiffs to the defendants proposal is not sufficient. In the peculiar facts of Bloxam 's case a contract to take shares was concluded by an oral application for shares followed by allotment though no notice of allotment was given to the applicant. Ordinarily there is no contract unless there is an acceptance of the application for shareholders and the acceptance is communicated to the applicants, see in re: Pellatt 's Case (4) , Fry on Specific Performance, 8th ed article 306, page 142, Pomeroy on Specific performance, 3rd ed., article 306. In re : Pellat 's ease, 1822 Madd. 316, 326= 1 2, 1115.

The appellants are office bearers of M/s. S.K.G Sugar Ltd., Ltd., (Lauriya). A complaint has been registered against them under sub rule (3) of rule 3 of the Sugarcane (Control) Order, 1955 read with section 7 of the , on the ground that they have failed to pay to the sellers the price of sugarcane purchased by them within the time prescribed. The said complaint is being investigated. The appellants are objecting to that investigation on various grounds. They unsuccessfully sought intervention of the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution in Cr. W.I.C. No. 11 of 1966. Hence this appeal. HELD: (i) The power conferred on the Government under section 3 of 'the Act cannot be challenged as invalid. There is no substance in the contention that the impugned order contravenes the fundamental right guaranteed to the citizens under article 19(1 ). No fundamental right is conferred on a buyer not to pay the price Of the goods purchased by him or to pay it whenever he pleases. The contention that in view of section 11 of the Act, no cognizance could have been taken of the offence alleged is premature. [677 E F] (ii) The question whether the cultivation and sale of sugarcane can be regulated under section 2(a) of the does not arise in this case. No court has yet taken cognizance of the case. That stage has Still to come. There was no substance In the contention of the appellants that the complaint made before the police did not disclose a cognizable offence and as such the police could not have taken up the investigation of that complaint. The offence complained of is punishable with three years ' imprisonment and as therefore it falls within the 2nd Sch. of the Cr.

The Government of Karnataka decided to adopt a policy to encourage rapid industrialisation. An Order No. CI 58 FMI 69 dated 30th June, 1969 was issued which recited that the Government, namely, the Government of the State was committed to a policy of rapid industrialization and that, in pursuance thereof, the Govern ment had on 30th November 1966, issued directions indicating the incentives that would be given to entrepreneurs starting new industries in the Mysore State. The material part of the said order ran thus: "Consequently, the Governor of Mysore is pleased to sanction the following incentives and concessions to the entrepreneurs for starting new industry in Mysore State: (1) Sales Tax A cash refund will be allowed on all sales tax paid by a new industry on raw materials purchased by it for the first five years from the date the industry goes into production, eligibility to the concession being determined on the basis of a certificate to be issued by the Department of Industries and Commerce. " By an order dated 11th August 1975, the procedure was prescribed for obtaining the concessions given under the orders referred to earlier. On 12th January 1977, the State Government issued another order which stated that the scheme of concessions adopted by the Government earlier had given room for many types of misuse and the earlier orders had not been prescribed any ceiling limits or restrictions on the quantum of refund of sales tax or concession to be granted. The said order dated 12th December, 1977 inter alia provided as under: "The concession of refund will he limited to 10 per cent of the cost of fixed assets per year, thus not exceeding the total of 50 per cent over a period of five years for which the concession is available.

A 1 to A 7 were tried for the offences under Sections 147, 148, 323, 379 and 302 read with Section 149 I.P.C. on the allegations that they caused the death of Madda Laksha mandas of village Ramaraogudem on November 1, 1980 near the Tobacco garden of A 1. The Trial Court acquitted A 7 of all the charges. A 1 to 6 were, however, found guilty for the offence punishable under Sections 148 and 302 I. P.C., and sentenced them to imprisonment for life. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of A 4 to A 6 under Section 148 and on applying 149 I 1.P .C. The appellants contended that after the acquittal of four accused persons by the courts below the conviction of the appellants under Section 302 read read with section 34 I.p.C cannot be sustained. It was argued that the appel lants being three in number, could not have formed an unlawful assembly within the definition of Section 141 I.A. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. There is force in the contention of the learned counsel for the appellants. The appellant being only three in numbers, there was no question of their forming an unlawful unlawful assembly along with some unidentified persons who were involved in the crime. The High Court clearly fell into error in confirming the conviction & sentence of the appell lants under Sections 149 and on apply ing 149 I .P. C. [8H; 9A] 2. There was force in this contention of PW 1, the wife of the deceased, PW 2, the daughter of the accused and PW 3 an adjoining land owner, are the three eye witnesses to the occurrence. It is in evidence that the complainant and the accused belonged to opposite factions and there was long standing enmity between the parties. During the last 30 years, there had been murders and rioting between the two factions. The deceased Madda Padshamandas was undergoing life imprisonment for the murder of one of the persons belonging to the group of the said accused. He had come on parole. On the day of occurrence at about 7.00 A.M., when he was passing near the field of A1 he was attacked by the accused party. According to the eye witness es, A 1 and A 3 were armed with spears, A 2, A 4, A 5 and A 6 with knives and A 7 was armed with a stick. All of them way laid the deceased and dragged him into the Tobacco plantation of A I. It cannot be said that apart from the seven accused persons there were some other unidentified person who were involvement in the offence. The non applicability of Section i49 I.

The assessee was the owner of a house situated in Ernakulam which he had purchased in 1958 for the price of Rs. 16,500 to his daughter in law and five of his children. The assessment of the assessee for the assessment year 1966 67 for which the relevant accounting year was the calendar year 1965 was completed in the normal course and in this assessment no amount was included by way of capital gains in respect of the transfer of the house since the house was sold by the assessee at the same price at which it was purchased and no capital gains accrued or arose to him as a result of the sale. On 4th April 1968, however, the Income Tax officer issued a notice under section 148 of the Income tax Act seeking to reopen the assessment for the year 196667 and requiring the assessee to submit a return of income within thirty days of the service of the notice. 48,500 were to tax because there was admittedly no under statement A of consideration in respect thereof of the transferred house and it was not possible to say that the transfer was effected by the assesee with the object of avoidance or reduction of his liability under section 45. The Income Tax Officer issued a show cause notice on 4th March, 1968 seeking to reopening the assessment of assessee for that year and requiring him to submit return of his income within 30 days of service of notice. On 5th April, 1968 the IncomeTax officer issued another notice under Section 148 of Act seeking reopen the assessments of the asses see for the years 1966 67 and 1967 68.

The appellant was charged in the Court of Presidency Magistrate, Bombay as follows: That you on 3 12 1968 at 8 a.m. at Bandra in contravention of provisions of section 2(1)(f) and 7(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, sold 450 grams of Til seeds to the Food Inspector and that the Til seeds were unfit for human consumption and thereby committed an offence under sec. 16(1) (a)(1) of that Act and within my cognizance". The two witnesses produced to support this charge were D. P. Tambe and section P. Gaydhani, P.W. 2, the prosecuting Food Inspector, who stated that after having gone into the grocery shop at Hill Road, Bandra, he disclosed his identity to the accused and demanded 450 grams for which he paid Rs. 1.35. He said that he himself divided this quantity into 3 parts each of which was put into a separate plastic bag and then sealed and labelled by him. He claimed to have obtained the signatures of the accused in the presence of Tambe whom he described as "the independent witness Tambe". The Presidency Magistrate after finding that it was more probable that there was talk about the purpose for which the Til plants were kept in the accused 's shop, held that the purpose was for human use and thus committed an offense under section 16(i)(a) (1) Of the Act. On appeal by the appellant the High Court set aside the conviction and sentence of six months rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs. 1000/ . Allowing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: 1. It is not correct to say that it is presumed from the nature of the article itself or the circumstances and manner of offering it for sale. Where circumstances raise a genuine doubt on the question whether what was kept by a seller was "food" at all, this must be resolved (1 ) A.I.R. , referred to. (2) In order to judge whether the Food Inspectors 's version or the accused`s explanation was more credible it became necessary to examine the evidence of the only witness produced to corroborate the food Inspector. [330 E] Bhagwan Das vs Delhi Administration, ; , followed.

The plaintiff, a Government servant of Madhya Pradesh was dismissed from service by the Collector on 13th January 1966. He preferred an appeal to the Divisional Commissioner and that appeal was dismissed on 31st August 1966. The order of dismissal was communicated to the plaintiff on 19th September, 1960 asking for a declaration that the order of dismiss ment was inoperative and he continued to be in service. This suit was dismissed in the Courts below on acceptance of the defence plea that it had not been filed within three years from the date when cause of action first arose, as required under Article 58 of the First Schedule of the . When this appeal came up for hearing before a Division Bench, reliance was placed on the decision of this Court in Sita Ram Goel vs The Municipal Board, Kanpur & Ors., ; in support of the contention that the suit was barred by limitation. On behalf of the appellant it was contended that Article 113 of the Act of 1963, corresponding to Article 120 of the old Act, is a general one and would apply to suits to which no other Article in the schedule applies; and that the principle of merger applicable to decrees of courts would not apply to orders of departmental tribunals. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The cause of actions shall be taken to arise not from the dates of the original adverse order but on the date When the remedy availed of has not been provided by law. It is proper that the position in such cases should be uniform.

The appellant filed a suit in forma pauperis in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Chittoor for his half share in the properties which once belonged to the joint family consisting of himself and his father and to this suit he impleaded his father, and several alienees from him. His case was that the alienations effected by his father as well as sales held in execution proceedings against his father were not binding on him and so his share in them covered by the said alienations was not affected by them. The trial court rejected his contention that the alienation did not bind him, upheld all the alienations and dismissed his suit. On appeal the High Court reversed the trial court 's decree in respect of alienations which covered items 2, 10 and 14 in Schedule A as well item 5 in Schedule B. It held that the transactions in respect Of these items did not affect that position. The appellant then applied to the High court for a certificate under article 133(1) of the Constitution. This application was rejected on the ground that the decree sought to be appealed from was one of affirmance and there was no substantial question of law raised by the proposed appeal. In coming to this conclusion the High COurt followed an earlier Full Bench decision in Chittam Subba Rao vs Vela Mankanni Chilamayya (I.L.R. [1953] Mad. i. It was urged on behalf of the appellant that the word "decision" does not mean the whole of the decision but the decision on that part of the controversy between the parties which is brought to this Court in appeal. Held, further, that in construing the clause it is obviously necessary to bear in mind that the clause under discussion deals with the constitutional right of the litigant to make an appeal to this court and so it would be inappropriate to adopt a technical or pedantic approach in interpreting the material words used in the relevant clause. It is a matter of comparing the appellate decree with the decision of the trial Court under appeal. If the Appellate decree affirms the decree of the Trial Court it is not a decree of affirmence but variation, and this position would not be affected whether the variation is made in favour of the intending appellant or against him and whether the variations made are minor or major.

Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, read with section 115 of C.P.C., provided that in respect of cases decided before 20th September, 1972 and also all cases arising out of original suits or other proceedings of any valuation, decided by the District Court, the High Court alone was competent to exercise revisional power under section 115 C. P.C. In 1970, the provisions of section 115 were amended and the result was that : (i) The High Court possessed exclusive jurisdiction under section115 in cases arising from original suits of a value of Rs. 20,000/ and above; and 36 (ii) The District Judge possessed exclusive juris diction under section 151 C.p.C.; (iii) A revision proceeding pending immediately before 1st August 1978 of the nature in which a District Court would exercise revisional powers under section 25 would vest in the High court. On 1st February, 1977, section 115 was amended and substituted by section 2, U.P., Civil Laws (Amendment) Act, 1976, with effect from 20th Septem ber, 1972. In consequence: (i). The High ' Court possessed jurisdiction under Section 115 C P. C. in cases which the District Judge and the High Courts respectively exercise revisional juris dic tion of the High 'Court under section 5 of the Provincial Small Cause Courts Act; (ii). The District Court possessed concurrent jurisdiction under sec tion 115 in a case arising out Of an original suit of the value of more than Rs.20,000 and above, including such suits or proceedings instituted before 1 st August 1978; (iii). The two salient features of revisional jurisdiction under s 115 are, on the one hand, the closely limited grounds on which the court is permitted to interfere and on the other, the wide expanse of discretion available to the Court, when it decides to interfere, in making an appropriate order. The intent is that so serious an error as one of jurisdiction, if committed by a subordinate court should not remain uncorrected, and should be removed and the record healed of the infirmity by an order shaped to re instate the proceeding within the proper jurisdictional confines of the subordinate Court. It is a power of superintendence, and fittingly it has been conferred in terms enabling the High COurt to exercise it, not only when moved by an aggrieved person but also suo motu; while considering the nature and scope of the revisional jurisdiction, it is necessary however, to advert to prime circumstance that in civil cases the jurisdiction has been entrusted to the highest court of the State, demonstrating that broadly the order under section 114 is to be regarded, in the absence of anything else, as a final order within the State judiciary.

The respondents filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution in the Calcutta High Court and the rule nisi thereon requiring the reasons as to why a writ in the nature of mandamus should not be issued directing the appellants herein, the State of Rajasthan, the Jaipur Development Authority, Jaipur and the Land Acquisition Officer, Jaipur to forbear from giving effect to the impugned notification dated February 8, 1984 and passed an ad interim prohibitory order restraining them from taking any steps requiring the respondents under sub section (5) of 52 of the Act to surrender or deliver possession of the lands acquired forthwith or upon their failure to do so to take immediate steps under sub s.(6) thereof to secure such possession. The State Government in its special leave petition have explained that the notification under section 52(1) of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959 could not be issue till February 8 , 1984 because the Government were primarily thinking of making the land available for construction of residential houses before making provisions for construc tion of a Three Star Hotel on an area of 6,000 square yards as their real object was to get the notified land released from acquisition. The respondents have been shifting their stand before the Special Officer. As already stated , they had in their reply dated September 8, 1975 alleged that they genuinely required the land for starting new businesses in the State , to open a branch office at Jaipur and to construct residential quarters for their Director and other Senior Executives but at a later stage they alleged that there was no possibility of an exemption being granted under section 20 of the Urban Land (Ceiling & Regulation) Act, 1976 or the legality and propriety of the notice issued by the Special officer under s. 52(2) or his jurisdiction to proceed with the inquiry under section52(3). Nor did the respondents place any material before the special Officer to show that they really needed the notified lands for the purpose of expansion of their business activities to the State Government of Rajasthan.

Section 2 of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of letting, Rent and Eviction) Act 1972 provides various kinds of buildings to which the new Rent Act has no application. Sub section (2) of section 2 contemplates that the new rent Act will not apply to a building during a period of ten years from the date on which its construction is completed. Explanation I to sub s.(2) enumerates the dates on which the building shall be deemed to have been completed : Provided that there may be different dates of completion of construction in respect of different parts of a building which are either designed as separate units or are occupied separately by the landlord and one or more tenants or by different tenants: Explanation II A building shall he deemed to be constructed substantially out of funds obtained from sources mentioned in the proviso, if the funds obtained by way of loan or advance from the State Government or the Life Insurance Corporation of India or a bank or a Co operative society. and the period of repayment of such loan or advances exceeds the aforesaid period of 10 years, then reference in this sub section to a period ten years or the period ending with the date of actual repayment of each loan or the periods ending with that date of the actual repayment Of each loan of advance, including interest, whichever is shorter. Explanation 1 to sub section (3) enumerates certain dates onwhich the building may be deemed, to have be completed : (i) The date on Which the completion thereof is reported to or otherwise is recorded by the local authority having jurisdiction. (ii) In case of building subject to assessment, that date onwhich it is actually occupied for the first time. In the absence of any such report, record or assessment, the date, on which it is originally actually occupied (not including occupation merely for the purposes of supervising the construction or guarding, the building under construction) for the second time.

The appellant company entered into three contracts for the construction of aerodrome, hangarettes, buildings and other works at Ranchi, the first of them being contract No. 21 of 1942 dated November 5, 1942, and the other two being contracts Nos. 6 and 8 dated April 5, 1943. After the above works were completed, disputes arose between the parties over the bills and eventually by an agreement dated February 6, 1948, they were referred to arbitration of one Col. A. W. section Smith. The arbitrator made his award on June 4, 1948 and sent a copy thereof to the parties. The respondents thereupon filed a petition under sections 17 and 20 of the Indian , for a decree in terms of the award. The appellant contended that the agreement was not one relating to execution of works as that had been completed and the dispute related only to payment of the bills, and that further the essential feature of an arbitration agreement was the constitution of a private Tribunal and it could not therefore be brought within item 2 and that accordingly it fell within item 12. Held (per curiam) that in view of section 175(3), the copy of an instrument cannot be validated: That was held in The Rajah of Bobbili vs Inuganti China Sitaramasani Garu, A.I.R. , referred to. Held further, that the document actually before the court is, what it purports to be, "a certified copy" and that under section 35 of the Stamp Act there can be validation only of the original when it is unstamped or insufficiently stamped, that in consequence no decree could be passed thereon. The law is no doubt well settled that the copy Of an instrument can be validated by a notification in the Official Gazette but there is nothing in the section itself to preclude authorisation being conferred ad hoc on any person and when that is established the requirements of the section must be held to be satisfied. In the present case, it was not necessary for the arbitrator to prepare the award in triplicate, sign all of them and send one each to the party and the third to the court.

The respondent was working as Executive Engineer in the Public Works Department in the State of Punjab in the year 1979. On various dates in that year, he placed orders for the purchase of sign boards which were required by the Department to avoid accidents on roads and for traffic safety. The requisite sign boards were purchased in pursuance of the aforesaid orders. The plea raised by the respondent found favour with the High court which relying on an earlier decision of that Court in Des Raj Singhal vs State of Haryana, quashed the First Information report by its order dated February 12, 1986. The respondent company was floated as a public limited company under the Indian Companies Act 1913, to acquire and carry on the business of manufacture and sale of "Amrutanjan". The authorised capital of the company was 7,000 ordinary shares and 3,000 preference shares. Under the Articles of Association of the Company, both preference and ordinary shareholders were entitled to vote at the meeting of the Board of Directors each shareholder being entitled to exercise one vote for each share. In the course of assessment proceedings of the respondent company, the Income tax Officer found that for the three years ending March 31, 1947, March 31. 1948 and March 31., 1949, the company had declared each year a total dividend of Rs. 38,750/ at the rate of 71/2 per cent on the preference shares and 61 per cent of the amount available for distribution as computed under section 23 A of the Income Tax Act, 1922. As it stood at the material time, no order could be passed in respect of any company in which the public were substantially interested and to a subsidiary company of such a company if the whole of the share capital of such subsidiary company was held by the parent company or by the nominees thereof. The respondent company took over the business conducted by it for Rs. 5,50,0001 paid in the form of 2,500 ordinary and 3200 preference shares fully paid up shares. This company was managed by a firm which after the death of 12 Nageswara Rao Panthulu, consisted of Ramayamma, widow of Nageswara Rama Rao and Kamakashamma ma 's husband Sambu Prasad. Between April 1, 1946 to March 31 , 1949, Ramayma, widow Of Nageswararao Rao was holding 2,185 ordinary shares, and her daughter Kamakhamma was holding 250 ordinary shares. Out of the preference share only 385 were held by directors including Ramayamamma and Kamakshamma. Under section 23A of the Indian Income tax Act, a company shall be deemed to be a company in Which the public are substantially interested, but in considering whether shares carrying not less than twenty five per cent or more of the voting power have been allotted uncoiiditionally to, or acquired unconditionally by, and are at the end of the previous year beneficially held by, the public. shares entitled to a fixed rate of dividend have to be excluded. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Explanation to sub section (1) of section 23 of the Act is in reality a clause which defines what a company, in which it the public arc substantially interested. On an analysis of the provisions of the third proviso to section 23 and its explanation, the following position emerges: (i) Where there is no individual member or a group of shareholders acting in concert holding fifty one per cent share or more or of the controlling power, which controls the working of a company it is from its very nature a Company in which there isno controlling member or group and therefore the public is substantially interested; (ii) where not less then twenty five percent of the shares are held by persons other than the controlling group. If a director does not belong to the controlling groups, he will be regarded as a member of the public for the purposes of the second proviso and the Explanation thereto to section 22 A even though such director was directly entrusted with the management of the affairs of the companies. The Commissioner contended that the explanation to sub s (1 ) of section 24A is in substance a clause whereby defines what "a company" in which, the Public are substantially con tended, is. In terms, however, the Explanation raises a conclusive presumption and does not purport to define a company as in which 'the public are not substantially interested", but on different grounds. The interpretation of the Explanation by the High Court for reasons already set out was incorrect. The Revenue authorities have not made any investigation on the question whether there existed any controlling interest in a group Of persons.

The first appellant was a registered joint stock company, the Seksaria Mills Ltd. He was sentenced to two months ' rigorous imprisonment and a fine of RS. 2,00,000 for each count. In appeal the sentence of imprisonment was set aside and the fine reduced to Rs. 1,00. On receipt of this advice slip the first appellant prepared what it had called a " ready sale note " on the same day, 21st February, 1947 authorising the purchaser to take delivery within a week. Dharsi Moolji wrote to the first appel lant that he had effected a sale, (2) the selling agent had paid the first Appellant for the goods, (3) specific bales had been set aside, and appropriated to the sale and consequently the property in the goods had passed, (4) the goods have actually left the Mills ' premises, and (5) they were in the Dady Seth godown under the control of Dwarkadas Khetan. The first appellant then sent a " advice slip " telling it that the money has been received and asking it to prepare a delivery order. The third appellant then debits Dwarkadash Khetan & Company with the price and not the purchaser. For payment it looks to Dwarkad as and Company who, after making the necessary entries in their books, return the order to the Mills office was sent to "our godown ", Whether the goods " refers to Dwaradas" godown or to a godown jointly shared between Dwarkadandas Khetan & Co., and the first appellants were responsible for orders ' which were placed through them. Held, that the charge on the second count relating to the 6 bales is a similar one and the facts follow the same pattern. They have been detailed in the High Court 's judgment and they cannot be said to have concerned themselves with the question of actual physical possession because they say: " It would not be correct to say that there had been anything beyond a technical and unintentional breach of the law.
