The respondent was a Senior Lecturer in a Government College affiliated to the Gujarat University. One of the centres was Surendranagar, which is a Government college. Vallabhdas Gordhandas Thakkar was a legal practitioner conducting cases before the Income tax and Sales Tax Departments. He was also a resident of Jamnagar. It was alleged that in April 1964 the Physics practical examination for the first year B.Sc. was to be held by the Gujarat university. One Of the centres which was Surethranagar Dwivedi had been appointed as an Examiner for Physics practical. He accepted gratification of Rs. 500/ other than legal remuneration for showing favour to a candidate Jayendra Jayantilal Shah by giving him more marks than he deserved in the Chemistry practical examination. It is stated that he had obtained that amount through Thakkar. Dwivedi was charged with commission of offences under section 161, Indian Penal Code and section 5(2) read with section 5 (1) (d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act 1947 read with Section 114 of the Indian Penal code. The Special Judge who tried both these persons found them guilty of the offence with which they were charged. He imposed a sentence of 2 years ' rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs, 1,000/ . Both the convicted persons filed appeals to the High Court. The High Court took the view that even an Examiner was a public servant and as such could be regarded as a public Servant within the meaning of ninth clause of section 21, Indian penal Code, it was necessary that the person committing that offence must be a public servants. Allowing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: (1)(a) The word "otherwise" has wide connotation and if no limitation is placed on it, the words "corrupt", "illegal" and "otherwise ' mentioned in the clause become surplusage, for on that construction every abuse of position is gathered by the clause. So some limitation will have to be put on that word and that limitation is that it takes colour from the preceding words along with which it appears in the cl, that is to say something savouring of dishonest act on his part. The court entertained no doubt that every benefit obtained by the public servant for himself or for any other person by abusing his position as a Public servant fell within the mischief of the said clause. But the abuse being either by corrupt or illegal means or by other means of the nature mentioned in Narayanan Nambiar 's(1) case. (b) relating to obtaining of the valuable thing etc. relates to the object of the public servants, namely, the obtaining of a bribe. " If the meaning to be given to the word " otherwise" is, as earlier stated, the two words "by corrupt or unlawful means" stand by themselves and as soon as it is established that a public person has by such means obtained any valuable thing or pecuniary advantage he will be guilty of an offence as contemplated by section 5.(1)(d).

The petitioners alleged that notwithstanding the fact that each of them had put in continuous service for quite a long period, the Railway Administration, respondent herein, has not treated them as temporary servants and have applied discriminatory rates of wages. They also asked for a direction to treat the petitioners at par with maintenance workers and to declare that they are entitled to equal pay for equal work and have asked for their absorption in the regular cadre in the permanent category as per the circulars issued by the Administration. The Senior Signal & Telecom Engineer (Power Signalling) has filed a counter affidavit on behalf of the respondents challenging the claim of the petitioners. According to them five out of forty four petitioners in this group of writ petitions had undergone medical examination and were granted temporary status as Khallasisis. One of them has been directed to be absorbed against a permanent vacancy in the open line; five others have refused to go to the open Line for permanent absorption. He further averred that though prior to the issue of the Railway Board 's directions on January 1, 1984, project casual labourers were not entitled to all the privileges like House Rent Allowance, Casual Leave, increment etc., they are now entitled to be all the benefits as applicable to open line temporary railway servants after attaining temporary status. In Paragraph 23 of the counter affidavit it has been specifically pleaded that as per extant rules, temporary status will first be given in the cadre of Khallasi and then promotion to skilled category after conducting the trade test is admissible. A number of documents and circulars issued from the Administration have been produced in support of their claim. The senior Signal and Telecom Engineer, (Powerignalling) have filed a Counter affidavit on their behalf. At the hearing of the applications, counsel for the petitioners as also the learned Additionaly Solicitor General were given full opportunity of placing their arguments and documents. In addition, they have also furnished written submissions. 141 It is stated on behalf that out of Forty four petitioners sixteen have now been empanelled and of them five have been given temporary appointments; eleven are said to have refused not to join and seventeen are still continuing with temporary status, and eleven seem to have joined, while seventeen are continuing on temporary status on temporary basis. The respondents have placed reliance on the definition of 'Project ' which means: "a project should be taken as construction of new lines, major projects, restoration of dismantled lines and major important open line works, line doubling, widening of tunnels etc. which are completed within a definite time limit". Admittedly the petitioners have put in more than 360 days of service. Though counsel for them had pointed out that the Administration was requiring continuous service of purpose of eligibility, learned Additional Solicitor General on instructions obtained from the Railway officers present in Court during arguments has clarified that continuity is not insisted upon and though there is break in such continuity the previous service is also taken into account. It is also conceded that on eventual absorption in regular employment half the service rendered with temporary Status is counted as qualifying service for pensionary benefits. In view of the submission, learned Counsel for the respondents has pleaded that the allegation of discrimination does not exist.

The Forest Conservation Act, 1980 aims to prevent depleting forests, conservation thereof and protection of wild life in the country to maintain ecological balance. The State Acts regulate preservation of forest produce and regulates possession of the forest produce failing of trees in the forest area and removal from the forest or reserved forest area by transit permits etc. When Sandalwood Oil either was found in transit or in possession of manufacturers, it was seized in the respective cases and laid the complaints under section 5 1 (1) (or contravention thereof. As the jurisdictional question was raised on the premise that Sandal Wood Oil is not a wood oil as defined under section 2(f)(1) of the Act, the High Court quashed the complaint holding that Sandrial Wood Oil was not 'wood oil ' as defined in section 2 (f) (i) of Kerala Forest Act, 1961 for short the Act. Allowing the appeals by Special Leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The word wood oil used in the Act will require purposive interpretation drawing the context in which the words are used and its meaning will have to be discovered having regard to the intention and object which legislature seeks to subserve. The restricted meaning sought to put up by the accused would frustrate the object and the literal interpretation would defeat the purpose of the statute and the strict interpretation giving narrow meaning to the word wood Oil ' should be excluded. Undoubtedly, the Karnataka Forest Act 1963 incorporated in its definition of forest Produce Sandal wood oil after the word "wood oil" and the legislature in Andhra Pradesh and Tamilnadu, like the Act do not specifically incorporate Sandal timberwood oil in the definition of Forest produce. From this could it be concluded, if it be otherwise interpretable that wood oil would not include Sandal trees as well. to mean wood oil oleo resin from Dipterocarpus alatus (family Diptersocarpuceae), a tree of India and other regions of Southern Asia. Khori in his 'Materia Medica of 504 India and theirrapeutics ' and Pharmacaignhia Indica by Willim Dymock defined wood oil in The same strain. All these technical literatures were concerned in finding out physio chemical properties contained in wood oil and the source from which they are drawn for use in industrial purposes.

The prosecution alleged that the canal after a temporary closure restarted flowing on May 5, 1953, and although it was not his turn of water the deceased Shivlal was allowed to take the water to irrigate his fields. On May 6 the canal was flowing to its full capacity and Shivlal had been to take his turn for water which was of 6 hours duration from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m., but he watered his lands from 8 A.I.R. 1954 section C. 28, 859 and sentenced to transportation for life. The order as to Mt. Rameshwari was reversed and they were convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the High Court should not set aside an acquittal unless there are " substantial and compelling reasons for doing so; because ordinarily a dying declaration of the kind which the prosecution has relied upon is by itself insufficient for sustaining a conviction on a charge of murder. The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in Stephen Seneviratne vs The King, Aher Raja Khima vs The State of Maharastra, ; , referred to. Held further, that where the evidence was such that no Tribunal could legitimately infer from it that the accused is guilty this court would set aside the conviction.

The appellant company was an all India complex having establishments in different parts of the country. In Bihar alone, it has two factories one at Jamshedpur and the other at Ranchi and have depots at Patna and other towns. The factory at Jamshedpur is an establishment under the Bihar Shops and Establishments Act. Certain disputes having arisen between the management of the appellant company and its workmen employed in the factory at Ranchi, the com pany and the said workmen represented by their union called the Indoxco Labour Union. As required by r. 3 of the Industrial Disputes (Bihar) Rules, 1961, the statement accompanying the said application signed by the District Manager on behalf of the Company and the General Secretary of the said union representing the said workman contamed inter alia the following information: "Whereas the Governor of Bihar is of opinion that an industrial dispute exists or is apprehended between the Management of Indian Oxygen Limited. Jamshedpur, regarding the matters specified in their joint applications dated 7 9 1963 annexed hereto . Now therefore in exercise of powers conferred by sub section (2) of section 10 of the , the Governor is pleased to refer the said dispute for adjudication. " The notification thus makes it clear that the disputes referred to the Tribunal were disputes set out in the agreement and state 554 and were between the company 's management of I.N.T.U.C. If held at Jamshedpur; (2 ) a letter dated January 21, 1963 by the General Manager of Golmuri Tinplate Workers Uni , Jamshedpur, to the effect that members of the executive committee of that union were relieved from duty with pay to attend meetings of the Executive Committee or any other meeting called by the union except mass meetings and the union 's delegates were also allowed special leave with p.ay to attend I. N.T.; (3) a letter by the Secretary of Telco Workers Union, Jamshedpur to the affect that members Of the executive Committee of that Union and office bearers were allowed to attend union ' meetings without loss of pay. The Tribunal found that the company had been allowing without loss to pay the representatives of the workmen to attend proceedings before conciliation officers and Industrial Tribunals. This concession was sufficient and, therefore, rejected the demand for special leave to attend the law courts. But it awarded that the Union 's representatives should be given special leave as required by section 28(3) of the . In appeal to this Court on the question: whether the union "s constitution was duly amended on January 6, 1963 as claimed by the company and held by the Tribunal. HELD : (i) The Tribunal was not justified in obliging the appellant Company to grant special leave demanded by the Union. [352 B C] (ii) It is obvious that if the company were asked to pay at the rate equivalent to the ordinary rate of wages for work done beyond 39 hours but not exceeding 48 hours a week, it would be paying no extra compensation at all fo.r the work done within the agreed hours of wo.k. The company would in that case be indirectly increasing the hours of work and consequently altering its conditions of service. If after taking into consideration the fact of the comparatively higher scale of wages prevailing in the appellant 's Company the Tribunal fixed the rate for overtime work at 1 1/4 times the ordinary. rate of wage, it is impossible to say that the Tribunal erred in doing so or acted unjustly. [353 G] (iii) It was not as if the provisions of that Act govern overtime payment payable by an employer where maximum hours of duty are governed by the conditions of services prevailing in his establishment.

The assessee was assessed to tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1918 in respect of income from business inter alia in timber at Abdullapur. In 1939 there was a partition of the Hindu undivided family and five members of that family entered into an agreement of partnership to carry on the business in the name of R. B. Jodha Mal Kuthiala son of Lala Hakam Mal Tani Mal, the business which was originally carried on by the undivided family. Accounts of this firm were settled till March 31, 1939 and the firm was dissolved. The timber business was taken over by two partners of the firm Gajjan Mal and Jodhara Mal. In assessment proceedings for 1943 44 the assessee contended that the firm had ceased to carry On April 1, 1939, before the Income tax (Amendment) Act 7 of 1939 came into force and the first succession to the business after April 1. 1939 was in March 1943 when the assessee was dissolved and on that account the assessee 's firm alone was entitled to relief under section 25(3). The Income tax Officer completed the assessment without giving to the assessee the benefit of sub sections (3) or (4) of section 25 of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922. The Appellate Tribunal agreed with the view of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and held that succession to a family firm was not admissible in relation to the assessment in question. On appeal by certificate the High Court held that in the facts and circumstances of the case the Tribunal was correct in law in holding that the assessee firm was entitled on the dissolution of that firm in March, 1943 to the benefit under section 5(3) of the Act.

The appellant was granted a stage carriage permit under section 48 of the (briefly the Act) for the route Devenagere to Shimoga via Honnali by the Regional Transport Authority, Shimandhar, by its order dated May 3/4, 1963. Some of the respondents preferred appeals against the said order to the State Transport Appellate Tribunal and obtained stay of the operation of the order. The appellant produced the same on April 26, 1967 and the permit was issued on the same day. Against the order of the issue of the permit, respondents 4 to 13 preferred appeals to the Mysore Revenue Appellate Tribunal constituted under sub section (2), who shall after giving such person and the original authority an opportunity of being heard, give a decision thereon which shall be final. The District Judge however dissented. An appeal filed by the appellant to the Revenue Appellate Tribu nal against the order granting the permit had been dismissed on September 27, 1963 on the ground that the Secretary to the Regional ' Transport Authority had no jurisdiction to issue a permit under rule 119 of the Mysore Motor Vehicles Rules, 1963 after a lapse of such a long time from the date of the grant of the permits. It was contended by the appel lant before the appellate authorities that there was no period of limitation under rule 151 of the old Rules which was applicable to his case, for the issue Of a permit. The appeals of the Respondents were allowed by the State transport Appellate Tribunal by majority on January 29, 1969 and the District Judge dissented. On appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant before this Court that there is no dispute that section 64 of the Act is the only section creating rights of appeal against the grant Of permit and other matters with which we are not concerned here. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. There is no appeal provided for under section 64 against an order issuing a permit in pursuance of the earlier resolution of the Regional transport Authority granting the said permit.

The appellant contested the election on the ticket of the Republican Party. He was then a sitting member of Parliament. Among the rival candidates, Prakash Vir Shastri secured 1,49,943 votes while the appellant secured 34,274 votes. The Congress candidate respondent Smt. Kamla Chaudhury secured 33,988 votes and the appellant challenged the election of the appellant on grounds of corrupt practices as mentioned in sub sections (2), (3A) and (4) of section 123 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. At the hearing of the appeal, the appellant appeared in person after counsel on his behalf had obtained leave of this Court to withdraw and to allow the appellant to appear in person. The various corrupt practices on which the appellant relied relate to occurrences at six places. The appellant did not press the other occurrence. The first occurrence relates to a meeting held at Hapur Town Hail Maidan at Hapur on 7 February, 1967. The respondent was not called upon to state as to whether there was a meeting on 6 February,1967 and thereby the appellant was denied the opportunity of meeting that case. Trading(1) and the observations appearing at page 547 of the report in support of the contention that under the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure 'and in particular, the provisions contained in Order VIII of the C.P.C., respondent Shastri should have alleged in the pleadings that the meeting was held on 6 2 1967 and in the absence of such allegations respondent Shastri could not have been allowed to make that case, and that there was rejection of evidence on behalf of the appel lant on consideration that the appellant 's witnesses belonged to particular castes and sects. The High Court correctly came to the conclusion that no meeting was con sidered at Hapur town HailMaidan on 7 2 1967, and there was no attack on the office of the Sta te Party. With regard to the meeting at the Town Hall Maidyan at Hapur it held that respondent Shastri in answer to the petition did not state that there had been a meeting at Hapur.

The mortgagee decree holder in execution of the final decree for mortgage himself purchase the disputed property in auction sale held on July 14, 1978 at a sum of Rs.30,000. On September 20, 1978, the judgment debtor Ganpat Singh, since deceased, the predecessor in interest of the appellants, filed an application under Order XXI Rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the sale. Two other petitions of objections were filed by one Chiranji Lal and another judgment debtor Mst. Abhey Kanwar. All these objections including the applica tion of Ganpat Singh under Order 21 Rule 95 of the C.P.C., were dismissed for default and, consequently, the sale was con firmed by the District Judge on January 2, 1979. On July 17, 1980, that is more than one year after the sale, was confirmed, the decree holder auction purchaser filed an applica tions under Order XXII Rule 95 C. P.C. for setting it aside the auction sale which was opposed by the judgment debtors Ganpat Singh on the ground that as the application was filed more than two years after the confirmation of sale, it was barred by limitation under Article 134 of the . 360 It was held by the learned District Judge that in view of the provision of Explanation I1 of Section 47 read with Article 136 of the , an application for setting setting aside sale can also be made within a period of 12 years from the date on which the decree or order becomes enforceable or where the decree, or any subsequent order directs any payment of money or the delivery of any property to be made at a certain date or at recurring periods when default in making any payment or delivery in respect of which execution is sought, takes place. After a decree is out into execution within the period of limitation under article 136, questions relating to execution, discharge or satisfaction of the decree may arise and such questions including the question as to the delivery Of possession shall be determined by the executing court. When a property is sold in execution Of a decree, an applicationfor setting aside t he sale may be made under Rules 89, 90 or 91 of Order XXI of the code of Civil Proce dure by the persons and on grounds as mentioned therein. Article 134 prescribes a limitation of one year for an application to delivery of possession by a purchaser of immovable property which is purchased in the course of execution of a decree. Such an application can be made only after the decree is put into execution for the period prescribed by Article 136.

Section 123(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 provides that where the corrupt practice is committed not by the candidate or his election agent but by an agent other than the election agent and in his interest, and the corrupt practices by such agent has materially affected the result of his election, the High Court may decide that the election of the returned candidate is not void. Sub section (2) of Section 100 enacts a rider to sub section (1) thereof, and states that even if the agent has committed the corrupt provi sions in the interest of the returning candidate, if the High court is satisfied that the said corrupt practice was not committed by the candidates or his Election Agent and every such corrupt practices was committed contrary to the orders and without the consent of the candidateor his election agents and that the candidate and his election Agent took all reasonable means for pre venting the commission of the corrupt ties at the elec tion, and that in all other respects the election was free from any corrupt practice the part of the candidates, or any of his agents, the Election Commission may decide whether the election should be declared void. The appellant 's election to the Kerala Legislative Assembly from Mattancherry Constituency No. 73 was declared void on the ground that he had committed two corrupt practices within the meaning of Section 123(1) of Act. In support of the petition, the first respondent alleged various corrupt practices on the part Of the appel lant. The High Court negatived all the said allegations except two, viz., (i) printing and publication on March 22, 1987 a day prior to the election; (ii) publication of a wall poster, both maligning the personal character and conduct of the first Respondent. The pamphlet containing the reprint of the daily "Malayala Manorama" dated May 22, 1983 was marked as exhibit P 1 and two photographs of the wall poster were marked as exhibits P 1, and two photograph of the walls poster were also marked as Exhibits P 1. The election petitioner filed an Election Petition claiming a declaration that the appellant ' s election was void and that he was entitled to be declared duly elected from the said constituency. In the petition it was alleged inter alia that the pamphlet was printed and distributed with a view to create a false impression among the elector ate that he Was a murderer, he had not stated as to why it will create such an impression amongst the electorate. The Marxist leader arrested also is known" were a clear and a direct reference to the first respond ent, be cause it was an admitted fact that the first re spondent was arrested for an offence of harbouring the accused in that murder case. It was further alleged that he has not stated in his petition that it was because he was a Marxists leader and was also arrested for harbouring and harbouring his murderers that the elector Ate was likely to construe the said two statements as accus ing him as the murderer. The Election Tribunal held that both these acts amounted to corrupt practices under Section 123 (4) read with Section 100 of the Act, and were sufficient to void the election. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (i). It is not the usual practice in libel actions to plead particular acts of publication if the words com plained of had been published in a newspaper, in cases where the action was based on a legal, or 'true ', innuendo and the ordinary readers of the paper would not have derived from the words complained of; (2).

The respondent No. 5 proposed to construct a five star hotel on a tract of land measuring 44,820.49 square yards at Bandra, Bombay bearing R.S. Nos. 416 (Part) and 417. The land in question had been purchased by the respondent No 5 from its erstwhile owner, Byramji Jeejeebhoy Pvt. Ltd., In the 1966 sanctioned Development Plan of Greater Bombay, the said land was shown in the residential zone and a contiguous parcel of land admeasuring 18,000 sq. was shown as a green belt. With a view to developing the disputed land, the respondent NO. 5 submitted a plan to the Municipal Corporation of GreaterBombay for the construction of a five Star hotel. The Commissioner of the Municipal corporation rejected the plan on the sole ground that it was proposed to earmark the said property under reference as a recreational ground with suitable internal network of roads during the revision of the development plan which was in the offing. Being aggrieved by the rejection of the plan, the Respondent No. 1 filed an appeal before the State Government under section 47 of the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966. The respondent No 2 set aside the order of the Commissioner of Municipal Corporation rejecting the plan submitted by the Respondent NO.5 after hearing the petitioners as also the Municipal Commissioner and directed sanctioning of the Plan on certain conditions which will be referred to later in this judgment. The Municipal Corporation accepted the appellate order and did not challenge the order granting sanction of the building plan submitted on the said plot. Being dissatisfied with the rejection, the appellant filed a writ petition challenging the legality and validity of the resolution dated 14.3.1974 and also the provision of section 20 of the Urban Land Ceiling Act. The Writ Petition was dismissed by the Division Bench of the High Court by the judgment under appeal. At this stage, it may be mentioned that some of the provisions of the Act have been considered by the High court in Life Insurance Corporation of India and Another vs Municipal Corporation, Greater Bombay and Others, Writ Petition No. 2944 of 1932 disposed of on 6.3 .1984. In that case, a development application was rejected by the Municipal Corpora tion on the ground that the property was proposed for to be reserved for public purposes or for recreational ground in the draft revised development plan, and the High COurt repelled the challenge to the decision taking the view that even the proposed revision could be taken into account as one of the relevant factors. The petitioners have not challenged the judgment on review applications. They have not assailed the judgment of the Division Court passed on the review applications after considering all the points including certain additional grounds to the effect that certain contentions had not been dealt with earlier by the Judgment dated October 9/10, 1985. In support of his contention, the learned Counsel has placed reliance on an unreported decision of a Single Judge of the Bombay High Court in Life Assurance Corporation ofIndia and Another v Municipal Corporation Of Greater Bombay & Ors., Writ Petition NO.

The employers were guilty of imposing and continuing a lock out as provided in Item 6 of Schedule II of the Maharashtra Recognition of Trade Unions and Prevention of Unfair Labour Practices Act, 1971. After hearing the parties, the learned Judge answered the issue in negative and dismissed the complaints. The appellant Union filed two special civil applications in Bombay High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution questioning the correctness of the decision of the Industrial Court. Both the applications were dismissed in limine. The Union thereupon filed these appeals by special leave. 66 At the hearing of the appeals, Mr. Govind Dass, learned counsel for the employers stated that the industrial undertakings of the employers had never been closed or at any rate have resumed working in full and that the old workmen are not being re employcd and new hands are being recruited. The Industrial Court observed as under: "During that the undertaking is carried out in letter and spirit we direct the Industrial court Maharashtra Bombay to depute its senior ministerial officer to visit the industrial establishments of the employer and to satisfy itself that the new workmen are being re inducted in service and that as resumption of production is gradually expanded, the old workman will be re inducted into service. There will be a continuous watch by the ministerial officer and to be appointed by the Industrial Judge till all the old employees who are willing to be reappointed in service are taken back in service. In fact this undertaking should have concluded the matter. But there is a statement of law made by the industrial Court while rejecting the complaints filed by the appellant union which does not command to us and to avoid any such error being repeated in future, we, with a view to set right the matter proceed to examine the same in this judgment. 67 The complaints of the union were that the employers were innocent of imposing unfair labour practice by imposing and terminating continuing a strike out which under the law was illegal. On the other hand, the submission on behalf of the respondents was that there was a closure of the industrial undertaking and it was not a case of lock out. In such a situation there the parties are at variance whether the employers have imposed a lockout or have closed the establishment it is necessary to approach the matter from this angle that the closure has to be irrevocable, final and permanent and that lockout is necessarily temporary or for a period. The employer may close down industrial activity bonafide on such eventualities as suffering continuous loss, no possibility of revival of business or inability for various other reasons to continue the industrial activity. There may be a closure for any of these reasons though these reasons are not exhaustive but are merely illustrative. To say that the closing down of the industry was a consequence of imposing lock out or the owner employer had decided to close down the industrial activities, the Industrial Tribunal before which the action of the management is questioned must keep in view all the relevant circumstances at the time of closure decide and determine whether the closure was a bonafide one or was a device or a pretence to determine the services of the workmen. Answer to this question would permit A the Industrial Industrial Court to come to the conclusion one way or the other. Having clarified the position in law, we dispose of the appeal in terms of the undertaking of Dr. P.D. Meghani as recorded in this Judgment. Both these appeals are disposed of accordingly.

The appellant company was incorporated on July 29, 1924 as an investment company. The objects of which are set out in el. III of the memorandum of association and more particularly in sub cls. 1, 2, 15 and 16 of that cl. III provided: "In relation to the purchases made by the petitioner company as stated above no appreciable sales of shares were made during the period 29th July, 1924 to 30th June, 1942, the sales made in the year ended 30th September, 1946, of the value of Rs. 1.29,333 included shares of the values of Rs 45,000 in the Loyal Mills Ltd., sold to the members of the staff and shares of that value representing sterling investments handed over to the creditors of the petitioner Company in part repayment of the loan taken from them in the years ended 30st June, 1931, shares of shares the value Of Rs. 7,48,356 were handed over by the appellant company during the year ending 30th December, 1946. The sales were contained in paragraph 3(b) which states: " In relation to purchases made on behalf of the Petitioner Company as stated below no appreciable sale of shares was made during that period 29st July, 1925 to 30rd June, 1941, the said sales were included shares in the value for the assessment years 1940 41, 1941 42 and 1942 43 the Income Tax Department accepted the plea of the assessee company and treated it as a dealer in shares, securities and immovable properties and assessed it on that basis. For these years and for the year 1943 44 the appellant Company made its return in that basis but after the return had been filed for the years 1943 44, 1941 41 and 194243 the Income tax department accepted the contention of the appellant assessee company treating it as an investor but it was rejected by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner on the ground that no question of law arose out of its order. The Appellate Tribunal held that in the case of the asses see company not only the Memorandum of Association gave the power to the company to deal in investments but the case and of the company all along in the past was that it was a dealer dealing in shares and properties, and therefore, the profits and losses arising from the sale of share, securities etc. could be taxed as business profits. The High Court also held that the assessee Company was a "dealer" within the meaning of section 2(22) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf Of the appellant that (1 ) most of the shares, security and properties acquired by the assessee were the properties of E.D. Sassoon & Co., and the family of Sassoons continued to be interested in the said Group of Mills and they were realised by sale only when E. D. Sassoon and Co. decided to relinquish their interest in the aforesaid group of Mills, and (2) neither the mode of acquisition of these shares nor the mode and manner of their disposal have any of the distinctive characteristics of business dealings. HELD: The question as to what are the characteristics of the business in shares or that of an investor is a mixed question of fact and law and what was the legal effect of the facts found by the Tribunal and whether as a result the assessee can be treated as a " dealer" or an investor was itself a question of ' law. [52 E F] G.

The appellant was recruited to the Madras Provincial Judicial Service as District Munsif in 1935. In 1949 he was promoted to the office of Subordinate Judge and on June 19, 1950, he was posted as Subordinate Judge of Masulipatnam, Krishna District. On August 22, 1950 when judgment was still pending in the High Court of Madras a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for a writ quashing the order of suspension dated January 28, 1954 on the grounds: (1) that under the Andhra Civil Services (Disciplinary Proceedings Tribunal) Rules, 1953, which had been published by the Andhra Government on October 22, 1953 with effect from October 1, 1953 the enquiry into the conduct of Government servants on a monthly salary of Rs. 150 and above could be held only by a Tribunal to which the Government might refer the same; and (2) that the order in question was void as it was in contravention of article 311 of the Constitu tion. Held, that the High Courts had no authority under the rules to suspend a judicial officer pending final orders of the Government. The order passed by the High court on January 28 was merely one of suspension pending final proceedings by the Government and such an order was neither one of dismissal nor removal from service within article 311 Of the Constitution. Held further, that in view of this conclusion it became unnecessary to consider the contention of the appellant that having regard to its setting, the proviso should more properly be read as qualifying sub rule (2), and that read as a whole, the Rule did not show an intention to depart from the procedure laid down in the Madras Civil Services Rules.

The income tax Officer then issued notice under s 34(2) (b) to " James anderson"s appeals against the order of the Incometax Officer to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and to the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, Bombay, were unsuccessful. Whether in the facts and circumstances of the case the dividends of Rs. 61,051 and "Rs. 3,73,099 deemed to had been distributed on 26th May 1947 and 22nd December 1947 respectively under section 23A of the Act was assessable in the hands of the applicant?

The appellant was the Ruler of the State of Baster. After the passing of the Indian Independence Act, 1947, the appellant executed an Instrument of Accession to the Dominion of India on August 14, 1947. Thereafter he entered into an agreement with the Government of India whereby he ceded the State to the Government and to make provisions for other matters connected therewith. Under section 3 of the Act vesting of proprietary rights in the State Government takes place on certain conditions mentioned in that section being complied with. The definition of 'proprietor ' is stated in section 2(j) and it is "in relation to merged territories, means any area other than land in possession of a raiyat which has been separately assessed to land revenue, whether such land revenue be payable or has been released, compounded for or redeemed in whole or in part". The definition includes an inferior proprietor, a protected thekadar or other thekadadar, or protected headman; and (ii) the merged territories means a maufidar including an ex Ruler of an Indian State merged with Madhya Pradesh. Under article 366(22) of the Constitution any dispute arising out of the Merger Agreement or the Instrument of accession is beyond the competence of the courts to enquire into. The High Court was of the opinion that in these circumstances it was for the appellant to establish that the villages in question had never been assessed to the land revenue but no evidence had been led to this effect. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the appellant was an ex ruler and that article 366 (22) did not make him a Ruler for the purposes of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950, which required a court to recognise such a person as a Ruler.

The respondent was a Garden Curator in the Office of the Scientist SE, Botanical Survey of India, Eastern Circle, Shillong. By order dated January 29, 1991 he was transferred from Shillong to Pauri (Uttar Pradesh) by the Senior Administrative Officer, office of the Director, Botsotanual Survey ofIndia, (Ministry of Environment and Forests, Government of India). As many as 19 persons were transferred under the said order including the respondent. The respondent approached the Gauhati Bench of the Central Administrative Tribunal ( Original Application No. 33 of 1991) questioning the order of his transfer. He submitted that his wife is also employed at Shillong in and off ice of the central Government, that his children are studying at Shillong and further that he himself had suffered back bone fracture injuries some time ago. He relied upon certain executive instructions issued by the Government in that behalf. Those instructions were in the nature of guidelines. They do not have statutory force. Who should be transferred where, is a matter for the appropriate authority to decide. Unless the order is vitiated by mala fides or is made in violation of any statutory provisions, the Court cannot interfere with it. While ordering the transfer, there is no doubt, the authority must keep in mind the guidelines issued by Government on the subject. Similarly if a person makes any representation with respect to his transfer, the appropriate Authority must consider the same having regard to the exigencies of administration and enable the two spouses to live together at one station if it is possible without any detriment to the administrative needs and the claim of other employees. [431C E] Bank of India vs Jagjit Singh Mehta [1992] 1 S.C.C., 306, followed.

The appellants were tried for the murder of one Jawahar. Three charges were framed against them. A7 was charged under Section 302 read with Section 109, I.P.C. for instigating A1 to 6 to commit the murder. The second charge related to rioting wherein A1, A2, A4, A5 and A6 armed with sticks, A3 armed with aruval (bill hook) and A 6 armed with stick (spear stick), attacked Jawahar at about 8.30 A.M. on January 2, 1977 and caused him multiple injuries as a result of which he died on the same day. All the ac cused persons were acquitted by the Trial Judge. On appeal the High Court maintained the acquittal of A4 to A7 but reversed the findings in respect of A1to A3. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The intention of the appellants was to cause grievous hurt and as such the offence committed by them comes within the parameters of Section 325 read with 34, I P.C., and instead convict them under Section 325, IP. C. [3E] 2.1 In view of the nature of injuries on the person of the deceased and the facts and circum stances of this case, the offence com prised by the appellants came within the mischief of Section 324 read with section 34, IPC. Thirteen external in juries were found on the dead body of Jawahar. Out of those 11 were on lower legs and arms. The High Court while consid ering the nature o offence observed as under: "The accused and their associates who be set themselves on Jawahar could never have intended to cause the death of Jawahar for, if such was their intention, they could have certainly killed him especially after carrying him into the cholam field and left him dead there instead of merely causing simple and grievous injuries to him. Even with reference to the aspect whether the accused persons could have intended ted to cause such injuries as would be sufficient, in the ordinary course of nature, to cause death, it is not able to give a finding in favour of the prosecution. Even according to Jawahar 's statement (Exhibit P 6) all that first accused had remarked was that the attack on him was in retaliation for the injuries Jawahar had caused on the first accused a few weeks earlier.

The appellant Bank filed a suit in the Sub Court, Eluru on February 10, 1975 against the respondents including the respondent firm and its partners to recover a sum of Rs.18,14,817.91 being the balance (inclusive of interest) of three principal amounts of Rs,3.00,000 and Rs.80,000 advanced by the Bank to the firm under cash credit account on 28 11 1967, 3 4 1968 and 17 2 1972 respectively. It may be noticed that the Bank was nationalised on July 7, 1969 under the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act V of 1970, which came into force on July 19, 1969. The respondent firm owns certain motor vehicles which are mentioned in A and Schedules to the plaint of the said suit. The firm was carrying on its business at Madras as fleet owners and gasolene carriers. It had two partners, namely, one section Doranna Choudhury, since deceased, the father of the respondent No. 3 and the respondent Nos. 4 to 12, the alienees, since the deceased also created an equitable mortgage in favour of the Bank on December 22, 1969 in respect of E Schedule properties of the plaint. Section Doranna Choudhary, sincedeceased, also created a equitable mortgage by the deceased partner and the respondents Nos.4 to 12 created another equitable mortgage on September 6, 1974 in respect thereof to secure repayment of the aforesaid amounts of loan, the other partner, the respondent no. 2, created an ' equitable mortgage ' in favour favour of Bank on February 28, 1970 in respect Of E Schedule property of the suit. Section 120B I.P.C. provides that on the commencement of the Act there shall be constituted such corresponding new Banks as are specified in the First Schedule. In view of section 4(e) of the Madras Agriculturists Relief Act IV of 1938, which after the creation of the State of Andhra Pradesh, was made applicable to that State as the Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Agriculturists Relief Acts IV of 1939, were not applicable to the Bank and, as such, the bank was entitled to recover the entire amount without the same being scaled down as provided in section 13 of the Banking companies Act. The appellant Bank contested the suit by filing written statements, inter alia, denying the creation or creation of any equitable mortgage, by the erstwhile partner and also the respondents nos.

By section 3 of the Sugar (Control) Order, 1955, the Central Government was given the power, if it was of opinion that it was necessary or expedient so to do for maintaining or increasing supplies of any essential commodity or for securing their equitable distribution and availability at fair prices. The Central Government issued a notification fixing ex factory price per maund of sugar produced in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and North Bihar. In exercise of these powers the Central Govern ment promulgated the Sugar Export Promotion Ordinance No. V of 1958 empowering it to appoint an export agency for carrying out the work of buying sugar in the Indian market and exporting the same to foreign markets and fixing the quantity of sugar for export. The petitioners challenged the validity of the notification on the ground that it did not fix any price at which the persons purchasing sugar from the mills would sell it, so that it could be open to the middleman who bought sugar from factories to sell it at any price, thus creating discrimination between factories and factories and between the producers selling sugar and the middlemen who buy sugar selling the same in their turn. Held, that the impugned notification was beyond the authority conferred on the Central Govt. by section 3 Of the Act and cl. 5 of the Order. The object of the Act is to provide for control of production, supply and distribution of trade and commerce in, essential commodities in the interests of the general public so that the supplies of such commodities may be maintained or increased, their equitable allocation secured and they may be available to the general Public at fair price prices.

The Government of West Bengal by its order dated September 13, 1956 transferred the dispute from the file of the Second Industrial Tribunal to that of the Fifth Industrial Tribunal. The Fifth Industrial Disputes (Amendment and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1956 came into force on August 28, 1956. On April 9, 1956, the Government made an order transferring the said dispute from a file of Second Industrial Tribu nal to that Of the Fifth industrial Tribunal. Under the award the Tribunal held that there was a rise in the cost of living index and that to neutralise the said rise the employees should get an increase of Rs. 7 in dearness allowance on the pay scale up to Rs. 50 and Rs. 5 on the Pay Scale above Rs.50. On that basis the dearness allowance payable to the employees was worked out and awarded. The correctness of the award is questioned in these appeals by special leave. Held, that in regard to matters covered by it, the agreement replaced the earlier award and therefore the date of the agreement is the crucial one for ascertaining whether there was substantial change in the working class cost of live index in the year 1957. Pritam Singh vs The State of Madras, [1955] 1 S.C.R. 869, followed. Pritam singh vs The Union of India, ; , referred to. In regard to proceedings pending before a Tribunal constituted under the Act before the commencement of the Amending Act would be disposed of as if the Amending act had not been passed. Pritam Sing Singh vs State of Punjab, [1959] Supp. 2 S. C.R., followed.

The appellant was a religious institution dedicated to the propagation and promotion of the tenets of the Veera Saiva cult of Hinduism. This Mutt is situated at Uravakonda in the district of Anantapur. It appears that on 6th September, 1939, the Board of Hindu Religious Endowments constituted under the Madras Act 11 of 1927 framed a scheme under section 63 of the said Act for the proper administration of the Mutt and its endowments. The predecessor in office of the appellant then filed suit No. 21 of 1939 on the file of the District Judge Anantapur for getting the said scheme set aside. His suit substantially failed, because the District Court was persuaded to make only a few minor modifications in the scheme subject to which the scheme was confirmed. That decision was taken in appeal by the predecessor of the appel lant to the High Court of Madras (A.S. No. 269 of 1945). During the pendency of the appeal, the appellant 's predecessor died and the appellant brought himself on the record as the legal representative of his deceased predecessor. Thereafter, the present writ proceedings commenced and throughout the protracted period occupied by these proceedings. The status quo has continued. The scheme consists of 15 clauses and in substance it entrusts the administration of a Mutt and all its clothe ments in the hereditary trustee and two non hereditary trustees appointed by the Board. These latter are liable to be removed by the State Government for good and sufficient cause and the Board 's order in that behalf has to be final. The appellant moved the Madras High Court on the 28th April, 1952, by his writ petition and prayed for an appropriate writ quashing the notice served on him by the Executive Officer threatening to take over the administration and its properties under the scheme. This petition was heard by a single Judge of the same High Court and was allowed. The Division Bench took the view that some provisions of the earlier Act which were valid when it was enacted, could not be challenged on the ground that some of its provisions contravened the fundamental right guaranteed to the citizens of this country under article 19(1)(f) and so, it could not he enforced. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The scheme in question was framed and the Executive Authority was appointed as early as 1939. If the Executive officer could not take over possession of the properties and its property, it was partly because the appellant has continuously challenged the implementation of the scheme by legal proceedings and partly because he has otherwise obstructed the said implementation. But it is clear that when the scheme is framed and a challenge made by the appellant to its validity failed in courts of law, his property rights had been taken away. The fact that the order was not implemented does not make any difference to this legal position.

The appellant was appointed as Hindi Teacher in Banichha M.E. School (Orrisa) for a period of 89 days or till a candidate selected by the State Selection Board was made available. He joined the school on July 12, 1982. The appointment was made by the District Inspector (Schools) on the recommendation of the managing committee of the school. He continued to serve the school with repeated spells of 89 day appointments and one day break in between the spells till May 25, 1986. He was not paid the salary for the period of summer vacations during all these years. Although the period was of summer vacation during all those years, the appellant continues to serve as Hindi teacher in the school under orders of the Managing Committee yet his appointment after 1986 has not been approved by the educational authorities. The managing committee even passed a resolution on July 6,1987 requesting the educational Authorities of the State of Orissa to approve the continuous appointment of the appellant as Hindi Teachers but no action was taken by the said authorities. Aggrieved, the Appellant filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the Orissa High Court claiming regularisation as Hindi Pandit with effect from July 12.1982. The only argument raised before the High Court was that the appellant was entitled to be regularised in terms of the provisions of Section 3 of the Orissa Aided Educational Institutions (Appointment of Teachers Validation) Act, 1989. The High Court rejected the prayer for regularisation and held that the appel lant was not entitled to the benefit of the validation Act on the following reasoning: "Admittedly, the petitioner was appointed on 12.7.1982 and continued till 18.7 1986 with breaks in between and the petitioner 's appointment was conditioned by the stipulation that he would continue until replaced by a candidate from the Select List. His case, therefore will not come within the preview of the Validation Act and, therefore, the question of issuing any direction to regularise his service in a substantive vacancy because of the Validating Act does not arise. " The High court rejected the claim for regularisation on the ground that his initial appointment for 89 days was conditioned on by the stipulations that he will continue until replace by a candidates from the select list. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. Under the Constitution the State is committed to secure right to education for all citizens. Bulk of our population is yet illiterate. Till the time illiteracy is effaced from the country the resolution enshrined in the Preamble cannot be fulfilled. Education is the dire need of the country. There are neither enough schools nor teachers to teach. Insecurity is writ large on the face of the teaching community because of nebulous and unsatisfactory conditions of service. In order to make the existing educational set up effective and efficient it is necessary to do away with ad hocism in teaching appointments. An appointment on 89 day basis with one day breaks which deprives a teacher of his salary for tho period of vacation and other service benefits, is wholly arbitrary and suffers from the vice of discrimination. The Validation Act has been enacted by the Orissa legislature with the obvious object of granting relief to those members of teaching community who are being exploited for years together by keeping them in short spell appointments like 89 day appointment as here with oneday break and in the process denying them their rightful dues and other services. Inspite of repeated depreciation by this Court the practice continues to be followed by various State Governments in the country,. Under Article the State has been committed to securing right to Education for all citizen.

The respondent was the Chairman of a Panchayat Samiti and the ground that he was disqualified from being chosen as a member of the Assembly, because he was holding an office of profit under the State Government at the relevant time. The appellant challenged the election of the respondent in an election petition inter alia on the ground: (i) that the office of Chairman of the Panchayat Samiti was an office under the Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zila Parishads Non Official Members ( Payment of Allowances) Rules, 1965 which are as follows : "3. There shall be paid a monthly consolidated allowance in lieu of all other allowances, at the following rates. Category I . Rs. 6.00 per day. Category II. Rs. 4.00/ per day (2) A Chainnan, Vice Chairman or Member shall be allowed to travel by 1st Class and the Members by 2nd Class. The Chairman, ViceChairman and Members shall be entitled to draw single fare of the class of accommodation to which he is entitled: Provided that if the journey is performed in lower class, the Chairman, vice Chairman and Members should be paid the fare actually paid. (iii) Mileage allowance by road shall be admissible at the rates specified below, for the journeys performed by the Chainnan Vice Chairman/ Members between stations which are neither connected by rail nor by regular bus : Motor Cycle or Ordinary cycle other means of conveyance between the stations connected by road, where regular bus service plies and also for a journey between the station connected by railway but performed by bus by taking a single seat the Chairman. Vice Chairman and Member Members shall he paid the fares actually paid." The High Court dismissed the election petition on the view that the various questions involved were of considerable importance and should be settled by a larger Bench, referred the petition to a Full Bench. Allowing the appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) Under r. 3 of the Punjab Panchayats Samitis and Zilla Parishads Nonofficial Members (Payment of Allowances ) Rules, 1961, the members entitled to daily allowance are divided into two categories and a Chairman of Panchayat Samiti belonging to Category II is entitled to Rs.6/ per diem when a Member of the .Samiti belonging to category II is only entitled to 1/4th of the rate provided, if the Chairman was provided free board and lodging officially and at 1/2 rate if he was charged either for board or for lodging.

The appellant was tenant of Kothi No. 196 situated in Dholki Mohalla, Sadar Bazar, Meerut Cantt. ever since 1961 on a rent of Rs. 93 per mensem. The tenanted premises was let out to the appellant for running a Dal and Oil Mill. The respondents purchased the building from the erstwhile owners in 1963 a year later they filed a suit for eviction on a number of grounds including the 972 ground that the appel lant had made constructions materially altering the accommodation without their consent causing substantial damages to it. It was not necessary to refer to other grounds as the sole ground which survived for the decree of eviction relates to the material alterations made in the tenanted premises without obtaining the consent of the landlord. The disputed construc tions include a partition wall in a hail converting the same into two portions and tin sheds shown by letters ABHG and CDGH. The trial Court held that the partition wall did not constitute material alteration, it further held that since the constructions had been made with out permission of the respondent, the tenant was liable for eviction. On second appeal, the Additional Civil Judge set aside the order of the first appellate court on the findings that none of the construc tion constituted material alteration justifying appellant 's eviction under sec. 14(c) of the U.P. Cantonment Rent Control Act, 1952. Since the constructions have been made without permission of t he respondent,the tenant was not liable for ejectment. The Additional Civil judge set aside ted the trial court 's order and dismissed the respondents suit on the finding that none Of the constru cions constituted material alterations justifying appellant eviction under section 14(C) of U. P. Cantonment Act 10 of 1952. On a second appeal made by the respond ents a learned Single Judge of the High Court set aside tho judgment and decree of the First Appellate Court on the con struction that the tin shed indicated by letters C DGH as well as the parti tion wail made in th e hall converting the premises into two rooms, constituted material altera tions as contemplated by section 14 (c). The appellant company filed a suit for setting aside an ex parte decree for Rs. 28,479/ passed in favour of the respondent firm on 22 4 1975 against the appellant. The Additional District Judge held that summons in the suit was not duly served on the company and it came to know about the decree on 29 7 1975. Hence he set aside the ex parte order. The respondent firm filed a revision in the High Court under section 115 of the Code. The High Court allowed the revision, set aside that judgment of the Trial Court and upheld the passing of the ex exparte decree. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The judgment by the Trial Judge setting aside the decree was correct. In any event no error of jurisdiction was committed by it. [1031C] 2.1 Rule 17 of Order 5 of C.P.C. provides that where the defendant or his agent or such other person as aforesaid refuses to sign the acknowledgement, or where the serving officer, after using all due and reasonable diligence, cannot find the defendant, and there is no agent empowered to accept service of the summons on his behalf, nor any other person on whom service can be made, the serving Officer shall affix a copy of the notice on the outer door or some other conspicuous part of the house in which the defendant ordinarily resides or carries on business or personally works for gain, 1032 and shall then return the original to the Court from which it was issued, with a report endorsed thereon or annexed thereto stating that he has so affixed the copy, the circumstances under which he did so, and the name and address of the person (if any) by whom the house was identified and in whose presence the copy was affixed. [ 1031E F] 2(a) The word "Principal Officer" in clause (a) of Rule 2 would include managing agents and it can, under this rule, be on a juristic person. Therefore service on managing agents who are a corporation is valid under clause (b). The meaning of clause (c) has got to be understood in the background of the provisions of the code in Order 5 which is meant for issue and service of summons on natural persons. Sending a summons by post to the registered office of the company, unless the contrary is shown will be presumed to be service on the Company itself. But the first part of clause(b) has get to be read in the context of the provision contained in Order5 Rule 17 C. In other words, if the serving peon or bailiff is not able to serve the summons upon the Secretary or any Director or any other Principal Officer of the Corporation because either he refuses to signed the summons or is not to be found by the serving person even after due diligence then he can leave the summons at the registered Office of the Company and make a report to that effect. In the instant case, nothing of the kind was done. It was not the case of the Respondent in its rejoinder filed in the Miscellaneous case that the service of notice as effected in accordance with the first portion of clause 2(b).

The Magistrate passed a preliminary order on the 29th July, 1976 declaring the appellant to be in possession of the land in dispute. Against this order, the respondents moved the High Court under section 482 Cr. P.C. for quashing the order of the Magistrate. The High Court found that as there was no clear finding by the Magistrate in the final order that there was an apprehension of breach of peace, therefore, the final orders were bad and the High court accordingly allowed the petition and remitted the case to the Magistrate for passing a final order under sub section (1) and thereafter to pass a final orders under sub s.(6) of section 145. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there could be no dispute having ended so as to lead to cancellation of the order under subsection (5) of Section 145 nor was such a case set up by any party before the Magistrate or before the High Courts. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Under section 145 it is for the Magistrate to be satisfied regarding the existence of a breach of the peace and once he records his satisfaction in the preliminary order, he can continue the proceedings. It is not necessary that at each stage he should be satisfied that there exists an imminent apprehension of such breach of law. Unless such a contingency arises, the proceedings have to be carried to their logical end culminating in the finally order under section 145(6) Cr. [95C D] 2. The enquiry under section 146 is limited to the question whether the dispute has ceased to exist at all stages of the proceedings also.

The appellant carried on the business of manufacture and sale of blankets and other woollen cloth. For the assessment year 1948 49, the assessee paid a sum of Rs. 75,465 as commission to the General Manager Shri J.P. Vaish, who was also given free medical facility for himself and the members of his family. In terms of the letter of appointment Shri Vaish got no commission in the first year as the mill suffered a loss. The Income Tax Officer disallowed the claim on the ground that it was excessive and quite unreasonable looking to the salary paid to Shri Vaish. He also found that no general practice of giving commission at the rate of 25 % existed in the assessee 's line of business, but there was some collateral reason. But considering the practice in similar business concerns, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner expressed the view that the post of General Manager carried the responsibility equal to that of the Director who was given the charge of the conduct of business after the death of Shri Vaish, the General manager. Tiffs post carried a remuneration of Rs . 18,000 plus Rs. 6,000 i.e., a total remuneration of RS. 24,000 per annum and therefore the commission paid to Sri Vaish in excess of tiffs amount was not really paid wholly for the purpose of carrying on business. But it was pointed out on behalf of the assessee that Shri Vaish who worked in the mill at the initial stage and of the Managing Director was not comparable and the Appellate Tribunal was wrong in taking this circumstance into consideration. Held, further, that the question of law referred to the High Court must be answered in the manner indicated and this appeal is accordingly allowed with costs.

The appellant was a workman employed in the Digha factory of Bata Shoo Company. On January 13, 1954, the management served him with a charge sheet alleging that he had been doing anti union activities inside the factory during the working hours and so was guilty under section 12B(1) of the Standing Orders and Rules of the company. After written statements were filed by both the parties stating that all the disputes were going to be compromised. On November 16, 1956, however, a fresh application for time was filed but it was stated that agreement had already been reached on some of the matters and opportunity was asked for to settle the other matters. The case was adjourned to January 21, 1957, for filing a compromise or hearing. On December 20, 1956 the parties, that is, the Management and the Union filed a joint petition of compromise settling all points of dispute out of court. Prior to this on January 12, 1957 the present appellant had made an application praying that he should be allowed to represent his case before the Tribunal instead of Fateh Singh, the Secretary of the Union and that he did not want his case to be represented by Fateh Singh as he had no faith in him. The question was whether when a dispute concerning an individual workman is taken up by the Union of which the workman is a member, as 200 a matter affecting workmen in general and on that basis a reference is made under the Industrial Disputes Act the individual workman can claim to be heard independently of the union is undoubtedly of some importance. Held, further, that section 36 of the Industrial Dispute Act recognises this position by providing that the workman who is a party to a dispute shall be entitled to be represen ted by an officer of a registered trade union of which he is a Member. The scheme of the industrial Disputes Act does appear to contemplate that the machinery provided therein should be set in motion to settle only disputes which involve the rights of workmen as a class and that a dispute touching the individual rights of a workman was not intended to be the subject of adjudication under the Act, when the same had not been taken up for by the union or a number of workmen.

The appellant tenant was the tenant of a building in Delhi having been inducted into possession by the respondent landlord under a letting of May 19, 1954 evidenced by a deed which fixed the term merely as less than a year (a circumstance out of which a minor ripple of legal argument has arisen). At the time of the lease the appellant had not been extended to Delhi although later on December 1, 1962, the said Act was made applicable to this area. The landlord filed a petition for eviction against the tenant on the ground that no notice terminating the tenancy under section 106 was needed and further that the forfeiture of the tenancy caused by sub letting contrary to the terms of the deed of demise can be availed of by the landlord even in the absence of a notice as contemplated by section 111(g) because the TP Act, as amended by the Amending Act of 1929 did not apply proprio vigore to such demises and their determination, could the principles of justice, equity and good conscience, which alone applied, did not desiderate the technical requirement of a valid notice in writing of an intention to determine the lease. The Rent Controller dismissed the petition holding that no notices terminating the contractual tenancy under Section 106 was required and further held that forfeiture of tenancy caused thereby by sub let contrary to terms of deed of lease can be avail ed by the tenant even in absence of notice as envisaged by section III(g). In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant landlord that the lease has expired by efflux of time limited thereby under Section 111(a) and no notice terminates the tenancy. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The requirement of the notice in the writing could not be said to be based on any general rule of equity or good conscience and would not govern the bases made prior to 1929 or even prior to the coming into force of the TP act or to a lease executed prior to that coming into effect. [918C D] 2. A notice, as envisioned in section 111 (g) cannot be claimed by the lessor. Counsel for the respondent sought to sustain his case on the submission that the renewal Act does not apply to the lease in question and therefore a forfeiture giving rise to a determination of the demise follows upon breach of a condition in the lease, to wit, sub lease of a portion of the building, plus an act indicative of the landlord 's intention to terminate the tenancy.[919D E] 3.

The Governor of Assam was satisfied under sub cl. (c) of the proviso to clause (2) of article 311 of the Constitution that in the interest of the security of the State it was not expedient to give the said Shri P. K. Hore an opportunity to show cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him as stated above, and after such inquiry, the third step to be adopted under clause (3) of Article 311 was, according to the common case of the parties, held against the appellants when the Governor made these two orders his attention was not invited to the amended article 311(2) which had come into force on October 6, 1963. The impugned orders were accordingly made in terms of article 309 as it existed before its amendment by the Constitution (Fifteenth Amendment) Act, 1963 which had came into force with effect from October 6. 1963. On the same day an identical order was made with respect to the dismissal of the appellant B. C. Das except that in his order against him there is no mention of more charges having been received against him and given a reasonable opportunity of being heard in respect of those charges and where it is proposed, after such enquiry, to impose on him any such penalty, until he has been given a responsible opportunity of making representation on the penalty proposed, but only on the basis of the evidence adduced during such inquiry. Provided that this clause shall not apply (a) where a person is dismissed or removed or reduced in rank on the ground of conduct which has led to his conviction on a criminal charge; or (b) where an authority empowered to dismiss or remove a person or to reduce him in rank is satisfied that for some reason, to be recorded by that authority in writing it is not reasonably practicable to give to that person an opportunity of showing cause against such action proposed, the Governor must be satisfied that, in the interests of the public it was neither expedient to hold the inquiry under the principal clause that clause shall apply. In order that the opportunity to defend himself by cross examining the witnesses produced against him should have used these words in the sense in which they were used in the Constitution prior to its amendment and in the light of the interpretation placed on those words by this Court in Khem Chand vs The Union of India and Others, [1969] Vol.VI Assam Law Reports 192, it was held that consultation with the Public Service Commission in such cases cannot, therefore, be dispensed with. In the present case, in order to enable the Governor to pass an order of dismissal without holding an inquiry, without informing the Government servant of the charges against him, and without giving him a reasonable notice of being hearing in respect thereof, he must have used those words in his sense in Which they were use in the constitution prior to their amendment. The satisfaction recorded by the Governor, therefore related to the third one step to he taken under clause(2). Once it was borne in mind that the Governor 's attention was, for some reasons or the other drawn only to the unamended article 311 and not to the amend Article, and it was further kept in view that the amendment of article 31 in 1963 as already explained, was only designed to clarify and give effect to the judicial decisions interpreting the unamended Article, the reason for the form and the language used in these orders became clear and there could be no difficulty in understanding their true meaning. Khem Chand V. Union of lndia, ; Khemchand vs The State of U.P., [1969], Vol. VI Assam Law Report 192, referred to.
