The assessee company disclosed capital gains of Rs.3.10,200 but claimed set off of capital loss of Rs 3.17,500 sustained by it during the assessment year 1957 58 over sale of shares to three associate concerns. It was maintained by the asses see that the loss was sustained in the previous year rele vant to the assessment years 1957 58 and the same should be set off against the capital gains in the assessment Year in question. The Income Tax Officer disallowed the claim for set off on the footing that when in the assess ment year 195758, the loss is claimed it was excluded in the computa tion of income as capital loss and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner while disposing of the assessee 's appeal had stated that it was a notional capital loss. As no further appeal was carried by the assessee with the first appellate order, the matter had become final. The assessee challenged the rejection of its claim of set off before the Appellate Tribunal and reiterated its claim. The Tribunal came to the conclusion that the assessee was entitled to the benefit of setoff of loss provided it satisfied that its capital loss was computed under the old Act. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue: (1) that the benefit conferred under section 24 of 1922 Act continued to be given effect to under the 1961 Act and notwithstanding the wordings of section 80 of the latter Act, the High Court was Fight in holding that the claim of setting off was admissible in our view. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court reached the correct conclusion and there is no merit in the appeal. [1166C] 1.2 In the order for assessment year 1965 66 to which the Act of 1961 applied, it is necessary to turn attention to the relevant provisions thereof and they are in sections 74 and 80. For convenience they are extract ed: "Section 74(1)(a) Where in respect of any assessment year. the net result of the compu tation under the head "capital gains" is a loss such loss shall. subject to the other provisions of this Chapter. be dealt with as follows: "(i) such portion of the net loss (relating to short term capital/assets as cannot be or is not wholly set off under any head in accordance with the provisions of section 71 shall be carried forward to the following assessment year and so on; however, that no loss shall be carry forward for more than eight years.

The respondent was recruited as a Senior Scientific Officer on October 12, 1966 in the Defence Science Service. He was posted in the Directorate of Technical Development and Production (Air) (DTD & P). The recruitment when made was always to the Defence Engineering Service, and after the recruitment, the recruits were posted according to the exigency of the service, in any of the said three units. Their 22 services were inter changeable and inter transferable be tween the three units, and all the service conditions of the persons working in the three Units including scales of pay, superannuation age etc. were the same and regulated by the same set of Rules, viz. Defence Science Services Rules. In the year 1979, the Defence Research Service was trifurcated into three dif ferent services as stated above. However, at that time, admittedly no option was given to the employees working in different units to opt for one or the other of the units. It appears that those who were already working in either of the three unit were deemed to belong to the respective newly constituted service. This being so, their service conditions would have to run parallel and no discrim ination can be made between them by an unilateral action. The classification made between the parties further has no rational basis and no nexus of such classification to the object sought to be achieved has been shown to us by Mr. Subba Rao appearing for the appellants. In spite of the decision of the Tribunal, and even pending this appeal, when no stay was granted, the appellant Union of India retired the respondent at the age of 58 years, and those in the lower grade for which flexible complementing scheme was applicable would also retire at the said age of 60 years provided they had been promoted to the grades they were holding at the time of attaining the age Of 58 years within the preced ing five years. Subsequently by OM No. 7(3)/85 D (R & D) dated 10.2.86, the said decision was extended to all 23 Scientific and technical personnel of the DRDO i.e. DrDS as listed in the Appendix 'A ' of that Memo. By virtue of Rule 12 quoted above, this benefit given to members of the staff of DAQAS was also available to the members of DA QAS, since the said condition of service was not expressly provided for in the Service Rules. The Tribunal, therefore, held that the re spondent was not liable to be retired at the alleged superannuation age of 55 years, his superannuation age being deemed to have been increased to 60 years in view of the OM dated 24.12.85 read with OM dated 10th February, 1986 referred to above.

On June 3, 1967 election of councillors to the Sangli City Municipality was held under the Maharashtra Municipalities Act, 1965. The counting of votes took place with regard to Ward No. 25 on June 4, 1967. According to the election petition, the results were published in the Official Gazette on June 15, 1967 and the petition was filed on June 24, 1967 i.e. beyond time prescribed by the Act and as such it was not maintainable. The appellant denied that he was responsible for the publication of any of the impugned pamphlets. Of the four issues framed at the hearing of the petition the first was : "whether the petitioner proved that opponent No. 1 who was elected as Municipal Councillor for Ward No 25 had used malpractices at the time at the election by arousing religious sentiments of the voters and making defamatory statements against him thereby prejudicing the voters generally against him and in particular instigating the Muslim voters to vote against him by arouse their religious sentiments. Another similar ground based on a defamatory pamphlet dated 30th May 1967 was urged in the petition. charges of terrorising voters and securing votes by false personation were also levelled therein. statements were made in the election petitions that the appellant 's name as councillor had been declared in the official Gazette on 6th June, 1967, and he gave full particulars as to how he came to receive it. He further stated that he had attended a prayer meeting at a mosque on the 2nd June and after the Namaj was over the appellant had read over the pamphlet and one Moulana Hannanlent support to the appellant. In cross examination, it was elicited from him that although he had occasion to see the distribution of other pamphlets, he could give no details thereof i. e., either about the person who distributed them or the dates when that was done. The Judge accepted his testimony and came to the conclusion that the first publication having taken place on the 8th June the below mentioned candidates were elected from the above mentioned wards for the seats mentioned as against their names. He fixed August 24, 1968 for further hearing of this matter and directed issue of summonses to these two persons. These two persons were examined on the 24th August as court witnesses and thereafter the argument of counsel was resumed and concluded. By judgment delivered on August 30, 1968 the learned Judge allowed the election Petition holding in favour of the appellant on the first issue. The High Court dismissed the writ petition in limine on October 4, 1968 and the appellant has now come up before this Court by special leave. It was contended on behalf of the appel lant that having rejected this application, it is not open to the Judge to examine these two witnesses as court witness and this was a serious irregularity which the High Court should have set right by quasbing the order of the Judge based on the evidence of these witnesses. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) Under section 21(1) of the Maharashtra Municipal Act, 1966 which does not contain a similar provision it has been held by this Court that "although. the trial court should be at arms length and the court should not really enter into the dispute as a third party, but it is to be understood that the Court never has the power to summon a witness or to call for a document which would throw light upon the matter, particularly of corrupt practice which is alleged and is being sought to be proved. If the Court was satisfied that a corrupt practice had in fact been perpetrated, may be by one side or the other, it would have been absolutely necessary to find out who was the author of that corrupt practice. [975H; 976A B] (2) In the instant case, if the two persons had not been examined, the Judge might well have decided the issue the other way.

By a notification dated March 31, 1956, the State of Uttar Pradesh imposed a tax of one anna in the rupee on the sale proceeds of jute. Previously thereto the tax payable on sale of jute was six pies in the rupees. This notification having been struck down by the High Court of Allahabad as unauthorised and inoperative, the petitioner filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the said notification as from March 31. 1956. The High Court held that there was no power in the State to issue the impugned notification under section 3 A on March 31 as that section was itself to come into force only on April 1, 1956 and therefore it was not a law which the State legislature was competent to enact and it was therefore a nullity. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the Validation Act is not ultra vires the powers of the legislature under entry 54 in List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The power conferred on Parliament under article 286(2) is a legislative power, and such a power conferred upon a Sovereign Legislature carries with it authority to enact a law either prospectively or retrospectively unless there can be found in the Constitution itself a limitation on that power. In the exercise of such a powers, it will be competent for the legislature to impose a tax (1) ; 13 sales tax is an indirect tax which can be passed on by the seller to the purchaser. P. V. Sundararamier & Co. vs The State of Andhra Pradesh, ; , followed.

A philanderer of 22, appellant overpowered by sex stress in excess, hoisted himself into his cousin 's house next door, and in broad day light, overpowered the temptingly lonely prosecutrix of twenty four, Pushpa, raped her in hurried heat and made an urgent exist having fulfilled his erotic sortie. The screaming victim complained to her mother working in the field; thereafter a first information, prosecution and conviction ensued, a sentence of 4 years R.I. was imposed by the Sessions Court and the High Court affirmed it in appeal. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: (1) In prison treatment must, therefore, be geared to psychicaling, release of stresses, restoration of self respect and cultural normalisation, apart from training to adapt oneself to the life outside. The functional failure of our pachydermic prison projects, exacerbated by its tension and trauma on the one hand and the reverse ethos inside on the other, deserves judicial cognizance. [591C D] (2) In jail treatment must therefore be ge Obtained to psychics healing, released of stress es, restoration, restoration or cultural normalization apart from being deterrent. The insulated years behind the insensitive bars must possess a hospital setting if correction is a social purpose, as Gandhiji often insisted. [592D E] Sunil Batra 's case and later that, constitutionally viewed punitive deprivation of personal freedom must be goal oriented and humanely restorative apart frombeing deterrent. [593F G] (3) The special circumstances of this case constrain us to relent a little on principle because the restorative approach to sentencing has been jettisoned by the courts below. The task is not done by a negative reduction in the prison term. What is more important is a set of positive prescriptions which will ensure his turning a new leaf. One major method in securing this goal is to keep alive the family tie of the person in prison so that he may not deteriorate into a non person. Within limits of the Prison Act and Rules thereunder, the State Government or the Inspector General of Prisons will ensure that on parole, furlough or orders, the young appellant turns a newlic leaf of normal life. N.K.A. Appeal allowed in part.

The respondent was a limited company dealing in land. It maintains its accounts on the mercantile system. By an order dated June 21, 1946 under rule 75A(1) of the Defence of India Rules read with section 19 of the Act certain plots of land measuring about 19.17 acres in village Kankulia in the District of 24 Parganas and belonging to the assessee were requisitioned by the Government of West Bengal. Subsequently the land was acquired permanently in the State Government under s.5, Requisition of Land (Continuance of Powers) Act, 1951 by a notice of acquisition dated December 27, 1952 published in the Gazette dated January 8, 1953. The Land Acquisition Officer awarded a sum of Rs.24,97,249 as compensation payable to the respondent. On receipt of the amount the assessee credited it in its suspense account on the same date. During the assessment proceedings for the assessment year 1956 57, the relevant accounting period being the year ended March 31, 1956 the Income Tax Officer brought to tax a sum Rs.7,24,914 in the assessee 's business income. This represented the difference between the sum of RS.737,190 payable to it in terms of the award dated July 29, 1956 of the Arbitrator and a sum which had already been assessed to tax. The Income Tax officer treated the sum as liable to income tax during that year on the basis that the income accrued to the appellant on the date of the Award. The assessment was confirmed by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner of Income tax on first appeal. In second appeal by the assessee before the Income tax Appellate Tribunal two contentions were raised by it. It was urged that the amount of compensation received by the respondent related to the acquisition of land which was the stock in trade of the assessee, and was, therefore, a trading receipt of business carried on by the appellant, and therefore a receipt of a revenue nature liable to tax could be said to have accrued to it as income during the previous year ended on March 31. 1956 relevant to the assessment years 1956 57. The Appellate Tribunal accepted the other contention and held that the compensation received was not taxable in the assessment Year 1956 57 and that the sum received by it related to acquisition of the land which had been the stockin trade of trade of assessee, but was a trading receipts of the business carried out by the assesee, and that therefore a trading Receipt of the Business carried on for the purpose of assessment to tax in the year of assessment P. Jaganmohan Reddy, C.J., speaking for the Court, held that when land was taken over by the Govern ment the right of the owner to compensation was an inchoate right until the compensation had been actually determined and had become payable. It allowed the appeal accordingly by its order dated February 22, 1964. At the instance of the Revenue the Appellate Tribunal referred the question of law set out earlier to the Calcutta High Court for its opinion, and by its judgment dated January 9, 1973 answered the question in favour of the respondent assessee and against the Revenue.

The respondents landlords filed a suit against the appellants in the Court of Second Civil Judge, Class II, Gwalior for a decree for eviction from the suit premises and for certain other reliefs. The appellants ' eviction was sought on statement of facts mentioned in paragraph 3 of the plaint which squarely fell within clause (f) of sub section (1) of Section 12 of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961. The trial court accepted the appellants ' objection to the execution of the decree and dismissed the execution case. A miscellaneous appeal filed by the respondents was dismissed by the Third Additional District Judge Gwalior. They preferred a second miscellaneous appeal before the High Court. A learned single Judge following the decision of that Court in Smt. Chandan Bai vs Surja, ; came to the conclusion that the decree was not a nullity and was executable. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The language of section 12 of Madhya Pradesh and Ajmer Rent Control Act is somewhat different from many similar State statutes. Section 12(1) says "where it is proved to the satisfaction of the Court that a suit has been adjusted by any lawful agreement or compromise". The inhibition related to the filing of the suit only. No suit can be filed for eviction of a tenant except on one or more of the grounds enumerated in section 12(11). In sub sections (2) to (11) of section certain conditions have been engrafted to show under what circumstances an order for the eviction of the tenant cannot be passed in relation to some of the ground enumerated in sub section(1). Reading the section as a whole and remembering the beneficial object of the Act for the protection of a tenants based upon public policy, it would appear that the inhibition related only to the filling of the suits only. [882 G H; 883 A] 2. The bar related to filing of a suit only if it is satisfied on evidence that a ground for passing such a decree in accordance with the requirement of the statute has been established. Even when the trial proceeds ex parte, this is so. If, however, parties choose to enter into a compromise due to any reason such as to avoid the risk of protracted litigation expenses, it is open to them to do so. The Court can pass a decree on the basis of the compromise.

The assessee company was assessed on a total income of Rs. 1,61,089/ and taxes paid were Rs. 69,973/ leaving a distributable balance of RS. 91,116/ . The Income tax authorities disallowed an amount of Rs 11,88,000/ out of this loss on the ground that it relates to the price paid for the shares purchased for the sake of acquiring the managing agency of the Mills. In appeal the Asstt. Commissioner took the view that the loss incurred by the company was a capital loss. But all the same as there was no commercial profits in the relevant accounting years it was not reasonable to expect the assessee company to declare any dividend in respect of those years in view of the capital loss incurred and he, therefore, cancelled the orders of the Income tax Officer under section 23A(1). In appeal by the Department the Tribunal agreed with the conclusions reached by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. It held that under the circumstances the Directors were justified in not declaring any dividend because of the loss referred to earlier. The question was whether the Directors of a company acted as prudent businessmen in refraining from Declaring any dividend. The High Court answered that question in favour of the assessee. Dismissing the appeal by certificate, HELD: (1) In view of section 23 A(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, the provisions must be worked not from the standpoint of the tax collector but from that of a businessman. The reasonableness or unreasonableness of the amount distributed as dividends is judged by business considerations, such as the previous losses, the present profits, the availability of surplus money and the reasonable requirements of the future and similar others. The Income Tax Officer must take an overall picture of the financial position of the business. He should put himself in the position of a prudent businessman or the director of a Company and deal with the problem with a sympathetic and objective approach. On the facts found by the Tribunal there can be hardly any doubt that the assessee had suffered a capital gain of Rs, 12,00,000. [851 F G] Commissioner of Income tax West Bengal vs Gangadliar Bannerjee and Co. (Pvt.) Ltd., ; Commissioner of Incometax, West Bengal, vs Gangadharshree Banner & Co. , Commissioner of lncome tax, WestBengal, vsGangadlikar Bannerji and Co., , referred to.

The Consolidation Officer acting under section 12(4) of the Uttar Pradesh Consolidation of Holdings Act (U.P. Act V of 1954), referred the question of title to the Civil Judge, Aligarh who referred the same to the arbitrator, Shri Vikram Singh, who had been appointed under section 37 of the Act. Section 12(6) provides that where any matter is by or under this Act directed to be referred to an Arbitrator for determination, the Arbitrator will be appointed by the State Government from amongst Civil Judicial Offi cers or Assistant Collector of the I class of not less than five years ' standing and in all other respects the matter shall be determined in accordance with the provisions of the . The arbitrator gave his award on May 14, 1956 and submitted it to the civil court for final decision. On May 19, 1956, Charan Singh, Dungar Singh, Maharaj Singh and Lajja Ram filed an appeal before the District Judge against the order of the Civil judge dated September 8, 1956. Before the District judge a preliminary objection was raised that no appeal lay (1) I.L.R. [1959] 1 All. 65 against the award of the civil judge. The District Judge overruled the objection and held that the Civil Court was not justified under section 15 of the , in modifying the award merely because he disagreed with the finding. He, therefore, allowed the appeal and set aside the order passed by the Civil court. On appeal to the High Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that section 37 Of the Act applies only as far as procedure is concerned and section 39 of the which provides for appeals does not apply to arbitrations referred to in section 37. Held, further, that the effect of section 46 and section 47 of the is that all the provisions Of the except sub section (1), of section 6, sections 7, 12, 36 and 37 apply to arbitration proceedings under the Act; it is not necessary to rely (1)[1959] Supp. 1 S.C.R 928, followed.

The petitioner was diploma holder in Engineering and holds the post of Executive Engineer in the respondent Corporation. Till 1974, the promotion post of the superintending Engineer was available both for diploma holders and degree holders according to merit cum seniority. This was so according to the practice followed by the Corporation without making any rules or regulation in that behalf. The petitioner who was senior to respondent NO. 2 would have been promoted to the post on 31st October, 1990. However, since respondent No.2 was a degree holder, he got the said resolution and was promoted to that post on that date. It is this promotion which was challenged by the petitioner by a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that no classification could be made among the Executive Engineers on the basis of their educational qualification for the purpose of promotion to the posts of superintending Engineers, since they belong to the same cadre of Executive Engineers and do the same work. Aggrieved, the petitioner has preferred this special leave Petition. Dismissing the Special Leave Petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The proposition that in the absence of rule or regulation the authority can prescribe service conditions by executive instructions and this is what was done till the year 1988 and is also sought to be done since 1988 by the impugned resolution. [75C] 1.2 In the absence, of rule, or regulation, the authority could prescribe service condition by executive instruction and this was what was taken till the years 1988 and was also sought for to be achieved since 1988. [76E F] State of Jummu & Kashmir vs Triloki Nath Khosa & Ors., ; , relied on.

These applications under Article 32 of the Constitution have been clubbed together and heard from time to time. In response to the rule, the Union of India took the stand through the Attorney General that the petitions were not maintainable and the filling up of the vacancies in the superior courts was not a justiciable matter. Reliance was placed on the decision of this Court in the case of S.P. Gupta vs Union of lndia, [1982] 2 SCR 365. The objection raised by the Attorney Gener al was overruled by the Court by drawing a distinction between fixing the Judge strength in the Courts or selection of judges on one side and the filing up of vacancies on the basis of sanctioned strength on the other. This Court as an interim measure took the view that while the ratio in S. P. Gupta 's case left the matter of fixing up of Judge strength to the President of India under the constitutional scheme, and the choice of Judges to the prescribed procedure, once the sanctioned strength was determined it was the obligation of the Union Government to maintain the sanctioned cadre in superior courts and the default, if any, was a matter of public interest and the writ petitions requiring a direction to the Union o f India to fill up the vacancies were maintainable. Dismissing the applications, this Court, HELD: 1.1 It is clear on a plain reading of clause (2) of Article 124 that it is the President, which in effect and substance means the Central Government, which is empowered by the Constitution to appoint Judges of the Supreme Court. It would therefore be open to the Central Govern ment to over ride the opinion given by the constitutional function aries required to be consulted and to arrive at its own decision as to which opinion it should accept in deciding whether or not to appoint the particular person as a Judge. [462C D] 1.2 The primacy of the Chief Justice of India in the process of selection would improve the quality of selection. The matter is not, therefore, to be considered that the final say is the exclusive prorogative of the executive Government. There are preponderant and com pelling considerations why the views of the chief Justices of the States and that of the High Courts should be afforded a decisive import unless the executive has some material in its possession which may indicate that the appointment is otherwise undesirable. The view which the four learned Judges shared, in Gup ta 's Case, in our opinion, does not recognise the special and pivotal position of the institution of Chief Justice India.

The respondent C. Bernard while serving as a Relieving Head Cashier in the K.G. Road Branch availed of 15 days leave from April 17, 1978 to May 1, 1978 and was allowed an advance of Rs.2,500 on April 4, 1978 under LFC to be adjusted later on his submitting the LFC Bill. He submitted a bill for Rs. 2,800 on May 5, 1978 along with a stamped cash receipt purported to have been issued by M/s. Shri Manju Travels of Bangalore and claimed reimbursement for the same. The said bill was passed by the Bank on May 15, 1978 but subsequent investigations revealed that the firm of M/S. Shri Manu Travels was a spurious one which indulged in issuing fake travel receipts. Thereupon the respondent was served with a charge sheet dated October 12, 1978 followed by a departmental enquiry. However, during the pendency of the departmental enquiry he retired from service on January 31, 1979. Not withstanding his retirement he continued to function as an Enquiry Officer and concluded the enquiry against the re spondent by the end of 1979. He then gave an opportunity to the respondent to be heard on the question of punishment and then passed the impugned order of discharge on January 14, 1980. The respondent did not raise any objection against the continuance of the enquiry by the said Shri U.B. Menon at any time during the course of the pendency and till the disposal of the Departmental appeal preferred by him, he was served a Memo dated August 1,1978 by the Divisional office of the Bank calling for his expla nation. A letter was also addressed on the same day to M/ s. Shri MAF & Ors., requesting them to furnish the details of the persons who traveled and the amounts received by the firm. No reply was received from the said firm but the respondent sent a reply on August 10, 1978 which was not found to be satisfactory. Some correspondence ensued between the respondent and the appellant in this connection but finally the respondent remained served with the charge sheet on October 12.1978 followed by another departmental enquiry, which was followed by the departmental inquiry. It is not necessary to go into the details in regard to proceedings at the departmental enquiries but it would be sufficient to state that the respondent participat ed in the departmental proceed ing till it was completed by the enquiry officer Shri U B. Menon. 200 Paragraph 9.14 of the Memorandum of Bi par Khandsari Settle ment dated October 19, 1966 empowers the Chief Executive Officer, etc., of he Bank to decide which officer should be empowered to hold an enquiry and take disciplinary action in the case of each office or establishment. Accordingly, the respondent 's departmental appeal was also dis missed on June 17, 1980 by a Single Judge of the High Court. A learned Single Judge allowed the writ petition, quashed the impugned orders of punishment as well as directed that the respond ent be paid all consequential benefits. The appellant preferred a Letters Patent Appeal against the said order of the Single Judge. The Division Bench dismissed it by a one line order: "no ground for interfer ence is made out". It was contended on behalf of the appel lant that the High, Court ought not to have permitted the respondent t o question the competence or jurisdiction of Shri U .B. Shah to act as an enquiry Officer as well a Disciplinary Authority after his superannuation since he had participated in the enquiry throughout without a demur; that by conduct the respondent had been estopped from raising such a contention for the first time in Writ Petition No. 18 140 of 1980 filed against the impugned Order of discharge in the High court, and that even otherwise the appellant could have appointed a non official as an Inquiry Officer and therefore his decision could be saved on the de facto doctrine; that since the initial appoint ment of Shri M.B Menon was valid, his actions and decisions could not be invalidated by his subsequent retirement.

The respondents are owners and are in possession of the building bearing municipal door Nos. 3766 to 3776 situated in the main Chawri Bazar, Delhi. As the building was an old construction and required urgent and extensive repairs, on October 16, 1965, the respondents submitted to the appellant plans for its sanction for execution of work consisting of repairs, additions as well as alterations to the said building. The Commissioner of the appellant Corporation, by letter dated February 4, 1966 informed the respondents that their application for execution had been refused on the grounds "that the proposal was under acquisition and also effected in the ROW and the land was residential against proposal of commercial". A dispute arose between the parties regarding the construction of a building or the execution of a work unless such a building is or work would contravene any of the provisions of sub section (2) of section 336 or section 340 of the Corporation Act. The respondents contended that the Master Plan prepared by the Authority for Delhi, which has statutory force, has come into operation under the Development Act and that the plan submitted by them did not conform to bye laws or the provisions Of section 336(2) or any other law in respect of land use. They further referred to a letter dated April 30, 1966 of the Delhi Development Authority stating that the Zonal Development Plan had not been prepared for the area in question. The High Court accepted the contention of the respondents and issued a mandamus directing the appellant to accord sanction to the plan for execution work in respect thereof as per their application of October 16. 1965. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the Master plan prepared by him for Delhi which has Statutory force, had come into effect under the development Act; and (2)(a) there was no violation of any law or rules having failed, they filed Civil Writ Petition No. 410 D of 1966 in the Circuit Bench of the Punjab High Court at Delhi under article 226 of the Constitution praying for the issue of an order or direction in the nature of mandamus directing respondent to accord the sanction asked for by them. HELD: (1)(a). The Master Plan and the two maps relied on by the appellant do not give any indication that any part of the land belonging to the respondents will be covered by any portion of the proposed road. The provisions of section 7 of the Development Corporation Act clearly indicate and that is borne out by the various matters mentioned in the Master plans that the master plan will only give a very broad outline of DeLhi as it will look in future. Though there is an obligation on the Authority to prepare the Zonal development Plan simultaneously with the preparation of the Master Planning Plan, or as soon as there may be thereafter, no such Zonal Development plan has been prepared. That assumes considerable importance in this case because it is the Zonal Master Plan under section 8(2)(b) which will show the approximate location and extents of land uses proposed in a zone for roads; further, under sub cl. (d) of sub s.(2) Of section 8, the said Zonal Development Plans will also contain provision regarding the allotment or reservation of land for roads. If such an indication is made available by the Zonal Planning Plan then section 14 will quite naturally stand attracted, because any user of a land or building otherwise than in conformity with the Zonal Plan will be hit by that section.

The appellant No. 1 was the Minister of Industries and the appellant No 2 was the Secretary to the Government of the Commerce and Industries Department of the State of Vindhya Pradesh. He was charged with having committed offences under sections 120 B, 161, 465 and 466 of the Indian Penal Code as adopted by the Vindhya Pradesh Ordinance No. 48 of 1949 and the Special Judge acquitted both of them. The Judicial Commissioner reversed the order of acquittal passed by the Special judge and convicted both the appellants of the several offences with which they were charged. On appeal to the Supreme Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the statement made by the appellant to him was not recorded under the provisions of section 164 of the Criminal Procedure Code and was therefore inadmissible in evidence and could not be proved orally by him. Held, that the statements made by appellant No 1 before them were admissible in evidence there was no doubt that the appellant was asked by Shanti Lal Ahuja, the Additional District Magistrate to make the statements to these two witnesses not with a view to avoid the bar of section 16 of the Code of Criminal Procedure or by way of colourable pretence but by way Of greater caution particularly having regard to the fact that the accused No. 25,000, which were recovered from the top drawer of the dressing table exceeded by far the amount which according to him he had left with him by way 'of balance and the most natural reaction to the recovery of this large sum of money would have been that he would have certainly denied that these moneys were his and he would had been surprised at finding that such a large sum was found there.

The respondent was serving the State Police as a constable when an incident took place on 17.2.1971, which led to the prosecution of the plaintiff along with the Head Constable Kahan Singh and the Sub Inspector Baldev Singh. The charge made against the respondent was that he physically assaulted and detained one Gurdial Singh. On the question whether the suit was barred by limitation and whether the order of dismissal was illegal on the ground that the plain tiff was not served with a show cause notice before the impugned order was passed. Both the issues were decided by the learned Subordinate Judge against the plaintiff and the suit, was accordingly dismissed. The respondent preferred an appeal before the High Court against the decree of the first appellate court which was dismissed at the admission stage itself by merely saving: "HEARD. DISMISSED" It has been contended on behalf of the appellants that Rule 16.2(2) of the Punjab Police Rules, 1934 mandatorily directs that a police officer judicially sentenced to rigorous imprisonment exceeding one month shall be dismissed, and this mandate of law cannot be ignored on the grounds that in the case of another member of the police force a mistake was committed. The High Court should have examined the plaint for finding out the cause of action for the suit and then in that light deter mined the correct article of the Limitation Act applicable to the case. Serious objection has been taken against the observations of the First appellate court permitting the competent authority to inflict only minor punishment on the respondent in certain conditions, and the direction about the payment of salary and other emoluments.

The appellant, a private limited company carrying on business in tea garden tools and requisites and also acting as agents for selling tea; in fact the bulk of its income was from selling commission on tea. The assessment year in question is 1959 60 in the relevant previous year which ended on June 30,1958, the assessee for the first time in its history entered into certain transactions in jute. On April 17, 1958 the assessee had contracted to purchase 1100 bales of B Twill and 2500 bales of corn sacks: the contract for B T will was with two parties M/s. Raghunath & Sons (P) Ltd. for 500 bales and M/S. Mahadeo Ramkumar for 600 bales. The transactions thus resulted in a loss of Rs. 98,534 to the assessee and the assessee claimed adjustment of this loss in the computation of its Income for the assessment year 1959 60. The Income tax Officer held that the transactions were not speculative and the loss should be treated as business loss relying on two decisions of this Court: Bayana Bhimayya and Sukhdevi Rathi vs The Govt. of Andhra Pradesh, ; and D. M. Wadhwana vs Commissioner of Income tax, West Bengal, , referred to. In reaching this conclusion the Income tax officer held that transactions involving mere transfer of delivery notes and not actual delivery of the goods were of a speculative character as contemplated in Explanation 2 to section 24(1) read with explanation 2 and restored the order of the Income Tax Officer. On appeal by the assessee, the Tribunal referred to the High Court the following question of law: "Whether on the facts and circumstances of the case the Tribunal was right in holding that the transaction described above entered into by the appellant were speculative transactions within the meaning of Explanation 2 of section 24 (1) of the Act?" The High Court answered the question in the affirmative and against the assessee. Allowing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: 1. A transaction which is otherwise speculative would not be a speculative transaction within the mischief of explanation 2 if actual delivery is of the commodity or the scrips has taken place; on the other hand, a transaction which was not otherwise speculative in nature may yet be speculative according to explanation 2 If there is no actual delivery or physical delivery, the loss, if any, would be a loss in a speculative transactions which could be allowed to be set off only against a profit in a transaction of the same nature. The Explanation does not invalidate speculative According to explanation 1 says that where the speculative transactions are of such a nature as to constitute a business, I) the business shall be deemed to be distinct and separate from any other business. Explanation 2 defines a speculative transac tion as a transaction in which a contract for purchase and sale of any commodity is periodically or ultimately settled otherwise than by the actual delivery and having regard to the mischief which was sought to be averted by the promulgation of the ordinance to prevent persons who dealt in differences only and never intended to take delivery under any circumstances it was held that though the respondent and his transferees had not acquired any title to the goods, the title acquired by the ultimate endorsee of the delivery orders went to feed their previously defective titles and ensured to their benefit. His Lordship further observed that this was the principle that formed the basis of the decision in Bayanna Bhimayya & Sukhdevi Maheshwari vs The Government of Andhra Pra desh, [1955] 2 S.C.R. 869, which is also a case under the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939. The respondent in that case, a dealer in gunny bags purchased gunnies from the mills on terms of written contracts which were on printed forms. These contracts were entered into on brokers acting for the respondent who sent him 'Bought Notes setting out the terms upon which the purchases had been effected from the Mills.

Rule 2(2) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 requires each candidate to "deliver to the Returning Officer. a nomination paper completed in the prescribed form and subscribed by the candidate himself as assenting to the nomination and by two persons referred to in sub section (2) as proposer and seconder. The appellant was a candidate for the reserved seat but his nomination was rejected by the Returning officer at the scrutiny stage and so he was unable to contest the election. He filed an election petition challenging the rejection of his nomination papers on the ground that the nomination paper was not signed by the proposers and seconders in the usual way by writing their names, and as their marks were not attested it was evident that they had not been " subscribed" because " subscribing " imports a "signature" and as the Act sets out the only kinds of "signatures" which it will recognise as II signing", for the purposes of the Act, there is no valid signatures of either of a proposer or a seconder in any one of the four nomination papers. Held, that the attestation in the present case was not a mere technical or unsubstantial requirement and the attestation must exist at the presentation stage and a total omission of such an essential feature cannot be subsequently validated any more than the omission of a candidate to sign at all could have been. In the case of illiterate persons unable to write their names it is necessary to guard against misrepresentation and fraud by requiring that their signatures should be formally authenticated in a particular way. A special statutory cloak of protection is thrown around them just as the ordinary law clothes pardanish in women and illiterate and ignorant persons and others likely to be imposed on, with special protective covering.

The appellants, who were employees of the Company, went on an indefinite peaceful strike with effect from August 30, 1972 pursuant to the strike notice given to the Company by their registered union called 'the Association of Chemical Workers ' in support of its demand for re instatement of three of the Union leaders who had been dismissed by the Company. On September 7, 1972, the Company issued notices to the appellants and 10 others asking them to report for duty on or before September 18, 1972 failing which their absence would be construed as voluntary abandonment of service and their names would be struck off from the muster rolls of the company. On October 23, 1972 the union made a formal demand calling upon the Company to re instleate the appellants, and 10 other workmen informing them that since "by not reporting for duty they had confirmed its presumption that they were no longer interested to continue in service of the said Company and had totally abandoned the Company 's service" their names had been struck off. The Assistant Commissioner thereupon summoned the parties for discussion on July 19, 1973 but his attempts at conciliation did not bear any fruit. Thereafter, the appellants made the aforesaid complaints before the Industrial Tribunal with the result as stated above. On March 30, 1973, the union wrote a letter to the Labour Commissioner complaining about the arbitrary termination of service of 25 workmen (including the appellants) and emphasising that they had never abandoned the service of Company and did they wish to do so, and that they would report for work the moment the strike was called off by their union. On May 19,1973 certain proposals for settlements were made on behalf of the employees whose services were terminated by the company and requesting the Company for re dis instate ment of the appellants. The Labour Commissioner summoned the concerned parties for discussions on July 20, 1973 and his attempts to conciliation did Not bear any significance. Thereafter the appellant made the said complaints before it with the results as stated in their letter dated September 26, 1972 but his attempt at conciliation failed did not yield any fruit, whereupon the appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the action of the respondent Company in removing them from service and asserting that the said action was by way of victimization for their participation in the strike. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that there was no abandonment of services on the part of the appellant during the admitted pendency of the industrial dispute before the Labour Court which adversely affected them, and could not be countenanced. Allowing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: 1.1 An employee has abandoned or relinquished service is always a question of intention, and normally such an intention cannot be attributed to an employee without adequate evi 618 dence in that behalf. Thus whether there has been voluntary abandonment or relinquishment of service or not is a question Of fact which has to be determined in the light of the surrounding circumstances of each case. Question No. 2: This takes us to the consideration of the second question, namely, whether in the circumstances of the instant case it could be said that the appellants had voluntarily abandoned the services of the workmen on the ground of abandonment of their service because of their going on strike in enforcement of their demands, there can be no question of abandonment by them. [616C D] 1.2 In Buckingham Co. vs Venkatiah & Ors., it was held that if the employees absent themselves from the work because of strike in enforce of their demand, there cannot be any question of abandon of employment by them.[617E F] Express Newspaper (P) Limited Limited vs Michael Mark & Anr., ; Express Newspapers (P.) Ltd. vs Michasel Mark and Anr. , referred to. 1.3 In the instant ease also the appellant 's absence from duty was because of his peaceful strike to enforce their demand.

In March 1950 the trustees mortgaged a house belonging to the trust to one Saheba to secure repayment of Rs. 5,000. An action instituted by the mortgagee against the trustees to enforce the mortgage was compromised and it was decreed that the trustees do pay Rs. 3,910 due under the mortgage by monthly instalments of Rs 100 each and in default of three instalments the entire amount remaining unpaid shall become due and recoverable from the mortgagee property. The trustees did not pay the instalments due under decree, and in an application for execution by the mortgage ( mortgaged property) was put up for sale and the bid of the appellant was accepted for Rs.5,000 by the executing Court. The trial court passed an order disposing of the execution application and directed that Rs. 250 out of the amount deposited by the trustees be paid over to the appellant. In appeal the District Court reversed the order holding that since the trustees had failed to comply with the requirements of r. 89 of 0. 21, Code of Civil Procedure, the executing court had no jurisdiction to set aside the sale held in execution of the decree. The High Court of Gujarat in exercise of powers under section 115 of the Code of Criminal Procedure set aside that order and remanded the case to the District Judge "for decision on all the points correctly arising out of this matter". Against that order by the appellant, the District court reversed the said order holding: (1) that sale of the mortgaged property which belonged to a public trust was without the sanction of the Charity Commissioner being prohibited by section 36 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act; and (2) that the sale in execution was in law equivalent to payment to the decree holder of the money specified in the proclamation of sale for the recovery of which the sale was ordered. In an application under 0.21 r.89 of the C.P.C., for setting aside the order of the District judge, the High Court reversed that order holding : (1 ) that sale in the execution proceeding and to wait for six months for receiving payment of the mortgage dues from the trustees, abandonment of the Execution proceeding was in Law equivalent to, payment to, the decree holders of the amounts specified in proclamation of sales for the recovered which the auction purchaser was ordered, less any amount which may, since the date of such proclamation of Sale, have been received by the decreeholder; (2 ) that a judgment of a Full Bench of the High ' Court could be ignored by a Single Judge if the Full Bench judgment is given on a reference made on a question of law arising in a matter before a single Judge or a Division Bench of Judges to a larger Bench. HELD: (i) In considering whether a precedent of a court of coordinate authority is binding reference to section 165 of the Evidence Act is irrelevant. Undoubtedly, every judgment must be based upon facts declarded by the evidence Act to be relevant and duly proved. But when a Judge in deciding a case follows a precedent he only regards himself bound by the principle underlying the judgMent and not by the facts of that case.

Rule 2(2) of the Liberalised Pension Rules, 1950, which permits the Central Government to retire a Government serv ant at any time after he has completed 30 years of qualifying service provided that he shall give in this behalf a notice in writing to the appropriate authority at least three months before the date on which he wishes to retire. Government servants who have out lived their utility but there is no guide line provided in Rule 2(1) of Pension Rules on the other hand provides no guide lines and gives absolute discretion to the Govern ment. There is no requirement under the rule to act in 'Public Interest '. A person who joins Government service at the age of 21 years can be retired prematurely under F.R. 56(j) only on the ground of 'Public interest ' whereas another Government servant who is only 51 and has completed thirty years of ' qualifying service, can be picked up for premature retirement under the Rule. Since no safeguards are provided in the Rule, the discretion is absolute and is capable of being used arbi trarily and with an un even hand. [800C] Union of India & Ors. vs R. Narasimhan, ; , referred to. In the instant case, there was no challenge to any of the rules or para 620 of the manual on the grounds that it gives unguided power to the Railway authorities to pick and choose railway employees for the purpose of pre mature retirement. Rule 2046 having been framed under Article 309 of the Constitution and being a compendious rule, the railway employees are only gover ed by the said rule and para 620 was void and inoperative.

The assessee was an unregistered firm carrying on business of manufacture and sale of katechu. The chargeable account ing period was 1st April, 1943 to 31st March, 1944. There were two partners of the assessee firm, namely L. Phoolchand and M/s Biharilal Balkishan each having profits in proportion of 11 annas and 5 annas respectively. The work in connection with the extraction of Katechu was carried on in Nepal by 1.4.1943 to 31th March, 1941 failing in the financial year ending March 31, 1944, sales took place from May 30, 1941 to September 29, 1941. Thereafter another jungle was taken on lease in November 1942 and Katechhu were extracted from 23rd November, 1942 to June 29, 1940. The sales in this case were effected between 26th July, 1943 and March 31st, 1943. The assessee firm did not maintain any books of account and the entire record of the business transaction was maintained in the books of M/S BiharilalBalkishan in the account styled "Kalyanmal Phoolchand". The assessee Firm had taken a jungle on lease for this purpose and had extracted Katechku from October, 1940 to September, 1941, failing in their financial year ended March 31. 1945, sales were effected from April 1, 1944 to April 4, 1944 when the business was dis continued. Therefore, while there was manufacturing activity there was no sale during the financial years ending on 31st December, 1941 and 31st Decem ber, 1942.

The Kerala Public Service Commission invited applications for filling up 130 expected vacancies in the posts of Junior Engineers in the Public Works Department as per notification published in the Kerala Gazette dated 16th May, 1978. The qualifications specified for the posts were B.Sc. in Civil Engineering or Mechanical Engineering of the Kerala University or its equivalent as prescribed by the special rules of the Tamil Nadu Engineering Subordinate Service (General Branch). The applicants had to appear in the written test conducted by the KPSC and there after in an interview held by it. There was a common question paper which contained, in category I, questions in Civil engineering and in Category II, questions, in Mechanical Engineering. Petitioners who were qualified in Civil Engineers had to answer the questions in Category 1, and those who had qualified in Mechanical engineering and answered questions indicated in Category I in the question paper could not rationally be included in a common rank list after the interview. The learned Single Judge of the High Court allowed the Writ Petitions and directed the Government of Kerala and the K PSC to prepare "two lists, namely, one for the Civil Bench and the other for the Mechanical Branch on the basis of examination already conducted". He proceeded: "With respect to it the Service Commission has not yet published the rank list. On receiving information from the Government on the above lines, the Public Service Commis sioner is directed to prepare the two separate rank lists, one in the Civil Engineering and other for Mechanical Engineering graduate on the ground that there were directions to the K.PSC to preparing two separate seniority lists one for Civil Engineering graduates and the others for Mechanical Engi neers as stated above". The petitioner will be entitled to a post, if he has exercised his option in terms of this Court 's order and he is high enough in the common list for claiming the post.

The plaintiff respondent No. 1, a partner of a partnership business along with his brothers defendant Nos. 1 and 2, was later converted into a partnership firm by a regular deed. During his life time the business was under the control of Abdul Samad, but on his death the defendants Nos.1 and 2 have effectively taken charge of the business and excluded the plaintiff. A suggestion to re constitute and partnership made and repeated by the plaintiff has been ignored. In reply to the plaintiff 's letter seeking information the defendant No. 2 petitioner had stated in his letter that he has no interest in the firm. In paragraph 11 of the plaint it is stated that he had on enquiry discovered that the defendants nos. 1 & 2 have been falsely representing before the Income Tax Department inter alia, that a new deed of partnership had been executed on 15.1.1979 to be effective from 1.1 1979 in which the plaintiff had no interest. The Income Tax Officer passed an order on 26th December 1981 on the basis of the false allegations made by the defendants. The plaintiff challenged the valuation given by the defendant as grossly undervalued and arbitrary. The issues relating to the correct valuation and pecuniary jurisdiction of the court to enter the suit were taken up as preliminary issues and were decided in favour of the plaintiff, and the defendants challenged the order by a civil revision application before the Calcutta High Court which was dis missed. The defendant No 2 has now come to this Court against the High Court 's order. Special leave is granted. On behalf of the appellant it was contended that relief to the tune of lacs of rupees has been claimed by the Plaintiff in the suit, and he said that the plaintiff having laid claim to a sum of Rs.1,26,796.72 besides another sum over Rs.84,000 as his share in the profit for a particular period by reference to the proceeding of the Income tax department mentioned in paragraph 11 thereof, and it is, therefore preposterous on his part to suggest in paragraph 19 of the Plaint that it could be tentatively valued at Rs.50 only. According to the defence case which was challenged as incorrect by the defend ant, the plaintiff requested for and was allowed a larger share 'in the well established and reputed business of auctioneer known as "Russell Exchange" and its assets and goodwill as well as the amount lying in the Habib Bank, Karachi Branch solely and absolutely '. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The interpretation put by the learned counsel on the decisions of this Court is not correct and cannot be accepted. None of the two cited judgments relied upon by Mr. Chatterjee helps him. It is true that in a suit for accounts the plaintiff is not obliged to state the exact amount which would result after taking all the accounts and he may, therefore, put a tentative valuation upon the suit but he is not permitted to choose an unreasonable and arbitrary figure for that purpose. At page 392 of the judgment in Meenakshisundaram Chettiar vs Venkatachalam Chettiar, [1945] ILR XXIV Patna 334, the respondent filed a suit praying for accounts from appellant No.1 on the ground that the court was powerless to challenge the valuation put by him on the relief claimed in the plaint. " The plaintiff is, however, allowed to give his own tentative valuation. Ordinarily the Court shall not examine the correctness of the valuation chosen, but the plaintiff cannot act arbitrarily in this matter. If a plaintiff chooses whimsically a ridiculous figure it is tantamount to not exercising his right in this regard. In such a case it is not only open to the court but its duty to reject such a valuation. The cases of some of the High Courts which have taken a different view must be held to be wrongly decided.

Section 12 of the Madhya Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1958 lays down four requirements for grant of exemption from the provisions of the Act: (i) that any exemption to be granted under the section has to be by a notification; (ii) that the dealer should continue to furnish the pre scribed returns under the Sales Tax Acts; and (iii) that they should produce, at the time of their assessment, a certifi cate from the Director of Industries certifying that such dealer is eligible to claim exemption and have not opted for in part I of the scheme of deferred payment of tax under the rules framed for this purpose. However, when they approached the Director for the certificate of exemption envisaged under column (3) of the notification, it was denied to them on the ground that the industries run by them are "traditional industries" which were not eligible for exemption. The High Court took the view that these rules and instructions had no relevance to the claim for exemption put forward under the notifica tion of 23.10.1981 and that, in any event, the executive instruction could not override the provisions Of the statu tory notification. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The question of grant of eligibility certificate by the Industries Department is not an empty formality but before granting the certificate the Industries Depart ment has to see whether all the requirements as con cerned in the instructions are fulfilled and complied with or not. But, here: "as pointed out earlier, column 3 of the 1981 Notification does not contain any guidelines or a procedure in the matter of grant ing exemption certificate and condi tions therefore, in order to avoid the possibility of arbi trariness and injustice to any one the State Government was justified in issuing executive instructions laying down the guidelines and procedure for the same. No. To answer these contentions, one has to look first at the statutory instruments in this case viz. section 12 of Act and the notification thereunder.

Rule 17(1) of the Delhi Higher Judicial Service Rules, 1970 provides that not withstanding anything contained in these rules, the Administrator may fill substantive vacancies in the service by making temporary appointments thereto from amongst members of the State Judicial Service. Rule 17 provides for recruitment to the Delhi Judicial Service by promotion on the basis of selection from the members of Delhi Judicial Services who have completed not less than 10 years of service in the Delhi judicial Service. The petitioners who were direct recruits filed writ petitions in this Court contending that seniority between promotees and direct recruits must be determined in accordance with the respective dates of their continuous officiation as Additional District & Sessions Judges and that, direct recruits who are appointed to temporary posts of Additional District and Sessions Judges after the promotees are so appointed cannot rank higher in seniority over the promotees. On behalf of the respondents it was contended that there is no provision for probation for the appointments under Rules 16 and 17 of the said rules, but sub rule (2) of Rule 12 required that all candidates shall be on probation for a period of two years. Allowing the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The seniority of direct recruits vis a vis promotees shall be determined according to the dates on which direct recruits were appointed to their respective posts and the dates from which the promotees have been officiating continuously either in temporary posts created in the Service or in substantive vacancies to which were appointed in a temporary capacity. [362C] 2.1 The seniority list which is impugned in this case has been prepared on the foundation that the rule of `quota and rota ' will continue to apply notwithstanding the fact that appointments are made to the service under Rules16 and 17, her present position in the seniority list, which has been accorded to her on the strength of that rule cannot be maintained. The controversy in these two writ petitions is inter se seniority between the promotees and the direct recruits and for this, one must refer to some other relevant provisions of the aforesaid rules and mainly to rules 7 and 8 alongwith Rules 16 & 17 of Delhi Higher judicial Service Rules. [361E F] Chandramouleshwar Prasad vs Patna High Court & Ors., ; , referred to.

The Income tax Officer assessed the Ambala Flour Mills in the three years of assessment in the status of an association of persons. In appeals by Debi Parshad, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner set aside the order of assessment and directed that the direction for assessing the income should be deleted. The Tribunal referred the following questions at the instance of the Commis sioner of Income tax: "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the appeals. filed by DebiParshad were maintainable in law ?" The High Court answered the first question in the negative. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The expression 'any person ' in the setting in which it appears must be confined to a person intimately connected in the said sense with the assessment of the year under appeal. " In such cases, though the latter are not eo nomine parties to the appeal, their assessments depend upon the assessment Of the former. The said instances are only illustrative. It is not necessary to pursue the matter further. [395 C D] Commissioner off Income tax, U.P. vs Kanpur Coal Syndi cate, ; , followed. (ii) In making a direction against Debi Parthshad the Tribunal did not exercise his powers qua a stranger to the assessment proceeding. The power of the Appellate Assist ant Commissioner to make the direction was not and could not be referred to the High Court. [394 E G] Commissioner of Income Tax, U .P.v Kanpur Coal Co., ; , applied.

The appellant filed a suit for partition of his joint family properties and an account in respect of the joint family assets managed by the respondent. The plaint was valued at Rs. 1,000 under section 7(iv)(f) of the Madras Court Fees Act (which will be described hereafter as the Act). In regard to the relief for partition the fixed court fee of Rs. 100 was paid by the appellant under article 17 B(Madras) of Schedule II of the Act. For the purposes of jurisdiction, however, the appellant gave Rs. 15,00,000 as the value of his share. The respondent filed an application for a formal amendment of the valuation made in the plaint and it raised some interesting questions of law under the provisions of section 7 (iv)(b) of that Act. Pending the appeal the dispute was settled amicably between the parties and in consideration of payment of a specified sum and delivery of possession of certain sites, Subbiah agreed to release all his claims and those of his son, the present appellant in respect for the properties then in suit. According to the respondent, this compromise transaction did not bind the appellant and so he claimed to recover his share ignoring the said transaction between his father and the respondent and that was the basis on which a claim for partition and accounts was made by the appel lant in his suit. The trial court held that the plaint filed in the present suit did not attract the provisions Of section 7, sub section (iv) of Act and that the proper court fee to be paid was determined by article 17B of Schedule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. On appeal the High Court set aside the order under appeal and directed that the appellant should pay deficit court fees on the basis of Rs 15,000 at which he values the relief sought for by him for the purpose of jurisdiction and it was not open to him to value his relief on the memorandum of appeal under section 5 of the said Act. On the question whether the Division Bench was justified in directing the appellant to pay Court fees both on the plaint as well as on the Memorandum of appeal, HELD : (i) The High Court was in error in holding that the suit fell under section 6(iv) (b) or section 7.(iv)(c) ordinarily liberty should be given to the plaintiff to value the claim with any precision or definiteness. That is why legislature has left it to the option of the plaintiff 'to value his claim for the payment of court fees.
