In July 1985, Respondent No 1 sought permission to erect the high rise buildings on plot No 148, barakhambara Road NewDelhi of which the first respondent is the lessee. The sanction was again revalid ed for a period of 2 years. The NDMC raised the issue of applicability of Bye law 16.4.8 of the applicable Building Bye laws framed under the Punjab Municipal Act 1911 in relation to the Union territory of Delhi and that the proposed build ing did not also provide for a "podium/pedestrian walk way" made mandatory by the Zonal Development Plan for Zone D 1 (viz. Connaught Place Area) approved by the Central Govern ment on 30th April 1966 in No. 21023(7)66UD under Section 9(2) of the Delhi Development Act 1957. The High Court allowed the writ petition and directed the NDMC to convey its formal sanction of the building plans on or before the 5th day of May, 1989. Aggrieved by the decision of the High Court, Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 preferred an appeal before this Court. During the course of hearing, the standing counsel for the NDMC raised a ques tion of the applicability of bye law 16 and submitted that the clearance of the Chief Fire Officer did not prevent the NDMC from enforcing the applicable bye laws. However, the Court in the light of the statement of counsel for respondent No. I allowed the appeal and directed Respondent Nos 1 and2 to reconsider the question of according sanction to the plans in the context of the specific objectives of bye laws 16. 4.1. The eligibility of the proposed construction for sanction except on the point of adequacy of "Refuge areas" in the requirement of a "pedestarian walk way", and "Podium" is not otherwise disputed. 6.2.4, the building schemes shall also be cleared by the Chief Chief Fire Offi cer, Delhi Fire Service" "17.2 The additional provisions related to fire protection of buildings more than 15m in height and buildings identified in 6.3.1, shall be as given in Appendix K". The proposed building is over 15 meters in height, and attracts Bye law16.4 which, inter alia, provides: "Refuteuge area for all buildings exceeding 15 m in height. refuge area shall be provided as follows: (a) For floors above 15m and upto 24m. One refuge area on the floor immediately above 13m. The structural nature and basis of its calculation of the extent of these "Refaximum areas" are dealt with by Bye law 17.1 is that a wall abutting an inner vacant space is also an "external wall" and the acceptance of the cor rectness of this position was implicit in the clearance given by the chief Fire Officer.

The joint family carried on joint family business of a grocery shop, liquor shops, a ration shop, a motor bus service and also money lending under the name of "Sontakke Brothers". The family also Possessed immovable and movable property. Balkrishna Sontakke was the eldest of the brothers and was the plaintiff respondent in the present appeal. He will be referred to hereafter as the plain tiff. It is common ground that up to 1944 the brothers were living and messing together and the income from 101 the family business used to be kept with the plaintiff. From April 14, 1945, all the five brothers filed a suit for partition against the plaintiff of all joint family properties including the accounts of all the businesses. The compromise further declared that the plaintiff was to have one sixth share in the motor garage and that defendants 1 and 2 were to pay the price of one fifth share to him. These are the material provisions of the compromise. One of the two brothers was a minor and the Court finding the compromise to be for the benefit of the minor accepted it and passed a preliminary decree in terms of the compromised on July 25, 1947. If nothing else had happened to disturb the natural course of events, the proceedings would have ended in a final decree for partition. The plaintiff filed an application before the Civil Judge in which he alleged that when he agreed in the compromise that the accounts were to be taken up to March 31, 1946, he was under a misapprehension regarding his legal right inasmuch as he thought that when the accounts are to be took up to a certain date, the joint family property after that date would not be allowed to be utilized by some members only of the family for making profits for themselves to the exclusion of the plaintiff and for other damages and expenses incurred by him and will take a severe legal action against you therefor. The Civil Judge found that though the motor business carried on after the partition had ceased to be a joint family, yet as it was carried on by some member of a family their position was analogous to that of a partner carrying on partnership after dissolution and applying the principle underlying section 37 of the Partnership Act he held that the two brother brothers carrying on the motor bus business were liable to account. Accordingly he passed a preliminary decree directing accounts of the motor cycle business to be carried out from March 31 1946 up to the date on which a final judgment decree for payment of the amount found to be due would be made. A Commissioner was appointed to take the accounts to ascertain the profits earned by the use of the capital belonging to the shares of brothers other than those who carried on the Motor business. In appeal Bavdekar 'J. agreed with the findings of the Civil judge and held that although the motor car business carried out after the 1st of April, 1946 had ceased lo be a Joint family business yet as such it was carrying on by several members of a joint Hindu family their positions were analogous to those of a partners carrying on a partnership after the 31st March, 1946. Held, further, that the compromise closed once for all the controversy about taking any account of the joint Family businesses including the motorbusiness after the31st March 1946, and the plaintiff is bound by the terms of compromise and the consent decree following upon it.

The Salt Works were extended over an area of about two hundred and fifty acres. Some of the other salt works, however, have even larger areas. The only buildings on this land consist of temporary shelters constructed for the resident labour and for an office. At a few places, pucca platforms exist for fixing the water pump when required to pump water from the sea. When not required, this pump is kept in the office. With the exception of the constructions already mentioned, the entire area of Salt Works was open. On the sea side, it has bunds in order to prevent sea water flooding the salt pans. Clause (m) of section 2 of the Act provides that " the factory means any premises including the precincts thereof (i) whereon ten or more workers are working, or were working on any day of the preceding twelve months, and in any part of which a manufacturing process is being carried on with the aid of power, or is ordinarily so carried on, or (ii) whereon twenty or more workmen are working or were employed on any days of the following 12 months and in all parts of which A manufacturing process was being carried out without the aid Of power or is being ordinarily so brought on, but does not include a mine subject to the operation of the , or a railway running shed. " The word " premises " is not restricted in scope to buildings alone. of course, the building referred to in this clause is the building which is referred to In section 93 of the Indian Factories Act and would be a factory if the work carried on there comes within the definition of the word " factory " and would therefore be a ' factory if it had a building and unless the Factory Act definitely provided for the application of the provisions to it. This case too is distinguishable as the farm on which the workman was employed to drive a movable steam engine for the purpose of working a (1) (2) (3) 602 mill for grinding meal intended to be used for food for stock on the farm and not for sale, was held to be not a factory in view of the fact that the meal which was ground was not intended for the purposes of sale but was meant only for feeding the stock from the farm.

The respondent entered the service of the Princely State of Mysore in 1935 as Instructor in Tailoring and he joined duty there on December 1, 1949. One Shri K. Narayanaswamy Chetty who was also an Instructor in tailoring in the Department of Public Instructions was also deputed to the occupational Institute at Hassan and joined duty thereafter there on 12th December, 1949, but no order was passed in the case of the respondent despite repeated representations made by the latter. In 1953, the then State of Karnataka set up the Department for Technical Education and the Polytechnic at Devangere became part of that Department. The respondent continued to make representations to the effect that like other employees who were taken on deputation from other Departments, he should also be absorbed in the department of Technical Education with effect from November 28, 1949 which was the date on which he initially came on deputation. His specific grievance was that in any case, he could not be discriminated against and treated differently from K. N. Chetty who had been junior to him in the parent Department and came on his deputation to the Polytechnics subsequently. The State Government referred the respondent 's case to the Public Service Commission who examined it and by a communication dated February 2, 1960 made these recommendations in favour of the Respondent: "It is stated in the Government letter dated 26 10 1959 that the Director who was the Unit Officer for both the departments ordered the transfer of Sri Srinivasa Murthy who was fully qualified as Tailoring Instructor in the Technical Education Department and there was no need to classify the vacancy post to which he was transferred under the then existing rules. Along with him, Sri K.N. Chetty was absorbed with effect on November 28th, 1949 and his reversion at this distance of time for no fault of his would cause a great hardship to him, the Commission are of the opinion that he may be absorbed as tailoring Instructor from the date of his appointment as such as has been ordered in the ease of Sri K Narayanaswamy Chettiar. In the opinion of the Commission, the temporary reversion of the respond ent to his parent department in 1955 56 was not justified. However, by a notification dated May 17, 1950, the Government directed that the promotions of 63 petitioners therein from the post of Surveyors as Assistant Engineers were to take effect from that date irrespective of the dates on which they were put in charge of sub divisions. But by a subsequent notification dated June 11, 1956, the respondent was again posted on deputation as Instructor with effectfrom November 28. 1949, when he initially resumed duty on deputation to a Polytechnic at Devagere. The intervening period between his reversion and reposting to the polytechnic was treated as leave. On the re organisation of States with effect From November 1, 1956 another batch of 107 persons were similarly promoted as Assistant Engineer with retrospective effect from 11th November, 1956 when the new State of Madras emerged under the States Reorganization Act. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court for the issue of a writ of mandamus directing his absorption in the Depart ment Department of Technical education and the polytechnics at Devanagere became Part of that department. The High Court allowed the writ petition and issued a direction that the absorption of the re spondent in the Departments of technical Education be given effect from the dates of the order, in the vacancy in which he had been working, subject to these conditions. Hence this appeal by the State. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The respondent was not entitled to the benefit of revision of scales of pay that had been effected in 1957 and 1961 by way of increments or weightage accruing thereunder, (2) Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution cannot be invoked to enforce a mere concession. [259C D] (3) In the special circumstances of this case, the High court was fully justified in granting the relief, it did, to the respondent. The appeal fails and is dismissed with costs.

The petitioner, an advocate practising in this Court complaining of malpractices indulged in by social organisations and voluntary agencies engaged in the work of offering Indian children in adoption to foreign parents. The letter referred to a press report based on "empirical investigation carried out by the staff of a reputed foreign magazine" called "The Mail", and alleged that not only Indian children of tender age were under the guise of adoption "exposed to the long horrendous journey to distant foreign countries at great risk to their lives but in cases where they survive and where these children are not placed in the Shelter and Relief Homes, they in course of time become beggars or prostitutes for want of proper care from their alleged foreign foster parents. " The petitioner accordingly sought relief restraining Indian based private agencies "from carrying out further activity of routing children for adoption abroad" and directing the Govern ment of India to carry out their obligations in the matter of adoption of Indian children by foreign parents, on the ground that it would be unlawful to make or to give to any person any payment or reward for or in consideration of the grant by that person of any consent required in connection with the adoption of a child or the transfer by that foreigner of the care and custody of such child with a view to its adoption or the making by that persons of any arrangements for such adoption. " This letter was treated as a writ petition and by an order dated 1st September, 1982 the Court issued notice to the Union of India the Indian Council of Social Welfare and to appear in answer to the writ petition, and assist the Court in laying down principles and norms which should be followed in determining whether a child should be allowed to be adopted by foreign parent and if on a consideration of these reports and material, the court comes to the conclusion that it will be for the welfare of the child, the Court makes an order appointing the foreign parent as guardian of the minor child with liberty to him to take the child in adoption. The net effect of this provision is that in view of clause 17 no institution or organisation can make any arrangement for the adoption or of an Indian child by foreign father unless such institution or Organisation is licensed as a social welfare institution and under Clause 21, it would he unlawful to making or to provide to any persons any payment, or reward, for or consideration of grant by the said person of his consent required. The object of giving notice to Indian Council for Child Welfare or any other independent, reputed and publicly recognised social agency is obviously to ensure that the application of foreign parents for guardianship of the children with a particular view to their eventual adoption is properly and carefully scrutinised and evaluated by an expert body having experience in the area of child welfare with a consideration to assist the court in coming to the finding whether it will he in the interest of the Child, promotive of its welfare, to be adopt by the foreign parents making the application or in other words, whether such adoption will provide moral and material security to the child with an opportunity to grow into the full stature of its personality in an atmosphere of love and affection and warmth of a family hearth and home. The court thus has in most cases where an application is made by a foreign parent for being appointed guardian of a minor child in the courts in Bombay, Delhi and Gujarat, the child study report as also the home study report together with other relevant material in order to enable it to decide whether it would take the children in adopt adoption.

An order of pre mature retirement following close upon the heels of promotion and appointment to a coveted Selection post is bound to perplex any right thinking man and make him wonder whether the right hand knows what the left hand has done. If in the month of May a Government servant is found to possess 'such high merit and ability which naturally includes integrity, as to entitle him not merely to be promoted to a selection post but to be appointed to a very responsible and much desired post in that cadre, what could have happened between May and September to merit his being weeded out altogether from service in September under the rule which enables the Government to retire a Government Servant in the public interest after he has attained the age of SO years or after he had completed 25 years of qualifying service. One would expect that some grave and grim situation had developed in the interregnum to warrant the pursuit of such a drastic course. But surprisingly, we found nothing what soever had happened in this case during that period. Let us look at the totality of the facts. 77 The appellant appears to have quite a noteworthy career. A Starting at the lowest rung as a Lower Division Clerk in 1953 he was promoted as an Assistant Commercial Tax officer in 1954, next as a Deputy Commercial Tax Officer in 1957, then as a Joint Commercial Tax Office in 1962, thereafter as a Commercial Tax Officers in 1966, later as an Asstt. Commissioner of Commercial Taxes in 1972 and finally as Deputy Commissioner of Sales Tax on 7 S 1975. On promotion as Deputy Commis sioner of Commercial taxes he was posted as Member of the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal in the same cadre. On September 28,1975 he was retired under Fundamental Rule 56(d). His Service Book shows that he had an excellent record of service. He had earned several encomiums, commendations and appreciations. The several promotions gained by him react his good record of serv ice. But there was one dark spot. In 1969 when he was working as Commercial Tax officers it was noted in his Confidential file by the Deputy Commissioner as follows: "This is due to his unbending attitude. With a little more tact he will be an asset to the Department". One Wonders whether the failure to note the result of the enquiry in the personal file led to the impugned order ! In the face of the promotion of the appellant just a few months earlier and nothing even mildly suggestive of ineptitude or inefficiency thereafter, it is impossible to sustain the order of the Government retiring the appellant from service.

The appellants, among others, filed objections to the schemes and thereafter there was a hearing of these objections by the Transport Minister of the State under section 68 D(2) on the 11th of January, 1963. The Regional Transport Authority held that instead of the above order Kurnool Nellore and Cuddapah Districts in that order would be chosen for nationalisation and in the three schemes which were formulated in pursuance of this Resolution the western half of Kurnoo was selected as the area to be nationalised in the first instance, and that the choice of the Western part of K. was made by them alone. The appellants challenged the validity of these Schemes on the grounds: (1) That it was not in fact the Corporation formed the opinion indicated in section 68 C but really the Chief Minister; (2) assuming, however, that the Chief Secretary was actuated by political motives to hit at his opponents still, the schemes which are published by the Corporation had been framed by the Corpora tion not at the dictation of the Chief Ministers, but as a result of their own independent judgment; and (3) that it was done under the direction of the chief Minister who, it was alleged for reasons which were set out in the affidavits and to which we shall refer presently was to have compelled, directed or induced the Corporation to do so. HELD: (i) Rule 5 is repugnant to section 68 E(1) which provides that any scheme published under sub s.(3) of section 68D may at any time be cancelled or modified by the State Transport Undertaking and the procedure laid down in section68 C and section 68 F shall, so far as it can be made applicable be followed in every case where the scheme is proposed to be modified as if the modifications proposed were a separate scheme. [353 E] (ii) The Regional Authority which is specifically mentioned in s.68 F(1), is empowered to issue the permit to the transport undertaking "notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in Chapter IV" and that section rendered the provisions of Rule 141 of the Motor Vehicles Rules inapplicable to cases covered by section 68F(1). [353 G] Dosa Satyanaraya namurty etc. vs The Andhra Pradesh State Road Transport Corporation, ; , followed. (iii) It was not necessary to finally decide the larger question whether the mere prescription of the maxima and minima, particularly for the reasons set out therein in the affidavit of the Assistant Secretary to the Transport Department constitutes a violation of section68 E as also of r. 4 of the Andhra Pradesh Motor Vehicles Rule, 1957 as to require the same to be struck down. [355 G] (iv) It is not necessary that a policy decision contemplated by s.34 of the Road Transport Act could relate to a matter which under s. 68 C of the Act is left to the unfettered discretion and judg ment of the Corporation where that is the State Undertak ing, or again whether or not the policy decision has to be by a formal Government order in writing, for what is rele vant is whether the materials placed before the Court estab lish that the Corporation gave effect to it as a direction which they were expected to and did obey.

The appellant was a public limited company registered as a dealer under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. In respect of the accounting year ending with 31st December 1954 in the return for the year the assessee had shown its gross turnover at Rs. 70,99,928 10 0 and deposited the tax of Rs. 9 6 on the said amount in the treasury. The Commercial Tax Officer by notice dated April 22, 1955 fixed August 4, 1955 for hearing the assessee in respect of its return. Under section 5(2)(a)(ii) of the Act the furnishing of the declaration forms duly filled in and signed by the registered dealer to whom the goods were sold and containing the prescribed particulars on a prescribed form obtainable from the prescribed authority has to be furnished in the prescribed manner by the dealer who sells the goods. Under r. 27A of the Bengal Sales Tax Rules, 1941, a dealer who wishes to claim the said exemption shall on demand produce such a declaration in writing signed by him. Sub r. (2) thereof enjoins on a dealer not to accept and on the purchasing dealer not give a declaration except in the form prescribed. The other rules make stringent provisions to prevent the misuse of the forms by the purchasing dealers; they do not enable the selling dealer to either directly apply or to compel the buying dealers to apply for duplicate forms; nor do they enjoin on the appropriate authority to give the selling dealers a duplicate form to replace lost one. In the nature of things, in view of several transactions that may be entered into between dealers it will well nigh be impossible for the taxing authorities to ascertain in each case whether a dealer has sold the specified goods to another for the purposes mentioned in the section. Therefore, presumably to achieve the twofold object namely prevention of fraud and facilitating administrative efficiency, the exemption given is made subject to a condition that the person claiming the exemption shall furnish a declaration form in the manner prescribed under the section . The liberal construction suggested will facilitate the commission of fraud, and introduce administrative inconveniences, both of which the provisions of the said clause seek to avoid. The decision of this Court in the State of Orissa vs M.A. Tulloch and Co. Ltd., [1964] 7 S.C.R. 810 was concerned with section 5 (2)(b) (ii)of the Act in question, but there was no proviso to that section in the Orissa Act similar to the one found in the present section. That makes all the difference for it is the proviso that imposes the condition. But under r.27(2) made under the Orissa Sales Tax Act "a dealer shall produce a true declaration in the writing by the buying dealer or by such responsible person as may be authorized in writing in this behalf by such dealer that the goods in question are specified in the purchasingdealer 's certificate of registration as being required for resale by him or in the execution of any contract."

% The State of Bihar has assured us in the affidavit of Mrinmaya Choudhri that necessary steps for transferring women under "protective custody" in jails to the institutions run by the welfare department have been taken and directions to that effect are issued by the Government. It is not uncommon to find that under trial prisoners whose names are set out in the chart filed by Mrs. Hingorani to day have been in jail for periods longer than the maximum term for which they could have been sentenced, if convicted. The State should furnish to this Court the dates on which these under trial prisoner were remanded to judicial custody from time to time by the Magistrates so that we can satisfy themselves that the requirement of the proviso was complied with. This averment is wholly unsatisfactory and it does not inform the court as to what were the dates when these under trials prisoners who were directed to be released by this Court in regard to compliance with the proviso to section 167(2). The State Government will comply with this direction as far as possible within a period of six weeks from today and submit report of compliance to the High Court of Patna. [529D E] Maneka Gandhi vs Union of India, ; , referred to. In order to enable the court to discharge this constitutional obligation, it is necessary that the Court should have the requisite information bearing on the problem. The Court should also take this opportunity of impressing upon the Government of India as also the State Governments, the urgent necessity of introducing a dynamic and comprehensive legal service programme with a view to reaching justice to the common man. Today, unfortunately, in our country the poor are priced out of the judicial system with the result that they are losing faith in the capacity of our legal system to bring about changes in their life conditions and to deliver justice to them. The poor in their contract with the legal system have always been on the wrong side of the law. It was, therefore, necessary that this Court should inject equal justice into legality and that can be done only by dynamic and activist scheme of legal services. When only the rich can enjoy the law, as a doubtful luxury, and the poor, who need it most, cannot have it because its expense puts it beyond their reach, the threat to the continued existence of free democracy is not imaginary but very real, because democracy 's very life depends upon making the machinery of justice so effective that every citizen shall believe in an benefit by its impartiality and fairness. And also recall what was said by Leeman Abbot years ago in relation to affluent America.

The appellant landlord gave notice of termination of tenancy to the respondent on December 31, 1951 under section 34(1) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948. The tenant objected and claimed the benefit of the third clause of subs. (2 A), and the question that arose for determination was whether the tenant was entitled to the protection contained in this clause. Held, that the amendment did not affect any vested right of the landlords till the tenancy actually stood terminated after the expiry of the notice. Durlabbhai Fakirbhai vs Jhaverbhai Bhikabhai (1933) I.L.R. LX Cal. 1037 and Jeebankrishna Chakrabarti vs Abdul Kader Chaudhuri, (1933), I. L. R. LX All. 574, referred to. Held further, that in the circumstances of the present case it was obvious that the legislature could not have intended that the benefit should not be extended to tenants in whose cases the tenancy had not yet terminated, though notices had been given, when the further restrictions were being put on the right to terminate the tenancy. It is only when the period of notice has expired and the tenancy has terminated that the landlord acquires a vested right to obtain possession of the land. If there was any doubt about the meaning of sub section (2A) that doubt should be resolved in favour of the tenant, for whose benefit the Amending Act was passed, it would be taking away the vested right which of the landlord arising out of the notices of termination and therefore the Amending act did not affected any vested rights of landlords till then.

The petitioners were evacuees and the houses of one Khadim Ali who had never been declared an evacuee and had died on or about October 1, 1950 leaving three sons and five daughters who thereupon became entitled to them in certain shares. No notice under section 7 had at any time been issued to them nor were they ever declared to be evacueies. Neither of these two persons having appeared, a declaration was made by the Custodian on January 10, 1952 under that section that Nusrat Ali and Fateh Ali were evacuedes and their properties being the two houses in dispute, to be evacuee property. The petitioners contended that for a long time they had no knowledge of the proceedings taken under the Act in respect of the houses and when they came to know of the order of the Custodian, they took various steps to protect their rights but were unsuccessful. Held, that the acts of the custodian in so far as they deprive the petitioners of their property cannot be upheld. It was well established and not disputed that no property of any person can be declared to have been evacuee property unless that person had first been given a notice under B. 7 of the Act. Ebrahim Aboobaker vs Tek Chand Dolwani, , referred to. In the present case there was no judicial determination by the custodian General of any fact affecting Zafar Ali 's right in the houses. The acts of Custodian in so much as they deprived the petitioners Of their property could not be upheld on the sole ground that it had been filed beyond the time prescribed for it.

The assessee company was running at a loss as a result of which in 1952 the assessee Company decided to instal a plant for manufacture of worsted yarn from imported wool tops by raising a loan of Rs. 7 lakhs from the Industrial Finance Corporation. The plant went into production in September 1952 and the assessee company appointed M/s. Murlidhar Chiranjilal as the sole selling agents on certain specified conditions, the important of which being that the agents were to finance the assessee ' Company to the extent of Rs 2,50,000/ and the latter agreed to pay 6% interest on the advances to be made by the agents and further agreed to Pay 2% commission on the net proceeds of sales of goods in India. Before expiry of this agreement another agreement was entered into by the assessee with the agents on October 20, 1955 under which the agents agreed to share losses on net sales and 50% commission On December 15, 1953 the assessee assessee company entered into an agreement with Mis Saligram Premnath under which, the latter were appointed as the principal selling agents for the worsted cotton yarn on payment of 2% Commission. Subsequently on December 15. 1953 the appellant Company entered into a joint venture for distributing the net profits, after being ascertained between themselves and that is why there was an express provision in the agreement by which the agent agreed to part with the losses to the tune of 50% which were to be deducted from the remuneration payable to the agents. The selling agents M/S. Salig Ram Premnath advanced a sum of Rs 6,26,847 and Rs. 871,873 and Rs 37,157/ and Rs . The case of the assessee was that the two amounts mentioned above being in the nature of commission paid to the selling agents would be deemed expenses incurred by the company in order to earn profits and would therefore fall within the ambit of section 10(2)(xv) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The Income Tax officer disallowed the deduction and held that the deductions claimed were actually a division of profits after the profits had come into existence and had been ascertained, therefore could not be claimed as a valid deduction under the provisions of the Act but amounted to application of profits under section 10 (2)(XV) of Income tax 1922. On appeal by the Commissioner of Income Tax, the Tribunal held that there was a very thin line of distinction between a contract for payment of a share of profits simpliciter and a payment of remuneration which is deductible in truth from the profits divisible.

The assessee company maintains an accounts pertaining to him in its books. The accounts showed that as on March 31, 1958 a sum of Rs. 36,546.17 np was due to him by the company. In January 1959 for the first time he became indebted to the company in the sum of RS. 3,757.04 np. He was originally assessed for the assessment year 1959 60 on a total income of Rs 43,407. Thereafter, the Income Tax Officer came to know that the assessee had been withdrawing moneys from the company and in the belief that those amounts were liable to be treated as "dividend" under section 2(6A)(e) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 he reopened the assessment by virtue of section 147 of the Income tax Act, 1961. In the assessment proceedings which followed, the assessee claimed that the accumulated profits of the company amounted to Rs. 1,050 only and that amount alone could be considered as "accumulated profits" under Section 2(7A)(a) (e). The figure was worked out on the basis that a sum Of Rs. 11,000 as a provision for tax and of Rs 6,900 as a Provision for dividend had to be adjusted against the balance of Rs 18,950 in the Profit & Loss Account. The Income Tax officer rejected the contention of the assessee and determined a sum as dividend under section2(6 A)(e). He arrived at this figure by including the current profits of that company for the account year ending March 31. 1959. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed an appeal filed by the assessee. The High Court in second appeal upheld the claim of the asses see that the words "accuulated profits ' occurring in section 2 (6A) (c) could not be construed as including current profits, but it rejected the contentions of the assesses that the two sums of Rs 11,00 and Rs. 6, 900 had to he taken into account in determining the figure of the accumulated profit. Hence this appeal by the Revenue.

The appellant was the Mahant of a religious institution known as Rajgunj Asthal in Burdwan, and the suits out of which the present appeals arose were instituted by him to recover possession of various plots of land in the occupation of the defendants or in the alternative for assessment of fair and equitable rent. It was alleged in the plaint that the suit lands were comprised in Mouza Nala forming part of the permanently settled estate of Burdwan, that their income was taken into account in fixing the revenue payable by the estate, that they had been granted as Lakheraj to their predecessors in title long prior to the permanent settlement, that neither the Maharaja nor the plaintiff claiming under him had any title to them, and that the entry in the record of rights published during the settlement in 1931 was correct. The trial court held that the documents put forward by the defendants as containing assertions by them that they held under a Lakhearaj grant were not shown to relate to the suit land, that the relationship subsisting between the parties was one of landlord and tenant, that as there had been no determination of tenancy, no decree in ejectment could be passed but that the plaintiff was entitled to fair rent and that their claim was barred by reason of article 131 of the Limitation Act. On appeal, the District Judge held that as the defendants and their predecessors had been in possession of the lands for a long time without payment of rent, a presumption of a lost grant could be made in their favour; but before raising such a presumption, it must be established that the grant was one which could have legally been made by him. Held, further, that on the facts found, no presumption of lost grant had been made in favour of the predecessors of the respondents and they were within time from that date. There is no substance in this plea, which is accordingly rejected.

The appellant filed a suit for specific performance of a contract dated 15th December 1965 for sale of land admeasuring 45 acres 5 gunthas bearing Survey No. 25 situated in Sholapur Mouje Dongaon in Maharashtra State for a consideration of Rs. 42,000/ out of which Rs. 5,000 were paid as earnest money and a further amount of Rs 5,00,000 was paid on 22nd April 1966 when the period for performance of the contract for sale was extended by six months, which suit was dismissed by the trial Court and the plaintiff 's First Appeal No. 117/68 was dismissed. On appeal, the High Court agreed with the trial court observing that Civil Court has undoubtedly jurisdiction to entertain a suit relating to specific performance and while considering the main issue whether specific performance should be granted or not, civil Court will have jurisdiction to decide the incidental or subsidiary issue and recorded a finding that the plaintiff was not an agriculturist. In appeal by certificate, it was contended on behalf of the appellant (i) that if the court does not take note of Ext 78, an issue on the pleadings would arise whether the plaintiff is an agriculturist and in view of the provisions contained in section 70(a) read with sections 85 and 85A of the Tenancy Act, the issue would have to be referred to the Mamlatdar for decision and the Civil Court would have no jurisdiction to try the issue; and (ii) that even when a properly constituted suit is brought to the civil court having jurisdiction to deal with the same, prima facie on a contention being raised by the defendant an issue may arise which the Civil court would not be competent to try and the legislature stepped in to avoid the conflict of jurisdiction by introducing section 85A making it obligatory upon the civil Court to refer such an issue to the competent authority under the Tenancy Acts. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The jurisdiction of the Civil Courts to settle, decide or deal with any question which is required to be settled, decided or dealt with by any competent authority is totally ousted. Therefore, it an issue arises in a civil court whether a person is an agricultural labourer within the meaning of the said Tenancy Act and if section 85 A imposes an obligation on the Civil Judge to refer the issue to Mamlatdar as to whether the defendant is a lessee under Ext.

Section 15C(2)(i) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 provides that the profits or gains of an industrial undertaking to which this section applies shall be computed in accordance with the provisions of section 10. Section 15C partially exempts from tax a new industrial unit which is separate physically from the old one, the capital of which and the profits thereon are ascertainable. Under sub section (1) of section 15C the tax shall not be payable by an assessee on so much of the profits and gains derived from any industrial undertaking, to which the section applies as do not exceed six per cent per annum on the capital employed in the new industrial undertaking from the profits which alone exemption is claimed. Negatively, the new Industrial Undertaking of the assessee should not be formed (1 ) by the splitting up of the business already in existence, (2) by the reconstruction of business already existing and hence the assessee was not entitled to exemption under section 15 C(2) as rightly held by the High Court since they were formed by the con tended reconstruction of the old industrial undertakings. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The two new undertakings are independent and separate production units in the sense that the commodities produced or the results achieved are commercially tangible products and the undertakings can be carried on separately without complete absorption and losing their identity in the old business, they are not to be treated as being formed by reconstruction of their old business. [764C D] 2. The assessee continues to be the same for the purpose of assessment.

Section 44 B of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1926 authorises resumption even in cases where there has been an alienation of the inam either before or after 1934. Even apart from section 44 B, any inam whatever its nature could be resumed for failure to perform the conditions of the grant. Subject to certain restrictions and safeguards, paragraph 2 of the Board 's Standing Order No. 54 permitted resumption of religious and charitable inams on the ground that the land was alienated or otherwise lost to the institution or service to which it once belonged or on the grounds that the terms of the lease were not observed. The object of section 44B is to define and enlarge the grounds on which the inams could be resume and to devise a proper procedure for the resumption. On general grounds of public policy, the legislature has declared that the inam may be resumed on any of the three grounds mentioned therein. The first ground is that the holder of the Inam has made an alienation. The words "has failed" in sub section (2)(a)(ii) and the words "have ceased" and (1) (1870) 13 H.I.A.438,464. (2) and (3) similarly authorise resumption of the inams if the other grounds exist though they may have arisen earlier. Section 44 B does not apply to a personal inam burdened with a condition of service and the grant of land as remuneration for an office, see, Forbes vs Noor Muhammad Tuquee, [1870] 13 H .I. A. 4 38, referred to.

Section 21 of the Indore City Municipal Act, 1909 authorised a Municipality to levy and collect house tax on houses, buildings or lands within the municipal limits at a rate not exceeding 12 1/2% of such gross annual letting value for the financial years 1953 54 and 1954 55. This was objected to by the respondents on the ground that under the 1954 Act the tax could be assessed on the basis of gross annual rental letting value less 10% statutory allowance in lieu of costs of repairs or on any other account whatsoever. The difference came to Rs. 1,461 and of this the trustees claimed refund on the grounds that the Municipality had collected excess from them under pain of distress The Municipality having refused to refund the excess amount the respondents filed a suit to recover it on the allegation that the excess amounts were illegally recovered. The trial court decreed the suit and the appeals filed by the Corporation in the District Court and the High Court were dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation: (i) that under sec. 79(1) of the 1954 act the Municipality could levy the house tax at the rate of 7% of their gross annual rent and that it was not bound to deduct the 10% allowance provided by sec. 73(2) from such gross monthly letting value; and (ii) that saving coupled with the fact that the assessment list prepared for 1952 53 was saved and was deemed to have been made under the 1955 Act it could be deemed to had been so made in so far as it was consistent with the provisions of section 73 of the Act. HELD: The appellant Corporation was entitled to adopt the assessment lists prepared for the year 1952 53 for the two assessment years, 1953 54, 1954 55 and 1954 56 under secs. 75 and 76. [130 E] (i)(a) Under sections 75 and 77 when the assessment List is prepared in accordance with the provision of section 74 it has to be published and time has to he fixed for lodging objections against the entries therein. After such objections are heard and disposed of the assessment Lists have to be authenticated as provided by section 76(6). The list so adopted has therefore to be publish, has to invite objections and has to have to he authenticated in the manner prescribed by secs 76 (6) after disposing of the objections if any and it is then only that it becomes conclusive evidence of the valuation and the tax assessed thereon for that particular official year. If it were otherwise, the annual letting Value or the value estimated on a particular building or house would be static for 4 years during which the Corporation can go on adopting the assessment panel prepared in an earlier year and the owner or the occupier of the building would be deprived of the right to object to the valuation or the annual lease value or the tax assess thereon for at least 4 years even though the valuation Or the annual rental value thereof may have decreased for one reason or the other. [131 E F] (b) The word "if" appearing in sub sec. 2 of section 79 is obviously a mistake and must be read as "as if" because the word "where" standing by itself makes no sense at all.

The respondent company was incorporated in 1937 primarily with the object of acquiring and working the rights, title and interest in a match factory belonging to one A. V. Thomas at Medical. The Memorandum of Association empowered the Company to manufacture and deal in acids, alkalis and other chemicals. The assessee company carried on its business of manufacturing matches till the account year ending April 30, 1941. Thereafter, the profits from the business became less and less due to War conditions, and the assessee company started to manufacture plywood chests for tea, paints and lemon grass oil. These were contemplated by cl. (3) of the Memorandum of association. On May 9, 1943, the assessee Company entered into an agreement with one Rao Sahib Natesa Iyer for the sale of the lands, buildings, plant and machinery of its match factory for Rs. 5, 75,000. It was agreed that the price would not include manufactured goods, chemicals and other raw materials or any other asset not shown in the agreement of sale. The purchaser was allowed sixty days for the payment of the balance of the price, Rs. 57,500 having been already paid at the time the agreement was 'entered into. The purchase included chemicals and paper for manufacture which had not been sold in the first instance. In a confidential report made on August 1, 1944, to the shareholders, the 963 Directors stated that the prices obtained had shown a capital appreciation of about six times the cost price, and that the sale included chemicals & raw materials and obtained a larger price, that later it included chemicals, and raw materials for manufacture, which had resulted in a substantial profit. Meanwhile, the assessment of the company for the account years ending April 31, 1944 bad been completed by the Deputy Commissioner of Income tax and the asses see Company 's Liquidator took up the position that the match manufacturing had been stopped, and there thus only an appreciation of the capital assets and not a business profit which was liable to be assessed. The Official Liquidator took into consideration the Memorandum dated May 9. 1943, which allowed the assessee to manufacture, and sell chemicals and on the Directors report, held that the assessee firm was liable for income tax on a profit of Rs. 36,498 6 4. On appeal by the Commissioner of Incometax, the Tribunal reduced the assessable profits to Rs. 1,15,259. The High Court also held that by the sale no business was done and that there was legally a single transaction of the entire match factory inclusive of raw materials. In appeal to this Court on the question whether there can be said to be a sale in the carrying on of the business in respect of the chemicals and raw material, HELD : (i) There is a great danger of extracting a principle from the reported cases, divorced from the facts. The law as summarised from the cases, is stated as follows: "210. Mere realisation of assets is not trading; but the completion of outstanding contracts after the dissolution of a firm, the commencement of liquidation of a company, or the winding up of the affairs of a trader, has been held to be trading. The cases illustrating the question arising in such circumstances can be divided into two categories first, those where the sales formed part of trading activities, and, second, those, where the realisation was not an act of trading. This distinction is a sound one. The only difficulty is that whereas in the former, though the whole of the property was sold, it was sold at; a part of the trading, in the letter, the property, was sold not as part of trade but on a winding up sale. These cases were also considered and applied by the Privy Council in Doughty vs Commissioner of Taxes [1921] 2 A.C. 327 and Doughyty 's case (3), relied upon by the rival parties before us, and we shall consider them.
